0.title: The LORD Fights for His People: The Book of Joshua
0.overview:
The book of Joshua opens with a death and a charge. Moses, the servant of the LORD, is dead, and lies in an unmarked grave on the far side of the Jordan. And God says to Joshua, 'Moses my servant is dead. Now therefore arise' (1:2). The law could lead Israel to the edge of the land but not bring them in. The one who takes them across is Yehoshua, Joshua, later Yeshua: the name the angel would give a child in Bethlehem (Matt. 1:21). What the law could not accomplish, Jesus does. He brings us into the rest.

Joshua is the sixth book of the Old Testament and the first of the so-called Former Prophets in the Hebrew canon. It does not name its author; Jewish tradition credited Joshua, and phrases like “to this day” (4:9) show that it was completed after the events, how long after being debated. It records the conquest of Canaan, the division of the land, and the covenant renewals that bracket Israel's entry into its inheritance. Its driving claim is plain on every page: the LORD fights for his people. Israel does not earn the land; God gives it, and Jericho falls to trumpets and a shout so that no one may boast. The conquest is a prolonged sermon on the faithfulness of God to his promise to Abraham, the down payment on a redemption that reaches its consummation in Christ.

Did the conquest happen quickly, as “Joshua took the whole land” (11:23) suggests, or slowly, as Judges 1 shows? Both. Joshua records the campaigns that broke the power of the Canaanite kings in the centre, the south and the north; the settling of the land and the driving out of remaining peoples went on tribe by tribe for generations (13:1; Judg 1).

Does archaeology support it? The evidence is debated. Garstang found Jericho’s walls collapsed and dated it near 1400 BC; Kenyon later dated the destruction about 150 years earlier; others have argued again for Garstang’s date. The site of Ai is disputed. On the early date of the exodus (1 Kgs 6:1), the conquest falls about 1400 BC; many evangelical scholars prefer the thirteenth century, which suits the great burned layer at Hazor (11:11). Many scholars doubt the account; but the evidence is patchy and contested, and faith does not rest on the spade.

The hardest thing in the book is its violence. God commands the herem, the devotion of whole cities to destruction, and the text says plainly that this included men and women, young and old, and the animals (6:21). We must not soften that dishonestly, nor read it as a charter for human aggression; and its sweeping phrases (“all that breathed”) partly follow the stock language of ancient war reports, since Canaanites plainly remain afterwards (Judg 1). It is a time-bound, divinely commanded judgment upon a civilization whose iniquity had, in God's patient reckoning, finally become full (Gen. 15:16). The Canaanites burned their sons and daughters to their gods (Deut. 12:31). It was not a standing licence: it was given once, for this land, and it previews the final judgment when the King of kings returns (Rev. 19). Yet in the middle of this judgment Rahab the Canaanite is saved by faith (Heb. 11:31) and grafted into the line of the Messiah. Judgment and mercy meet, as they meet supremely at the cross.

Read Joshua, then, as gospel and not only as military history. Hear in 'Be strong and courageous' the voice that says 'I will never leave you nor forsake you' (Heb. 13:5). Its commands rest on what God has already given, and its failures (7:1; 24:19) send us to the one Joshua who never failed. The cities of refuge picture the refuge we have in him (Heb. 6:18), and the rest Israel entered points to the deeper rest that 'remains for the people of God' (Heb. 4:9). The God whose good promises did not fail (21:45) keeps every promise to us in his Son.

1.title: The Commissioning of Joshua
1.text: <sup>1</sup>After the death of Moses the servant of the LORD, the LORD said to Joshua the son of Nun, Moses' assistant,<sup>2</sup>"Moses my servant is dead. Now therefore arise, go over this Jordan, you and all this people, into the land that I am giving to them, to the people of Israel.<sup>3</sup>Every place that the sole of your foot will tread upon I have given to you, just as I promised to Moses.<sup>4</sup>From the wilderness and this Lebanon as far as the great river, the river Euphrates, all the land of the Hittites to the Great Sea toward the going down of the sun shall be your territory.<sup>5</sup>No man shall be able to stand before you all the days of your life. Just as I was with Moses, so I will be with you. I will not leave you or forsake you.<sup>6</sup>Be strong and courageous, for you shall cause this people to inherit the land that I swore to their fathers to give them.<sup>7</sup>Only be strong and very courageous, being careful to do according to all the law that Moses my servant commanded you. Do not turn from it to the right hand or to the left, that you may have good success wherever you go.<sup>8</sup>This Book of the Law shall not depart from your mouth, but you shall meditate on it day and night, so that you may be careful to do according to all that is written in it. For then you will make your way prosperous, and then you will have good success.<sup>9</sup>Have I not commanded you? Be strong and courageous. Do not be frightened, and do not be dismayed, for the LORD your God is with you wherever you go."<sup>10</sup>And Joshua commanded the officers of the people,<sup>11</sup>"Pass through the midst of the camp and command the people, 'Prepare your provisions, for within three days you are to pass over this Jordan to go in to take possession of the land that the LORD your God is giving you to possess.'"<sup>12</sup>And to the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh Joshua said,<sup>13</sup>"Remember the word that Moses the servant of the LORD commanded you, saying, 'The LORD your God is providing you a place of rest and will give you this land.'<sup>14</sup>Your wives, your little ones, and your livestock shall remain in the land that Moses gave you beyond the Jordan, but all the men of valor among you shall pass over armed before your brothers and shall help them,<sup>15</sup>until the LORD gives rest to your brothers as he has to you, and they also take possession of the land that the LORD your God is giving them. Then you shall return to the land of your possession and shall possess it, the land that Moses the servant of the LORD gave you beyond the Jordan toward the sunrise."<sup>16</sup>And they answered Joshua, "All that you have commanded us we will do, and wherever you send us we will go.<sup>17</sup>Just as we obeyed Moses in all things, so we will obey you. Only may the LORD your God be with you, as he was with Moses!<sup>18</sup>Whoever rebels against your commandment and disobeys your words, whatever you command him, shall be put to death. Only be strong and courageous."
1.overview:
The book begins with a death. Moses can bring a people to the threshold; he cannot bring them in. That is the law's limitation set out as a story, and the charge passes to Joshua.

One imperative dominates: three times God says be strong and courageous (vv. 6, 7, 9), and at the end the people say it back (v. 18). Each time the ground of the courage is outside the man: an outcome already decided, a book to keep, and a God who goes with him. The chapter ends in logistics and loyalty, with the eastern tribes sent to fight until everyone is home.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Moses is dead, and God's first word to his successor is a marching order (vv. 1-2). The land is spoken of as already given (v. 3), the promise of presence follows (v. 5), and the threefold command comes, each time with a different anchor (vv. 6-9).
verseByVerse.theology: Grace arrives before duty and grounds it. The land is given in verse 3 and fought for from chapter 6 onwards, which is the pattern of the whole Bible: God announces the accomplished gift and then calls his people to walk into it. Israel does not fight to earn Canaan; they fight because it is already theirs.
verseByVerse.examples: The middle command is the surprising one. The most courageous thing required of a general on the eve of a war is not to storm a wall but to keep a book — to meditate on it day and night and not turn from it to the right hand or to the left (vv. 7-8). Before a single battle plan is drawn, the campaign is located in the soul of the man who reads.

verseByVerse.quote: After the death of Moses the servant of the LORD, the LORD said to Joshua the son of Nun, Moses' assistant,
verseByVerse.commentary:
The book is hinged on a grave. The man who spoke with God as a friend and carried a nation for forty years is gone, and the work is not finished. Yet there is no interregnum, no anxious pause: Moses dies and God speaks. There is no power vacuum in the kingdom of God, because the King does not die.

Read the two titles side by side, because the writer has put them there on purpose. Moses is the servant of the LORD, among the highest titles the Old Testament gives anyone. Joshua is Moses' assistant, and had been, as Numbers puts it, from his youth (Num. 11:28).

That had been Joshua's job for decades. He led the fighting in the valley while Moses held up his hands on the hill (Ex. 17:9-12). He stayed behind in the tent of meeting after Moses had gone back to the camp (Ex. 33:11). He stood with Caleb against ten frightened men and a nation ready to stone him (Num. 14:6-10). None of it made him famous. All of it made him ready.

His name matters more than the chapter says out loud. Joshua is Yehoshua, later shortened to Yeshua, the name that would be given to a carpenter's son in Nazareth. The letter to the Hebrews makes the connection and then makes the limitation: if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken later of another day (Heb. 4:8). This man will get them into the land. He will not get them into the rest.
verseByVerse.note: Joshua means “the LORD saves.” The book covers Israel’s entry into Canaan and the division of the land, probably in the late 1400s or 1200s BC.

verseByVerse.quote: "Moses my servant is dead. Now therefore arise, go over this Jordan, you and all this people, into the land that I am giving to them, to the people of Israel. Every place that the sole of your foot will tread upon I have given to you, just as I promised to Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God says it himself: the grief is not denied and not hurried. But the next word is arise, and it is the right word to a man who has been sitting down for thirty days of mourning.

There is a kind of loss that persuades a person the story has stopped. It has not. God's answer to a funeral, here, is a river and a date.

Then the tense in verse 3, which is the engine of the entire book. Not I will give you but I have given to you — before a single Israelite has crossed the water, the land is deeded over. Every battle in the next eleven chapters is fought on ground that already belongs to them.

That is the shape of the Christian life and not merely an Old Testament curiosity. Nobody fights sin in order to become a child of God; the fighting is what a child of God does about territory the Father has already put in his name.

Yet the gift has to be walked on. Every place that the sole of your foot will tread — the promise is title deed, and the foot is possession. Faith is the foot set down on the promise. A man may own a field for years and never once walk it, and there is a way of holding the promises of God that amounts to exactly that.

verseByVerse.quote: From the wilderness and this Lebanon as far as the great river, the river Euphrates, all the land of the Hittites to the Great Sea toward the going down of the sun shall be your territory. No man shall be able to stand before you all the days of your life. Just as I was with Moses, so I will be with you. I will not leave you or forsake you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The borders are those God swore to Abraham (Gen. 15:18), and they are enormous. They were never occupied. Chapter 13 opens with God telling an old man that very much land remains, and something near the fullest extent was reached only briefly, centuries later, under Solomon (1 Kgs. 4:21). The book is honest about the gap between what was promised and what was held, and the gap is not a failure in the promise; it is a signpost. Paul says the promise to Abraham was never really about a strip of coastline but that he should be heir of the world (Rom. 4:13), and the last chapters of the Bible show what that finally means.

Verse 5 is the bedrock of the whole chapter, and it is worded with care. Not "no one will attack you", but no man shall be able to stand before you. Not "I will make it easy", but I will be with you. The promise is presence, not exemption.

The letter to the Hebrews lifts this sentence out of a general's commissioning and hands it to ordinary Christians worried about money, and the promise could hardly be stronger: I will never leave you nor forsake you. The conclusion drawn is a matter of nerve — so we can confidently say, The Lord is my helper; I will not fear (Heb. 13:5-6).

Does the land promise still belong to the Jewish people and modern Israel? Dispensationalists hold that it does: God’s promise to Abraham’s physical descendants remains literal, with its borders, and awaits fulfilment. But Joshua says that Not one word of all the good promises that the LORD had made to the house of Israel had failed (Josh 21:45), and the New Testament widens the promise: Abraham was to be heir of the world (Rom 4:13), and the patriarchs looked for a better country, that is, a heavenly one (Heb 11:16). This commentary reads the land as fulfilled in Christ and the new creation his people will inherit (Matt 5:5). Faithful Christians differ here, and many godly believers hold the dispensational view out of a desire to honour every word God spoke; both sides agree that the promises stand because God keeps his word.
verseByVerse.note: “The great sea” is the Mediterranean.

verseByVerse.quote: Be strong and courageous, for you shall cause this people to inherit the land that I swore to their fathers to give them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first of three commands is an imperative. Courage here is not a temperament some men are born with and others are not. It is commanded, which means it must be available to whoever is commanded to have it.

What makes it available is the clause attached to it. Joshua is not told to attempt the conquest and hope. He is told he shall cause this people to inherit, because God swore it to their fathers. The outcome is settled before the courage is required, and the courage is simply the appropriate response to a settled outcome.

Most fear works the other way round. We wait to see how a thing will turn out and take our courage from the evidence. God reverses it: here is how it turns out, now be strong.

The oath reaches back through Moses to Abraham, Isaac and Jacob, across centuries. God's covenant memory does not shorten with time, and his word does not expire with the generation that first heard it. Joshua leads as the trustee of a promise much older than himself.

verseByVerse.quote: Only be strong and very courageous, being careful to do according to all the law that Moses my servant commanded you. Do not turn from it to the right hand or to the left, that you may have good success wherever you go. This Book of the Law shall not depart from your mouth, but you shall meditate on it day and night, so that you may be careful to do according to all that is written in it. For then you will make your way prosperous, and then you will have good success.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second command raises the temperature, very courageous, and attaches it not to the walls of Jericho but to the law. Both directions off the road are named because a leader in a long campaign will be pressed to take either: the shortcut on one side, the compromise on the other.

Three organs are named, and the order is instructive: the mouth, then the mind, then the hands. The book is to be spoken, chewed over, and done.

The word for meditate is hagah, a low muttering — the same word Isaiah uses of a lion growling over its prey (Isa. 31:4). It does not mean an empty mind. The Book is not to depart from the mouth, so this is a man reading half-aloud to himself, turning the words over day and night like the blessed man of Psalm 1 (Ps. 1:2). Meditation in the Bible is not emptying but gnawing.

No one but Christ has kept this book without turning to right or left. He did it for us, and his obedience is counted ours (Rom. 5:19); and the Spirit he gives now writes the same word on our hearts and moves us to walk in it (Ezek. 36:27). So a believer who has turned aside comes back by confession, and opens the book again as a child, not a hireling.

A word about the prosperity, since the sentence is often quoted badly. The success promised is the success of this specific commission — getting a people into a land God had sworn to give them. It is not a formula for turning devotions into money. What the verse does teach, and teaches at the worst possible moment for it, is that the campaign will be won or lost long before the army forms up, in the quiet of one man's reading.

verseByVerse.quote: Have I not commanded you? Be strong and courageous. Do not be frightened, and do not be dismayed, for the LORD your God is with you wherever you go."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The third time opens with a question that lands like a hand on the shoulder. Joshua is not being encouraged. He is being reminded that he has orders.

This puts fear in an uncomfortable light. If courage is commanded, then settled fear is not merely a weakness of the nerves; it is a way of not taking God at his word. That should be said carefully — Scripture is full of frightened people who are handled gently, and God does not shout at the trembling. But it does mean that fear is answerable to something, and that a believer is allowed to argue with his own dread rather than obey it.

The last words are the best in the chapter. Not "wherever I send you," which would cover obedient errands only, but wherever you go, including the places Joshua would choose badly: the valley at Ai, the day he believed the Gibeonites without asking. The promise is hammered three times because it will need to be remembered three hundred.

The New Testament does not improve on those words so much as give them a face. A child is born and called Immanuel, God with us; and the last thing the risen Christ says on a hillside, to men about to be scattered across the world, is that he is with them always, to the end of the age (Matt. 1:23; 28:20). The promise made to one soldier at a river has turned out to be the standing arrangement. For the Christian the presence is nearer still, for the Spirit of Christ lives in us, and he is the courage the command asks for (2 Tim. 1:7).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–18 — The Charge to the People
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: What God said in private, Joshua says in public within a day: provisions and a deadline (vv. 10-11), the eastern tribes held to their promise (vv. 12-15), and the people's pledge, giving God's words back to him (vv. 16-18).
verseByVerse.theology: No tribe rests while its brothers are still fighting, and the new leader's authority rests on God's presence, not on his own.
verseByVerse.examples: When we repeat God's promises to a tired leader or a frightened friend, as Israel does in v. 18, we give them nothing of our own and nothing less than God's word.

verseByVerse.quote: And Joshua commanded the officers of the people, "Pass through the midst of the camp and command the people, 'Prepare your provisions, for within three days you are to pass over this Jordan to go in to take possession of the land that the LORD your God is giving you to possess.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The gap between the word in private and the order in public is nothing at all. Obedience that waits for better feelings has already begun to be disobedience.

The order is wonderfully unspiritual: pack food. Faith here gets the bread ready for the journey it believes God will provide. God has given the land, and the people are to pack lunches. Divine sovereignty and human effort are not rivals sharing out the work between them; the certainty of the outcome is what makes the preparation confident rather than anxious.

There is also a quiet change of era in that instruction. These are people who have eaten manna every morning for forty years and have never had to think about supplies. The manna will stop within a month of this order (5:12). God's provision does not become less; it stops being miraculous and starts being a harvest, which is how he feeds nearly everybody.

verseByVerse.quote: And to the Reubenites, the Gadites, and the half-tribe of Manasseh Joshua said, "Remember the word that Moses the servant of the LORD commanded you, saying, 'The LORD your God is providing you a place of rest and will give you this land.' Your wives, your little ones, and your livestock shall remain in the land that Moses gave you beyond the Jordan, but all the men of valor among you shall pass over armed before your brothers and shall help them, until the LORD gives rest to your brothers as he has to you, and they also take possession of the land that the LORD your God is giving them. Then you shall return to the land of your possession and shall possess it, the land that Moses the servant of the LORD gave you beyond the Jordan toward the sunrise."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two and a half tribes had been granted the land east of the river on one condition (Num. 32), and Joshua now collects on it. These men already have their inheritance, their families safe and their cattle grazing. They are told to leave all of it and cross a river to fight a war of some seven years (14:7, 10) for land that not one of them will ever own.

Verse 15 sets the term of service, and it is not a number of years: until the LORD gives rest to your brothers as he has to you. They go home when everyone else is home.

Here is the principle, and it is one the church needs about as badly as Israel did: my inheritance does not excuse me from my brother's battle. It is entirely possible to be settled, provided for, and spiritually comfortable while people you are bound to are still fighting for their lives, and this chapter treats that arrangement as a debt rather than a blessing. Paul says it in four words — bear one another's burdens (Gal. 6:2) — and this is what it looks like with boots on.

Something greater than Reuben is faintly visible here. One who was at rest, at home, and in possession of everything crossed over armed into a war he had no need to fight, for the sake of an inheritance that would belong to his brothers (Phil. 2:6-8; Heb. 2:11).

verseByVerse.quote: And they answered Joshua, "All that you have commanded us we will do, and wherever you send us we will go. Just as we obeyed Moses in all things, so we will obey you. Only may the LORD your God be with you, as he was with Moses! Whoever rebels against your commandment and disobeys your words, whatever you command him, shall be put to death. Only be strong and courageous."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The pledge is total, but it hangs on something they cannot give him: God's presence. Joshua's authority is borrowed, and their one anxiety about the new leadership is not competence but presence.

The clause about death is severe and it is not decoration. In a covenant nation crossing into a war, rebellion against God's appointed leader was rebellion against God, and the penalty says how seriously the arrangement was meant. It is one of the places where the Old Testament feels a long way from a Sunday morning, and the distance is real; the mediator now is not a man with an army but a Son with a cross, and the stakes have gone up rather than down.

The last words of the chapter are almost the words God used: he said them to Joshua three times, and now the people say them back to him.

That is how courage travels. It begins in the mouth of God, is spoken over one frightened man at a riverbank, and comes back to him out of the mouths of the people he is supposed to be leading. The LORD who will not leave or forsake gives his own words away, and they go round the camp all day and come home to him at evening, undiminished.

1.theology:
Grace before duty. The land is given in verse 3 before a foot has touched it. That order is never reversed in Scripture, and it is the whole difference between obedience and bargaining.

The sufficiency of God's presence. The promise of verses 5 and 9 is the foundation of the book: presence, not exemption.

The Word as the source of strength. Meditation is commanded before strategy (v. 8), and the 'good success' promised is the success of this commission.

No one rests alone. Being settled is not a discharge from a brother's battle (v. 15).
1.examples:
Then: A nation stood at a river with its leader newly buried and walled cities ahead, with no army to match Canaan's, only a sentence spoken over them: I have given to you (1:3).

Now: The cure for fear here is not a change of circumstances but a presence and a book. When a person dies, a job ends, or a diagnosis lands, the promise is not that the river will be easier but that the same God will be on both banks. If you are waiting for a change in the facts before you will be at peace, this chapter offers something else, and calls it better.

2.title: Rahab and the Spies
2.text: <sup>1</sup>And Joshua the son of Nun sent two men secretly from Shittim as spies, saying, "Go, view the land, especially Jericho." And they went and came into the house of a prostitute whose name was Rahab and lodged there.<sup>2</sup>And it was told to the king of Jericho, "Behold, men of Israel have come here tonight to search out the land."<sup>3</sup>Then the king of Jericho sent to Rahab, saying, "Bring out the men who have come to you, who entered your house, for they have come to search out all the land."<sup>4</sup>But the woman had taken the two men and hidden them. And she said, "True, the men came to me, but I did not know where they were from.<sup>5</sup>And when the gate was about to be closed at dark, the men went out. I do not know where the men went. Pursue them quickly, for you will overtake them."<sup>6</sup>But she had brought them up to the roof and hid them with the stalks of flax that she had laid in order on the roof.<sup>7</sup>So the men pursued after them on the way to the Jordan as far as the fords. And the gate was shut as soon as the pursuers had gone out.<sup>8</sup>Before the men lay down, she came up to them on the roof<sup>9</sup>and said to the men, "I know that the LORD has given you the land, and that the fear of you has fallen upon us, and that all the inhabitants of the land melt away before you.<sup>10</sup>For we have heard how the LORD dried up the water of the Red Sea before you when you came out of Egypt, and what you did to the two kings of the Amorites who were beyond the Jordan, to Sihon and Og, whom you devoted to destruction.<sup>11</sup>And as soon as we heard it, our hearts melted, and there was no spirit left in any man because of you, for the LORD your God, he is God in the heavens above and on the earth beneath.<sup>12</sup>Now then, please swear to me by the LORD that, as I have dealt kindly with you, you also will deal kindly with my father's house, and give me a sure sign<sup>13</sup>that you will save alive my father and mother, my brothers and sisters, and all who belong to them, and deliver our lives from death."<sup>14</sup>And the men said to her, "Our life for yours even to death! If you do not tell this business of ours, then when the LORD gives us the land we will deal kindly and faithfully with you."<sup>15</sup>Then she let them down by a rope through the window, for her house was built into the city wall, so that she lived in the wall.<sup>16</sup>And she said to them, "Go into the hills, or the pursuers will encounter you, and hide there three days until the pursuers have returned. Then afterward you may go your way."<sup>17</sup>The men said to her, "We will be guiltless with respect to this oath of yours that you have made us swear.<sup>18</sup>Behold, when we come into the land, you shall tie this scarlet cord in the window through which you let us down, and you shall gather into your house your father and mother, your brothers, and all your father's household.<sup>19</sup>Then if anyone goes out of the doors of your house into the street, his blood shall be on his own head, and we shall be guiltless. But if a hand is laid on anyone who is with you in the house, his blood shall be on our head.<sup>20</sup>But if you tell this business of ours, then we shall be guiltless with respect to your oath that you have made us swear."<sup>21</sup>And she said, "According to your words, so be it." Then she sent them away, and they departed. And she tied the scarlet cord in the window.<sup>22</sup>They departed and went into the hills and remained there three days until the pursuers returned, and the pursuers searched all along the way and found nothing.<sup>23</sup>Then the two men returned. They came down from the hills and passed over and came to Joshua the son of Nun, and they told him all that had happened to them.<sup>24</sup>And they said to Joshua, "Truly the LORD has given all the land into our hands. And also, all the inhabitants of the land melt away because of us."
2.overview:
The conquest of Canaan opens with a conversion, and the convert is a Canaanite prostitute. Two spies cross the Jordan and end up in the one house in Jericho where somebody is ready to believe. Rahab's trade and her nationality both marked her for destruction under the coming judgment, and she ends up in the roll of faith and in the family line of Christ.

Her confession on the roof (v. 11) is the summit of the chapter, and her scarlet cord its lasting picture.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — The Spies Sheltered and Hidden
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Two spies lodge with Rahab (v. 1); the king's men come to her door (vv. 2-3); she sends them off towards the fords while the spies lie hidden under flax on her roof (vv. 4-7).
verseByVerse.theology: Rahab is not improvising under pressure: she had chosen a side while there was still time to choose the other one (see v. 6).
verseByVerse.examples: Whatever is said about her lie (see below), what is beyond dispute is the direction she moved: away from her king, towards a God she had only heard about.

verseByVerse.quote: And Joshua the son of Nun sent two men secretly from Shittim as spies, saying, "Go, view the land, especially Jericho." And they went and came into the house of a prostitute whose name was Rahab and lodged there.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two men, sent secretly. The last time Israel sent spies into this country there were twelve of them and the report was made in public, and it cost the nation forty years (Num. 13). Joshua was one of the two who came back from that expedition telling the truth. He has learned something about how many people need to hear a scouting report.

Where they end up is the surprise. The narrator says it flatly, without euphemism and without a sneer: the house of a prostitute whose name was Rahab.

There were practical reasons. A house where strangers came and went at night attracted no attention, and a house built into the city wall had a window on the outside. But the practical explanation runs out quickly, because of all the doors in Jericho, these two men walked through the only one behind which somebody was ready to believe.

Scripture never tidies her up. Both New Testament writers who mention her keep the word: Rahab the prostitute (Heb. 11:31; James 2:25). The genealogy of Jesus does the same, naming her without explanation between Salmon and Boaz (Matt. 1:5) — which, on the face of the list, makes this woman David's great-great-grandmother (ancient genealogies often skip generations, so there may be more links than are written) and a direct ancestor of Christ.
verseByVerse.note: Shittim lay on the plains of Moab across the Jordan from Jericho, some miles east of the river.

verseByVerse.quote: And it was told to the king of Jericho, "Behold, men of Israel have come here tonight to search out the land." Then the king of Jericho sent to Rahab, saying, "Bring out the men who have come to you, who entered your house, for they have come to search out all the land."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The intelligence is good and it is fast. The spies have been in the city a matter of hours and the king already knows the house. Jericho is a frightened city watching its own gates, and frightened cities are observant.

The demand is issued directly to Rahab, and it puts her in an impossible position within a single sentence. Her king has sent men to her door. Handing over two foreigners costs her nothing and is what any loyal citizen would do. Refusing is treason, and treason inside a walled city under siege conditions has one penalty.

Weigh what she is being asked to weigh. On one side: her city, her king, her neighbours, her livelihood, and the roof over her family's heads. On the other: a rumour about a God she has never seen, whose people are camped across the river and have not yet won a single battle on this side of it.

Everyone in Jericho had the same information. The whole city had heard about the Red Sea. What separates Rahab from her king is not that she knew more; it is what she did in the ten seconds after the knock.

verseByVerse.quote: But the woman had taken the two men and hidden them. And she said, "True, the men came to me, but I did not know where they were from. And when the gate was about to be closed at dark, the men went out. I do not know where the men went. Pursue them quickly, for you will overtake them." But she had brought them up to the roof and hid them with the stalks of flax that she had laid in order on the roof. So the men pursued after them on the way to the Jordan as far as the fords. And the gate was shut as soon as the pursuers had gone out.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Verse 6 is told out of order on purpose: she had brought them up means the decision was not made under interrogation but earlier, when there was still time to make the other one. Faith that survives a crisis is nearly always faith that settled the question before the crisis arrived.

The flax is a domestic detail with weight in it. Stalks were spread on flat roofs to dry before being worked into linen; it was ordinary household work in progress, and she moved two grown men in under it without the soldiers seeing. She had thought about the roof.

Then she lies, in detail, with a false direction and a note of urgency. This is the honest difficulty of the chapter. Hebrews and James commend what her faith did (Heb. 11:31; James 2:25), not the lie. One older Reformed reading is that God accepted the genuine service of a believer a few days old without approving every part of it, a mercy the rest of us live on.

Was Rahab’s lie right? Some hold that every lie is sin, and that God honoured Rahab’s faith in spite of it; Scripture commends her faith and her protection of the spies (Heb 11:31; Jas 2:25), never her words. Others hold that deceiving those bent on murder in war is not the lie the ninth commandment forbids, which is false witness against a neighbour. The second view is the more likely: Rahab owed no truth to men coming to kill God’s servants, as the midwives owed none to Pharaoh (Exod 1:19). Christians who hid Jews from the Gestapo stood where she stood. Ordinary life is another matter: Do not lie to one another (Col 3:9).
verseByVerse.note: Once dried, flax stalks were soaked and beaten to free the fibres spun into linen.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–14 — The Confession on the Roof
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: On the roof Rahab states what she knows (v. 9), gives her evidence (v. 10), confesses the LORD as God of heaven and earth (v. 11), and asks mercy for her family (vv. 12-13); the spies pledge their lives for hers (v. 14).
verseByVerse.theology: She has no Scripture, no covenant, no priest and no temple, and out of a rumour she has reached a conclusion that half of Israel had failed to reach in the wilderness. Faith comes by hearing, and this is what it sounds like when the hearing is all there is.
verseByVerse.examples: Anyone who feels they have no claim on God may ask what Rahab asked, and on the same terms: not merit, but mercy promised on oath.

verseByVerse.quote: Before the men lay down, she came up to them on the roof and said to the men, "I know that the LORD has given you the land, and that the fear of you has fallen upon us, and that all the inhabitants of the land melt away before you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
She cannot wait until morning. I know: not I suspect, not I have heard it said. And what she knows is what God had said to Joshua a chapter earlier, that the land has been given. A Canaanite on a roof in Jericho and the LORD on the far bank of the Jordan are using the same sentence.

She also uses the covenant name. Not your god or the god of the Hebrews, which is how everyone else in the region speaks, but the LORD, the name given to Moses at the bush.

Her reading of the political situation is more accurate than her king's, and she gives the reason without flattering the men in front of her. It is not the Israelite army that has frightened the country; Israel has been walking in circles for forty years. What has fallen on Jericho is the fear of you, and behind that stands a promise made at the Red Sea that terror and dread would fall on the inhabitants of Canaan (Ex. 15:16). She is watching a song come true from the wrong side of it.

verseByVerse.quote: For we have heard how the LORD dried up the water of the Red Sea before you when you came out of Egypt, and what you did to the two kings of the Amorites who were beyond the Jordan, to Sihon and Og, whom you devoted to destruction. And as soon as we heard it, our hearts melted, and there was no spirit left in any man because of you, for the LORD your God, he is God in the heavens above and on the earth beneath.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Her evidence has two items, one forty years old and hundreds of miles away, the other recent and local: two pieces of news carried up the trade routes by men who had no interest in converting anybody.

The middle clause is regularly misquoted. It is usually said that Jericho melted in terror while Rahab melted in faith. The verse will not carry it. She says our hearts melted, and there was no spirit left in any man. She is inside that description, not outside it.

She was as frightened as everybody else, and that settles what faith is and is not. Faith here is not a steadier nervous system or a braver temperament; it is what one melted heart did with its melting. Every other person in that city took the same terror and locked the gate. She took it upstairs and asked for mercy.

Then the summit of the chapter, and one of the great confessions in the Old Testament: the LORD your God, he is God in the heavens above and on the earth beneath.

That is not a compliment paid to a strong local deity. It is a denial that there is anybody else, sky or soil, and it is almost word for word what Moses had told Israel to know and lay to heart (Deut. 4:39). She has never read Deuteronomy, and nobody taught her; she arrived where the covenant nation was still being argued into.
verseByVerse.note: “Devoted to destruction” means set apart to the LORD for destruction (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: Now then, please swear to me by the LORD that, as I have dealt kindly with you, you also will deal kindly with my father's house, and give me a sure sign that you will save alive my father and mother, my brothers and sisters, and all who belong to them, and deliver our lives from death." And the men said to her, "Our life for yours even to death! If you do not tell this business of ours, then when the LORD gives us the land we will deal kindly and faithfully with you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Confession turns immediately into petition, which is the order faith always runs in. She has said who God is; now she asks him for something, and what she asks for is her family's lives.

The word behind deal kindly is hesed, and it is one of the great words of the Old Testament: loyal love, the settled kindness of someone who has bound himself by covenant. It is what God shows Israel. Rahab asks a foreign God for the thing he gives to family, and she asks it as a Canaanite with no claim on him whatever.

The request is wide: her first instinct is to get everyone she is related to under the same roof. Salvation in this chapter is never a private arrangement.

The oath is startling. Two Israelite soldiers put their own lives up as the security for a Canaanite prostitute's — if she dies, they die. There is no reason on earth why either man should have offered that.

A woman with no standing asked for mercy and was answered with a life laid down as the price of hers. Her faith was enough to bring her inside a covenant she was born outside of. Many Christians have heard in that room an echo of the gospel, in which Christ laid down his own life for people who had no claim on him. The text does not make the spies a picture of Christ, and they had no idea of any such thing; but the echo is a fair one.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: She lets them down the wall and advises them where to hide (vv. 15-16); the spies set the terms of the rescue (vv. 17-20); she agrees and ties the cord that night (v. 21).
verseByVerse.theology: The terms are precise, and precision is mercy here rather than meanness: one sign, one house, and one condition.
verseByVerse.examples: Rahab's first thought was for her household, and a believer's first prayers still run the same way: for the people under our own roof.

verseByVerse.quote: Then she let them down by a rope through the window, for her house was built into the city wall, so that she lived in the wall. And she said to them, "Go into the hills, or the pursuers will encounter you, and hide there three days until the pursuers have returned. Then afterward you may go your way."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The detail about the wall is given because the story needs it twice — once now, for the escape, and once later, when that wall comes down.

Living in the wall was probably not a fashionable address. Houses built into a town wall were likely where the poor and the disreputable lived, and it tells you something of where Rahab stood in Jericho's social order. The place that made her marginal is the place that makes her useful to God.

Her advice is worth attention because it is not pious. She does not tell the spies that God will protect them. She tells them to run the wrong way — into the hills, not towards the Jordan where the search has gone — and to sit still for three days until the patrols give up.

Faith in this chapter has a working head on it. She has calculated how long a search party stays out and where they will not look. Trusting God has never meant declining to think, and the newest believer in the story is the one giving competent operational advice to professionals.
verseByVerse.note: The same house is the one the spies return to when the city falls (6:22–25).

verseByVerse.quote: The men said to her, "We will be guiltless with respect to this oath of yours that you have made us swear. Behold, when we come into the land, you shall tie this scarlet cord in the window through which you let us down, and you shall gather into your house your father and mother, your brothers, and all your father's household. Then if anyone goes out of the doors of your house into the street, his blood shall be on his own head, and we shall be guiltless. But if a hand is laid on anyone who is with you in the house, his blood shall be on our head. But if you tell this business of ours, then we shall be guiltless with respect to your oath that you have made us swear."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The terms are three, and they are exact. A cord in the window. Everyone she wants saved, inside her house. And no one steps out.

The cord may well be the rope she has just used to lower them down the wall, not a special object fetched for the purpose; it is the working equipment of the escape, left hanging where anyone could see it.

The Hebrew word for the cord, tiqvah, is spelled the same as the ordinary Hebrew word for hope. Most scholars think they are two different words that happen to sound alike, so the link should not be pressed, but a Hebrew reader could hardly miss the echo: what hung in that window for the next several weeks was a line of hope.

The line is drawn at the doorway. Inside, the spies carry the responsibility; outside, a man carries his own. The pattern is the Passover, structurally rather than by colour: a sign on the house, the family indoors, no one to go out, judgment passing over (Ex. 12:22-23).

Salvation in this arrangement has an address, and the only question on the day is which side of a doorway a person is standing on. Grace is free and it is not vague, and a man who preferred the street was not less loved on the day the walls came down. He was simply not in the house.

verseByVerse.quote: And she said, "According to your words, so be it." Then she sent them away, and they departed. And she tied the scarlet cord in the window.
verseByVerse.commentary:
She asks for no amendment. Not one clause is negotiated, which is remarkable given that she is agreeing to hand her entire family's survival to two foreign soldiers on the strength of their word.

Then the last sentence of the verse, which is the point of the whole scene: she tied the cord in the window. That night. Not on the morning the trumpets started, not when the dust of an approaching army appeared on the road — immediately, while the spies were still climbing the hills.

Consider what the next few weeks were like. Jericho carries on. The market opens, the gate opens, the king's men patrol, and in a window in the wall there is a red rope that everybody can see and nobody understands. She has to leave it there. She has to persuade a household of relations, who have almost certainly told her she has lost her mind, to come indoors and stay indoors.

Every believer knows something of those weeks: the sign is given, the promise is made, and the world goes on as if nothing had been said.

Rahab of Jericho, whose name was a byword in her own street, hung a rope in a window on the strength of a God she had heard about twice, and it held. She walked out of the falling city alive.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The spies follow Rahab's advice (v. 22), return to Joshua (v. 23), and give a one-sentence report (v. 24).
verseByVerse.theology: Same land, same walls, same giants as forty years before; the difference is not the intelligence but the men carrying it.

verseByVerse.quote: They departed and went into the hills and remained there three days until the pursuers returned, and the pursuers searched all along the way and found nothing. Then the two men returned. They came down from the hills and passed over and came to Joshua the son of Nun, and they told him all that had happened to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two men on a mission from Israel's leader take their orders from a Canaanite prostitute and are preserved by them. The narrator notes that the search found nothing and does not comment further; the chapter is not offering a rule about speech.

All that had happened to them does more work than it looks. What happened to them was not reconnaissance; the only thing recorded from three days inside enemy territory is a conversation on a roof. And this is why, when the city falls, Joshua knows the name of one household and sends the same two men to bring them out (6:22-25). The report saved her family a second time.

verseByVerse.quote: And they said to Joshua, "Truly the LORD has given all the land into our hands. And also, all the inhabitants of the land melt away because of us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The report has not a single military fact in it, no estimate of walls or garrison: just a verdict about who owns the country. It is what God said to Joshua (1:3) and Rahab said on the roof (2:9); the same sentence has travelled from God to a Canaanite to Israel's scouts unchanged.

Set it beside the report the last generation brought back from the same country: we are not able, the people are too strong, we seemed like grasshoppers (Num. 13:31-33). A generation had died in the desert learning the difference.

The LORD who dried a sea forty years before the news reached Jericho had been working on that city ever since, without an army, without a preacher, and without one word of written Scripture in it. By the time Israel arrived, the walls were still standing and the hearts behind them had already gone. He had a woman in that town before he had a soldier on that side of the river.

2.theology:
Grace reaching outside the covenant. Rahab has no claim of any kind. She is the wrong nationality, in the wrong trade, in a city under sentence, and she says out loud what God had said to Joshua, in almost his own words. If the conquest were a story about a deserving nation dispossessing an undeserving one, this chapter would be unwritable — which is why it stands where it does, at the front.

A faith that acts, and a faith that is afraid. Rahab is the rare figure cited by Hebrews for faith (11:31) and by James for works (2:25), and both specify the same actions: she welcomed the messengers and sent them out another way. Neither commends the lie. And verse 11 keeps her honest company for everyone who has ever been frightened: faith here is not the absence of fear but what a melted heart does next.

The cord, the house, and the line at the door. The text never calls the scarlet cord blood and never mentions the Passover, so the connection should be made the way the text makes it — structurally. A marked house, a family gathered inside, an instruction that no one go out, a judgment passing over: every element recurs. The Passover blood itself pointed to Christ, a lamb without blemish or spot (1 Peter 1:19), and many Christians have heard in the scarlet cord an echo of that blood. It is a fair echo so long as it stays an echo: the text's own point is the shelter of a marked house, and it never explains the cord's colour.

The conquest is God's before it is Israel's. No Israelite preached in Jericho, and no army had yet crossed the river, yet the city's courage was already spent (v. 24).
2.examples:
Then: A woman in a doomed city heard what God had done at a sea she had never seen, believed it, hid two enemy soldiers on her roof, and hung a red rope in her window. Then she lived under it for weeks, in a town going about its business, arguing her relatives indoors on the word of two men who had gone away and promised to come back.

Now: That is the position of every Christian between the promise and its keeping — living under a sign, in a world carrying on as normal, on the word of someone who has left and said he will return. Rahab's evidence was two pieces of news about what God had done in history; ours is a tomb that did not stay shut. She was saved not by her courage but by the mercy she asked for, and the same mercy is held out to us in Christ. If you are still waiting for more before you will trust him, remember that she had less information than anyone reading this, and she tied the cord that night.

3.title: Crossing the Jordan
3.text: <sup>1</sup>Then Joshua rose early in the morning and they set out from Shittim. And they came to the Jordan, he and all the people of Israel, and lodged there before they passed over.<sup>2</sup>At the end of three days the officers went through the camp<sup>3</sup>and commanded the people, "As soon as you see the ark of the covenant of the LORD your God being carried by the Levitical priests, then you shall set out from your place and follow it.<sup>4</sup>Yet there shall be a distance between you and it, about 2,000 cubits in length. Do not come near it, in order that you may know the way you shall go, for you have not passed this way before."<sup>5</sup>Then Joshua said to the people, "Consecrate yourselves, for tomorrow the LORD will do wonders among you."<sup>6</sup>And Joshua said to the priests, "Take up the ark of the covenant and pass on before the people." So they took up the ark of the covenant and went before the people.<sup>7</sup>The LORD said to Joshua, "Today I will begin to exalt you in the sight of all Israel, that they may know that, as I was with Moses, so I will be with you.<sup>8</sup>And as for you, command the priests who bear the ark of the covenant, 'When you come to the brink of the waters of the Jordan, you shall stand still in the Jordan.'"<sup>9</sup>And Joshua said to the people of Israel, "Come here and listen to the words of the LORD your God."<sup>10</sup>And Joshua said, "Here is how you shall know that the living God is among you and that he will without fail drive out from before you the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Hivites, the Perizzites, the Girgashites, the Amorites, and the Jebusites.<sup>11</sup>Behold, the ark of the covenant of the Lord of all the earth is passing over before you into the Jordan.<sup>12</sup>Now therefore take twelve men from the tribes of Israel, from each tribe a man.<sup>13</sup>And when the soles of the feet of the priests bearing the ark of the LORD, the Lord of all the earth, shall rest in the waters of the Jordan, the waters of the Jordan shall be cut off from flowing, and the waters coming down from above shall stand in one heap."<sup>14</sup>So when the people set out from their tents to pass over the Jordan with the priests bearing the ark of the covenant before the people,<sup>15</sup>and as soon as those bearing the ark had come as far as the Jordan, and the feet of the priests bearing the ark were dipped in the brink of the water (now the Jordan overflows all its banks throughout the time of harvest),<sup>16</sup>the waters coming down from above stood and rose up in a heap very far away, at Adam, the city that is beside Zarethan, and those flowing down toward the Sea of the Arabah, the Salt Sea, were completely cut off. And the people passed over opposite Jericho.<sup>17</sup>Now the priests bearing the ark of the covenant of the LORD stood firmly on dry ground in the midst of the Jordan, and all Israel was passing over on dry ground until all the nation finished passing over the Jordan.
3.overview:
Forty years earlier an older generation walked out of Egypt through the Red Sea on dry ground. Now their children walk into Canaan through the Jordan on dry ground. The two crossings bracket the wilderness, and between them they say one thing: the God who brings people out is the God who brings them in.

Throughout, the ark goes first, and at the end the priests who carry it stay in the riverbed until the last person is over.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel camps on the bank (v. 1) and is told to follow the ark at a distance (vv. 3-4), to consecrate themselves for tomorrow's wonders (v. 5), and to let the ark go first (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: The people were not asked to know the route; they were asked to keep something in sight.
verseByVerse.examples: A believer facing a road never walked before, a new country, a bereavement, an illness, is not required to know the way, only to keep the Lord in view.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Joshua rose early in the morning and they set out from Shittim. And they came to the Jordan, he and all the people of Israel, and lodged there before they passed over. At the end of three days the officers went through the camp and commanded the people, "As soon as you see the ark of the covenant of the LORD your God being carried by the Levitical priests, then you shall set out from your place and follow it. Yet there shall be a distance between you and it, about 2,000 cubits in length. Do not come near it, in order that you may know the way you shall go, for you have not passed this way before."
verseByVerse.commentary:
They camp on the bank, and the order to move comes only at the end of three days (v. 2). The three days here, the three of 1:11 and the spies' three days in the hills (2:22) probably overlap; the writer does not stop to fit them together. Whatever faith this generation had, it had to survive those days within sight of a river it could not cross.

The ark of the covenant was the gold-covered chest that held the tablets of the law: the sign of God's covenant, his binding promise to Israel and claim on it, and of his throne among them. The instruction is simple and the reason attached to it is the tender thing in the chapter: for you have not passed this way before. Nobody in that column knew the road. There was no map of the riverbed, no memory of the country, no veteran to ask.

They are not told to work it out. They are told to keep something in sight and walk after it.

The gap is the detail nobody would invent, and it does two jobs at once. A gap that size keeps the ark visible to every family in a column of that length — the person at the back can see where God is going. And it keeps everyone well out of arm's reach of it. Near enough to follow, far enough to fear, which is the working arrangement of the whole Christian life.
verseByVerse.note: Two thousand cubits is about 1,000 yards, a little over half a mile.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Joshua said to the people, "Consecrate yourselves, for tomorrow the LORD will do wonders among you." And Joshua said to the priests, "Take up the ark of the covenant and pass on before the people." So they took up the ark of the covenant and went before the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Before the river, a wash. Consecration probably meant what it had meant at Sinai (Exodus 19:10, 14-15): the ordinary business of cleaning up and setting apart — garments washed, households put in order, a night spent deliberately rather than casually. It is startling as a piece of military preparation: the night before the crossing is given to holiness rather than to logistics.

Joshua says not "may" but will, and puts a date on it in front of the whole nation. The consecration answers a promise; it does not buy one. Then the most protected object in Israel, normally screened behind a curtain, is carried to the head of the column, towards the water, first.

God does not send his people anywhere he has not gone. The order of march in this chapter is the order of the gospel: the presence goes in front, and the people follow into ground nobody has walked.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–13 — The Living God Among You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God begins to exalt Joshua (v. 7) and orders the priests to stand still in the river (v. 8). Joshua names the living God and the Lord of all the earth (vv. 9-11), appoints twelve men (v. 12), and makes the promise exact (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology: The title in verses 11 and 13, the Lord of all the earth, settles the question the whole book raises.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 13 asks for the first step to be taken before anything has changed, which is where faith is usually tested.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Joshua, "Today I will begin to exalt you in the sight of all Israel, that they may know that, as I was with Moses, so I will be with you. And as for you, command the priests who bear the ark of the covenant, 'When you come to the brink of the waters of the Jordan, you shall stand still in the Jordan.'" And Joshua said to the people of Israel, "Come here and listen to the words of the LORD your God." And Joshua said, "Here is how you shall know that the living God is among you and that he will without fail drive out from before you the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Hivites, the Perizzites, the Girgashites, the Amorites, and the Jebusites. Behold, the ark of the covenant of the Lord of all the earth is passing over before you into the Jordan. Now therefore take twelve men from the tribes of Israel, from each tribe a man. And when the soles of the feet of the priests bearing the ark of the LORD, the Lord of all the earth, shall rest in the waters of the Jordan, the waters of the Jordan shall be cut off from flowing, and the waters coming down from above shall stand in one heap."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The purpose clause is the important part. The exaltation is not for Joshua's benefit; it is so that they may know. A nation that had followed Moses through one body of water now has to learn to follow somebody else, and God gives them the evidence before he asks for the trust.

Joshua's name means the LORD saves, and in Greek it is Iēsous, Jesus. Hebrews sets the two men side by side (Hebrews 4:8), and sets Moses beside Christ too, who is faithful over God's house as a son and not as a servant (Hebrews 3:5-6). The God who exalted Joshua at the Jordan has highly exalted the greater Joshua, raised from the dead and seated at his right hand (Philippians 2:9).

The order to the priests is not to cross but to walk into a flooding river and stop. Standing still in a riverbed in spate, holding a gold box, while a nation files past behind you, is a harder assignment than running across.

Neither title is decoration. The living God is set against the gods of the country they are entering, who are carved and carried and cannot do anything, a contrast Isaiah will spend whole chapters on later. And the Lord of all the earth answers the question the conquest raises. If Israel's God is a regional deity, this is one tribe taking another tribe's land. If he owns the earth, then Canaan was never anyone else's to begin with, and he is disposing of his own property. That does not make the conquest easy to read, but it changes the question from theft to judgment.

Here is the difference from the Red Sea, stated in advance so that nobody can miss it. At the sea, Moses stretched out his hand, the water divided, and then Israel walked in. At the Jordan the water goes on flowing until there are feet in it.

The promise comes first and the path comes second, and between them is a step taken with nothing under it but a sentence. That is not a special demand made of priests. It is the ordinary shape of obedience: the evidence usually arrives after the foot goes down, and not before.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–17 — The Waters Stood in a Heap
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The priests reach a river in flood (vv. 14-15); it stops far upstream at Adam (v. 16); and they stand in the riverbed until the whole nation has crossed (v. 17).
verseByVerse.theology: The miracle is dated to the worst possible week of the year, and it echoes the Red Sea so that Israel will know the same God is with them.
verseByVerse.examples: The slowest in the column were not hurried or left: the people who feel they are always at the back are the ones verse 17 was written for.

verseByVerse.quote: So when the people set out from their tents to pass over the Jordan with the priests bearing the ark of the covenant before the people, and as soon as those bearing the ark had come as far as the Jordan, and the feet of the priests bearing the ark were dipped in the brink of the water (now the Jordan overflows all its banks throughout the time of harvest), the waters coming down from above stood and rose up in a heap very far away, at Adam, the city that is beside Zarethan, and those flowing down toward the Sea of the Arabah, the Salt Sea, were completely cut off. And the people passed over opposite Jericho. Now the priests bearing the ark of the covenant of the LORD stood firmly on dry ground in the midst of the Jordan, and all Israel was passing over on dry ground until all the nation finished passing over the Jordan.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The narrator mentions the river's condition only now, in brackets, the driest way of saying something enormous. God brought them to the river in the one season of the year, the spring snowmelt, when it could not be waded. In late summer it could be forded in places, as the fords of 2:7 show. The timing is not bad luck; it is the removal of every other explanation.

The geography is exact enough to check: everything below Adam ran on to the Dead Sea and left the bed dry. This is not a story about a river politely dividing at the point of crossing. It is a story with a place name in it.

The picture of waters that rose up in a heap is borrowed, not coined. It echoes the song Moses sang at the Red Sea, the floods stood up in a heap (Ex. 15:8), and the generation crossing here had learned that song from parents who died in the desert. Their fathers sang about it. They walked on it.

Everything in the chapter has been building to verse 17. The ark does not go across and wait on the far side. It stays until all the nation has passed: not most, not the strong and the quick. The priests hold that ground while the last of the flock straggles by — the old, the pregnant, the children, the man with the lame leg who has been at the back of this column all his life.

The throne of God went down into the riverbed and would not come up until everyone was across. Many Christians, and many of their hymns, have heard in the Jordan a picture of death, and the New Testament gives them a Priest to match: Christ, our great high priest (Hebrews 4:14), went down into death itself and keeps every last one the Father has given him. Of those whom you gave me, he said, I have lost not one (John 18:9).

Some explain the crossing by a landslide damming the Jordan upstream at Adam, as has happened in later centuries. Even if God used such a means, the timing is the miracle: the water stopped the moment the priests’ feet touched it, in flood season, and returned when they came out (4:18).
verseByVerse.note: Adam was probably Tell ed-Damiyeh, a town about 16 miles upstream.

3.theology:
The presence goes first. The ark leads, and the reason given is the people's ignorance rather than their weakness (v. 4).

The step before the sight. The promise is exact and it is conditional on a movement: when the soles of the priests' feet rest in the waters, the Jordan shall be cut off (v. 13). Had they waited on the bank for the river to open first, they would still be there.

The Lord of all the earth. The title is given twice at the crossing (vv. 11, 13), before a single Canaanite city falls, and it carries the moral weight of the whole conquest. The owner may give or judge as he wills, and Scripture adds that he waited centuries before judging (Genesis 15:16).

The ark in the riverbed. The priests hold the ground until the slowest child is across (v. 17), and in them Christians hear a greater Priest who loses none of his own.
3.examples:
Then: A nation stood on a bank in the barley harvest, looking at a river in flood, with no boats and no bridge, and was told to follow a gold box into it.

Now: Much of what God asks of a Christian is asked at that spot, and the difficulty is the order of events: we would like the river opened and then to walk. The step is not taken alone: the God who has gone ahead in Christ goes with us by his Spirit, and when we have hung back on the bank, his mercy calls us again rather than leaving us there. The water moved when there were feet in it, and not one moment sooner.

4.title: The Twelve Memorial Stones
4.text: <sup>1</sup>When all the nation had finished passing over the Jordan, the LORD said to Joshua,<sup>2</sup>"Take twelve men from the people, from each tribe a man,<sup>3</sup>and command them, saying, 'Take twelve stones from here out of the midst of the Jordan, from the very place where the priests' feet stood firmly, and bring them over with you and lay them down in the place where you lodge tonight.'"<sup>4</sup>Then Joshua called the twelve men from the people of Israel, whom he had appointed, a man from each tribe.<sup>5</sup>And Joshua said to them, "Pass on before the ark of the LORD your God into the midst of the Jordan, and take up each of you a stone upon his shoulder, according to the number of the tribes of the people of Israel,<sup>6</sup>that this may be a sign among you. When your children ask in time to come, 'What do those stones mean to you?'<sup>7</sup>then you shall tell them that the waters of the Jordan were cut off before the ark of the covenant of the LORD. When it passed over the Jordan, the waters of the Jordan were cut off. So these stones shall be to the people of Israel a memorial forever."<sup>8</sup>And the people of Israel did just as Joshua commanded and took up twelve stones out of the midst of the Jordan, according to the number of the tribes of the people of Israel, just as the LORD told Joshua. And they carried them over with them to the place where they lodged and laid them down there.<sup>9</sup>And Joshua set up twelve stones in the midst of the Jordan, in the place where the feet of the priests bearing the ark of the covenant had stood; and they are there to this day.<sup>10</sup>For the priests bearing the ark stood in the midst of the Jordan until everything was finished that the LORD commanded Joshua to tell the people, according to all that Moses had commanded Joshua. The people passed over in haste.<sup>11</sup>And when all the people had finished passing over, the ark of the LORD and the priests passed over before the people.<sup>12</sup>The sons of Reuben and the sons of Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh passed over armed before the people of Israel, as Moses had told them.<sup>13</sup>About 40,000 ready for war passed over before the LORD for battle, to the plains of Jericho.<sup>14</sup>On that day the LORD exalted Joshua in the sight of all Israel, and they stood in awe of him just as they had stood in awe of Moses, all the days of his life.<sup>15</sup>And the LORD said to Joshua,<sup>16</sup>"Command the priests bearing the ark of the testimony to come up out of the Jordan."<sup>17</sup>So Joshua commanded the priests, "Come up out of the Jordan."<sup>18</sup>And when the priests bearing the ark of the covenant of the LORD came up from the midst of the Jordan, and the soles of the priests' feet were lifted up on dry ground, the waters of the Jordan returned to their place and overflowed all its banks, as before.<sup>19</sup>The people came up out of the Jordan on the tenth day of the first month, and they encamped at Gilgal on the east border of Jericho.<sup>20</sup>And those twelve stones, which they took out of the Jordan, Joshua set up at Gilgal.<sup>21</sup>And he said to the people of Israel, "When your children ask their fathers in times to come, 'What do these stones mean?'<sup>22</sup>then you shall let your children know, 'Israel passed over this Jordan on dry ground.'<sup>23</sup>For the LORD your God dried up the waters of the Jordan for you until you passed over, as the LORD your God did to the Red Sea, which he dried up for us until we passed over,<sup>24</sup>so that all the peoples of the earth may know that the hand of the LORD is mighty, that you may fear the LORD your God forever."
4.overview:
The crossing is finished and God is not. Before a single soldier moves on Jericho, he stops the campaign to have a monument built: twelve stones lifted out of the middle of the riverbed, from the exact spot where the priests had stood, and carried to that night's camp. The first thing Israel does in the promised land is remember the last thing God did.

The reason is given twice, and both times it is a child's question (vv. 6, 21). There are two sets of stones: one heap at Gilgal, where the whole camp walks past it daily, and another left standing in the riverbed, where the returning flood hides it from everyone but God (v. 9). The chapter ends by naming the point of it all, which faces two ways: a witness to the nations and lasting reverence in Israel (v. 24).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — Twelve Stones Out of the Riverbed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The nation is across and God speaks before anyone marches: take twelve men, one per tribe, and twelve stones out of the middle of the Jordan, from the exact spot where the priests' feet had stood (vv. 1-3). The stones are to be laid down at that night's camp, because a question is coming from the children, and the answer is supplied in advance (vv. 6-7). The people obey (v. 8), and then a second set is mentioned: Joshua set up twelve stones in the riverbed itself, where the priests had stood (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: The battle waits while a monument is built: the first order after the miracle is not to advance but to remember.
verseByVerse.examples: Every Christian has some stones of this kind: a mercy that would be forgotten unless it were marked. Name yours, and keep them where you will pass them.

verseByVerse.quote: When all the nation had finished passing over the Jordan, the LORD said to Joshua, "Take twelve men from the people, from each tribe a man, and command them, saying, 'Take twelve stones from here out of the midst of the Jordan, from the very place where the priests' feet stood firmly, and bring them over with you and lay them down in the place where you lodge tonight.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The nation is across, the enemy city is a few miles off, and God's first instruction is about rocks.

Nothing in the military situation calls for a pause. What calls for it is the human memory, and God is under no illusion about how it works. A wonder like this one will be vivid for a month, argued about for a year, and gone in a generation unless something is done about it, so the first act of Israel in the promised land is to build a monument.

Look at where the stones come from. Not the bank, which would have been easier, but from the very place where the priests' feet stood firmly — out of the middle of the riverbed, from the ground that had been dry only because God was standing on it.

Twelve men are named, one for each tribe, and each carries his own stone on his own shoulder. The memorial could have been built by a work party in an hour. Instead every tribe in Israel has a man with a wet stone on his back, and nobody in the nation can look at that heap later and say it was somebody else's deliverance.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Joshua called the twelve men from the people of Israel, whom he had appointed, a man from each tribe. And Joshua said to them, "Pass on before the ark of the LORD your God into the midst of the Jordan, and take up each of you a stone upon his shoulder, according to the number of the tribes of the people of Israel, that this may be a sign among you. When your children ask in time to come, 'What do those stones mean to you?' then you shall tell them that the waters of the Jordan were cut off before the ark of the covenant of the LORD. When it passed over the Jordan, the waters of the Jordan were cut off. So these stones shall be to the people of Israel a memorial forever." And the people of Israel did just as Joshua commanded and took up twelve stones out of the midst of the Jordan, according to the number of the tribes of the people of Israel, just as the LORD told Joshua. And they carried them over with them to the place where they lodged and laid them down there. And Joshua set up twelve stones in the midst of the Jordan, in the place where the feet of the priests bearing the ark of the covenant had stood; and they are there to this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The purpose of the monument is not commemoration but a conversation that has not happened yet: a child at Gilgal, not born when this happened, asking his father what the stones are for. The stones teach nothing on their own; they provoke a question, and a parent answers it. Moses had made the same provision — When your son asks you in time to come, “What is the meaning of the testimonies and the statutes and the rules that the LORD our God has commanded you?” (Deut. 6:20).

The second set nobody will ever see again: within the hour the flood closes over them. No child will ask about them. They stand under a running river with nobody but God to look at them, and the narrator's aside — they are there to this day — is written by a man who knows they are invisible and knows they are there.

Some translations read verse 9 as Joshua setting up at Gilgal the stones taken from the riverbed, so that there is only one set. The Hebrew most naturally reads as a second set, standing in the riverbed itself, and the ESV and the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint) take it that way.

Not every witness to what God has done is public. Most of the evidence in most Christian lives is submerged: prayers answered that nobody else heard about, sins killed that nobody knew were alive, a marriage still standing for reasons that were never explained to anyone. The water goes back over it and it is still there.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The people cross in haste and the ark comes up last (vv. 10-11); the eastern tribes cross armed (vv. 12-13); God exalts Joshua (v. 14); and the river returns the moment the priests step out (vv. 15-18).
verseByVerse.theology: God's presence goes in first into the water (3:6) and comes out last, behind the people (v. 11).
verseByVerse.examples: Because the ark led them in and stayed to see them out, at no point was anybody the last one in the river. Christ's people are never left alone in the water.

verseByVerse.quote: For the priests bearing the ark stood in the midst of the Jordan until everything was finished that the LORD commanded Joshua to tell the people, according to all that Moses had commanded Joshua. The people passed over in haste. And when all the people had finished passing over, the ark of the LORD and the priests passed over before the people. The sons of Reuben and the sons of Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh passed over armed before the people of Israel, as Moses had told them. About 40,000 ready for war passed over before the LORD for battle, to the plains of Jericho. On that day the LORD exalted Joshua in the sight of all Israel, and they stood in awe of him just as they had stood in awe of Moses, all the days of his life.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two small phrases do quiet work. The first is in haste: with water standing in a heap upstream, every family crossed as fast as it could carry the children. The event was glorious and it was also frightening, and the writer lets both stand.

The second is the order in verse 11: the presence of God stood between them and the river until the last was clear.

The promise of chapter 1 is kept: forty thousand men who already had their land cross to fight for somebody else's. It cost them years.

What God said he would begin (3:7) he did, and the verb is the one to notice: the LORD exalted Joshua. He did not exalt himself, campaign for it, or manage his reputation. He carried out an instruction about a river and God did the rest, which is the arrangement Peter describes when he tells frightened church leaders to humble themselves under God's mighty hand so that he may exalt them at the proper time (1 Pet. 5:6).

Why only 40,000 from tribes that numbered over 110,000 men (Num 26)? These were picked fighters; the rest stayed east of the Jordan to guard families and flocks (1:14).

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Joshua, "Command the priests bearing the ark of the testimony to come up out of the Jordan." So Joshua commanded the priests, "Come up out of the Jordan."
