And when the priests bearing the ark of the covenant of the LORD came up from the midst of the Jordan, and the soles of the priests' feet were lifted up on dry ground, the waters of the Jordan returned to their place and overflowed all its banks, as before.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God speaks to Joshua; Joshua repeats it to the priests, adding nothing. It is a small picture of what leadership in this book is.

The river does not subside back over hours. It stopped when feet went in (3:15) and returned at the instant they came out: not an ebb that happened to coincide with a crossing, but a thing that started and stopped on command.

Then look at what the returning flood does to the way home. Behind them is a river in spate that no one is crossing back over. The wilderness is now unreachable. Every complaint about Egypt, every proposal to go back, every option but forward has just been closed by God himself — and he waited to close it until every last one of them was safely on the other side.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 19–24 — What Do These Stones Mean?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel camps at Gilgal on the tenth day of the first month and the stones go up (vv. 19-20). The children's answer now includes the Red Sea (vv. 21-23), and the purpose looks outward and inward (v. 24).
verseByVerse.theology: The date links the entry to the Passover, and the stones join two crossings, forty years apart, into one story.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 24 keeps the whole event from turning inward: what God does for his people is meant to be heard about by others.

verseByVerse.quote: The people came up out of the Jordan on the tenth day of the first month, and they encamped at Gilgal on the east border of Jericho. And those twelve stones, which they took out of the Jordan, Joshua set up at Gilgal.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The date is not a filing detail. On the tenth day of the first month, in Egypt, the lamb was chosen, four days before the blood went on the doorframes (Ex. 12:3). Forty years later to the day, the nation walks into the land, and four days later it keeps the Passover there (5:10), so the calendar of their slavery becomes the calendar of their inheritance, without a single date being changed.

They camp at Gilgal, on Jericho's doorstep, and the stones go up there. Not on a hilltop and not at a shrine, but in the middle of the camp, where the washing is done and the children play and everyone walks past them a dozen times a day.
verseByVerse.note: The first month is Abib, later called Nisan, in early spring.

verseByVerse.quote: And he said to the people of Israel, "When your children ask their fathers in times to come, 'What do these stones mean?' then you shall let your children know, 'Israel passed over this Jordan on dry ground.' For the LORD your God dried up the waters of the Jordan for you until you passed over, as the LORD your God did to the Red Sea, which he dried up for us until we passed over, so that all the peoples of the earth may know that the hand of the LORD is mighty, that you may fear the LORD your God forever."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The question comes round a second time, and now the Red Sea is in the answer. Watch the pronouns, because they carry the whole point. The Jordan was dried up for you; the Red Sea was dried up for us. Joshua was a grown man at both. He stands in front of a nation whose older members were children when the sea opened and most of whom were not yet born, and he puts the two events in one sentence, so that no child grows up thinking God did something for his grandparents and something else, unrelated, for him.

That is how a family teaches faith: not by handing on a doctrine but by handing on a story with the child's own name in it. The people who came out and the people who came in are one people, and the God who did the one did the other.

The last verse turns the monument outward before it turns it inward. The river was dried up so that the news would travel, as it already had to a woman in Jericho (2:10). And the right response to a memorial is not nostalgia. Twelve stones in a camp are not there to make anyone wistful about the good old days at the river; they are there to produce awe, permanently.

The hand that stopped a flooded river at a town sixteen miles upstream, and held it, and let it go again at the exact second the last priest stepped out, is mighty. He arranged the whole thing so that a child not yet born would ask a question, and so that a stranger in a foreign country would hear the story and be saved by it. Two rivers, forty years apart, and one hand over both.

4.theology:
Memory is commanded, not assumed. God halts a military campaign to build a heap of stones. The instinct runs through the whole Bible and lands on a table in an upper room: do this in remembrance of me (1 Cor. 11:24-25). Christian memory is not nostalgia; it is a discipline with physical objects attached — water, bread, wine, stones.

Faith is handed on in conversations. The arrangement here puts the next generation's faith in the hands of parents answering questions. Moses had made the same provision, and the psalmist describes the chain running four generations deep so that children not yet born would set their hope in God (Ps. 78:4-7). A generation that falls silent puts the next at risk, though God is not limited to parents, as a Canaanite in Jericho shows.

One work, two waters. Joshua puts the Red Sea and the Jordan in the same sentence (v. 23), and the date makes the same point (v. 19). The God who brings people out of slavery and the God who brings them into the inheritance are not two Gods with two projects. Paul reads the sea crossing as a kind of baptism into Moses (1 Cor. 10:1-2), and the same pattern holds for the church: the Saviour who brings his people out of sin's slavery is the one who will bring them into an inheritance kept in heaven for them (1 Peter 1:4).

Salvation aimed at the nations. The stated purpose reaches further than Israel: that all the peoples of the earth may know that the hand of the LORD is mighty (v. 24). This is not a private deliverance with a religious souvenir. It is a public act meant to travel.
4.examples: In Israel the story survived because a child asked about a heap of stones and a parent answered beside a cooking fire. The question still has to be answered by somebody who was there. What do the children and younger believers around you know of God's deeds: what he did at the cross, and what he has done in your house? The telling is not a burden laid on us to keep the faith alive by our own effort; God gave the question and the answer, and his Spirit uses ordinary words. Most Christians have a Gilgal they have never described to anyone, and it is not too late to begin.

5.title: Circumcision, Passover, and the Commander of the LORD's Army
5.text: <sup>1</sup>As soon as all the kings of the Amorites who were beyond the Jordan to the west, and all the kings of the Canaanites who were by the sea, heard that the LORD had dried up the waters of the Jordan for the people of Israel until they had crossed over, their hearts melted and there was no longer any spirit in them because of the people of Israel.<sup>2</sup>At that time the LORD said to Joshua, "Make flint knives and circumcise the sons of Israel a second time."<sup>3</sup>So Joshua made flint knives and circumcised the sons of Israel at Gibeath-haaraloth.<sup>4</sup>And this is the reason why Joshua circumcised them: all the males of the people who came out of Egypt, all the men of war, had died in the wilderness on the way after they had come out of Egypt.<sup>5</sup>Though all the people who came out had been circumcised, yet all the people who were born on the way in the wilderness after they had come out of Egypt had not been circumcised.<sup>6</sup>For the people of Israel walked forty years in the wilderness, until all the nation, the men of war who came out of Egypt, perished, because they did not obey the voice of the LORD; the LORD swore to them that he would not let them see the land that the LORD had sworn to their fathers to give to us, a land flowing with milk and honey.<sup>7</sup>So it was their children, whom he raised up in their place, that Joshua circumcised. For they were uncircumcised, because they had not been circumcised on the way.<sup>8</sup>When the circumcising of the whole nation was finished, they remained in their places in the camp until they were healed.<sup>9</sup>And the LORD said to Joshua, "Today I have rolled away the reproach of Egypt from you." And so the name of that place is called Gilgal to this day.<sup>10</sup>While the people of Israel were encamped at Gilgal, they kept the Passover on the fourteenth day of the month in the evening on the plains of Jericho.<sup>11</sup>And the day after the Passover, on that very day, they ate of the produce of the land, unleavened cakes and parched grain.<sup>12</sup>And the manna ceased the day after they ate of the produce of the land. And there was no longer manna for the people of Israel, but they ate of the fruit of the land of Canaan that year.<sup>13</sup>When Joshua was by Jericho, he lifted up his eyes and looked, and behold, a man was standing before him with his drawn sword in his hand. And Joshua went to him and said to him, "Are you for us, or for our adversaries?"<sup>14</sup>And he said, "No; but I am the commander of the army of the LORD. Now I have come." And Joshua fell on his face to the earth and worshiped and said to him, "What does my lord say to his servant?"<sup>15</sup>And the commander of the LORD's army said to Joshua, "Take off your sandals from your feet, for the place where you are standing is holy." And Joshua did so.
5.overview:
Israel is in the land, and God's first command is not a battle plan but a knife. Every fighting man is to be circumcised, because the covenant sign had lapsed in the wilderness (vv. 2-7).

Then the reproach of Egypt is rolled away (v. 9), Israel keeps its first Passover in the land (v. 10), and the manna stops the morning after they eat its grain (vv. 11-12).

The chapter ends outside the walls with a man holding a drawn sword, who comes not to take sides but to take command (vv. 13-15).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — The Knife Before the Battle
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The kings of Canaan lose heart (v. 1). God's first command in the land is a flint knife (v. 2), because the generation born on the way had never received the covenant sign (vv. 4-7). The nation lies still until healed (v. 8), and God names the place (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: A generation grew up belonging to God by promise and carrying nothing in their bodies to say so, and the first thing God does with them in the land is put the mark back on.
verseByVerse.examples: When obedience leaves us weak, we are not thereby left unguarded: the God who asks it is also at work on the other side of the wall.

verseByVerse.quote: As soon as all the kings of the Amorites who were beyond the Jordan to the west, and all the kings of the Canaanites who were by the sea, heard that the LORD had dried up the waters of the Jordan for the people of Israel until they had crossed over, their hearts melted and there was no longer any spirit in them because of the people of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The wording is Rahab's, almost word for word, from her roof three chapters ago: their hearts melted, and there was no spirit left in any man (2:11). What she reported about her own city has now happened to every king in the country.

Israel has not yet fought anybody west of the Jordan. There has been no battle, no siege, no demonstration of arms — only a river that behaved oddly for an afternoon, and the news travelling faster than the army.

Now hold this verse against what God commands in the next one, because the two belong together. Within days Israel will circumcise every fighting man in the nation and lie helpless in the camp. The one week in which Israel could have been wiped out by a determined attack is the exact week in which no king in Canaan can bring himself to move.

God empties the enemy of nerve on the same morning he empties his own army of strength. That is not luck and it is not tidy timing; it is how this book says the conquest was won.

verseByVerse.quote: At that time the LORD said to Joshua, "Make flint knives and circumcise the sons of Israel a second time." So Joshua made flint knives and circumcised the sons of Israel at Gibeath-haaraloth. And this is the reason why Joshua circumcised them: all the males of the people who came out of Egypt, all the men of war, had died in the wilderness on the way after they had come out of Egypt. Though all the people who came out had been circumcised, yet all the people who were born on the way in the wilderness after they had come out of Egypt had not been circumcised. For the people of Israel walked forty years in the wilderness, until all the nation, the men of war who came out of Egypt, perished, because they did not obey the voice of the LORD; the LORD swore to them that he would not let them see the land that the LORD had sworn to their fathers to give to us, a land flowing with milk and honey. So it was their children, whom he raised up in their place, that Joshua circumcised. For they were uncircumcised, because they had not been circumcised on the way.
verseByVerse.commentary:
God's first order inside the promised land is for a knife, not a sword. Flint, not metal, and Israel had metal. Circumcision was done with a flint blade, the ancient instrument; the same word appears when Zipporah takes a flint and circumcises her son on the road (Ex. 4:25). This is deliberately the old rite, performed the old way.

The writer takes his time over a painful piece of history. The text does not say exactly why the rite was not kept on the journey, but it sets the lapse beside the reason for the journey: their fathers had not obeyed, God swore they would not see the land, and it seems the sign lapsed with them. Israel spent four decades still fed with manna every morning, still led by the pillar, and unmarked.

Then think what this order costs, with Jericho a few miles away. Israel knew from its own family history: when Shechem's men were circumcised, Simeon and Levi came in on the third day, when they were sore, and killed every male in the city (Gen. 34:25). That is the precedent. God tells this army to do to itself, in sight of an enemy stronghold, what once left a whole town defenceless.

That settles what the conquest is going to rest on: not readiness. God will have a people marked as his before he has a people fit to fight.
verseByVerse.note: “Gibeath-haaraloth” means “the hill of the foreskins” (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: When the circumcising of the whole nation was finished, they remained in their places in the camp until they were healed. And the LORD said to Joshua, "Today I have rolled away the reproach of Egypt from you." And so the name of that place is called Gilgal to this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
An entire army lies still in enemy country, waiting to be able to walk. Then God speaks about shame rather than strength. The reproach of Egypt is the whole weight of what they had been. Slaves. A people whose God had, on the evidence, brought them out into a desert and left them there for forty years to die, which may well be the taunt Moses had twice warned God the Egyptians would make (Ex. 32:12; Num. 14:13-16). Every year in the wilderness had made the sneer look more reasonable.

The place is named Gilgal, which sounds like the Hebrew for to roll. The picture is of a weight the size of a millstone rolled off a nation, and it is done in one day, and it is done by God — I have rolled it away. Israel did not answer the taunt. They were not required to.

That is the pattern of everything God does about shame: the people concerned are lying still, unable to do anything at all, and the weight is moved from outside by somebody else. The New Testament carries both halves of this scene to Christ. It speaks of a circumcision made without hands, the circumcision of Christ, by which the old life is put off (Colossians 2:11), a circumcision of the heart worked by the Spirit (Romans 2:29), who now enables the obedience the outward sign could only mark. And it speaks of the reproach Christ himself endured when he suffered outside the gate to make his people holy by his own blood (Hebrews 13:12-13). The shame that matters most is rolled away by one who bore shame himself.
verseByVerse.note: Gilgal became Israel's base camp for the early campaigns (9:6; 10:6).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–12 — Passover, and the Last Morning of Manna
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel keeps its first Passover inside the land (v. 10), eats grain from fields it never planted (v. 11), and the manna ceases (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: The first four days in the land follow the Passover calendar, and the order in verse 12 is exact and kind: the new food comes before the old supply stops.
verseByVerse.examples: The provision had not failed; it had changed form, because the promise it was covering had arrived.

verseByVerse.quote: While the people of Israel were encamped at Gilgal, they kept the Passover on the fourteenth day of the month in the evening on the plains of Jericho. And the day after the Passover, on that very day, they ate of the produce of the land, unleavened cakes and parched grain. And the manna ceased the day after they ate of the produce of the land. And there was no longer manna for the people of Israel, but they ate of the fruit of the land of Canaan that year.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Count the days. They came up out of the Jordan on the tenth (4:19), the day the lamb was chosen in Egypt. Now it is the fourteenth, the night the lamb was killed. The first four days of Israel's life in the promised land follow the Passover calendar exactly, and this is the first Passover ever kept inside the land. Every one of those meals looked beyond itself, as the New Testament says plainly: Christ, our Passover lamb, has been sacrificed (1 Corinthians 5:7).

Forty years of these meals had been eaten in tents in a desert, remembering a rescue and waiting for a country. This one is eaten in the country, in sight of the first city they will have to take.

Parched grain is the plainest food in the Bible: new barley held over a fire and eaten in the hand. What makes it remarkable is whose field it came out of — grain they did not sow, in a land they had owned for less than a week, exactly as Moses had promised them: houses they did not build, vineyards they did not plant (Deut. 6:10-11).

One sentence ends forty years. Every adult in that camp had found breakfast lying on the ground every morning of his life, and then one morning there was nothing there. The order is the mercy: the harvest was in their hands before the miracle ended.

Hold onto that when a form of God's care leaned on for years comes to a stop: a job, health, a person, a season of nearness in prayer. The manna ending was not the withdrawal of God's kindness. It was the arrival of what the manna had been standing in for.

It was always standing in for something. Jesus, arguing with a crowd who wanted the bread trick repeated, said their fathers ate the manna in the wilderness and died, and that he himself was the bread that came down from heaven, which a man may eat and live for ever (John 6:49-51). The manna stopped at Gilgal because the land had come. It stopped for good because the true bread had.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 13–15 — The Commander of the LORD's Army
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Joshua challenges a man with a drawn sword (v. 13), is refused his question and falls on his face (v. 14), and is told to take off his sandals (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: Joshua offers two options and is told neither. God does not join sides in this book; he takes command of it.
verseByVerse.examples: The orders for Jericho come in the next chapter. This encounter settles who is in charge before anything is planned.

verseByVerse.quote: When Joshua was by Jericho, he lifted up his eyes and looked, and behold, a man was standing before him with his drawn sword in his hand. And Joshua went to him and said to him, "Are you for us, or for our adversaries?" And he said, "No; but I am the commander of the army of the LORD. Now I have come." And Joshua fell on his face to the earth and worshiped and said to him, "What does my lord say to his servant?" And the commander of the LORD's army said to Joshua, "Take off your sandals from your feet, for the place where you are standing is holy." And Joshua did so.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joshua is walking the ground before an assault, and he goes straight up to an unknown man with a drawn sword and asks the only question a soldier can think to ask. It is a reasonable question and the wrong one, and the answer says so in a single syllable: neither option applies.

God does not enlist. He commands. The question that this man's answer refuses is the question most of us bring to God about anything difficult — is he on my side in this argument, this decision, this dispute — and the refusal is not unkind. It is a promotion of the whole subject. The right question was never whether God had joined Israel's war. It was whether Israel had joined his.

Joshua's response points to who this is. He bows down in worship, and he is not stopped. The Hebrew word can mean simply bowing low before a superior, so this alone would not settle it, but it is telling: elsewhere in Scripture, when a man falls at the feet of an angel, the angel will not have it — You must not do that!... Worship God (Rev. 22:8-9). This one receives it.

The sentence that settles it is one Israel had heard before: what was said out of a burning bush to a shepherd on the far side of a desert, in almost the same words (Ex. 3:5). The same voice that commissioned Moses is standing outside Jericho.

The ground is not holy because of the soil. It is a field on the edge of a Canaanite city and there is nothing sacred about it. It is holy because of who is standing on it, which is the only thing that has ever made any ground holy.

No orders are given at all; it ends with Israel's general lying in the dirt with his shoes in his hand. The Captain of the LORD's host came to Jericho with his sword already drawn, and he did not come to be recruited. He came to take the field. Every wall in the country was already his, and the man he was speaking to would not swing a sword for seven days.

Who is the commander? Some take him as a high angel, like Michael (Dan 10:13). But he receives worship, and Joshua is told to remove his sandals because the place is holy, as Moses was at the bush (Exod 3:5). The best reading is the LORD himself, the Son before his incarnation. Such an appearance is called a theophany, a visible appearing of God. And his answer, “No”, means he is not on anyone’s side; the question is whether we are on his.

5.theology:
Consecration before conquest. The order of this chapter is the argument of the book. Circumcision, then Passover, then worship on holy ground, and only then a battle. The conquest never rested on Israel's readiness, and while Israel lay helpless God emptied the kings of Canaan of nerve (v. 1).

The reproach rolled away. The taunt that God had brought a nation into a desert to die is removed in a day, by God, while the people concerned lie still. Shame is lifted from outside, by someone else.

When the manna stops. The provision that had defined a generation ends the morning after the first harvest is eaten (v. 12), and nothing is wrong. God does not withdraw an old kindness and then ask for trust about a new one, and the manna itself pointed to the true bread from heaven.

He does not take sides. Joshua's question assumes two armies and asks which one this man belongs to. The answer is No. The commander of the LORD's army, most likely the LORD himself (see vv. 13-15), gives no instructions at all. The encounter exists to settle who is in charge, which is the question every believer is tempted to get the wrong way round.
5.examples: Joshua's question is the one nearly everybody brings to God in a conflict: are you for me in this argument, this church split, this decision I have already made? The answer outside Jericho was No, and an invitation to ask a better question: what does my lord say to his servant? We can ask it without fear, because the Lord who will not take our side has already given himself for us.

6.title: The Fall of Jericho
6.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Jericho was shut up inside and outside because of the people of Israel. None went out, and none came in.<sup>2</sup>And the LORD said to Joshua, "See, I have given Jericho into your hand, with its king and mighty men of valor.<sup>3</sup>You shall march around the city, all the men of war going around the city once. Thus shall you do for six days.<sup>4</sup>Seven priests shall bear seven trumpets of rams' horns before the ark. On the seventh day you shall march around the city seven times, and the priests shall blow the trumpets.<sup>5</sup>And when they make a long blast with the ram's horn, when you hear the sound of the trumpet, then all the people shall shout with a great shout, and the wall of the city will fall down flat, and the people shall go up, everyone straight before him."<sup>6</sup>So Joshua the son of Nun called the priests and said to them, "Take up the ark of the covenant and let seven priests bear seven trumpets of rams' horns before the ark of the LORD."<sup>7</sup>And he said to the people, "Go forward. March around the city and let the armed men pass on before the ark of the LORD."<sup>8</sup>And just as Joshua had commanded the people, the seven priests bearing the seven trumpets of rams' horns before the LORD went forward, blowing the trumpets, with the ark of the covenant of the LORD following them.<sup>9</sup>The armed men were walking before the priests who were blowing the trumpets, and the rear guard was walking after the ark, while the trumpets blew continually.<sup>10</sup>But Joshua commanded the people, "You shall not shout or make your voice heard, neither shall any word go out of your mouth, until the day I tell you to shout. Then you shall shout."<sup>11</sup>So he caused the ark of the LORD to circle the city, going about it once. And they came into the camp and spent the night in the camp.<sup>12</sup>Then Joshua rose early in the morning, and the priests took up the ark of the LORD.<sup>13</sup>And the seven priests bearing the seven trumpets of rams' horns before the ark of the LORD walked on, and they blew the trumpets continually. And the armed men were walking before them, and the rear guard was walking after the ark of the LORD, while the trumpets blew continually.<sup>14</sup>And the second day they marched around the city once, and returned into the camp. So they did for six days.<sup>15</sup>On the seventh day they rose early, at the dawn of day, and marched around the city in the same manner seven times. It was only on that day that they marched around the city seven times.<sup>16</sup>And at the seventh time, when the priests had blown the trumpets, Joshua said to the people, "Shout, for the LORD has given you the city.<sup>17</sup>And the city and all that is within it shall be devoted to the LORD for destruction. Only Rahab the prostitute and all who are with her in her house shall live, because she hid the messengers whom we sent.<sup>18</sup>But you, keep yourselves from the things devoted to destruction, lest when you have devoted them you take any of the devoted things and make the camp of Israel a thing for destruction and bring trouble upon it.<sup>19</sup>But all silver and gold, and every vessel of bronze and iron, are holy to the LORD; they shall go into the treasury of the LORD."<sup>20</sup>So the people shouted, and the trumpets were blown. As soon as the people heard the sound of the trumpet, the people shouted a great shout, and the wall fell down flat, so that the people went up into the city, every man straight before him, and they captured the city.<sup>21</sup>Then they devoted all in the city to destruction, both men and women, young and old, oxen, sheep, and donkeys, with the edge of the sword.<sup>22</sup>But to the two men who had spied out the land, Joshua said, "Go into the prostitute's house and bring out from there the woman and all who belong to her, as you swore to her."<sup>23</sup>So the young men who had been spies went in and brought out Rahab and her father and mother and brothers and all who belonged to her. And they brought all her relatives and put them outside the camp of Israel.<sup>24</sup>And they burned the city with fire, and everything in it. Only the silver and gold, and the vessels of bronze and of iron, they put into the treasury of the house of the LORD.<sup>25</sup>But Rahab the prostitute and her father's household and all who belonged to her, Joshua saved alive. And she has lived in Israel to this day, because she hid the messengers whom Joshua sent to spy out Jericho.<sup>26</sup>Joshua laid an oath on them at that time, saying, "Cursed before the LORD be the man who rises up and rebuilds this city, Jericho. "At the cost of his firstborn shall he lay its foundation, and at the cost of his youngest son shall he set up its gates."<sup>27</sup>So the LORD was with Joshua, and his fame was in all the land.
6.overview:
Jericho was a fortress and Israel was given a plan with no military content in it at all: walk round the city once a day for six days, and on the seventh walk round seven times, blow, and shout. No ladders, no ram, no tunnel, no assault on the gate. The one thing this method guarantees is that when the wall comes down, nobody will be able to explain how, and that is the object of the exercise.

Then the wall falls flat, the city is devoted to destruction, and one household walks out alive. The hardest question in the book is raised by verse 21 and faced in the commentary on verses 17-19. The writer sets the judgment and the rescue side by side on purpose, and gives the last word to a Canaanite prostitute who, he says, has lived in Israel to this day (v. 25).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–7 — The Plan No General Would Write
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jericho is sealed (v. 1), and God's first word about it is in the past tense (v. 2). Then the instructions no military academy would pass (vv. 3-5), which Joshua relays exactly as given (vv. 6-7).
verseByVerse.theology: What is asked of Israel at Jericho is not strength, courage or tactics. It is a week of doing something that cannot possibly work.
verseByVerse.examples: Jericho falls not to the noise of an army but to the sound of Israel's worship, carried round the walls before the ark.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Jericho was shut up inside and outside because of the people of Israel. None went out, and none came in. And the LORD said to Joshua, "See, I have given Jericho into your hand, with its king and mighty men of valor.
verseByVerse.commentary: Two sentences describe the same city from two sides. From the ground, Jericho is in total lockdown. From heaven, it is already handed over, past tense as at 1:3, with the best troops in the city listed on the delivery note. Everything Jericho has done to protect itself is real and competent, and already a completed transaction in somebody else's favour. Walls keep out armies. They have never once kept out God.

verseByVerse.quote: You shall march around the city, all the men of war going around the city once. Thus shall you do for six days. Seven priests shall bear seven trumpets of rams' horns before the ark. On the seventh day you shall march around the city seven times, and the priests shall blow the trumpets. And when they make a long blast with the ram's horn, when you hear the sound of the trumpet, then all the people shall shout with a great shout, and the wall of the city will fall down flat, and the people shall go up, everyone straight before him."
verseByVerse.commentary:
No army in history has been given a plan like it. Paul, writing about God's habit of choosing what looks foolish to shame the wise, gives the reason: so that no human being might boast in the presence of God (1 Cor. 1:27-29). Jericho is that sentence acted out over a week.

Count the sevens: seven priests, seven trumpets, seven days, seven circuits on the last one. The Bible's number of completion is stamped over all of it: nothing here is improvised.

These are not war trumpets but rams' horns, the instrument of Israel's worship, and the Hebrew word behind them, yobel, is the word that gave the jubilee its name: the fiftieth year, announced on the Day of Atonement, when debts were cancelled, land went back to its families, and slaves went home (Lev. 25:9-10).

Whether the writer means us to hear the jubilee here is uncertain, and nothing should be built on it. What is certain is that the sound going round Jericho is a priestly sound before it is a military one, and that inside the city there is a woman with a red rope in her window for whom it will mean release.

The outcome is told in advance, including the manner: not breached but flattened.

verseByVerse.quote: So Joshua the son of Nun called the priests and said to them, "Take up the ark of the covenant and let seven priests bear seven trumpets of rams' horns before the ark of the LORD." And he said to the people, "Go forward. March around the city and let the armed men pass on before the ark of the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joshua passes the order on and changes nothing. A soldier who has fought since Rephidim is handed a plan with no military content, and there is no record of a question or a battering ram quietly kept at the back. A general who has been face down in a field (5:14) is not in a hurry to improve on the instructions.

The shape of the column matters: armed men first, then priests with horns, then the ark, then the rear guard. The soldiers are at the front and the back, and the ark is in the middle, which is exactly where it was in the riverbed. The presence of God is not out of harm's way behind the lines but in the centre of the formation, in full view of the walls.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The procession forms up (vv. 8-9) under Joshua's order of total silence (v. 10), walks round once and returns (v. 11), and does the same each day (vv. 12-14).
verseByVerse.theology: The wall is exactly as high on the sixth evening as it was on the first morning, and the only instruction is to come back tomorrow and do it again.
verseByVerse.examples: There are seasons when the faithful thing is to keep walking and say nothing back.

verseByVerse.quote: And just as Joshua had commanded the people, the seven priests bearing the seven trumpets of rams' horns before the LORD went forward, blowing the trumpets, with the ark of the covenant of the LORD following them. The armed men were walking before the priests who were blowing the trumpets, and the rear guard was walking after the ark, while the trumpets blew continually. But Joshua commanded the people, "You shall not shout or make your voice heard, neither shall any word go out of your mouth, until the day I tell you to shout. Then you shall shout." So he caused the ark of the LORD to circle the city, going about it once. And they came into the camp and spent the night in the camp.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The horns do not stop: the trumpets blew continually is repeated until the reader begins to hear it.

Joshua adds the order of silence himself, and it is the hardest part of the week: absolute silence. Thousands of men walk within earshot of a wall lined with defenders, and whatever may have been shouted down from the ramparts, no Israelite may answer it. The instinct when mocked is to reply, and the reply always feels like strength. Israel was ordered to walk past the insult with a closed mouth, on the grounds that the answer was coming on a day God had chosen and not before.

Day one ends with nothing. This is what obedience looked like on the first evening, and it looked like a wasted day.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Joshua rose early in the morning, and the priests took up the ark of the LORD. And the seven priests bearing the seven trumpets of rams' horns before the ark of the LORD walked on, and they blew the trumpets continually. And the armed men were walking before them, and the rear guard was walking after the ark of the LORD, while the trumpets blew continually. And the second day they marched around the city once, and returned into the camp. So they did for six days.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The writer repeats the formation for day two and then covers four more early mornings and four more evenings in one line. By the fourth day the defenders may well have started finding it funny. Israel had no way of explaining what they were doing, because the explanation was a sentence from God and nothing else.

This is the part of the chapter most Christians actually live in. The dramatic seventh day gets preached; the six days are where the years go — praying for the same person, turning up to the same duty, keeping the same promise, and seeing the wall unchanged. Six days of obedience with no visible result is not failure. It is what the seventh day is made of. They knew there would be a seventh; they did not know what it would bring. They walked on the word alone, and the God who gave the word keeps his people walking by his Spirit when their own resolve runs out (Gal. 6:9; Phil. 2:13).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–21 — The Wall Fell Down Flat
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Seven circuits on the seventh day (v. 15); the command to shout (v. 16) and the terms of the ban (vv. 17-19); the wall falls (v. 20), and verse 21 records what happened inside without softening.
verseByVerse.theology: The order of Joshua's sentence in verse 16 is the point of the chapter: not "shout, and the LORD will give you the city", but shout, FOR the LORD has given.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 18 plants a warning in the middle of a victory, and somebody in the crowd is already thinking about a Babylonian cloak.

verseByVerse.quote: On the seventh day they rose early, at the dawn of day, and marched around the city in the same manner seven times. It was only on that day that they marched around the city seven times. And at the seventh time, when the priests had blown the trumpets, Joshua said to the people, "Shout, for the LORD has given you the city.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seven circuits on foot, in armour, in the Jordan valley, is most of a day's work, and nothing on the ground suggests the last will differ from the others.

The silence of six days ends in one word, and the reason attached is the theology of the chapter: shout, FOR the LORD has given you the city. The gift comes first, in the perfect tense, exactly as in verse 2 and exactly as at 1:3. The shout is not the cause of anything. It is the response of people who have been told that a thing is already settled and are finally allowed to say so out loud.

We do not praise in order to be accepted; we praise because we have been. The shout comes after the giving, and it comes on the day God names.

verseByVerse.quote: And the city and all that is within it shall be devoted to the LORD for destruction. Only Rahab the prostitute and all who are with her in her house shall live, because she hid the messengers whom we sent. But you, keep yourselves from the things devoted to destruction, lest when you have devoted them you take any of the devoted things and make the camp of Israel a thing for destruction and bring trouble upon it. But all silver and gold, and every vessel of bronze and iron, are holy to the LORD; they shall go into the treasury of the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the hardest thing in the book, and it should be met head on rather than hurried past.

The word is herem, usually translated devoted to destruction. It means something handed over to God entirely, taken permanently out of ordinary use. Jericho is the first city in the land, the firstfruits of the conquest, and like every firstfruit it belongs to God rather than to the people. Nobody profits from this one. That is why no plunder may be taken.

Verse 21, four verses later, states what that meant on the ground without any softening at all: men and women, young and old. Children died at Jericho. Any treatment of this passage that does not say so plainly is not worth reading.

What the Bible itself puts around this, taken in order:

First, the timing was announced centuries in advance, and the reason given was mercy. God told Abraham his descendants would not receive this land for four generations, because the iniquity of the Amorites is not yet complete (Gen. 15:16). The delay was deliberate. Judgment came late, not early, and it came to a culture that by then was burning its own children in fire to Molech — which is the practice Scripture names, again and again, as the reason (Lev. 18:21-25; Deut. 12:31).

Second, and decisively, Israel is told at length that none of this is about their being better. Not because of your righteousness, says Moses, three times in three verses, for you are a stubborn people (Deut. 9:4-6). The land is said to vomit out its inhabitants for what they do, and Israel is warned in the same breath that it will vomit them out too if they do the same things (Lev. 18:26-28). That warning was kept. Some eight centuries later the same God brought the same judgment on Jerusalem through Babylon, and the prophets said so in advance and at length.

Third, the ban was never about ancestry, and this chapter is the proof. A Canaanite household walks out of Jericho alive. Not because of nationality or morality, both against her, but because she believed what she had heard of God and acted on it. The door out of the judgment was open, and one household went through it.

Fourth, this was a specific, dated, geographically limited command, and Scripture never treats it as a template. No prophet urges Israel to repeat it elsewhere; no apostle applies it to the church. The New Testament is explicit that the weapons of the Christian war are not of the flesh (2 Cor. 10:4), and anyone who has ever used Joshua to justify violence has had to ignore the entire New Testament to do it.

Does all that close the question? No. Verse 21 still says young and old, and no argument set out above makes that easy, and it should not be made to feel easy. The Westminster Confession (10.3) teaches that elect infants dying in infancy are saved by Christ; Scripture says no more about which children those are, and this commentary, with many Christians, trusts the Judge of all the earth to do right with every child (Gen. 18:25), a Judge more merciful than we are. And the God who did this is the same God who, in the same book, took a prostitute out of the condemned city and put her name in the family tree of his own Son.

Then a warning, dropped into the middle of the victory: take any of it, and the ban falls on you. The whole of the next chapter comes out of verse 18.

verseByVerse.quote: So the people shouted, and the trumpets were blown. As soon as the people heard the sound of the trumpet, the people shouted a great shout, and the wall fell down flat, so that the people went up into the city, every man straight before him, and they captured the city. Then they devoted all in the city to destruction, both men and women, young and old, oxen, sheep, and donkeys, with the edge of the sword.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A week of walking, and one sentence. The detail that matters is flat. The wall does not breach; it drops where it stands, so the whole circumference becomes the way in at once, and no fighting is recorded at the wall.

The letter to the Hebrews puts this on its list of what faith has done, and words it carefully: by faith the walls of Jericho fell down, after they had been encircled for seven days (Heb. 11:30). Not by shouting. By faith — and faith, in that verse, is thirteen laps of a city by people who had no idea what walking was supposed to achieve.

Verse 21 is written flatly and it is meant to be read that way. Nothing is celebrated here and nothing is described in detail; the writer states what was done and stops.

Jericho had heard for forty years what this God had done at the sea (2:10), as Rahab had, and one household acted on it.

Why kill the animals too? Under the ban everything was given wholly to God and none of it taken for Israel’s gain (vv. 17–19).

Was it just? The fuller answer is given on verses 17–19: a judgment on sin ripened over centuries, a unique command, and no pattern for any later war, nation or church, for Christ’s kingdom is not of this world (John 18:36).

Rahab’s house was in the wall (2:15). The wall fell; the text does not say how her house survived, but God evidently spared the part where she lived, and her family came out alive (vv. 22–23).

Does archaeology support the fall of Jericho? The evidence is disputed. Excavations at the site, Tell es-Sultan, in the 1950s concluded that the city had been destroyed long before Joshua and was hardly occupied in his day; a later reassessment of the pottery argued for a destruction, with fallen walls and burned stores of grain, around 1400 BC, which fits the earlier of the two dates believing scholars give for the exodus (about 1446 or about 1260 BC). Three thousand years of erosion on an exposed mound have removed much. Honestly put, the digging neither proves nor disproves the account; Christians receive it as history because Scripture does (Heb. 11:30), and stay open to what further work may show.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 22–27 — Rahab Brought Out, and the City Cursed
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The spies keep their oath and bring Rahab's household out (vv. 22-23); the city is burned (v. 24) and she lives in Israel (v. 25); Jericho is cursed (v. 26), and the chapter ends where chapter 1 began (v. 27).
verseByVerse.theology: The one household that walked out of that city alive is not a footnote to the judgment; it is the writer's comment on it.
verseByVerse.examples: Jericho was left a ruin as a monument, so that every traveller on that road could see how the conquest began: by God's hand, not Israel's.

verseByVerse.quote: But to the two men who had spied out the land, Joshua said, "Go into the prostitute's house and bring out from there the woman and all who belong to her, as you swore to her." So the young men who had been spies went in and brought out Rahab and her father and mother and brothers and all who belonged to her. And they brought all her relatives and put them outside the camp of Israel. And they burned the city with fire, and everything in it. Only the silver and gold, and the vessels of bronze and of iron, they put into the treasury of the house of the LORD. But Rahab the prostitute and her father's household and all who belonged to her, Joshua saved alive. And she has lived in Israel to this day, because she hid the messengers whom Joshua sent to spy out Jericho.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The city is coming down and Joshua stops to keep somebody else's promise: two soldiers swore their lives away on a roof, and their commander treats that oath as binding on the whole nation. Every name she asked for is read back as a list of survivors.

The last clause of verse 23 is honest about the awkwardness: outside the camp. A Canaanite family at the edge of Israel, ceremonially unclean, alive but not yet belonging. Grace got them out of the fire before it got them a tent.

Outside the camp is not where the story ends. She has lived in Israel to this day: whether the writer means Rahab herself, still alive when he wrote, or her family after her depends on when the book was written, and that is uncertain. Either way, she ended inside the nation.

The narrator keeps calling her the prostitute to the last line, not from cruelty but refusing to tidy up the person grace actually saved, as Matthew does when he writes her into the genealogy of Jesus (Matt. 1:5), so that the Redeemer of Israel has a Canaanite in his family tree and the record says out loud what she used to be.

verseByVerse.quote: Joshua laid an oath on them at that time, saying, "Cursed before the LORD be the man who rises up and rebuilds this city, Jericho. "At the cost of his firstborn shall he lay its foundation, and at the cost of his youngest son shall he set up its gates." So the LORD was with Joshua, and his fame was in all the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Jericho is to stay down, and the curse was not rhetoric. Centuries later, in the reign of Ahab, a man called Hiel of Bethel rebuilt the city, and the historian records the price in one grim sentence: he laid its foundation at the cost of Abiram his firstborn and set up its gates at the cost of his youngest son Segub, according to the word of the LORD, which he spoke by Joshua the son of Nun (1 Kings 16:34).

The chapter closes on the promises of 1:5 and 3:7, signed off in a single line. Joshua had done nothing a soldier would put on a record; his reputation is entirely the visible edge of somebody else's presence.

The Commander with the drawn sword took a fortified city without Israel drawing a blade. He did it slowly, in daylight, to the sound of rams' horns, and carried out of the ruin only a household that had believed him. That is the shape of the judgment the New Testament still announces: a day fixed, a trumpet sounding (1 Thess. 4:16), and a door held open until then for anyone who will trust the greater Joshua, Jesus, who carries his people safely through the judgment because he bore it for them (Rom. 5:9).
verseByVerse.note: The site was not left wholly empty meanwhile (18:21; Judg. 3:13); the curse fell on rebuilding it as a fortified city.

6.theology:
The gift comes before the shout. The city is handed over in the perfect tense before anything happens (vv. 2, 16). Every act of Christian obedience has that grammar.

The six days. The faith Hebrews commends is not the shout on the last morning but the walking on the first six, when nothing whatever happened. Obedience without visible result is not a failure of faith; it is most of what faith consists of.

The ban, faced honestly. Verse 21 says men and women, young and old. The commentary on verses 17–19 sets out what Scripture puts around it, and admits that none of it closes the question.

Judgment and mercy in the same morning. The writer sets them side by side without comment: a city devoted to destruction, and a household walked out of it (v. 25). Grace in this chapter is not a softening of the judgment. It is a door held open in the middle of it.
6.examples: Jericho was promised to Israel, on a named day. God has not promised that the wall in your marriage or your prayers will fall on a timetable. He has promised to be with his people, that labour in the Lord is not in vain (1 Cor. 15:58), and that in Christ they will enter the inheritance Joshua's victory pointed to. So keep walking in the six days. And if you stopped walking long ago, the way back is not to make up the lost laps but to return to the Lord, who runs to meet those who come home (Luke 15:20).

7.title: Achan's Sin and the Defeat at Ai
7.text: <sup>1</sup>But the people of Israel broke faith in regard to the devoted things, for Achan the son of Carmi, son of Zabdi, son of Zerah, of the tribe of Judah, took some of the devoted things. And the anger of the LORD burned against the people of Israel.<sup>2</sup>Joshua sent men from Jericho to Ai, which is near Beth-aven, east of Bethel, and said to them, "Go up and spy out the land." And the men went up and spied out Ai.<sup>3</sup>And they returned to Joshua and said to him, "Do not have all the people go up, but let about two or three thousand men go up and attack Ai. Do not make the whole people toil up there, for they are few."<sup>4</sup>So about three thousand men went up there from the people. And they fled before the men of Ai,<sup>5</sup>and the men of Ai killed about thirty-six of their men and chased them before the gate as far as Shebarim and struck them at the descent. And the hearts of the people melted and became as water.<sup>6</sup>Then Joshua tore his clothes and fell to the earth on his face before the ark of the LORD until the evening, he and the elders of Israel. And they put dust on their heads.<sup>7</sup>And Joshua said, "Alas, O Lord GOD, why have you brought this people over the Jordan at all, to give us into the hands of the Amorites, to destroy us? Would that we had been content to dwell beyond the Jordan!<sup>8</sup>O Lord, what can I say, when Israel has turned their backs before their enemies!<sup>9</sup>For the Canaanites and all the inhabitants of the land will hear of it and will surround us and cut off our name from the earth. And what will you do for your great name?"<sup>10</sup>The LORD said to Joshua, "Get up! Why have you fallen on your face?<sup>11</sup>Israel has sinned; they have transgressed my covenant that I commanded them; they have taken some of the devoted things; they have stolen and lied and put them among their own belongings.<sup>12</sup>Therefore the people of Israel cannot stand before their enemies. They turn their backs before their enemies, because they have become devoted for destruction. I will be with you no more, unless you destroy the devoted things from among you.<sup>13</sup>Get up! Consecrate the people and say, 'Consecrate yourselves for tomorrow; for thus says the LORD, God of Israel, "There are devoted things in your midst, O Israel. You cannot stand before your enemies until you take away the devoted things from among you."<sup>14</sup>In the morning therefore you shall be brought near by your tribes. And the tribe that the LORD takes by lot shall come near by clans. And the clan that the LORD takes shall come near by households. And the household that the LORD takes shall come near man by man.<sup>15</sup>And he who is taken with the devoted things shall be burned with fire, he and all that he has, because he has transgressed the covenant of the LORD, and because he has done an outrageous thing in Israel.'"<sup>16</sup>So Joshua rose early in the morning and brought Israel near tribe by tribe, and the tribe of Judah was taken.<sup>17</sup>And he brought near the clans of Judah, and the clan of the Zerahites was taken. And he brought near the clan of the Zerahites man by man, and Zabdi was taken.<sup>18</sup>And he brought near his household man by man, and Achan the son of Carmi, son of Zabdi, son of Zerah, of the tribe of Judah, was taken.<sup>19</sup>Then Joshua said to Achan, "My son, give glory to the LORD God of Israel and give praise to him. And tell me now what you have done; do not hide it from me."<sup>20</sup>And Achan answered Joshua, "Truly I have sinned against the LORD God of Israel, and this is what I did:<sup>21</sup>when I saw among the spoil a beautiful cloak from Shinar, and 200 shekels of silver, and a bar of gold weighing 50 shekels, then I coveted them and took them. And see, they are hidden in the earth inside my tent, with the silver underneath."<sup>22</sup>So Joshua sent messengers, and they ran to the tent; and behold, it was hidden in his tent with the silver underneath.<sup>23</sup>And they took them out of the tent and brought them to Joshua and to all the people of Israel. And they laid them down before the LORD.<sup>24</sup>And Joshua and all Israel with him took Achan the son of Zerah, and the silver and the cloak and the bar of gold, and his sons and daughters and his oxen and donkeys and sheep and his tent and all that he had. And they brought them up to the Valley of Achor.<sup>25</sup>And Joshua said, "Why did you bring trouble on us? The LORD brings trouble on you today." And all Israel stoned him with stones. They burned them with fire and stoned them with stones.<sup>26</sup>And they raised over him a great heap of stones that remains to this day. Then the LORD turned from his burning anger. Therefore, to this day the name of that place is called the Valley of Achor.
7.overview:
The chapter turns on its first word: but. Jericho has fallen and Joshua's fame fills the land, and then one man reaches into a burning city and takes a coat, and God is angry with a nation that does not know it has done anything.

What follows is a defeat, a day of prayer, a slow search through the tribes, a confession, and a grave in a valley named Trouble.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel is charged for Achan's sin, and nobody in the camp knows it (v. 1). Scouts recommend a small force for Ai (vv. 2-3); three thousand go and run (v. 4); thirty-six die, and Israel's heart melts (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: Yesterday's victory had become this morning's assumption, and the hidden sin was doing its work unseen.
verseByVerse.examples: Success is often more dangerous to faith than failure, because it makes asking God feel unnecessary.

verseByVerse.quote: But the people of Israel broke faith in regard to the devoted things, for Achan the son of Carmi, son of Zabdi, son of Zerah, of the tribe of Judah, took some of the devoted things. And the anger of the LORD burned against the people of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One word turns the book over: but. The last chapter ended with Joshua's fame filling the land. This one begins with God angry.

The grammar is deliberate: the subject of the sentence is the people of Israel, and the subject of the crime is Achan. The devoted things were the goods of Jericho handed over wholly to God (the Hebrew word is herem), to be destroyed or given to his treasury (6:17-19).

That offends a modern reader immediately, and it should be met rather than smoothed over. We think of ourselves as separate units who are responsible for our own actions and nobody else's. Scripture consistently does not. A family, a church, a nation is treated as a body, and what one member does gets into all of it — which is precisely why the whole Bible can turn on two men, so that in Adam all die and in Christ all are made alive (1 Cor. 15:22).

The cases are not the same, for Achan was not Israel's head as Adam is ours and Christ is his people's. But the principle that people are bound together, so that one person's act reaches those who belong with him, is the same one; and if it were simply unjust, no one could be saved by one man's obedience (Romans 5:19).

Note also that the writer gives Achan's full pedigree — son of Carmi, son of Zabdi, son of Zerah — three generations, before anything else about him. He is not an anonymous thief. He is somebody's son and somebody's grandson, from the tribe of Judah, and every one of those names will matter before the chapter is finished.

Nobody knows. Israel wakes up the next morning under the anger of God, and the whole camp is entirely unaware of it.

verseByVerse.quote: Joshua sent men from Jericho to Ai, which is near Beth-aven, east of Bethel, and said to them, "Go up and spy out the land." And the men went up and spied out Ai. And they returned to Joshua and said to him, "Do not have all the people go up, but let about two or three thousand men go up and attack Ai. Do not make the whole people toil up there, for they are few." So about three thousand men went up there from the people. And they fled before the men of Ai, and the men of Ai killed about thirty-six of their men and chased them before the gate as far as Shebarim and struck them at the descent. And the hearts of the people melted and became as water.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The reconnaissance is competent; any staff officer would have written the same report. What is missing is the whole of chapter 6: nobody asks God anything. At Jericho every detail came from outside; here the plan is assembled by men looking at a hill and doing arithmetic. It is not rebellion. It is something more ordinary and far more common: a victory so complete that praying about the next one felt unnecessary.

The phrase for they are few is the giveaway. Israel has started counting the enemy. The week before, the size of the opposition had been the least relevant fact on the field.

Thirty-six men. It is a small number for a battle and an enormous number for this book, because until now Israel has not lost a single soldier. Somebody had to carry that news back into thirty-six houses.

They died for a sin they did not commit and never heard about. That is the ugliest fact in the chapter and the writer does not soften it: this is what hidden sin does, and it does not stop at the person who committed it.

Then the last sentence, and it is an echo. The hearts of the people melted and became as water recalls what Rahab said about her own city (2:11) and what happened to the kings of Canaan when they heard about the Jordan (5:1). Israel has caught the enemy's condition. The terror that had been fighting on their side has changed ends.

Where was Ai? It is usually identified with et-Tell, which seems to have been unoccupied in Joshua’s time; others identify it with a nearby site such as Khirbet el-Maqatir, where remains of a fortress of the right period have been found. The question is open, and it does not touch the truth of the account.
verseByVerse.note: Ai means “the ruin.”

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Joshua lies before the ark all day (v. 6) and prays no polished prayer (vv. 7-8), until he reaches its best argument (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: Joshua's prayer begins badly and ends well, and Scripture prints both halves.
verseByVerse.examples: Under enough pressure a believer can find himself saying the very thing he once stood against. God does not cast him off for it; he answers, and sets him on his feet.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Joshua tore his clothes and fell to the earth on his face before the ark of the LORD until the evening, he and the elders of Israel. And they put dust on their heads. And Joshua said, "Alas, O Lord GOD, why have you brought this people over the Jordan at all, to give us into the hands of the Amorites, to destroy us? Would that we had been content to dwell beyond the Jordan! O Lord, what can I say, when Israel has turned their backs before their enemies! For the Canaanites and all the inhabitants of the land will hear of it and will surround us and cut off our name from the earth. And what will you do for your great name?"
verseByVerse.commentary:
He holds the posture of a funeral from morning to evening. And this is not a good prayer, yet Scripture prints it: you brought us over here to destroy us. Those are almost exactly the words of the wilderness generation at Kadesh — why is the LORD bringing us into this land to fall by the sword?... Would it not be better for us to go back to Egypt? (Num. 14:2-3). Joshua had stood up in front of that crowd and contradicted them, and nearly been stoned for it.

Forty years later, one bad afternoon, and the man who opposed the complaint is making it. There is no comment from the narrator and no rebuke from God about this part; Scripture records it without excusing it or condemning him for it.

Then the prayer turns. Joshua does not say Israel deserves better; he has just watched thirty-six men die and has no idea why. He says: your reputation is attached to this. It is exactly how Moses prayed when God offered to destroy the nation and start again — not a word about Israel's merits, only why should the Egyptians say... (Ex. 32:12; Num. 14:13-16).

That is the one plea in prayer that does not depend on the person making it. A believer with nothing to say for himself can still say: your name is on this, and I am asking for your sake and not mine.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God's first word is Get up (v. 10). The diagnosis comes in four verbs (v. 11), then the sentence that empties the conquest of its ground (v. 12), and the remedy: consecration and a slow public process (vv. 13-15).
verseByVerse.theology: The presence of God has been the whole argument of the book since 1:5. Verse 12 says it can be withdrawn, and names the condition. Sin in the camp does not merely displease God; it removes the one thing Israel had going for it.
verseByVerse.examples: When God puts his finger on a hidden sin, it is not to crush us but to free the whole household of faith, and the way out is the way Joshua points: tell the truth.

verseByVerse.quote: The LORD said to Joshua, "Get up! Why have you fallen on your face? Israel has sinned; they have transgressed my covenant that I commanded them; they have taken some of the devoted things; they have stolen and lied and put them among their own belongings. Therefore the people of Israel cannot stand before their enemies. They turn their backs before their enemies, because they have become devoted for destruction. I will be with you no more, unless you destroy the devoted things from among you. Get up! Consecrate the people and say, 'Consecrate yourselves for tomorrow; for thus says the LORD, God of Israel, "There are devoted things in your midst, O Israel. You cannot stand before your enemies until you take away the devoted things from among you." In the morning therefore you shall be brought near by your tribes. And the tribe that the LORD takes by lot shall come near by clans. And the clan that the LORD takes shall come near by households. And the household that the LORD takes shall come near man by man. And he who is taken with the devoted things shall be burned with fire, he and all that he has, because he has transgressed the covenant of the LORD, and because he has done an outrageous thing in Israel.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
God's first word to a man who has been praying all day is to stop.

That deserves attention, because prayer is not usually the thing that needs interrupting. But there is a kind of praying that is a substitute for obedience — agonising before God about a situation he has already told us how to fix, or has been trying to. Joshua is asking why God has abandoned Israel. God's answer is that nobody has abandoned anybody, and there is a man in the camp with stolen property under his tent.

Four verbs, and they are a descent. Taken is the act. Stolen names what kind of act it was. Lied is what had to happen next, because Achan has been walking around the camp for days behaving normally. And put them among their own belongings is the settled state: the thing is in the tent now, and life has arranged itself around it.

Verse 12 is one of the most frightening sentences in the book. Everything since chapter 1 has rested on one promise: I will be with you. Here God says it is conditional, and states the condition.

He does not say Israel will be forgiven when they feel worse about it. He says the devoted thing has to go. There is no route round the object itself, and a great deal of religious distress is the attempt to find one — genuine grief, genuine prayer, genuine resolve, and the thing still under the floor of the tent.

The detection is deliberately slow. God knew the name on the first day; instead the lot walks toward Achan in four public stages, over a morning, in front of everybody. Four times he watches it come nearer, and four times he could have stood up. The machinery that exposes him is also, right up to the last moment, an invitation.

“I will be with you no more” (v. 12): does this contradict 1:5? God’s promise to fight for Israel as a nation depended on its faithfulness, and the nation could forfeit his help in battle. That is different from the bond with each believer in Christ, who promises I will never leave you nor forsake you (Heb 13:5). A Christian can grieve the Spirit and lose the sense of God’s help, but not lose God.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–21 — I Saw, I Coveted, I Took, I Hid
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The lot narrows to Achan (vv. 16-18); Joshua speaks to him gently (v. 19); and Achan confesses in a sequence of four verbs (vv. 20-21).
verseByVerse.theology: Achan's four verbs, saw, coveted, took, hid, are the oldest sequence in the Bible.
verseByVerse.examples: What we hide is usually small. Its smallness is what makes it easy to keep, and costly to everyone near us.

verseByVerse.quote: So Joshua rose early in the morning and brought Israel near tribe by tribe, and the tribe of Judah was taken. And he brought near the clans of Judah, and the clan of the Zerahites was taken. And he brought near the clan of the Zerahites man by man, and Zabdi was taken. And he brought near his household man by man, and Achan the son of Carmi, son of Zabdi, son of Zerah, of the tribe of Judah, was taken. Then Joshua said to Achan, "My son, give glory to the LORD God of Israel and give praise to him. And tell me now what you have done; do not hide it from me." And Achan answered Joshua, "Truly I have sinned against the LORD God of Israel, and this is what I did: when I saw among the spoil a beautiful cloak from Shinar, and 200 shekels of silver, and a bar of gold weighing 50 shekels, then I coveted them and took them. And see, they are hidden in the earth inside my tent, with the silver underneath."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The pedigree from verse 1 is read out again in public. The tribe is Judah: the royal tribe, the one Jacob had blessed with the sceptre, the tribe the Messiah would come from. The first recorded sin in the promised land is committed by a man of the line that produces the King.

Joshua's first two words are the surprise of the chapter. My son. He is speaking to a man who has cost thirty-six lives and is about to be executed, and he addresses him the way a father would.

Then the framing he gives to confession: telling the truth is giving glory to God. Not clearing the record, or making things easier, or getting it off his chest. To confess is to agree with God about what happened, which is a way of honouring him — and it means the last useful thing Achan can do in his life is available to him. Whether his confession was the repentance that brings life, Scripture does not say; it was at least true, and the God who heard a dying thief (Luke 23:42-43) can be trusted with him.

Four more verbs, and every one of us has used them in that order: I saw, I coveted, I took, I hid. It is Eve at the tree, who saw, took, and then hid (Gen. 3:6-8); it is David on a roof; and it is James's account of how sin gestates: desire conceives, gives birth to sin, and sin grown up brings forth death (James 1:15).

The inventory is pitifully small. A coat. Five pounds of silver. A bar of gold he could hold in one hand. For that, thirty-six men are dead and his own family is finished.

The coat came from Shinar. That is the plain where men once said come, let us build ourselves a city and a tower (Gen. 11:2-4); it is the Bible's name for Babylon. In the first week of the conquest, a man of Judah smuggled a piece of Babylon into the camp of God and buried it under the place where he slept.
verseByVerse.note: A shekel was about 2/5 ounce: Achan took about 5 pounds of silver and over a pound of gold.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The goods are found and laid before the LORD (vv. 22-23); Achan and all he has are taken to a valley and the sentence is carried out (vv. 24-25); a heap of stones is raised and the valley named Trouble (v. 26).
verseByVerse.theology: Judgment is carried out in the open and before God, and the valley's name keeps the memory.
verseByVerse.examples: No one reading this is beyond the reach of the God who turns valleys of trouble into doors of hope.

verseByVerse.quote: So Joshua sent messengers, and they ran to the tent; and behold, it was hidden in his tent with the silver underneath. And they took them out of the tent and brought them to Joshua and to all the people of Israel. And they laid them down before the LORD. And Joshua and all Israel with him took Achan the son of Zerah, and the silver and the cloak and the bar of gold, and his sons and daughters and his oxen and donkeys and sheep and his tent and all that he had. And they brought them up to the Valley of Achor. And Joshua said, "Why did you bring trouble on us? The LORD brings trouble on you today." And all Israel stoned him with stones. They burned them with fire and stoned them with stones. And they raised over him a great heap of stones that remains to this day. Then the LORD turned from his burning anger. Therefore, to this day the name of that place is called the Valley of Achor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They run, and what was buried in the dark under a man's bed is dug up, carried across the camp, and spread out on the ground in the open, in front of everybody, before God.

That is what happens to everything eventually. Nothing is covered up that will not be revealed, or hidden that will not be known (Luke 12:2). The only question about any concealed thing is whether it is brought into the light by confession or by exposure.

The list in verse 24 is long and it is meant to be. Everything he owned, everything he took, and everyone he loved goes up that valley with him.

The death of his children is the second hard thing in this book, and it should not be managed. Two things can honestly be said and neither closes the matter. The goods were buried under the family tent, in a dwelling shared by a household, which makes it difficult to believe that nobody knew — and Israel's own law forbids putting children to death for their fathers' sins (Deut. 24:16), which means the reader who finds this troubling is standing on ground the Old Testament itself provides. The text does not spell out what the family knew; the likeliest reading, given below, is that they shared the concealment, but it should be held with care rather than used to make the scene feel easy.

There are two monuments in the land now: one at Gilgal where a river opened, and this one over a man buried under the rocks, and the writer says to this day about both. The name Trouble is the last word of the chapter, but not the last word about the valley. Hosea, describing how God will win back an unfaithful nation, speaks tenderly to her in the wilderness and then promises and make the Valley of Achor a door of hope (Hos. 2:15).

The valley of trouble is issued as a doorway. God takes the name of the worst place in Israel's early history — a heap of stones over a thief, the site of a nation's shame — and hands it back as the entrance to the future. That is not sentiment; it is what he does. Centuries later he took the instrument of a criminal's execution and made it the sign under which the world is saved. Achan, of the tribe of Judah, brought trouble on Israel and died under it for his own sin. Another son of Judah would take his people's trouble on himself and die for sins that were not his (2 Corinthians 5:21), so that the valley of trouble could become a door of hope.

Why were Achan’s children put to death with him? Some think only Achan was stoned and his goods destroyed. But the stolen goods were buried in the family tent, which suggests his household shared the theft and the concealment. The likeliest reading is that they were complicit, so the law that children must not die for a father’s sin (Deut 24:16) was not broken.
verseByVerse.note: “Achor” means “trouble” (ESV note).

7.theology:
Sin is never private. God treats a body as a body: a church, a family, a nation is not a collection of separate units whose choices stay inside them. The doctrine that offends here is the same doctrine that saves at Romans 5.

Yesterday's victory is not today's permission. Nobody in verses 2-3 does anything wicked. Presumption in this chapter is not arrogance; it is the quiet assumption that God's involvement can be inferred from the last time.

The condition on the promise. Verse 12 attaches a condition to the promise of 1:5, and no amount of prayer substitutes for dealing with the thing itself.

The Valley of Trouble as a door of hope. The place of a nation's shame becomes, in Hosea, the way back in (Hos. 2:15), as the cross later became the sign of salvation.
7.examples: Achan buried a coat and some silver under his tent, and nothing happened to him for days while others paid for it. The four verbs run in order and each one is small, and most of us are somewhere in that sequence about something. The counsel is not to feel worse but to dig the thing up, and we can, because the trouble it deserves has already fallen on Christ, who obeyed where we took and hid. Bring it into the light: If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins (1 John 1:9), and his Spirit gives the strength to put away what we have been hiding. The word spoken to the confessing sinner is my son.

8.title: Ai Defeated and Covenant Renewal at Mount Ebal
8.text: <sup>1</sup>And the LORD said to Joshua, "Do not fear and do not be dismayed. Take all the fighting men with you, and arise, go up to Ai. See, I have given into your hand the king of Ai, and his people, his city, and his land.<sup>2</sup>And you shall do to Ai and its king as you did to Jericho and its king. Only its spoil and its livestock you shall take as plunder for yourselves. Lay an ambush against the city, behind it."<sup>3</sup>So Joshua and all the fighting men arose to go up to Ai. And Joshua chose 30,000 mighty men of valor and sent them out by night.<sup>4</sup>And he commanded them, "Behold, you shall lie in ambush against the city, behind it. Do not go very far from the city, but all of you remain ready.<sup>5</sup>And I and all the people who are with me will approach the city. And when they come out against us just as before, we shall flee before them.<sup>6</sup>And they will come out after us, until we have drawn them away from the city. For they will say, 'They are fleeing from us, just as before.' So we will flee before them.<sup>7</sup>Then you shall rise up from the ambush and seize the city, for the LORD your God will give it into your hand.<sup>8</sup>And as soon as you have taken the city, you shall set the city on fire. You shall do according to the word of the LORD. See, I have commanded you."<sup>9</sup>So Joshua sent them out. And they went to the place of ambush and lay between Bethel and Ai, to the west of Ai, but Joshua spent that night among the people.<sup>10</sup>Joshua arose early in the morning and mustered the people and went up, he and the elders of Israel, before the people to Ai.<sup>11</sup>And all the fighting men who were with him went up and drew near before the city and encamped on the north side of Ai, with a ravine between them and Ai.<sup>12</sup>He took about 5,000 men and set them in ambush between Bethel and Ai, to the west of the city.<sup>13</sup>So they stationed the forces, the main encampment that was north of the city and its rear guard west of the city. But Joshua spent that night in the valley.<sup>14</sup>And as soon as the king of Ai saw this, he and all his people, the men of the city, hurried and went out early to the appointed place toward the Arabah to meet Israel in battle. But he did not know that there was an ambush against him behind the city.<sup>15</sup>And Joshua and all Israel pretended to be beaten before them and fled in the direction of the wilderness.<sup>16</sup>So all the people who were in the city were called together to pursue them, and as they pursued Joshua they were drawn away from the city.<sup>17</sup>Not a man was left in Ai or Bethel who did not go out after Israel. They left the city open and pursued Israel.<sup>18</sup>Then the LORD said to Joshua, "Stretch out the javelin that is in your hand toward Ai, for I will give it into your hand."
