And Joshua stretched out the javelin that was in his hand toward the city.<sup>19</sup>And the men in the ambush rose quickly out of their place, and as soon as he had stretched out his hand, they ran and entered the city and captured it. And they hurried to set the city on fire.<sup>20</sup>So when the men of Ai looked back, behold, the smoke of the city went up to heaven, and they had no power to flee this way or that, for the people who fled to the wilderness turned back against the pursuers.<sup>21</sup>And when Joshua and all Israel saw that the ambush had captured the city, and that the smoke of the city went up, then they turned back and struck down the men of Ai.<sup>22</sup>And the others came out from the city against them, so they were in the midst of Israel, some on this side, and some on that side. And Israel struck them down, until there was left none that survived or escaped.<sup>23</sup>But the king of Ai they took alive, and brought him near to Joshua.<sup>24</sup>When Israel had finished killing all the inhabitants of Ai in the open wilderness where they pursued them, and all of them to the very last had fallen by the edge of the sword, all Israel returned to Ai and struck it down with the edge of the sword.<sup>25</sup>And all who fell that day, both men and women, were 12,000, all the people of Ai.<sup>26</sup>But Joshua did not draw back his hand with which he stretched out the javelin until he had devoted all the inhabitants of Ai to destruction.<sup>27</sup>Only the livestock and the spoil of that city Israel took as their plunder, according to the word of the LORD that he commanded Joshua.<sup>28</sup>So Joshua burned Ai and made it forever a heap of ruins, as it is to this day.<sup>29</sup>And he hanged the king of Ai on a tree until evening. And at sunset Joshua commanded, and they took his body down from the tree and threw it at the entrance of the gate of the city and raised over it a great heap of stones, which stands there to this day.<sup>30</sup>At that time Joshua built an altar to the LORD, the God of Israel, on Mount Ebal,<sup>31</sup>just as Moses the servant of the LORD had commanded the people of Israel, as it is written in the Book of the Law of Moses, "an altar of uncut stones, upon which no man has wielded an iron tool." And they offered on it burnt offerings to the LORD and sacrificed peace offerings.<sup>32</sup>And there, in the presence of the people of Israel, he wrote on the stones a copy of the law of Moses, which he had written.<sup>33</sup>And all Israel, sojourner as well as native born, with their elders and officers and their judges, stood on opposite sides of the ark before the Levitical priests who carried the ark of the covenant of the LORD, half of them in front of Mount Gerizim and half of them in front of Mount Ebal, just as Moses the servant of the LORD had commanded at the first, to bless the people of Israel.<sup>34</sup>And afterward he read all the words of the law, the blessing and the curse, according to all that is written in the Book of the Law.<sup>35</sup>There was not a word of all that Moses commanded that Joshua did not read before all the assembly of Israel, and the women, and the little ones, and the sojourners who lived among them.
8.overview:
God speaks first, before Joshua asks, and gives back the words of the original commission almost unaltered (v. 1; cf. 1:9). There is no probation and there are no reduced terms. Two things are corrected without a word of reproach: take the whole army this time, and keep the plunder of this city, which one week earlier a man died for taking.

Ai falls to an ambush that God himself ordered (v. 2), and the bait in the trap is Israel's own humiliation: the plan depends on Ai believing that Israel will run, because Israel ran last time.

Then the campaign stops, and the nation marches twenty miles north into unconquered country to build an altar on Mount Ebal, write the law on stones, and hear every word of it read aloud — women, children and foreigners standing in the valley with everyone else. The first structure Israel builds in the promised land is not a fort. It is an altar, on the mountain of the curse.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–2 — The Same Words, After the Failure
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God speaks first and renews the commission to a man who has spent a day face down in the dust (v. 1). Two things are then corrected. Take all the fighting men, not a detachment of three thousand; and the spoil of this city, unlike Jericho's, may be kept (v. 2). With them comes an instruction no one expected in this book: lay an ambush.
verseByVerse.theology: The words of chapter 1 are given back almost unaltered. God does not re-commission a chastened man on reduced terms or with a warning attached; the sentence he had used before the failure is the sentence he uses after it.
verseByVerse.examples: In everyday life, this guards against two opposite mistakes. One is to turn a particular no from God into a permanent law for every case; the other is to think that because God later says yes, his earlier no did not matter. Achan's sin and Israel's freedom here rest on the same thing: what God has actually said.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Joshua, "Do not fear and do not be dismayed. Take all the fighting men with you, and arise, go up to Ai. See, I have given into your hand the king of Ai, and his people, his city, and his land. And you shall do to Ai and its king as you did to Jericho and its king. Only its spoil and its livestock you shall take as plunder for yourselves. Lay an ambush against the city, behind it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joshua has not asked. After Achan, after thirty-six funerals, after a day face down in the dirt, God opens the conversation, and do not fear and do not be dismayed is almost verbatim from the original commission (1:9). The promise was never resting on Joshua's record, so Joshua's record has not altered it.

Two corrections are folded in without a syllable of reproach. Take all the fighting men — last time three thousand went, because the scouts had done the arithmetic. And I have given into your hand, the perfect tense again, exactly as at Jericho.

Then a permission that ought to stop the reader cold: take the plunder. A week ago a man was executed for taking a coat and some silver from a captured city. The difference was never the goods, as if wealth were unclean. Jericho was the firstfruits and belonged wholly to God; Ai is given away. The only thing that changed between the two cities is what God said, and Achan died because he decided that a command about property was a suggestion.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Joshua takes thirty thousand men and sends them out at night to lie in ambush west of the city, with orders to stay close and stay ready (vv. 3-4). The main force will advance, be beaten, and run — because the men of Ai will say they are fleeing from us, just as before (vv. 5-6). When the city is empty the ambush is to take it and burn it (vv. 7-8). The trap is laid overnight (v. 9), the army musters at dawn and camps north of Ai with a ravine between (vv. 10-11), a further five thousand are positioned to the west (v. 12), and Joshua spends the night in the valley (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology: Jericho fell to a shout and no tactics at all. Ai falls to reconnaissance, a night march, a concealed force and a feigned retreat, and God is the one who says lay an ambush. Both victories are entirely his. What changes is the instrument, and nothing in this book lets a reader turn either method into a rule.
verseByVerse.examples: The bait is Israel's own humiliation. The plan works precisely because Ai has beaten them once and will believe it is happening again — just as before. The defeat that shamed the nation a chapter ago is the thing God uses to take the city.

verseByVerse.quote: So Joshua and all the fighting men arose to go up to Ai. And Joshua chose 30,000 mighty men of valor and sent them out by night. And he commanded them, "Behold, you shall lie in ambush against the city, behind it. Do not go very far from the city, but all of you remain ready. And I and all the people who are with me will approach the city. And when they come out against us just as before, we shall flee before them. And they will come out after us, until we have drawn them away from the city. For they will say, 'They are fleeing from us, just as before.' So we will flee before them. Then you shall rise up from the ambush and seize the city, for the LORD your God will give it into your hand. And as soon as you have taken the city, you shall set the city on fire. You shall do according to the word of the LORD. See, I have commanded you." So Joshua sent them out. And they went to the place of ambush and lay between Bethel and Ai, to the west of Ai, but Joshua spent that night among the people.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Here there is a night march, a concealed force, a decoy, a feigned retreat, a signal and a coordinated turn: competent soldiering. This is not Joshua reverting to human wisdom after the miracle ran out; the ambush is as much a divine instruction as the trumpets were.

Where did Joshua spend the night? Among the people. The commander does not withdraw to a tent to wait. He sleeps in the camp with the men who will be doing the running in the morning.

verseByVerse.quote: Joshua arose early in the morning and mustered the people and went up, he and the elders of Israel, before the people to Ai. And all the fighting men who were with him went up and drew near before the city and encamped on the north side of Ai, with a ravine between them and Ai. He took about 5,000 men and set them in ambush between Bethel and Ai, to the west of the city. So they stationed the forces, the main encampment that was north of the city and its rear guard west of the city. But Joshua spent that night in the valley.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Up early again, the fifth time the writer has mentioned it (3:1; 6:12, 15; 7:16): a man who does not lie in bed on the morning of an obedience. Israel camps in plain view across a ravine, where the whole city can count them, while a second detachment west of the city also blocks the road from Bethel.

Is this five thousand the same ambush as the thirty thousand of verse 3? Some think there were two forces, a large one sent by night and a smaller one placed later; others think one of the figures has suffered in copying, or that thousand here means a military unit rather than an exact count. The text can bear more than one reading, and nothing in the story depends on settling it.

Once more Joshua sleeps in the valley: not behind the lines, but on the low ground between two armies, the night before a battle in which he personally is the decoy.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The king of Ai sees the army and hurries out early, and the narrator adds the sentence the whole plan rests on: he did not know that there was an ambush against him behind the city (v. 14). Israel pretends to be beaten and runs for the wilderness (v. 15), and every fighting man in Ai and Bethel goes after them, leaving the city open (vv. 16-17). Then God tells Joshua to stretch out his javelin, the hidden force rises, takes the city and sets it alight (vv. 18-19). The men of Ai look back and see the smoke, and the army they were chasing turns round (vv. 20-21). Caught between the two, not one escapes, and the king is taken alive (vv. 22-23).
verseByVerse.theology: Their confidence was built on a real memory. Ai had beaten Israel, and the men running out of the gates that morning were reasoning from evidence. Presumption is rarely irrational; it is usually a sound argument from a previous week.
verseByVerse.examples: The outstretched javelin is the gesture Moses made with his staff over the sea and with his hands at Rephidim (Ex. 14:16; 17:11). It does nothing mechanically. It is a man standing in plain view with his arm up, so that nobody watching can mistake whose victory this is.

verseByVerse.quote: And as soon as the king of Ai saw this, he and all his people, the men of the city, hurried and went out early to the appointed place toward the Arabah to meet Israel in battle. But he did not know that there was an ambush against him behind the city. And Joshua and all Israel pretended to be beaten before them and fled in the direction of the wilderness. So all the people who were in the city were called together to pursue them, and as they pursued Joshua they were drawn away from the city. Not a man was left in Ai or Bethel who did not go out after Israel. They left the city open and pursued Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
He hurried. He has beaten these people once and watched them run, and the evidence he trusts is about to kill him. It is precisely the error Israel made in chapter 7, when the scouts counted the defenders and did not think to ask God. The king of Ai is now making Israel's mistake.

Then they left the city open: the gates shut against Israel a week ago stand wide, because every man in the place is out on the hillside chasing a defeat that is not happening.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Joshua, "Stretch out the javelin that is in your hand toward Ai, for I will give it into your hand." And Joshua stretched out the javelin that was in his hand toward the city. And the men in the ambush rose quickly out of their place, and as soon as he had stretched out his hand, they ran and entered the city and captured it. And they hurried to set the city on fire. So when the men of Ai looked back, behold, the smoke of the city went up to heaven, and they had no power to flee this way or that, for the people who fled to the wilderness turned back against the pursuers. And when Joshua and all Israel saw that the ambush had captured the city, and that the smoke of the city went up, then they turned back and struck down the men of Ai. And the others came out from the city against them, so they were in the midst of Israel, some on this side, and some on that side. And Israel struck them down, until there was left none that survived or escaped. But the king of Ai they took alive, and brought him near to Joshua.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A raised spear kills nobody at that distance, but it is the agreed signal: the ambush rose as soon as he had stretched out his hand (v. 19).

The fire is the second signal: when the pursuers look back, the retreat was staged, the city is gone, and the road home is burning. An army caught between the men it was chasing and the men who took its houses is not defeated by superior force; it is defeated by having believed something.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 24–29 — A King on a Tree, Taken Down by Sunset
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The killing is total and the number is given: twelve thousand, the whole population (vv. 24-25). Joshua does not lower his arm until it is finished (v. 26), the spoil is taken this time by command (v. 27), and the city is burned to a mound that is still there when the book is written (v. 28). Then the king of Ai is hanged on a tree, taken down at sunset, and buried under a great heap of stones at the city gate (v. 29).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 29 is written to the letter of the law. A body was not to remain on a tree overnight, because a hanged man is cursed by God and would defile the land (Deut. 21:22-23). Israel executes a Canaanite king and then observes, to the hour, a commandment about how to handle the cursed.
verseByVerse.examples: Paul takes that exact law and puts it on Christ: he redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us, for it is written, Cursed is everyone who is hanged on a tree (Gal. 3:13).

verseByVerse.quote: When Israel had finished killing all the inhabitants of Ai in the open wilderness where they pursued them, and all of them to the very last had fallen by the edge of the sword, all Israel returned to Ai and struck it down with the edge of the sword. And all who fell that day, both men and women, were 12,000, all the people of Ai. But Joshua did not draw back his hand with which he stretched out the javelin until he had devoted all the inhabitants of Ai to destruction. Only the livestock and the spoil of that city Israel took as their plunder, according to the word of the LORD that he commanded Joshua. So Joshua burned Ai and made it forever a heap of ruins, as it is to this day. And he hanged the king of Ai on a tree until evening. And at sunset Joshua commanded, and they took his body down from the tree and threw it at the entrance of the gate of the city and raised over it a great heap of stones, which stands there to this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Twelve thousand people, stated as a number and not dressed up. The book neither celebrates this nor hides it, and the hard question it raises is faced below, as it was at Jericho (6:21). To devote to destruction (herem) meant to hand over wholly to God, which in war meant to destroy.

The arm stayed up the whole time, a spear held out over a burning city until the thing was done, as Moses' hands were held up until Amalek was beaten (Ex. 17:12).

The plunder is taken according to the word of the LORD: the same action that damned one man is righteous when God commands it.

The king was probably put to death first and his body then hung up for display, as the five kings are at 10:26. The body comes down at sunset, not from squeamishness or convenience but in obedience to the law of Deuteronomy 21 described above.

Another King was hanged on a tree outside a city gate. He was taken down before sunset, because the law required it and the sabbath was coming. A stone was rolled over him. And the curse that fell on a Canaanite king because he was an enemy of God fell on this one although he was not, so that his enemies could stop being cursed.

Was it just to destroy Ai? As at Jericho, this was God’s judgment on peoples whose sin had ripened over centuries (Gen 15:16; Deut 9:4–5), including child sacrifice (Deut 12:31), and Israel was warned that the land would vomit it out too for the same sins (Lev 18:24–28). It was a unique command, carried out through Israel at one moment in redemptive history. It is no pattern for any later war, nation or church: Christ’s kingdom is not of this world (John 18:36), and the church’s weapons are not of the flesh (2 Cor 10:4).

Twelve thousand at a small city? Ai’s people were joined by the men of Bethel (v. 17), and some read “thousand” here as a military unit rather than an exact count, as with the figures in verses 3 and 12.

The mound is called a heap of ruins to this day, which raises the question of where Ai was (see on 7:2). If the usual site, et-Tell, is the wrong one, the main archaeological objection loses its force; if it is the right one, the question stays open.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The campaign stops. Joshua builds an altar on Mount Ebal of uncut stones that no iron tool has touched, exactly as Moses commanded, and burnt offerings and peace offerings are made on it (vv. 30-31). He writes a copy of the law on stones in front of everybody (v. 32). The whole nation is then drawn up in the valley, half facing Gerizim and half facing Ebal, with the ark and the priests between them, sojourners standing with the native born (v. 33), and Joshua reads the whole law aloud, blessing and curse (vv. 34-35). In the Greek Old Testament (the Septuagint) these verses come after 9:2, and one Dead Sea Scroll seems to place the altar-building just after the Jordan crossing; the Hebrew order, which our Bibles follow, sets it here, after Ai.
verseByVerse.theology: Ebal and Gerizim are twenty miles north of Ai, in country nobody had taken. Israel broke off a war, marched the entire nation — women, children and foreigners — deep into unconquered territory, and held a service. This is not a pause between campaigns. It is a claim staked in the middle of the land.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 35 is exact about who was there: the women, and the little ones, and the sojourners who lived among them. Not a word was left out and nobody was left outside. The foreigners standing in that assembly are what happened to Rahab's household, and to everyone since who has come in from outside.

verseByVerse.quote: At that time Joshua built an altar to the LORD, the God of Israel, on Mount Ebal, just as Moses the servant of the LORD had commanded the people of Israel, as it is written in the Book of the Law of Moses, "an altar of uncut stones, upon which no man has wielded an iron tool." And they offered on it burnt offerings to the LORD and sacrificed peace offerings. And there, in the presence of the people of Israel, he wrote on the stones a copy of the law of Moses, which he had written.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Ebal stands above Shechem, with walled cities on every side and no line of supply. How the nation got there safely the text does not say; Shechem may not have been hostile, and many think the writer places the scene here for its meaning as much as for its date.

The altar is built to a specification: uncut stones, no iron tool ever laid on them (Ex. 20:25; Deut. 27:5-6). The one place where human skill is forbidden is the place where atonement is made. Whatever else a man may improve by his craftsmanship, he may not improve the way back to God.

Two kinds of offering are made on it. Burnt offerings, which went up entirely — nothing kept back, the whole animal consumed. And peace offerings, which were eaten: the sacrifice that ended in a shared meal, the sign that the quarrel was over and the parties were at table. Atonement first, then dinner.

Then he writes the law on stones in public. A nation that had spent forty years being carried and fed takes its first act of settled ownership, and the act is to put God's words up where the country can read them.

verseByVerse.quote: And all Israel, sojourner as well as native born, with their elders and officers and their judges, stood on opposite sides of the ark before the Levitical priests who carried the ark of the covenant of the LORD, half of them in front of Mount Gerizim and half of them in front of Mount Ebal, just as Moses the servant of the LORD had commanded at the first, to bless the people of Israel. And afterward he read all the words of the law, the blessing and the curse, according to all that is written in the Book of the Law. There was not a word of all that Moses commanded that Joshua did not read before all the assembly of Israel, and the women, and the little ones, and the sojourners who lived among them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The valley between the two ridges is a natural amphitheatre where a voice carries. Moses had assigned their parts: Gerizim the mountain of blessing, Ebal the mountain of curse (Deut. 27:12-13). The altar was built on Ebal. If there is to be any dealing with God at all, it happens where the curse is, because that is the thing standing in the way.

One small textual point: in Deuteronomy 27:4, where Moses commands this altar, the Samaritan Pentateuch (the Samaritans' own copy of the five books of Moses) reads Gerizim, their holy mountain, instead of Ebal. The Hebrew text reads Ebal, and Joshua follows it.

Not a word was left out: the whole law, including the parts that indict the people listening, read in one sitting, with children too young to follow much of it standing through the reading.

Every word of the law is read over them, and every word of it will eventually be broken by them. The law was written on stones that day. Centuries later God promised, through a prophet watching the whole arrangement fail, to write it on the heart: I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts (Jer. 31:33). That is the Spirit's work in believers now (Ezek. 36:27), and where we still fall short, Christ has already kept every word in our place.

8.theology:
Restoration on the original terms. The words God gives Joshua after the disaster are the words he gave him before it. Nothing is withheld and no conditions are added, because the promise never rested on Joshua's record in the first place. It is the pattern of Peter on the beach, who was not asked how he could have done it but whether he loved him (John 21:15-17).

Miracle and means are both his. The shout at Jericho and the ambush at Ai were both commanded by God. Christians divide into those who think faith waits and those who think faith works, and each side has a favourite chapter here. The question in Joshua is never which approach is holier; it is what God has actually said.

The same act, damned and commanded. Achan died for taking spoil; Israel is ordered to take spoil, and the writer notes that they did it according to the word of the LORD (v. 27). The moral weight sat entirely on the command and not on the object, which is the thing to remember wherever Christians build permanent rules out of God's particular instructions.

Hanged on a tree, taken down by sunset. The king of Ai's body is removed before nightfall because a hanged man is cursed by God (Deut. 21:22-23), and Paul applies that same law to the cross (Gal. 3:13). And the altar in this chapter is built on Ebal, the mountain of cursing, not on Gerizim. Atonement is always made where the curse is.
8.examples:
Then: A defeated army went back to the town that had beaten it, won by pretending to run away again, and then walked twenty miles into enemy country with its wives and children to stand in a valley and listen to the whole law read out, every word, including the parts about what would happen if they broke it.

Now: The word to take from this chapter is the first one. God opened the conversation after the failure, and used the sentence he had used before it. If you are carrying something you assume has permanently changed the terms — a collapse, a disqualifying failure, a year you would not repeat — notice what God did not say to Joshua. He did not review the incident. He said do not be afraid, take the whole army, and go back to the place where it went wrong. The failure was real and had been dealt with; the promise had never rested on Joshua in the first place, and it does not rest on you.

9.title: The Gibeonite Deception
9.text: <sup>1</sup>As soon as all the kings who were beyond the Jordan in the hill country and in the lowland all along the coast of the Great Sea toward Lebanon, the Hittites, the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites, heard of this,<sup>2</sup>they gathered together as one to fight against Joshua and Israel.<sup>3</sup>But when the inhabitants of Gibeon heard what Joshua had done to Jericho and to Ai,<sup>4</sup>they on their part acted with cunning and went and made ready provisions and took worn-out sacks for their donkeys, and wineskins, worn-out and torn and mended,<sup>5</sup>with worn-out, patched sandals on their feet, and worn-out clothes. And all their provisions were dry and crumbly.<sup>6</sup>And they went to Joshua in the camp at Gilgal and said to him and to the men of Israel, "We have come from a distant country, so now make a covenant with us."<sup>7</sup>But the men of Israel said to the Hivites, "Perhaps you live among us; then how can we make a covenant with you?"<sup>8</sup>They said to Joshua, "We are your servants." And Joshua said to them, "Who are you? And where do you come from?"<sup>9</sup>They said to him, "From a very distant country your servants have come, because of the name of the LORD your God. For we have heard a report of him, and all that he did in Egypt,<sup>10</sup>and all that he did to the two kings of the Amorites who were beyond the Jordan, to Sihon the king of Heshbon, and to Og king of Bashan, who lived in Ashtaroth.<sup>11</sup>So our elders and all the inhabitants of our country said to us, 'Take provisions in your hand for the journey and go to meet them and say to them, "We are your servants. Come now, make a covenant with us."'<sup>12</sup>Here is our bread. It was still warm when we took it from our houses as our food for the journey on the day we set out to come to you, but now, behold, it is dry and crumbly.<sup>13</sup>These wineskins were new when we filled them, and behold, they have burst. And these garments and sandals of ours are worn out from the very long journey."<sup>14</sup>So the men took some of their provisions, but did not ask counsel from the LORD.<sup>15</sup>And Joshua made peace with them and made a covenant with them, to let them live, and the leaders of the congregation swore to them.<sup>16</sup>At the end of three days after they had made a covenant with them, they heard that they were their neighbors and that they lived among them.<sup>17</sup>And the people of Israel set out and reached their cities on the third day. Now their cities were Gibeon, Chephirah, Beeroth, and Kiriath-jearim.<sup>18</sup>But the people of Israel did not attack them, because the leaders of the congregation had sworn to them by the LORD, the God of Israel. Then all the congregation murmured against the leaders.<sup>19</sup>But all the leaders said to all the congregation, "We have sworn to them by the LORD, the God of Israel, and now we may not touch them.<sup>20</sup>This we will do to them: let them live, lest wrath be upon us, because of the oath that we swore to them."<sup>21</sup>And the leaders said to them, "Let them live." So they became cutters of wood and drawers of water for all the congregation, just as the leaders had said of them.<sup>22</sup>Joshua summoned them, and he said to them, "Why did you deceive us, saying, 'We are very far from you,' when you dwell among us?<sup>23</sup>Now therefore you are cursed, and some of you shall never be anything but servants, cutters of wood and drawers of water for the house of my God."<sup>24</sup>They answered Joshua, "Because it was told to your servants for a certainty that the LORD your God had commanded his servant Moses to give you all the land and to destroy all the inhabitants of the land from before you—so we feared greatly for our lives because of you and did this thing.<sup>25</sup>And now, behold, we are in your hand. Whatever seems good and right in your sight to do to us, do it."<sup>26</sup>So he did this to them and delivered them out of the hand of the people of Israel, and they did not kill them.<sup>27</sup>But Joshua made them that day cutters of wood and drawers of water for the congregation and for the altar of the LORD, to this day, in the place that he should choose.
9.overview:
Chapter 9 changes the kind of danger. Jericho and Ai were assaults; this is a confidence trick. The Gibeonites hear what Israel's God has been doing, work out that they cannot win, and decide to survive by fraud — patched sandals, split wineskins, bread deliberately left to go hard, and a story about a journey from a distant country. The disguise is aimed at a specific sentence of Israel's own law, which allows terms of peace only with cities that are very far from you (Deut. 20:10-18).

Israel nearly catches it (v. 7), and is then talked round by a speech built out of true statements with a hole in the middle. Israel inspects the evidence competently, finds it genuine, and the chapter turns on eight words: but did not ask counsel from the LORD (v. 14).

The rest is what God does with a blunder. The oath was sworn in his name and therefore holds, even against a furious congregation, and the Gibeonites live, sentenced to cut wood and carry water for the altar: a strange curse for a Canaanite city, and stranger still in the light of where the tabernacle eventually stood.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–2 — Three Ways of Hearing the Same News
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The kings of the whole country — hill country, lowland and coast, six nations named — hear what has happened at Jericho and Ai (v. 1), and they do the one thing that has not been tried yet: they combine. Six armies gather as one to fight Joshua and Israel (v. 2).
verseByVerse.theology: Three groups in this book hear the same reports and do three different things. Rahab heard and asked for mercy. These kings hear and form a coalition. The Gibeonites, in the next verse, hear and start sewing patches onto sandals. The news was identical every time.

verseByVerse.quote: As soon as all the kings who were beyond the Jordan in the hill country and in the lowland all along the coast of the Great Sea toward Lebanon, the Hittites, the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites, heard of this, they gathered together as one to fight against Joshua and Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Six nations and every region of the country, and for the first time they act together. Until now Canaan has been a patchwork of city-states that were at least as interested in each other as in Israel. Two burned towns have done what nothing else could and made them one.

Nobody in Canaan is short of information. What separates these people is what they do with it, which is one of the oldest patterns in Scripture: the same word softens one man and sets another hard.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 3–13 — Worn Sandals and Mouldy Bread
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Gibeon hears the same reports and takes a third route (v. 3). They load donkeys with split and mended wineskins, put on patched sandals and worn clothes, take bread that has gone dry and crumbly, and walk into the camp at Gilgal claiming to be from a distant country (vv. 4-6). Israel is suspicious and says so — perhaps you live among us (v. 7) — so the Gibeonites talk. They cite the name of the LORD, Egypt, Sihon and Og (vv. 9-10), quote their own elders (v. 11), and then produce the exhibits: bread that was warm when they left home, wineskins that were new, garments and sandals worn out by the length of the road (vv. 12-13).
verseByVerse.theology: Every fact in their speech is chosen. They mention Egypt and the two Amorite kings — old news that would have reached a distant country — and say nothing whatever about Jericho and Ai, which happened last month and only a neighbour would know. The gaps in the story are as carefully made as the story.
verseByVerse.examples: They are also standing inside a clause of Israel's own law. Deuteronomy permits terms of peace with a city that is very far and forbids it absolutely with the cities of Canaan (Deut. 20:10-18). The Gibeonites are not improvising a lie; they have worked out precisely which sentence of Israel's law they need to be standing in, and then dressed for it.

verseByVerse.quote: But when the inhabitants of Gibeon heard what Joshua had done to Jericho and to Ai, they on their part acted with cunning and went and made ready provisions and took worn-out sacks for their donkeys, and wineskins, worn-out and torn and mended, with worn-out, patched sandals on their feet, and worn-out clothes. And all their provisions were dry and crumbly. And they went to Joshua in the camp at Gilgal and said to him and to the men of Israel, "We have come from a distant country, so now make a covenant with us."
verseByVerse.commentary:
This took time and thought. Somebody in Gibeon worked out what a man would look like after weeks on the road and produced a whole wardrobe, down to the state of the food. They have studied the God they are afraid of well enough to find the one clause in his law with room in it, which is more attention than the kings up the road have paid.

Then they walk into Gilgal — the camp where the stones from the Jordan are standing, where the nation was circumcised, where the Passover was kept — and open with the lie.
verseByVerse.note: Gibeon lay about six miles north-west of Jerusalem.

verseByVerse.quote: But the men of Israel said to the Hivites, "Perhaps you live among us; then how can we make a covenant with you?" They said to Joshua, "We are your servants." And Joshua said to them, "Who are you? And where do you come from?" They said to him, "From a very distant country your servants have come, because of the name of the LORD your God. For we have heard a report of him, and all that he did in Egypt, and all that he did to the two kings of the Amorites who were beyond the Jordan, to Sihon the king of Heshbon, and to Og king of Bashan, who lived in Ashtaroth. So our elders and all the inhabitants of our country said to us, 'Take provisions in your hand for the journey and go to meet them and say to them, "We are your servants. Come now, make a covenant with us."' Here is our bread. It was still warm when we took it from our houses as our food for the journey on the day we set out to come to you, but now, behold, it is dry and crumbly. These wineskins were new when we filled them, and behold, they have burst. And these garments and sandals of ours are worn out from the very long journey."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel very nearly catches it. The first response is suspicion, and it is exactly the right suspicion: perhaps you live among us. Somebody in that meeting had read Deuteronomy and knew what question to ask.

That makes what follows worse. They saw the danger, named it out loud, and were then talked out of it. The silence about Jericho and Ai is deliberate, for verse 3 has told us that is precisely what the Gibeonites heard; the most effective lying is generally done with true statements and a hole cut in the middle.

One clause in the whole performance is entirely true: they came because of the name of the LORD your God. They had heard the report and were terrified, and that part needed no invention at all.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–15 — They Did Not Ask Counsel from the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Israel does the due diligence. They take some of the provisions and examine them — the bread really is dry, the skins really are split — and the evidence checks out (v. 14). And then the eight words that the whole chapter turns on: but did not ask counsel from the LORD. Joshua makes peace, cuts a covenant, and the leaders of the congregation swear to it (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: The failure is not laziness and it is not wickedness. They investigated competently and reached a reasonable conclusion from real evidence. What they did not do was ask the one party who knew where these men lived.
verseByVerse.examples: The means were standing in the camp. The high priest carried the Urim and Thummim for exactly this — so that Israel could put a question to God and get an answer (Num. 27:21). It was not that God was silent. Nobody asked him.

verseByVerse.quote: So the men took some of their provisions, but did not ask counsel from the LORD. And Joshua made peace with them and made a covenant with them, to let them live, and the leaders of the congregation swore to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel did inspect: they took some of their provisions and tested the story against them. The failure is competence without enquiry. Every piece of their real data had been manufactured the week before, and Eleazar the priest, who could have put the question to God, was in the camp.

Why did they not ask? The case looked closed. When the evidence is ambiguous we pray; when it is obvious we act. The Gibeonites' entire strategy was to make the case look obvious, and it worked, and it will work again on anybody who only prays about the decisions that are difficult.

Then the covenant is cut and the leaders swear. That oath is about to become the most important thing in the chapter, and at the moment it is sworn nobody thinks it matters much at all.

Must Christians keep every oath, however foolishly made? Israel kept this one, and God later held Saul guilty for breaking it (2 Sam 21:1). A Christian should keep his word even when it costs him (Ps 15:4), unless keeping it would mean sin. Better still, make fewer and more careful promises: Let what you say be simply “Yes” or “No” (Matt 5:37).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Three days later the truth is out: these men are neighbours, and their towns are Gibeon, Chephirah, Beeroth and Kiriath-jearim, three days' march away (vv. 16-17). Israel does not attack them, because the leaders had sworn by the LORD, and the whole congregation grumbles about it (v. 18). The leaders' answer is short and it settles the matter: we have sworn by the LORD, we may not touch them, and if we break it wrath will come on us (vv. 19-20). So the Gibeonites live, as woodcutters and water-carriers for the congregation (v. 21).
verseByVerse.theology: The treaty was obtained by fraud, and everybody knows it. Israel could have voided it on those grounds in ten seconds, and the congregation clearly wanted to. The leaders hold to it because of whose name was invoked, not because of who deserved it.
verseByVerse.examples: That the oath was genuinely binding was proved centuries later, and expensively. Saul broke it and killed Gibeonites, and a three-year famine came on Israel in David's reign with the reason given plainly: there is bloodguilt on Saul and on his house, because he put the Gibeonites to death (2 Sam. 21:1).

verseByVerse.quote: At the end of three days after they had made a covenant with them, they heard that they were their neighbors and that they lived among them. And the people of Israel set out and reached their cities on the third day. Now their cities were Gibeon, Chephirah, Beeroth, and Kiriath-jearim. But the people of Israel did not attack them, because the leaders of the congregation had sworn to them by the LORD, the God of Israel. Then all the congregation murmured against the leaders.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The lie survives three days, and Israel walks to their cities in three days more: the truth was a short walk away the entire time. Now the army stands outside four Canaanite towns it is under orders to destroy and does not attack, and the reason is a name: the leaders had sworn by the LORD, the God of Israel.

The word for what they do is the word used all through the wilderness years: they murmured. This is the old sin surfacing in a new situation, and this time they are grumbling in favour of obedience to a command about Canaanites, which shows how easily a bad instinct can find a good text to stand on.

verseByVerse.quote: But all the leaders said to all the congregation, "We have sworn to them by the LORD, the God of Israel, and now we may not touch them. This we will do to them: let them live, lest wrath be upon us, because of the oath that we swore to them." And the leaders said to them, "Let them live." So they became cutters of wood and drawers of water for all the congregation, just as the leaders had said of them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The leaders' reasoning has two steps. First, we have sworn by the LORD. When a man swears in God's name he is calling God as guarantor of what he says. Breaking it does not merely make the man a liar; it makes God look like the sponsor of a lie. That is why the third commandment is about taking the name in vain, and it is far wider than swearing in the street.

Second, lest wrath be upon us. They are not being sentimental about promises, and Saul's reign would prove them right: an oath sworn by deceived men to lying men was still binding on their great-grandchildren.

That is the man of Psalm 15:4, who swears to his own hurt and does not change. If men kept a promise made to deceivers because God's name was on it, God will not break the oath he swore to his own people (Hebrews 6:17-18), and every one of his promises is Yes in Christ (2 Corinthians 1:20).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Joshua summons them and asks the obvious question — why did you deceive us (v. 22)? — and pronounces the sentence: you are cursed, and some of you shall never be anything but servants, cutters of wood and drawers of water for the house of my God (v. 23). Their answer is honest at last: we were told your God had given you this land and commanded the destruction of everyone in it, so we feared greatly for our lives (v. 24), and now we are in your hand, do what seems right (v. 25). Joshua delivers them from the people and they are not killed (v. 26), and the last verse fixes their work: woodcutters and water-carriers for the congregation and for the altar of the LORD (v. 27).
verseByVerse.theology: The sentence Joshua passes is a curse, and the reader should feel how strange a curse it is. It condemns a Canaanite people to spend the rest of their history carrying firewood and water to the altar of the God of Israel. Every other Canaanite city in this book is destroyed; these men are sentenced to lifelong proximity to the sacrifices.
verseByVerse.examples: For worship, notice what the Gibeonites' work was: wood for the fire and water for the washing. It was unglamorous, endless and necessary. No sacrifice was offered without somebody having carried the fuel, and Scripture troubles to record who did it. Much faithful service in a church still looks like this, and God sees it.

verseByVerse.quote: Joshua summoned them, and he said to them, "Why did you deceive us, saying, 'We are very far from you,' when you dwell among us? Now therefore you are cursed, and some of you shall never be anything but servants, cutters of wood and drawers of water for the house of my God." They answered Joshua, "Because it was told to your servants for a certainty that the LORD your God had commanded his servant Moses to give you all the land and to destroy all the inhabitants of the land from before you—so we feared greatly for our lives because of you and did this thing. And now, behold, we are in your hand. Whatever seems good and right in your sight to do to us, do it."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joshua does not pretend nothing happened. The deception is named, and a sentence is passed, and it is called a curse.

But look at what the curse actually is: wood and water for the house of my God. Gibeon is put on the sanctuary's staff.

Their explanation is the first honest thing they have said, and it is not an excuse. It is a statement of fact: we were told what your God had ordered, we believed it, and we were terrified.

Six armies to the north heard the same thing and concluded that they could fight it; Gibeon concluded that they could not, and everything they did afterwards, the lying included, followed from taking God at his word.

Then total surrender: they do not argue that the treaty binds Israel, though it does. They put themselves in his hand and stop negotiating.

Is this slavery, and does the Bible approve of it? The Gibeonites became permanent servants at the sanctuary, a lower and lasting status, but not property to be bought and sold; they were protected by an oath in God's name, which even a king was punished for breaking (2 Sam. 21:1). Many think the temple servants of later centuries were partly their descendants (Ezra 2:43; 8:20). Scripture records the arrangement as the merciful outcome of a deception, not as a model for society, and the gospel goes further: in Christ there is neither slave nor free (Galatians 3:28).

verseByVerse.quote: So he did this to them and delivered them out of the hand of the people of Israel, and they did not kill them. But Joshua made them that day cutters of wood and drawers of water for the congregation and for the altar of the LORD, to this day, in the place that he should choose.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joshua delivered them out of the hand of the people of Israel. The danger to the Gibeonites at this point is not the Canaanite kings; it is the congregation of Israel, which is still grumbling and would happily have finished them. Joshua stands between an angry nation and the men who fooled it.

In the place that he should choose is Deuteronomy's language for the future sanctuary: Joshua attaches these men to whatever God is going to do next, permanently.

And it went further than Joshua could have known. Centuries later the tent of meeting came to rest at Gibeon, with Zadok stationed before it (1 Chron. 16:39), and there Solomon went up to sacrifice and God said to him, Ask what I shall give you (1 Kings 3:4-5; 2 Chron. 1:3). God took a prayerless blunder, a wardrobe of stage props and a nation's fury, and out of the three of them made a place where he met people. He has never yet been prevented from doing that by the poor quality of the material.

9.theology:
Prayerlessness is not laziness. Israel investigated, and the evidence was real. What they did not do was ask the only party who knew where these men lived (Num. 27:21).

An oath in God's name binds even when it was obtained by fraud. The leaders refused to void it because the name of the LORD had been invoked. Behind this stands a God who keeps his own oath to his people (Heb. 6:17-18).

Same news, three responses. What divided Rahab, the kings of Canaan and Gibeon was not knowledge but what each did with it. The Gibeonites, for all their lying, had the better theology: they believed what God had said about the land, and the kings did not.

What God did with the blunder. The deceivers are sentenced to serve the altar, and centuries later the tent of meeting itself stood in their town. A prayerless decision and an elaborate lie ended in a place where God met his people.
9.examples:
Then: Four Canaanite towns survived the conquest because they dressed up in old clothes, carried stale bread on a journey of a few days, and told a story with the recent news left out of it. Israel checked the evidence, found it convincing, and signed. Three days later they were standing outside the towns of the people they had sworn to protect.

Now: The verse to take away is the eight words in the middle of verse 14, and the reason they are frightening is that nothing else in the chapter went wrong. There was no rebellion, no laziness, no obvious sin — only a sensible decision made on good evidence without asking God, because the case looked clear. Think of the last significant decision you did not pray about: almost certainly the answer seemed obvious. The God who invites us to ask gives wisdom generously and without reproach (James 1:5), and, as Gibeon shows, he is not defeated by the blunders we make when we forget to.

10.title: The Sun Stands Still
10.text: <sup>1</sup>As soon as Adoni-zedek, king of Jerusalem, heard how Joshua had captured Ai and had devoted it to destruction, doing to Ai and its king as he had done to Jericho and its king, and how the inhabitants of Gibeon had made peace with Israel and were among them,<sup>2</sup>he feared greatly, because Gibeon was a great city, like one of the royal cities, and because it was greater than Ai, and all its men were warriors.<sup>3</sup>So Adoni-zedek king of Jerusalem sent to Hoham king of Hebron, to Piram king of Jarmuth, to Japhia king of Lachish, and to Debir king of Eglon, saying,<sup>4</sup>"Come up to me and help me, and let us strike Gibeon. For it has made peace with Joshua and with the people of Israel."<sup>5</sup>Then the five kings of the Amorites, the king of Jerusalem, the king of Hebron, the king of Jarmuth, the king of Lachish, and the king of Eglon, gathered their forces and went up with all their armies and encamped against Gibeon and made war against it.<sup>6</sup>And the men of Gibeon sent to Joshua at the camp in Gilgal, saying, "Do not relax your hand from your servants. Come up to us quickly and save us and help us, for all the kings of the Amorites who dwell in the hill country are gathered against us."<sup>7</sup>So Joshua went up from Gilgal, he and all the people of war with him, and all the mighty men of valor.<sup>8</sup>And the LORD said to Joshua, "Do not fear them, for I have given them into your hands. Not a man of them shall stand before you."<sup>9</sup>So Joshua came upon them suddenly, having marched up all night from Gilgal.<sup>10</sup>And the LORD threw them into a panic before Israel, who struck them with a great blow at Gibeon and chased them by the way of the ascent of Beth-horon and struck them as far as Azekah and Makkedah.<sup>11</sup>And as they fled before Israel, while they were going down the ascent of Beth-horon, the LORD threw down large stones from heaven on them as far as Azekah, and they died. There were more who died because of the hailstones than the sons of Israel killed with the sword.<sup>12</sup>At that time Joshua spoke to the LORD in the day when the LORD gave the Amorites over to the sons of Israel, and he said in the sight of Israel, "Sun, stand still at Gibeon, and moon, in the Valley of Aijalon."<sup>13</sup>And the sun stood still, and the moon stopped, until the nation took vengeance on their enemies. Is this not written in the Book of Jashar? The sun stopped in the midst of heaven and did not hurry to set for about a whole day.<sup>14</sup>There has been no day like it before or since, when the LORD heeded the voice of a man, for the LORD fought for Israel.<sup>15</sup>So Joshua returned, and all Israel with him, to the camp at Gilgal.<sup>16</sup>These five kings fled and hid themselves in the cave at Makkedah.<sup>17</sup>And it was told to Joshua, "The five kings have been found, hidden in the cave at Makkedah."<sup>18</sup>And Joshua said, "Roll large stones against the mouth of the cave and set men by it to guard them,<sup>19</sup>but do not stay there yourselves. Pursue your enemies; attack their rear guard. Do not let them enter their cities, for the LORD your God has given them into your hand."<sup>20</sup>When Joshua and the sons of Israel had finished striking them with a great blow until they were wiped out, and when the remnant that remained of them had entered into the fortified cities,<sup>21</sup>then all the people returned safe to Joshua in the camp at Makkedah. Not a man moved his tongue against any of the people of Israel.<sup>22</sup>Then Joshua said, "Open the mouth of the cave and bring those five kings out to me from the cave."<sup>23</sup>And they did so, and brought those five kings out to him from the cave, the king of Jerusalem, the king of Hebron, the king of Jarmuth, the king of Lachish, and the king of Eglon.<sup>24</sup>And when they brought those kings out to Joshua, Joshua summoned all the men of Israel and said to the chiefs of the men of war who had gone with him, "Come near; put your feet on the necks of these kings." Then they came near and put their feet on their necks.<sup>25</sup>And Joshua said to them, "Do not be afraid or dismayed; be strong and courageous. For thus the LORD will do to all your enemies against whom you fight."<sup>26</sup>And afterward Joshua struck them and put them to death, and he hanged them on five trees. And they hung on the trees until evening.<sup>27</sup>But at the time of the going down of the sun, Joshua commanded, and they took them down from the trees and threw them into the cave where they had hidden themselves, and they set large stones against the mouth of the cave, which remain to this very day.<sup>28</sup>As for Makkedah, Joshua captured it on that day and struck it, and its king, with the edge of the sword. He devoted to destruction every person in it; he left none remaining. And he did to the king of Makkedah just as he had done to the king of Jericho.<sup>29</sup>Then Joshua and all Israel with him passed on from Makkedah to Libnah and fought against Libnah.<sup>30</sup>And the LORD gave it also and its king into the hand of Israel. And he struck it with the edge of the sword, and every person in it; he left none remaining in it. And he did to its king as he had done to the king of Jericho.<sup>31</sup>Then Joshua and all Israel with him passed on from Libnah to Lachish and laid siege to it and fought against it.<sup>32</sup>And the LORD gave Lachish into the hand of Israel, and he captured it on the second day and struck it with the edge of the sword, and every person in it, as he had done to Libnah.<sup>33</sup>Then Horam king of Gezer came up to help Lachish. And Joshua struck him and his people, until he left none remaining.<sup>34</sup>Then Joshua and all Israel with him passed on from Lachish to Eglon. And they laid siege to it and fought against it.<sup>35</sup>And they captured it on that day, and struck it with the edge of the sword. And he devoted every person in it to destruction that day, as he had done to Lachish.<sup>36</sup>Then Joshua and all Israel with him went up from Eglon to Hebron. And they fought against it<sup>37</sup>and captured it and struck it with the edge of the sword, and its king and its towns, and every person in it. He left none remaining, as he had done to Eglon, and devoted it to destruction and every person in it.<sup>38</sup>Then Joshua and all Israel with him turned back to Debir and fought against it<sup>39</sup>and he captured it with its king and all its towns. And they struck them with the edge of the sword and devoted to destruction every person in it; he left none remaining. Just as he had done to Hebron and to Libnah and its king, so he did to Debir and to its king.<sup>40</sup>So Joshua struck the whole land, the hill country and the Negeb and the lowland and the slopes, and all their kings. He left none remaining, but devoted to destruction all that breathed, just as the LORD God of Israel commanded.<sup>41</sup>And Joshua struck them from Kadesh-barnea as far as Gaza, and all the country of Goshen, as far as Gibeon.<sup>42</sup>And Joshua captured all these kings and their land at one time, because the LORD God of Israel fought for Israel.<sup>43</sup>Then Joshua returned, and all Israel with him, to the camp at Gilgal.
10.overview:
The treaty Israel should never have made becomes the reason for the greatest day in the campaign. Five Amorite kings mobilise, and their target is not Israel but Gibeon, the city that changed sides (v. 4).

Gibeon calls in the oath, and Joshua marches all night to fight for the men who had lied to his face only days earlier. Then God takes the field, with a panic, a pursuit and a hailstorm, and in the middle of it Joshua speaks to the sun and the moon in front of the whole army. The narrator is quoting a poem, and he says where the wonder of that day lies: not in the astronomy, but that the LORD listened to a man (v. 14).

The chapter ends with five kings under the feet of Israel's officers, a catalogue of captured cities written in one repeated sentence, and one short reason for all of it: the LORD fought for Israel (v. 42).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — A Coalition Against the Traitors
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Adoni-zedek of Jerusalem hears about Ai and about Gibeon's peace with Israel, and is badly frightened — Gibeon is a great city, bigger than Ai, and its men are fighters (vv. 1-2). He sends to four other kings, Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish and Eglon, with a proposal (v. 3), and note who the target is: come up to me and help me, and let us strike Gibeon (v. 4). Five armies march, and they besiege not Israel but the city that changed sides (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: Israel's blunder in chapter 9 has just drawn the entire southern coalition out of five fortified cities and concentrated it in one place in open country. Nothing Joshua could have planned would have done that.
verseByVerse.examples: The name of the king of Jerusalem is Adoni-zedek. Centuries earlier a king of Salem, which most identify with Jerusalem (Ps. 76:2), met Abram and blessed him, and his name was Melchizedek, king of righteousness (Gen. 14:18; Heb. 7:2), the man Hebrews takes as the pattern of Christ's priesthood. Melchizedek came out of probably the same city to bless Abram with bread and wine; his namesake raises an army to destroy Abram's descendants. Jerusalem has been capable of both since the beginning.

verseByVerse.quote: As soon as Adoni-zedek, king of Jerusalem, heard how Joshua had captured Ai and had devoted it to destruction, doing to Ai and its king as he had done to Jericho and its king, and how the inhabitants of Gibeon had made peace with Israel and were among them, he feared greatly, because Gibeon was a great city, like one of the royal cities, and because it was greater than Ai, and all its men were warriors. So Adoni-zedek king of Jerusalem sent to Hoham king of Hebron, to Piram king of Jarmuth, to Japhia king of Lachish, and to Debir king of Eglon, saying, "Come up to me and help me, and let us strike Gibeon. For it has made peace with Joshua and with the people of Israel." Then the five kings of the Amorites, the king of Jerusalem, the king of Hebron, the king of Jarmuth, the king of Lachish, and the king of Eglon, gathered their forces and went up with all their armies and encamped against Gibeon and made war against it.
verseByVerse.commentary:
What terrifies Jerusalem is not the fall of Ai. It is the defection of Gibeon.

The reasoning is military. While Gibeon was Canaanite it was part of the wall; now it is a gap, with fighting men in it. So the five kings march on Gibeon first: punishing the traitor comes before fighting the invader. People who throw in their lot with God's people inherit their enemies, and generally meet them sooner than the people they joined. Gibeon lied its way into this covenant, and within days it is under siege by everyone it used to drink with.
verseByVerse.note: Adoni-zedek probably means “my lord is righteous,” a name like that of Melchizedek, king of Salem.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Gibeon sends word to Gilgal, and the message is a claim on the treaty: do not relax your hand from your servants... come up to us quickly and save us (v. 6). Joshua takes the whole army (v. 7), God says do not fear them, I have given them into your hands (v. 8), and the attack lands at first light after a march that took all night (v. 9). Then God does the fighting: he throws the coalition into a panic, and Israel chases them down the pass at Beth-horon (v. 10) while the LORD throws large stones out of the sky — and more of them die from the hail than from Israel's swords (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: Israel marches all night to rescue the people who conned them a chapter earlier. The oath they got by fraud is now costing them a forced march up a mountain, and nobody reopens the question of whether it was binding.
verseByVerse.examples: Gilgal is in the Jordan valley, several hundred feet below sea level; Gibeon sits over three thousand feet higher, some twenty miles away. This is a night climb of more than three thousand feet by an army that then fought a battle at the top of it.

verseByVerse.quote: And the men of Gibeon sent to Joshua at the camp in Gilgal, saying, "Do not relax your hand from your servants. Come up to us quickly and save us and help us, for all the kings of the Amorites who dwell in the hill country are gathered against us." So Joshua went up from Gilgal, he and all the people of war with him, and all the mighty men of valor. And the LORD said to Joshua, "Do not fear them, for I have given them into your hands. Not a man of them shall stand before you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The message is a claim on the treaty, and it is put in the language of the treaty: your servants. They are not asking a favour. They are calling in an oath.

There is real nerve in it: the last time these men spoke to Joshua he called them cursed. He goes, with no recorded council about whether an oath obtained by fraud is really binding.

Then God says what he always says in this book: do not fear; I have given, the perfect tense before the march has started. Israel is going into battle to honour a treaty God was never consulted about, made by men he had told to consult him. He does not say "you made this bed". He says he has already handed them the enemy.

verseByVerse.quote: So Joshua came upon them suddenly, having marched up all night from Gilgal. And the LORD threw them into a panic before Israel, who struck them with a great blow at Gibeon and chased them by the way of the ascent of Beth-horon and struck them as far as Azekah and Makkedah. And as they fled before Israel, while they were going down the ascent of Beth-horon, the LORD threw down large stones from heaven on them as far as Azekah, and they died. There were more who died because of the hailstones than the sons of Israel killed with the sword.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joshua took an entire army up that long climb in the dark, arrived before dawn, and attacked immediately.

Israel had walked round a city for a week and shouted; here they climb a mountain all night. There is no formula in this book for what obedience will require on a given day. Yet the credit goes elsewhere: the writer says the rout came because the LORD threw them into a panic. Whatever the tactical brilliance of the night march, what actually broke the coalition was terror arriving from outside.

The descent at Beth-horon is a steep, rocky defile where running men could not scatter or shelter. The hail killed more than Israel did, and it was aimed weather: Israelites were in that pass too, and the stones fell on one side of a running battle and not the other.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: In the middle of the battle Joshua speaks, in the sight of Israel, to the sun and the moon: stand still at Gibeon, and in the Valley of Aijalon (v. 12). The narrator reports what happened and then quotes his source — is this not written in the Book of Jashar? — adding that the sun did not hurry to set for about a whole day (v. 13). Then the verse that says where the wonder actually lies: there has been no day like it before or since, when the LORD heeded the voice of a man, for the LORD fought for Israel (v. 14). And then, flatly, everyone goes back to camp (v. 15).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 14 does not say that the astonishing thing was the astronomy. It says the astonishing thing was that God listened to a man. The heavens moving is the smaller half of that sentence.
verseByVerse.examples: Sun and moon were not neutral objects to anybody watching. They were worshipped as gods across Canaan and its neighbours. Joshua gave them orders in the name of the LORD, in public, and they did as they were told.

verseByVerse.quote: At that time Joshua spoke to the LORD in the day when the LORD gave the Amorites over to the sons of Israel, and he said in the sight of Israel, "Sun, stand still at Gibeon, and moon, in the Valley of Aijalon." And the sun stood still, and the moon stopped, until the nation took vengeance on their enemies. Is this not written in the Book of Jashar? The sun stopped in the midst of heaven and did not hurry to set for about a whole day. There has been no day like it before or since, when the LORD heeded the voice of a man, for the LORD fought for Israel. So Joshua returned, and all Israel with him, to the camp at Gilgal.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Joshua spoke to the LORD, and then said this in the sight of Israel. The command to the sun is a prayer said out loud in front of the army. Whatever happened next, he had committed himself publicly and there was no quiet way back.

The narrator cites a source. The Book of Jashar was a collection of Hebrew verse, now lost, quoted once more in the Old Testament when David laments Saul and Jonathan (2 Sam. 1:18). So the words about the sun and moon are poetry, quoted from a song Israel already knew.

That matters for how the sentences work, and it does not settle the question of what happened. Poetry can describe a real event with complete accuracy and still describe it as poetry does — and the narrator's own comment in the second half of verse 13, that the sun did not hurry to set for about a whole day, is written as plain report.

The words stand still describe the sun as it appears from the ground, as we still speak of sunrise and sunset; they make no claim about whether the earth or the sun moves.

Readers have taken this in more than one way: the earth's rotation halted or slowed; light prolonged in some other way; or, since the verb can mean "be silent" as well as "be still", a darkening, with the hail cloud giving Israel cool cover through the heat of the afternoon. The reading this commentary prefers is given at the end of this note. What no honest reading can do is remove God from the middle of it, because that is what both the poem and the narrator are for.

A God who requires nothing from anybody, who set the sun in its place, listened to a soldier standing in a field and did what he asked. So the question the chapter raises is not primarily what happened to the light. It is what kind of God takes instructions from a man who is out of daylight and still has work to do: the same God of whom James says, when he wants ordinary Christians to pray, that Elijah was a man with a nature like ours (James 5:17).

Verse 14 is true of that day: no day before or since was like it. But the Gospels tell of one Man whose voice the Father always hears (John 11:41-42), and he still speaks for his people at God's right hand (Hebrews 7:25). The day at Gibeon lasted one afternoon; his intercession has no sunset.

Did the sun really stand still? Some read it as poetry from the book of Jashar; some suggest a prolonged darkness under the hailstorm, or light lengthened in some other way. The text presents it as a real event, There has been no day like it before or since (v. 14). The best reading is a real miracle of prolonged daylight; how God did it, Scripture does not say, and the God who made the sun is not limited by it.
verseByVerse.note: The Valley of Aijalon runs west from Gibeon towards the coastal plain, along the line of Israel's pursuit.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 16–27 — Feet on the Necks of Kings
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The five kings run and hide in a cave at Makkedah (v. 16). Joshua has large stones rolled over the mouth and a guard posted, and tells the army not to stop — keep after the enemy, do not let them reach their cities (vv. 17-19). When the pursuit is over and everyone is back, not a man dares to open his mouth against Israel (vv. 20-21). Then the cave is opened, the kings are brought out, and Joshua has his commanders put their feet on their necks (vv. 22-24), with a sermon attached: do not be afraid, be strong and courageous, this is what the LORD will do to all your enemies (v. 25). The kings are executed and hanged on five trees, taken down at sunset, and thrown into the cave they hid in, with large stones set over the mouth (vv. 26-27).
verseByVerse.theology: The foot on the neck is the oldest picture of total defeat there is. It is hard to read, and Scripture does not soften it; instead it carries the image all the way to Christ's final victory over every enemy, and to his people's share in it.
verseByVerse.examples: Note what Joshua says over the kings in verse 25. It is his own commissioning, almost word for word from 1:9, handed on to the men under him. What God said to him on the day Moses died, he now says to his officers with the evidence lying at their feet.

verseByVerse.quote: These five kings fled and hid themselves in the cave at Makkedah. And it was told to Joshua, "The five kings have been found, hidden in the cave at Makkedah." And Joshua said, "Roll large stones against the mouth of the cave and set men by it to guard them, but do not stay there yourselves. Pursue your enemies; attack their rear guard. Do not let them enter their cities, for the LORD your God has given them into your hand." When Joshua and the sons of Israel had finished striking them with a great blow until they were wiped out, and when the remnant that remained of them had entered into the fortified cities, then all the people returned safe to Joshua in the camp at Makkedah. Not a man moved his tongue against any of the people of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary: Joshua knows what the day is for. He seals the cave and keeps the army chasing, because the kings are not going anywhere and the armies still are; every man who reaches a walled town becomes a siege. The army comes back safe; the writer bothers to say it, after a night march and a day of battle. Then not a man moved his tongue against Israel: a country with nothing left to say. The kings who had been sending each other messages at the start of the chapter are in a cave, and everyone else has stopped talking.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Joshua said, "Open the mouth of the cave and bring those five kings out to me from the cave." And they did so, and brought those five kings out to him from the cave, the king of Jerusalem, the king of Hebron, the king of Jarmuth, the king of Lachish, and the king of Eglon. And when they brought those kings out to Joshua, Joshua summoned all the men of Israel and said to the chiefs of the men of war who had gone with him, "Come near; put your feet on the necks of these kings." Then they came near and put their feet on their necks. And Joshua said to them, "Do not be afraid or dismayed; be strong and courageous. For thus the LORD will do to all your enemies against whom you fight." And afterward Joshua struck them and put them to death, and he hanged them on five trees. And they hung on the trees until evening. But at the time of the going down of the sun, Joshua commanded, and they took them down from the trees and threw them into the cave where they had hidden themselves, and they set large stones against the mouth of the cave, which remain to this very day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The gesture is not gratuitous cruelty but a formal act before the whole army, meaning total and final conquest. Scripture keeps the image and never softens it: God tells the Messiah to sit at his right hand until his enemies are made his footstool (Ps. 110:1), the Old Testament verse the New Testament quotes most often. Paul says Christ must reign until the last enemy, death itself, is under his feet (1 Cor. 15:25-26), and tells a small, squabbling congregation that God will soon crush Satan under your feet (Rom. 16:20). Under theirs.

Joshua hands on his own commission (1:9), and he can point at the floor while he says it. Courage in this book keeps travelling outward: from God to Joshua in chapter 1, from the people back to Joshua at the end of that same chapter, and now from Joshua to his officers with the evidence under their boots.

Once again the bodies come down at sunset, as the law required (Deut. 21:22-23; cf. 8:29). They are thrown into the cave they chose as a hiding place, behind the stones that had kept them in that morning. The place a man picks to hide from God has a way of becoming the place he stays.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The rest of the chapter is a list, and it is deliberately repetitive: Makkedah, Libnah, Lachish, Gezer's king coming to help and falling with him, Eglon, Hebron, Debir (vv. 28-39). Each entry uses the same words — captured, struck with the edge of the sword, none remaining, as he had done to the city before. Verse 40 sums up the whole southern country, hill country and Negeb and lowland and slopes, and verse 41 gives the map from Kadesh-barnea to Gaza. Verse 42 gives the reason for all of it in nine words, and verse 43 sends the army home to Gilgal.
verseByVerse.theology: The flat, formulaic repetition is the writer's method rather than his laziness. City after city falls in identical language, and the effect is of something advancing that nothing in the country can vary or slow. The morality of it is faced at Jericho (6:17-19), and answered briefly again in the commentary below.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 42 is the sentence the whole book exists to say: because the LORD God of Israel fought for Israel. Every campaign in the chapter is credited to somebody who never appears in the casualty lists.

verseByVerse.quote: As for Makkedah, Joshua captured it on that day and struck it, and its king, with the edge of the sword. He devoted to destruction every person in it; he left none remaining. And he did to the king of Makkedah just as he had done to the king of Jericho. Then Joshua and all Israel with him passed on from Makkedah to Libnah and fought against Libnah. And the LORD gave it also and its king into the hand of Israel. And he struck it with the edge of the sword, and every person in it; he left none remaining in it. And he did to its king as he had done to the king of Jericho. Then Joshua and all Israel with him passed on from Libnah to Lachish and laid siege to it and fought against it. And the LORD gave Lachish into the hand of Israel, and he captured it on the second day and struck it with the edge of the sword, and every person in it, as he had done to Libnah. Then Horam king of Gezer came up to help Lachish. And Joshua struck him and his people, until he left none remaining. Then Joshua and all Israel with him passed on from Lachish to Eglon. And they laid siege to it and fought against it. And they captured it on that day, and struck it with the edge of the sword. And he devoted every person in it to destruction that day, as he had done to Lachish. Then Joshua and all Israel with him went up from Eglon to Hebron. And they fought against it and captured it and struck it with the edge of the sword, and its king and its towns, and every person in it. He left none remaining, as he had done to Eglon, and devoted it to destruction and every person in it. Then Joshua and all Israel with him turned back to Debir and fought against it and he captured it with its king and all its towns. And they struck them with the edge of the sword and devoted to destruction every person in it; he left none remaining. Just as he had done to Hebron and to Libnah and its king, so he did to Debir and to its king.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A writer who wanted to celebrate would vary the telling and name the heroes; this one records it all without a word of triumph. Two details break the pattern, and both should be caught. Lachish takes two days (v. 32), the only city in the list said to have held out into a second day: a small honest note in a chapter that could easily have rounded everything off. And when Horam king of Gezer marches out to help Lachish, he is dealt with in a single verse and his city is never taken (v. 33). He came to the aid of a doomed ally and lost his army for it.

Was it just to destroy these cities? As at Jericho, this was God’s judgment on peoples whose sin had ripened over centuries (Gen 15:16; Deut 9:4–5), including child sacrifice (Deut 12:31), and Israel was warned that the land would vomit it out too for the same sins (Lev 18:24–28). It was a unique command, carried out through Israel at one moment in redemptive history. It is no pattern for any later war, nation or church: Christ’s kingdom is not of this world (John 18:36), and the church’s weapons are not of the flesh (2 Cor 10:4).

verseByVerse.quote: So Joshua struck the whole land, the hill country and the Negeb and the lowland and the slopes, and all their kings. He left none remaining, but devoted to destruction all that breathed, just as the LORD God of Israel commanded. And Joshua struck them from Kadesh-barnea as far as Gaza, and all the country of Goshen, as far as Gibeon. And Joshua captured all these kings and their land at one time, because the LORD God of Israel fought for Israel. Then Joshua returned, and all Israel with him, to the camp at Gilgal.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The phrase just as the LORD God of Israel commanded is doing the same job it did at Ai, where taking plunder was righteous because God said so and had been fatal at Jericho because he had said the opposite. Nothing in these chapters is Israel's initiative.

Then the reason. Not because Joshua marched at night, though he did, nor because the coalition blundered, though it did, but because the LORD fought. And the army walks home to Gilgal, to the twelve stones and the place where the reproach of Egypt was rolled away: a people who had been slaves inside living memory.

But Canaanites survive in later chapters. This is the summary language of ancient war: the armies were broken and the kings killed, not every person in every place.
