Joshua itself says that much land remained to be taken (13:1), and Judges 1 tells of tribes still driving out the inhabitants. Hebron and Debir, struck here, have to be taken again by Caleb and Othniel (15:13-17): the kings fell and the cities were struck, but survivors returned. Many think this summary style, common in ancient war reports, also means the killing was less total than the phrases sound; that does not remove the moral question, but it is part of reading the text honestly.

10.theology:
Covenant faithfulness when it costs. Israel marches through the night to rescue the men who deceived them, and the narrative records no debate about it. The oath was obtained by fraud and it is kept anyway, uphill, at night, at risk — and God meets the army on the way with do not fear them, for I have given them into your hands (v. 8). Keeping your word to people who do not deserve it is not naivety in this book; it is an imitation of God.

The long day, and where the miracle is. Verses 12-13 are quoted poetry from the Book of Jashar, and the narrator names his source. This commentary takes the event as a real miracle of prolonged daylight, while Scripture does not say how God did it. And verse 14 does not locate the marvel in the sky at all: what had never happened before or since was that the LORD heeded the voice of a man.

The gods of Canaan take orders. Sun and moon were worshipped throughout the country Israel was invading. Joshua addresses them out loud, in front of the army, in the name of the LORD, and they do as they are told. The theological claim underneath the miracle is the same one the whole book makes: the LORD is not a regional deity competing for territory. He is the Lord of all the earth, and the opposition's gods are on his staff.

Feet on the necks of kings. The image is the ancient world's picture of final conquest, and Scripture carries it to Christ, who reigns until every enemy is under his feet, death last of all (1 Cor. 15:25-26). Then Paul hands it to an ordinary congregation (Rom. 16:20).
10.examples:
Then: An army climbed more than three thousand feet of hill road in the dark to save the people who had swindled it, arrived at dawn, watched the sky kill more of the enemy than they did, and stayed on the field so long that the day itself became a national memory. Then five kings were pulled out of a cave and buried in it, behind the stones they had chosen for shelter.

Now: Two things transfer directly. The first is the march: a promise made carelessly is still a promise, and God met Israel on the road they took to keep it rather than lecturing them about how they got there. The second is verse 14. Before you decide what you think happened to the sun, notice what the writer thought was remarkable — that God listened to a man. Whatever you were about to conclude about the size of your own requests, he heard a soldier ask for more daylight.

11.title: The Northern Campaign Completed
11.text: <sup>1</sup>When Jabin, king of Hazor, heard of this, he sent to Jobab king of Madon, and to the king of Shimron, and to the king of Achshaph,<sup>2</sup>and to the kings who were in the northern hill country, and in the Arabah south of Chinneroth, and in the lowland, and in Naphoth-dor on the west,<sup>3</sup>to the Canaanites in the east and the west, the Amorites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, and the Jebusites in the hill country, and the Hivites under Hermon in the land of Mizpah.<sup>4</sup>And they came out with all their troops, a great horde, in number like the sand that is on the seashore, with very many horses and chariots.<sup>5</sup>And all these kings joined their forces and came and encamped together at the waters of Merom to fight against Israel.<sup>6</sup>And the LORD said to Joshua, "Do not be afraid of them, for tomorrow at this time I will give over all of them, slain, to Israel. You shall hamstring their horses and burn their chariots with fire."<sup>7</sup>So Joshua and all his warriors came suddenly against them by the waters of Merom and fell upon them.<sup>8</sup>And the LORD gave them into the hand of Israel, who struck them and chased them as far as Great Sidon and Misrephoth-maim, and eastward as far as the Valley of Mizpeh. And they struck them until he left none remaining.<sup>9</sup>And Joshua did to them just as the LORD said to him: he hamstrung their horses and burned their chariots with fire.<sup>10</sup>And Joshua turned back at that time and captured Hazor and struck its king with the sword, for Hazor formerly was the head of all those kingdoms.<sup>11</sup>And they struck with the sword all who were in it, devoting them to destruction; there was none left that breathed. And he burned Hazor with fire.<sup>12</sup>And all the cities of those kings, and all their kings, Joshua captured, and struck them with the edge of the sword, devoting them to destruction, just as Moses the servant of the LORD had commanded.<sup>13</sup>But none of the cities that stood on mounds did Israel burn, except Hazor alone; that Joshua burned.<sup>14</sup>And all the spoil of these cities and the livestock, the people of Israel took for their plunder. But every person they struck with the edge of the sword until they had destroyed them, and they did not leave any who breathed.<sup>15</sup>Just as the LORD had commanded Moses his servant, so Moses commanded Joshua, and so Joshua did. He left nothing undone of all that the LORD had commanded Moses.<sup>16</sup>So Joshua took all that land, the hill country and all the Negeb and all the land of Goshen and the lowland and the Arabah and the hill country of Israel and its lowland<sup>17</sup>from Mount Halak, which rises toward Seir, as far as Baal-gad in the Valley of Lebanon below Mount Hermon. And he captured all their kings and struck them and put them to death.<sup>18</sup>Joshua made war a long time with all those kings.<sup>19</sup>There was not a city that made peace with the people of Israel except the Hivites, the inhabitants of Gibeon. They took them all in battle.<sup>20</sup>For it was the LORD's doing to harden their hearts that they should come against Israel in battle, in order that they should be devoted to destruction and should receive no mercy but be destroyed, just as the LORD commanded Moses.<sup>21</sup>And Joshua came at that time and cut off the Anakim from the hill country, from Hebron, from Debir, from Anab, and from all the hill country of Judah, and from all the hill country of Israel. Joshua devoted them to destruction with their cities.<sup>22</sup>There was none of the Anakim left in the land of the people of Israel. Only in Gaza, in Gath, and in Ashdod did some remain.<sup>23</sup>So Joshua took the whole land, according to all that the LORD had spoken to Moses. And Joshua gave it for an inheritance to Israel according to their tribal allotments. And the land had rest from war.
11.overview:
The north assembles what the south could not: every king from the hill country to the coast, a horde like the sand on the seashore, with very many horses and chariots (v. 4).

God's answer comes with a clock on it, tomorrow at this time (v. 6), and with an order that has nothing to do with winning the battle: hamstring the horses, burn the chariots. Israel could have become the strongest power in the region by nightfall, and God would not let it.

Hazor, the head of the northern kingdoms, is burned, and verse 15 gives the verdict the writer wants on Joshua's whole career: he left nothing undone. Then the giants that had frightened a generation into the desert are cut off in a single verse (v. 21), a remnant is noted in three Philistine towns including Gath, and the conquest narrative ends in seven words: and the land had rest from war.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — Chariots at the Waters of Merom
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Jabin of Hazor does what Adoni-zedek did, on a larger scale: a summons to every king in the north, hill country, Arabah, lowland and coast, six nations named (vv. 1-3). What assembles is the largest force in the book, a horde with very many horses and chariots (v. 4), camped at the waters of Merom (v. 5). God's word to Joshua comes with a timetable attached: do not be afraid, tomorrow at this time I will give over all of them (v. 6). And with an odd instruction: hamstring the horses, burn the chariots. Israel attacks suddenly, the coalition breaks, and Joshua does exactly what he was told with the captured equipment (vv. 7-9).
verseByVerse.theology: Israel has no chariots. The enemy's advantage is not numbers alone but technology, and God's answer is not to give Israel better technology but to destroy the enemy's and forbid his people to keep any of it.
verseByVerse.examples: The phrase in verse 4, like the sand that is on the seashore, is the promise God made to Abraham about his own descendants (Gen. 22:17). Here it describes the army coming to kill them. The writer knew what he was doing with it.

verseByVerse.quote: When Jabin, king of Hazor, heard of this, he sent to Jobab king of Madon, and to the king of Shimron, and to the king of Achshaph, and to the kings who were in the northern hill country, and in the Arabah south of Chinneroth, and in the lowland, and in Naphoth-dor on the west, to the Canaanites in the east and the west, the Amorites, the Hittites, the Perizzites, and the Jebusites in the hill country, and the Hivites under Hermon in the land of Mizpah. And they came out with all their troops, a great horde, in number like the sand that is on the seashore, with very many horses and chariots. And all these kings joined their forces and came and encamped together at the waters of Merom to fight against Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two things about this army are new. The first is its size, described in the very words of God's promise to Abraham. The second is the equipment: very many horses and chariots. A chariot in that world was the decisive weapon, expensive, fast and terrifying, and infantry generally broke in front of it. Israel has none. They are a nation of foot soldiers who were slaves within living memory, and they are looking at massed armour.

They camp together, which is their mistake and God's arrangement. Every king in the north is now in one valley, and the entire northern war will be settled in a single morning.
verseByVerse.note: Hazor, north of the Sea of Galilee, was the largest city in Canaan.

verseByVerse.quote: And the LORD said to Joshua, "Do not be afraid of them, for tomorrow at this time I will give over all of them, slain, to Israel. You shall hamstring their horses and burn their chariots with fire." So Joshua and all his warriors came suddenly against them by the waters of Merom and fell upon them. And the LORD gave them into the hand of Israel, who struck them and chased them as far as Great Sidon and Misrephoth-maim, and eastward as far as the Valley of Mizpeh. And they struck them until he left none remaining. And Joshua did to them just as the LORD said to him: he hamstrung their horses and burned their chariots with fire.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The same sentence as always, and this time with a clock on it: tomorrow at this time. Then an instruction about what happens after the battle. Militarily it is close to insane. Chariots and trained horses were the most valuable plunder on any ancient battlefield, and Israel could have equipped itself in a day and become the strongest power in the region by nightfall.

God will not have it, and the reason is not that technology is wicked. It is that a nation which owns chariots will, sooner or later, trust them. Moses had written the rule into the law of the king before Israel had a king at all: he must not acquire many horses for himself (Deut. 17:16). The psalmist puts it in a sentence: some trust in chariots and some in horses, but we trust in the name of the LORD our God (Ps. 20:7).

Israel did not keep it: Solomon accumulated fourteen hundred chariots and imported horses from Egypt (1 Kings 10:26-29), buying back at great expense precisely what Joshua was ordered to burn.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Joshua turns back and takes Hazor, which had been the head of all those kingdoms, kills its king and burns the city (vv. 10-11). The other royal cities are captured, but verse 13 notes something practical: none of the cities standing on their mounds were burned, only Hazor. The spoil and livestock are taken as plunder while every person is destroyed (v. 14). And then verse 15, which is the summit of Joshua's whole career: as the LORD commanded Moses, so Moses commanded Joshua, and so Joshua did — he left nothing undone.
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 13 is not squeamishness; it is housekeeping. Israel is about to live in these towns. They burn the capital that organised the war and leave standing the houses they will move into — the houses Moses had promised them, which they did not build (Deut. 6:10-11).
verseByVerse.examples: The chain in verse 15 has four links and no slippage in any of them: the LORD commanded Moses; Moses commanded Joshua; Joshua did it; nothing was left out. It is the sentence the writer wants on Joshua's record, and it is the exact opposite of what will be said about the generation in the book of Judges.

verseByVerse.quote: And Joshua turned back at that time and captured Hazor and struck its king with the sword, for Hazor formerly was the head of all those kingdoms. And they struck with the sword all who were in it, devoting them to destruction; there was none left that breathed. And he burned Hazor with fire. And all the cities of those kings, and all their kings, Joshua captured, and struck them with the edge of the sword, devoting them to destruction, just as Moses the servant of the LORD had commanded. But none of the cities that stood on mounds did Israel burn, except Hazor alone; that Joshua burned. And all the spoil of these cities and the livestock, the people of Israel took for their plunder. But every person they struck with the edge of the sword until they had destroyed them, and they did not leave any who breathed. Just as the LORD had commanded Moses his servant, so Moses commanded Joshua, and so Joshua did. He left nothing undone of all that the LORD had commanded Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Hazor was the largest and most important city in the north, and the writer says so plainly: it had been the head of all those kingdoms. Killing the coalition in the field was the battle; burning its capital is the end of the war.

Excavations at Hazor have uncovered a great Canaanite city destroyed by an intense fire in the Late Bronze Age. Scholars debate who burned it and when, and the answer depends partly on when the exodus is dated, but the burned city fits verse 11 well.

The plunder is taken here by permission, exactly as at Ai.

Verse 15's last clause goes further than the others: he left nothing undone. Almost every failure in the rest of Israel's history is a failure of exactly this kind: not open defiance but things left undone, tribes that did not drive out the inhabitants, commands obeyed in the parts that suited. The book of Judges opens with a list of them.

The verdict on Joshua is that there was nothing outstanding. It is said fully of only one other servant, who could tell his Father, I glorified you on earth, having accomplished the work that you gave me to do (John 17:4). Our own obedience is always partial; his is complete and counted to those who trust him, and the Spirit he gives finishes in us what God began (Phil. 1:6).

Judges 4 has another Jabin, king of Hazor. Jabin seems to have been a royal name, and Hazor was rebuilt in the generations between.

Was it just, in the north as in the south? This was God’s judgment on peoples whose sin had ripened over centuries (Gen 15:16; Deut 9:4–5), including child sacrifice (Deut 12:31), and Israel was warned that the land would vomit it out too for the same sins (Lev 18:24–28). It was a unique command, carried out through Israel at one moment in redemptive history. It is no pattern for any later war, nation or church: Christ’s kingdom is not of this world (John 18:36), and the church’s weapons are not of the flesh (2 Cor 10:4).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The summary covers the whole country, from Mount Halak in the south to Baal-gad under Hermon in the north, and states plainly that this took a long time (vv. 16-18). Verse 19 records that not one city made peace except Gibeon — and verse 20 gives the reason behind the reason: it was the LORD's doing to harden their hearts. Then the Anakim, the giants who had frightened a whole generation into the wilderness, are cut off from the hill country, with a remnant surviving in three Philistine cities (vv. 21-22). And the chapter ends in seven words that the book has been walking towards: and the land had rest from war (v. 23).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 20 is hard and verse 19 is its control. Peace was available — the text says so by noting the one city that took it. The hardening is judicial: God gives a people over to what they have already chosen, exactly as with Pharaoh (Ex. 9:16; Rom. 9:17-18), and in the same book he takes a prostitute and four Gibeonite towns out of the same judgment.
verseByVerse.examples: The Anakim were the reason Israel spent forty years in a desert. Ten spies had come back saying we seemed to ourselves like grasshoppers (Num. 13:33), and the nation believed them. Here one verse disposes of the giants.

verseByVerse.quote: So Joshua took all that land, the hill country and all the Negeb and all the land of Goshen and the lowland and the Arabah and the hill country of Israel and its lowland from Mount Halak, which rises toward Seir, as far as Baal-gad in the Valley of Lebanon below Mount Hermon. And he captured all their kings and struck them and put them to death. Joshua made war a long time with all those kings. There was not a city that made peace with the people of Israel except the Hivites, the inhabitants of Gibeon. They took them all in battle. For it was the LORD's doing to harden their hearts that they should come against Israel in battle, in order that they should be devoted to destruction and should receive no mercy but be destroyed, just as the LORD commanded Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The narrative has been moving fast, a city a verse, and here the writer stops to say that Joshua made war a long time: years.

Gibeon got its treaty by fraud, and it need not have been fraud; the terms existed and any city could have sought them. Rahab needed no treaty at all, only belief. What the country did, almost without exception, was fight.

Then one of the hardest sentences in this book: behind their resistance stood God, hardening. Scripture says the same of Pharaoh, who had first hardened his own heart (Ex. 9:16; Rom. 9:17-18). It is not arbitrary cruelty: the same God had taken a Canaanite prostitute out of a burning city and put her in the family of the Messiah. Hardening in Scripture is judicial, God confirming people in the direction they have already set, and never the whole story of what he was doing in that country.

What it does mean is that the outcome was never in the balance. The kings gathering at Merom believed they were making a decision. They were being gathered.
verseByVerse.note: The conquest took “a long time” (v. 18): about seven years, judging from Caleb’s ages (14:7, 10).

verseByVerse.quote: And Joshua came at that time and cut off the Anakim from the hill country, from Hebron, from Debir, from Anab, and from all the hill country of Judah, and from all the hill country of Israel. Joshua devoted them to destruction with their cities. There was none of the Anakim left in the land of the people of Israel. Only in Gaza, in Gath, and in Ashdod did some remain. So Joshua took the whole land, according to all that the LORD had spoken to Moses. And Joshua gave it for an inheritance to Israel according to their tribal allotments. And the land had rest from war.
verseByVerse.commentary:
One verse settles a question that had cost the nation forty years. Joshua was one of the two spies who did not believe the report; now an old man, he cuts those same giants out of those same hills. The giants were exactly as advertised. What changed was who the people were measuring them against.

A remnant survived in three Philistine cities on the coast, and one of them is Gath.

Centuries later a champion came out of the Philistine camp to challenge Israel, nearly ten feet tall in the Hebrew text (the Greek Old Testament and a Dead Sea Scroll of Samuel give about six and a half feet, still a giant to the men of that day), and the text is careful to say where he came from: Goliath of Gath (1 Sam. 17:4). An army of Israelites was paralysed by him, exactly as their ancestors had been, and a shepherd boy who had not been at Merom killed him with a stone.

Behind the land had rest from war stand four hundred years in Egypt, blood on the doorframes, a sea, forty years of walking in circles, a river, a walled city, and years of fighting. It did not last, and Hebrews puts it exactly: if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken of another day later on, and therefore there remains a Sabbath rest for the people of God (Heb. 4:8-9).

The rest under Joshua was real, and it was a copy. The one who gives the real thing carries the same name and made the offer in the plainest words anyone has ever used about it: come to me, all who labour and are heavy laden, and I will give you rest (Matt. 11:28). The land had rest from war because God fought it. So does the soul.

How does “took the whole land” fit 13:1, “very much land remains”? Joshua broke the organised power of the Canaanite coalitions, so Israel was at rest from war, but local pockets remained for each tribe to take. Both statements are true.
verseByVerse.note: The three Philistine towns where Anakim survived were Gaza, Gath and Ashdod (v. 22).

11.theology:
Burning the chariots. God destroys the enemy's technology and forbids his people to keep any of it (v. 6), because possession leads to reliance (Ps. 20:7; Deut. 17:16). Every generation has its own version of the captured chariot: the thing that would make the church formidable, and would quietly make God unnecessary.

Nothing left undone. Verse 15 is the high-water mark of the book. Partial obedience is the ordinary form disobedience takes among religious people, because from a distance it looks like the real thing.

The hardening, and its control. Verse 20 is not softened, but the hardening is judicial rather than arbitrary: peace was available, and one city took it (v. 19).

Rest, and the rest that remains. The rest that closes the conquest did not last, and Hebrews draws the conclusion that a Sabbath rest remains for the people of God (Heb. 4:8-9). The rest under Joshua was real and it was a copy; the one who gives the original carries the same name (Matt. 11:28).
11.examples:
Then: A nation of foot soldiers walked towards massed chariots at Merom, won, and then spent the evening crippling horses and burning the best military equipment in the country because God had told them to. Years of fighting later, an old man cut the giants out of the hills that had terrified his own generation when he was young, and the land was quiet.

Now: Two questions come straight out of this chapter. The first is what your chariots are: the resource, position or security that would make you formidable and would quietly make God optional. Joshua stood on a won field and set fire to his. The second is verse 15: not whether you have disobeyed anything, but whether anything has been left undone. That is where Israel actually lost the land, and it never felt like rebellion at the time. The question is asked by a God who fought every battle in this chapter for them, and the one who left nothing undone for us gives his Spirit for what remains.

12.title: The Roll Call of Defeated Kings
12.text: <sup>1</sup>Now these are the kings of the land whom the people of Israel defeated and took possession of their land beyond the Jordan toward the sunrise, from the Valley of the Arnon to Mount Hermon, with all the Arabah eastward:<sup>2</sup>Sihon king of the Amorites who lived at Heshbon and ruled from Aroer, which is on the edge of the Valley of the Arnon, and from the middle of the valley as far as the river Jabbok, the boundary of the Ammonites, that is, half of Gilead,<sup>3</sup>and the Arabah to the Sea of Chinneroth eastward, and in the direction of Beth-jeshimoth, to the Sea of the Arabah, the Salt Sea, southward to the foot of the slopes of Pisgah;<sup>4</sup>and Og king of Bashan, one of the remnant of the Rephaim, who lived at Ashtaroth and at Edrei<sup>5</sup>and ruled over Mount Hermon and Salecah and all Bashan to the boundary of the Geshurites and the Maacathites, and over half of Gilead to the boundary of Sihon king of Heshbon.<sup>6</sup>Moses, the servant of the LORD, and the people of Israel defeated them. And Moses the servant of the LORD gave their land for a possession to the Reubenites and the Gadites and the half-tribe of Manasseh.<sup>7</sup>And these are the kings of the land whom Joshua and the people of Israel defeated on the west side of the Jordan, from Baal-gad in the Valley of Lebanon to Mount Halak, that rises toward Seir (and Joshua gave their land to the tribes of Israel as a possession according to their allotments,<sup>8</sup>in the hill country, in the lowland, in the Arabah, in the slopes, in the wilderness, and in the Negeb, the land of the Hittites, the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites):<sup>9</sup>the king of Jericho, one; the king of Ai, which is beside Bethel, one;<sup>10</sup>the king of Jerusalem, one; the king of Hebron, one;<sup>11</sup>the king of Jarmuth, one; the king of Lachish, one;<sup>12</sup>the king of Eglon, one; the king of Gezer, one;<sup>13</sup>the king of Debir, one; the king of Geder, one;<sup>14</sup>the king of Hormah, one; the king of Arad, one;<sup>15</sup>the king of Libnah, one; the king of Adullam, one;<sup>16</sup>the king of Makkedah, one; the king of Bethel, one;<sup>17</sup>the king of Tappuah, one; the king of Hepher, one;<sup>18</sup>the king of Aphek, one; the king of Lasharon, one;<sup>19</sup>the king of Madon, one; the king of Hazor, one;<sup>20</sup>the king of Shimron-meron, one; the king of Achshaph, one;<sup>21</sup>the king of Taanach, one; the king of Megiddo, one;<sup>22</sup>the king of Kedesh, one; the king of Jokneam in Carmel, one;<sup>23</sup>the king of Dor in Naphath-dor, one; the king of Goiim in Galilee, one;<sup>24</sup>the king of Tirzah, one: in all, thirty-one kings.
12.overview:
The chapter is an inventory: two kings east of the Jordan, then thirty-one west of it, each entered with a single word after his name, one.

The tally starts not at Jericho but east of the river, with Sihon and Og, victories won under Moses before Joshua commanded anything. What one leader began and another finished is counted in a single column, because it had a single author.

Two things are easy to miss. About fifteen of these kings have no story in the book, only a name. And the king of Jerusalem is counted (v. 10) although Jerusalem was not taken. That is the hinge into the second half of the book: a defeated king is not an occupied city, and the very next verse says so (13:1).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — The Two Kings East of the Jordan
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The roll opens on the wrong side of the river and before Joshua's time. Sihon king of the Amorites at Heshbon, with his territory mapped from the Arnon to the Jabbok (vv. 1-3), and Og king of Bashan, one of the remnant of the Rephaim, ruling Hermon and Salecah and all Bashan (vv. 4-5). Verse 6 names who beat them and what became of the land: Moses the servant of the LORD, and the eastern tribes who were given it as a possession.
verseByVerse.theology: The tally of the conquest begins with two victories Joshua had nothing to do with. The writer is refusing to let the book be about Joshua: what was begun under one leader and finished under another is counted as a single work with a single author.
verseByVerse.examples: Moses is called the servant of the LORD twice in verse 6, which is the title the book opened with in its first sentence (1:1). Joshua does not get it here; the book gives him that title only at his death (24:29), and until then the honour of it is left where it was.

verseByVerse.quote: Now these are the kings of the land whom the people of Israel defeated and took possession of their land beyond the Jordan toward the sunrise, from the Valley of the Arnon to Mount Hermon, with all the Arabah eastward: Sihon king of the Amorites who lived at Heshbon and ruled from Aroer, which is on the edge of the Valley of the Arnon, and from the middle of the valley as far as the river Jabbok, the boundary of the Ammonites, that is, half of Gilead, and the Arabah to the Sea of Chinneroth eastward, and in the direction of Beth-jeshimoth, to the Sea of the Arabah, the Salt Sea, southward to the foot of the slopes of Pisgah; and Og king of Bashan, one of the remnant of the Rephaim, who lived at Ashtaroth and at Edrei and ruled over Mount Hermon and Salecah and all Bashan to the boundary of the Geshurites and the Maacathites, and over half of Gilead to the boundary of Sihon king of Heshbon. Moses, the servant of the LORD, and the people of Israel defeated them. And Moses the servant of the LORD gave their land for a possession to the Reubenites and the Gadites and the half-tribe of Manasseh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Both kings were formidable. Sihon had refused Israel passage and come out to fight them; Og was one of the last of the Rephaim, the giant peoples, and Deuteronomy records the size of his iron bed as a matter of public curiosity: nine cubits long, something over thirteen feet (Deut. 3:11).

These two had been beaten before Israel ever saw the Jordan, and their story is told in Numbers. Rahab had heard about them on her roof and named them in her list of what God had done (2:10); the Gibeonites cited them in their sales pitch (9:10). They are the reason the whole country was frightened before the invasion started.

The writer could have started the tally at chapter 6. He starts it with a dead man's victories instead: what Moses began and could not finish, Joshua completed, and neither of them is the subject of the sentence.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–24 — Thirty-One, Counted One at a Time
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The list turns west, sets the boundaries from Baal-gad to Mount Halak, and runs through every kind of terrain and all six nations (vv. 7-8). Then the roll itself: Jericho, Ai, Jerusalem, Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish, Eglon, Gezer, Debir and twenty-two more, each one followed by the same single word — one. The northern names come at the end, Hazor among them, and Megiddo, and the chapter closes with the total: in all, thirty-one kings (v. 24).
verseByVerse.theology: About fifteen of these kings have no battle and no story anywhere in the book: Geder, Hormah, Arad, Adullam, Tappuah, Hepher, Aphek, Lasharon, Taanach, Megiddo, Kedesh, Jokneam, Dor (named only in passing at 11:2), Goiim, Tirzah. The list is longer than the narrative.
verseByVerse.examples: The king of Jerusalem is counted in verse 10, and Jerusalem was not taken (see the note on vv. 9-16). The very next verse of this book says what that means: there remains yet very much land to possess (13:1).

verseByVerse.quote: And these are the kings of the land whom Joshua and the people of Israel defeated on the west side of the Jordan, from Baal-gad in the Valley of Lebanon to Mount Halak, that rises toward Seir (and Joshua gave their land to the tribes of Israel as a possession according to their allotments, in the hill country, in the lowland, in the Arabah, in the slopes, in the wilderness, and in the Negeb, the land of the Hittites, the Amorites, the Canaanites, the Perizzites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites):
verseByVerse.commentary:
The clause in brackets is doing quiet work. Joshua gave their land to the tribes: the conquest is already being spoken of as an inheritance being distributed, which is what the next nine chapters are about. The war is finished; the paperwork is not.

Six kinds of country and six nations, and every one had its own way of being difficult. Hill country favours the defender. The lowland is chariot country. The Arabah is furnace-hot below sea level. The Negeb is desert.

A nation of former slaves who had spent forty years in one kind of terrain has now fought in all six, and the geography is listed so that the reader can see the size of what was given.

verseByVerse.quote: the king of Jericho, one; the king of Ai, which is beside Bethel, one; the king of Jerusalem, one; the king of Hebron, one; the king of Jarmuth, one; the king of Lachish, one; the king of Eglon, one; the king of Gezer, one; the king of Debir, one; the king of Geder, one; the king of Hormah, one; the king of Arad, one; the king of Libnah, one; the king of Adullam, one; the king of Makkedah, one; the king of Bethel, one;
verseByVerse.commentary:
The roll has a sound: Jericho, one. Ai, one. It is written the way a quartermaster writes, and the flatness is the point. These were thrones. Each name is a walled city with a court, an army and a god, and each one is entered in a ledger with a single digit beside it.

What terrified a generation is now stock-taking.

The early names walk the reader back through the book. Jericho, where the wall fell flat. Ai, where thirty-six men died for plunder buried under a tent. Then Jerusalem, Hebron, Jarmuth, Lachish and Eglon in a row: the five kings of the southern coalition, in the order they came out of the cave at Makkedah.

The third name will not stay quiet. Adoni-zedek is dead, and Jerusalem is not taken. The book of Judges records that the Jebusites went on living there alongside Benjamin (Judges 1:21), and the city is not held until David takes it, generations later (2 Samuel 5:6-9). Readers who know Judges 1:8, where Judah sets the city on fire, are not looking at a contradiction: a raid that burns a town is not a garrison that holds it, and the Jebusites stayed or returned. A defeated king is not an occupied city.

That gap between victory and possession is the honest note this list is quietly sounding, and the next verse says it out loud (13:1).

verseByVerse.quote: the king of Tappuah, one; the king of Hepher, one; the king of Aphek, one; the king of Lasharon, one; the king of Madon, one; the king of Hazor, one; the king of Shimron-meron, one; the king of Achshaph, one; the king of Taanach, one; the king of Megiddo, one; the king of Kedesh, one; the king of Jokneam in Carmel, one; the king of Dor in Naphath-dor, one; the king of Goiim in Galilee, one; the king of Tirzah, one: in all, thirty-one kings.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Whole campaigns happened that the writer never wrote up, and if the account of the conquest were all we had, we would assume Israel fought about eight battles. They fought at least thirty-one, and chapter 11 already told us it took a long time.

Most of what God does never gets written down. There is no chapter for the king of Lasharon, and he is on the list.

Hazor, the head of all those kingdoms, is entered with the same single digit as everybody else. And Megiddo, the town on the pass that controlled the road across the plain of Jezreel, whose name most likely lies behind Armageddon (in Greek Harmagedon, probably ‘mountain of Megiddo’), the name John hears in his vision for the place where the kings of the whole world are gathered at the end (Rev. 16:16). The king of Megiddo is number twenty-six on Joshua's inventory.

The chapter ends with a number. Paul, describing the cross, uses the language of a Roman victory parade: God disarmed the rulers and authorities and put them to open shame, leading them in triumph, and the place he did it was a cross (Col. 2:15). The same accounting is still being kept, and the last enemy on the list has a name too, and it is death (1 Cor. 15:26).

Not one of the thirty-one thrones is standing. The LORD God of Israel counted them out, one at a time, and gave the ground they had been sitting on to a nation of former slaves who could not have taken a single city on their own.

12.theology:
One work, two leaders. The roll begins with Moses' victories east of the Jordan, which Joshua had no part in, and the title the servant of the LORD is given to Moses twice in the verse that closes them (v. 6). The conquest is presented as a single act of God spanning two generations and two mediators — begun under the man who could not enter, and finished under the man who carried the name Yeshua (see 1:1 and Heb. 4:8).

The list is longer than the story. Most of what God did in those years was never written up, which is a fair description of most faithful work in most centuries.

Victory is not yet possession. Jerusalem's king is counted while Jerusalem stands (Judg. 1:21). The whole Christian life sits in that gap: the decisive battle fought and won, the ground still being walked.

The accounting continues. Paul pictures the cross as God's triumph over the rulers and authorities (Col. 2:15), and the last entry on that ledger is already named: death (1 Corinthians 15:26).

Why count the dead? A reader may flinch at a page that tallies slain kings. The book has given its reasons in the battle chapters: this was God’s judgment on peoples whose sin he had borne with for centuries (Genesis 15:16; Deuteronomy 9:5), commanded for this land at this moment, and never a licence for any later war. The list records that God kept his word to Abraham, through a people who could not have taken one city alone, and it waits for the King who wins his war by dying rather than by killing.
12.examples:
Then: Somebody sat down and wrote out the names of thirty-one kings with the word one after each, and added them up at the bottom. It is the least dramatic page in the book and it is the receipt for everything in the eleven chapters before it.

Now: Two things to take from a list. Many of these kings have no story, and they are still counted, which is worth remembering for anyone whose work nobody writes up. And the king of Jerusalem is on the list while the city is still occupied, which is the shape of the Christian life exactly: the decisive victory is a matter of record, and there is a great deal of ground you have not yet walked on. The next verse of the book says so, and says it to a man who was old and tired.

13.title: Land Still to Be Possessed
13.text: <sup>1</sup>Now Joshua was old and advanced in years, and the LORD said to him, "You are old and advanced in years, and there remains yet very much land to possess.<sup>2</sup>This is the land that yet remains: all the regions of the Philistines, and all those of the Geshurites<sup>3</sup>(from the Shihor, which is east of Egypt, northward to the boundary of Ekron, it is counted as Canaanite; there are five rulers of the Philistines, those of Gaza, Ashdod, Ashkelon, Gath, and Ekron), and those of the Avvim,<sup>4</sup>in the south, all the land of the Canaanites, and Mearah that belongs to the Sidonians, to Aphek, to the boundary of the Amorites,<sup>5</sup>and the land of the Gebalites, and all Lebanon, toward the sunrise, from Baal-gad below Mount Hermon to Lebo-hamath,<sup>6</sup>all the inhabitants of the hill country from Lebanon to Misrephoth-maim, even all the Sidonians. I myself will drive them out from before the people of Israel. Only allot the land to Israel for an inheritance, as I have commanded you.<sup>7</sup>Now therefore divide this land for an inheritance to the nine tribes and half the tribe of Manasseh."<sup>8</sup>With the other half of the tribe of Manasseh the Reubenites and the Gadites received their inheritance, which Moses gave them, beyond the Jordan eastward, as Moses the servant of the LORD gave them:<sup>9</sup>from Aroer, which is on the edge of the Valley of the Arnon, and the city that is in the middle of the valley, and all the tableland of Medeba as far as Dibon;<sup>10</sup>and all the cities of Sihon king of the Amorites, who reigned in Heshbon, as far as the boundary of the Ammonites;<sup>11</sup>and Gilead, and the region of the Geshurites and Maacathites, and all Mount Hermon, and all Bashan to Salecah;<sup>12</sup>all the kingdom of Og in Bashan, who reigned in Ashtaroth and in Edrei (he alone was left of the remnant of the Rephaim); these Moses had struck and driven out.<sup>13</sup>Yet the people of Israel did not drive out the Geshurites or the Maacathites, but Geshur and Maacath dwell in the midst of Israel to this day.<sup>14</sup>To the tribe of Levi alone Moses gave no inheritance. The offerings by fire to the LORD God of Israel are their inheritance, as he said to him.<sup>15</sup>And Moses gave an inheritance to the tribe of the people of Reuben according to their clans.<sup>16</sup>So their territory was from Aroer, which is on the edge of the Valley of the Arnon, and the city that is in the middle of the valley, and all the tableland by Medeba;<sup>17</sup>with Heshbon, and all its cities that are in the tableland; Dibon, and Bamoth-baal, and Beth-baal-meon,<sup>18</sup>and Jahaz, and Kedemoth, and Mephaath,<sup>19</sup>and Kiriathaim, and Sibmah, and Zereth-shahar on the hill of the valley,<sup>20</sup>and Beth-peor, and the slopes of Pisgah, and Beth-jeshimoth,<sup>21</sup>that is, all the cities of the tableland, and all the kingdom of Sihon king of the Amorites, who reigned in Heshbon, whom Moses defeated with the leaders of Midian, Evi and Rekem and Zur and Hur and Reba, the princes of Sihon, who lived in the land.<sup>22</sup>Balaam also, the son of Beor, the one who practiced divination, was killed with the sword by the people of Israel among the rest of their slain.<sup>23</sup>And the border of the people of Reuben was the Jordan as a boundary. This was the inheritance of the people of Reuben, according to their clans with their cities and villages.<sup>24</sup>Moses gave an inheritance also to the tribe of Gad, to the people of Gad, according to their clans.<sup>25</sup>Their territory was Jazer, and all the cities of Gilead, and half the land of the Ammonites, to Aroer, which is east of Rabbah,<sup>26</sup>and from Heshbon to Ramath-mizpeh and Betonim, and from Mahanaim to the territory of Debir,<sup>27</sup>and in the valley Beth-haram, Beth-nimrah, Succoth, and Zaphon, the rest of the kingdom of Sihon king of Heshbon, having the Jordan as a boundary, to the lower end of the Sea of Chinnereth, eastward beyond the Jordan.<sup>28</sup>This is the inheritance of the people of Gad according to their clans, with their cities and villages.<sup>29</sup>And Moses gave an inheritance to the half-tribe of Manasseh. It was allotted to the half-tribe of the people of Manasseh according to their clans.<sup>30</sup>Their region extended from Mahanaim, through all Bashan, the whole kingdom of Og king of Bashan, and all the towns of Jair, which are in Bashan, sixty cities,<sup>31</sup>and half Gilead, and Ashtaroth, and Edrei, the cities of the kingdom of Og in Bashan. These were allotted to the people of Machir the son of Manasseh for the half of the people of Machir according to their clans.<sup>32</sup>These are the inheritances that Moses distributed in the plains of Moab, beyond the Jordan east of Jericho.<sup>33</sup>But to the tribe of Levi Moses gave no inheritance; the LORD God of Israel is their inheritance, just as he said to them.
13.overview:
The war is over and the book changes shape. What follows is a land registry, and it opens on an old man being told that he is old and that there remains yet very much land to possess (v. 1).

Verse 13 sounds the note that will run through the rest of the book and then open Judges: Geshur and Maacath were not driven out, and they dwell in the midst of Israel to this day. And the whole survey is framed by one tribe that receives none of it: Levi, whose inheritance is the LORD himself (vv. 14, 33).
13.theology:
Given and not yet taken. Chapter 1 says God has given the land; chapter 13 says very much of it remains to be possessed; and verse 6 holds both together. That is the position of every Christian: in possession of every spiritual blessing and still required to put on the armour and stand.

Whose land, and for how long? A reader today will ask what these boundaries mean now, and Christians answer in more than one way. Many in the Reformed tradition hold that the land promise is fulfilled and enlarged in Christ: Abraham was to be heir of the world (Romans 4:13), the meek will inherit the earth (Matthew 5:5), and the patriarchs were looking for a better, heavenly country (Hebrews 11:16). Others, including many Reformed and Puritan writers, expect God still to show great mercy to Abraham’s physical descendants, because the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable (Romans 11:29), and some of them expect a future for Israel in this land. Faithful Christians differ here and should do so kindly. All agree that no one inherits anything from God except through Christ, the true offspring of Abraham (Galatians 3:16, 29).

What is not driven out does not stay still. The failure at verse 13 is not defiance and it costs nothing that year. Centuries later it is a marriage alliance, a grandson in exile, and a rebellion (2 Sam. 3:3; 13:37-38; 15:8). Scripture keeps records of this kind, and what a generation tolerates because it is tired is inherited by people who did not choose it.

A name in a list of fields. Balaam is named in the register among the slain (v. 22), and what he did should be remembered. He could not curse Israel, because blessings came out every time he tried, so he taught Balak to seduce them instead, and twenty-four thousand died at Peor (Num. 25:9; 31:16). The danger to God's people was never chiefly military.

Levi's portion. The other tribes walked away from the allotment holding a map. Levi was handed nothing at all, and the explanation is one sentence: the LORD God of Israel is their inheritance. The rest of Scripture treats that as the richest outcome of the day, in surveyor's language: the LORD is my chosen portion and my cup; you hold my lot; the lines have fallen for me in pleasant places (Ps. 16:5-6). Everything else in this chapter has since changed hands. And Levi’s portion is no longer one tribe’s: in Christ every believer is made part of a royal priesthood (1 Peter 2:9) and is given an inheritance that is imperishable, undefiled and unfading, kept in heaven (1 Peter 1:4), which is God himself, possessed through his Son.
13.examples:
Then: An old soldier was told there was more to do than he had time for, and Israel was ordered to divide up a country it did not yet hold. The tribes were read their allotments one by one, and when the reading finished the men of Levi were still standing there with nothing in their hands.

Now: Two things to take. The first is verse 13, and the question it asks is not whether you have rebelled against God but what you have simply stopped short of finishing, and let go on living in the middle of your life because the war got long. Geshur was a small compromise for about four hundred years. The God who says I myself will drive them out (v. 6) has not left that work to your willpower: his Spirit is given to put to death what we have let stay (Rom. 8:13), and what we confess he forgives (1 John 1:9). The second is the test at the end: if everything on your side of the register were repossessed tomorrow, what would you still have? The other tribes were given things God had made. Levi was given God.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The chapter opens on an old man being told he is old. Joshua is advanced in years, and God says it back to him in the same breath as the news that there remains yet very much land to possess (v. 1). What follows is an inventory of what is not yet taken: the whole Philistine coast with its five cities, the Geshurites, the Sidonians, Lebanon as far as Lebo-hamath (vv. 2-5). Then two sentences that sit side by side without apology: I myself will drive them out, and only allot the land to Israel for an inheritance (v. 6). Divide it among the nine and a half tribes (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: The land was given in chapter 1 and most of it is still occupied in chapter 13. That is not a contradiction the book is embarrassed by; it states both facts in one verse. The inheritance is theirs by deed and not yet theirs in fact.
verseByVerse.examples: The first item on the unconquered list is the Philistines, with all five of their cities named. They are about to be Israel's chief enemy for generations: through Samson, through the loss of the ark, through Saul's death on Gilboa, until David finally breaks them. Centuries of trouble are listed here as unfinished business.

verseByVerse.quote: Now Joshua was old and advanced in years, and the LORD said to him, "You are old and advanced in years, and there remains yet very much land to possess. This is the land that yet remains: all the regions of the Philistines, and all those of the Geshurites (from the Shihor, which is east of Egypt, northward to the boundary of Ekron, it is counted as Canaanite; there are five rulers of the Philistines, those of Gaza, Ashdod, Ashkelon, Gath, and Ekron), and those of the Avvim, in the south, all the land of the Canaanites, and Mearah that belongs to the Sidonians, to Aphek, to the boundary of the Amorites, and the land of the Gebalites, and all Lebanon, toward the sunrise, from Baal-gad below Mount Hermon to Lebo-hamath, all the inhabitants of the hill country from Lebanon to Misrephoth-maim, even all the Sidonians. I myself will drive them out from before the people of Israel. Only allot the land to Israel for an inheritance, as I have commanded you. Now therefore divide this land for an inheritance to the nine tribes and half the tribe of Manasseh."
verseByVerse.commentary:
God tells an old man that he is old, and there is nothing cruel in it: it is plain honesty to a man who has been fighting for years and is not going to finish. Set very much land against 1:3 and 11:23. All are true: the land is given, most of it is not yet taken, and the man who was supposed to take it is out of time. Among the Philistine cities is Gath, where the giants were left standing two chapters ago.

Then two sentences that ought to pull against each other and do not: God will drive them out, and Israel is to allot territory that is still full of Philistines: to draw the boundaries of fields nobody has walked on, and hand out title deeds to towns still held by somebody else. That is a strange instruction and it is exactly the instruction the church lives under. Paul writes to people who have every spiritual blessing already and tells them, before the letter ends, to put on the armour and stand (Eph. 1:3; 6:11).

Then how could 11:23 say that Joshua took the whole land? Because that is the summary language of ancient war: the armies were broken and the kings killed, not every person in every place. This verse says much land remained, and Judges 1 tells of tribes still driving out the inhabitants. Both are true: the Canaanite kingdoms were broken, and the long work of settling had only begun.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–14 — What Was Not Driven Out
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The record turns to the two and a half tribes east of the Jordan, whose land Moses had given them: the tableland, the cities of Sihon, Gilead, Bashan, the whole kingdom of Og (vv. 8-12). Then verse 13, dropped into the middle of a property register without comment: the people of Israel did not drive out the Geshurites or the Maacathites, and they dwell in the midst of Israel to this day. And then verse 14, which is not about land at all: to Levi alone Moses gave no inheritance, because the offerings made by fire to the LORD are their inheritance.
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 13 is the first of a series that will run through the next few chapters and then open the book of Judges: the towns that were not taken. Nobody rebelled. The war simply stopped somewhere short of the orders, and the writer keeps a list.
verseByVerse.examples: Geshur did not stay quiet. Centuries later David married Maacah, daughter of the king of Geshur; their son Absalom murdered his half-brother and fled to his grandfather's kingdom for three years, and came home to raise the revolt that nearly ended David's reign (2 Sam. 3:3; 13:37-38; 15:8). What was left in the midst of Israel here came back as David's in-laws.

verseByVerse.quote: With the other half of the tribe of Manasseh the Reubenites and the Gadites received their inheritance, which Moses gave them, beyond the Jordan eastward, as Moses the servant of the LORD gave them: from Aroer, which is on the edge of the Valley of the Arnon, and the city that is in the middle of the valley, and all the tableland of Medeba as far as Dibon; and all the cities of Sihon king of the Amorites, who reigned in Heshbon, as far as the boundary of the Ammonites; and Gilead, and the region of the Geshurites and Maacathites, and all Mount Hermon, and all Bashan to Salecah; all the kingdom of Og in Bashan, who reigned in Ashtaroth and in Edrei (he alone was left of the remnant of the Rephaim); these Moses had struck and driven out. Yet the people of Israel did not drive out the Geshurites or the Maacathites, but Geshur and Maacath dwell in the midst of Israel to this day. To the tribe of Levi alone Moses gave no inheritance. The offerings by fire to the LORD God of Israel are their inheritance, as he said to him.
verseByVerse.commentary: Verse 13 is dropped into a property list with no comment. There is no story of a command refused; two peoples went on living where they had always lived, still there to this day. The same note will sound through the next chapters (Judah, Manasseh, Ephraim), and Judges opens by explaining what it cost. In Geshur's case the cost came due under David, when its princess became Absalom's mother and Absalom's rebellion drove the king barefoot out of Jerusalem (2 Sam. 15:30).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 15–33 — Fields for Eleven Tribes, and God for One
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The rest of the chapter is a survey: Reuben's towns on the tableland (vv. 15-23), Gad's territory in Gilead and the valley (vv. 24-28), and the half-tribe of Manasseh with all Bashan and the sixty towns of Jair (vv. 29-31). One person is named in the middle of all this property: Balaam son of Beor, killed with the sword (v. 22). Verse 32 closes the eastern register, and then the chapter ends where verse 14 began, and says it more plainly: to Levi, Moses gave no inheritance, for the LORD God of Israel is their inheritance (v. 33).
verseByVerse.theology: The lists are dull on purpose and they are a receipt. Every boundary and village in them was a sentence spoken to a childless man in Genesis, and here it is surveyed, divided and handed over. God's promises do not arrive as sentiments; they arrive as addresses.
verseByVerse.examples: The chapter is framed by the tribe that got none of it. Verse 14 and verse 33 sit at either end of the survey like bookends, and both say the same thing in different words: Levi has no fields, and Levi has the LORD.

verseByVerse.quote: And Moses gave an inheritance to the tribe of the people of Reuben according to their clans. So their territory was from Aroer, which is on the edge of the Valley of the Arnon, and the city that is in the middle of the valley, and all the tableland by Medeba; with Heshbon, and all its cities that are in the tableland; Dibon, and Bamoth-baal, and Beth-baal-meon, and Jahaz, and Kedemoth, and Mephaath, and Kiriathaim, and Sibmah, and Zereth-shahar on the hill of the valley, and Beth-peor, and the slopes of Pisgah, and Beth-jeshimoth, that is, all the cities of the tableland, and all the kingdom of Sihon king of the Amorites, who reigned in Heshbon, whom Moses defeated with the leaders of Midian, Evi and Rekem and Zur and Hur and Reba, the princes of Sihon, who lived in the land. Balaam also, the son of Beor, the one who practiced divination, was killed with the sword by the people of Israel among the rest of their slain. And the border of the people of Reuben was the Jordan as a boundary. This was the inheritance of the people of Reuben, according to their clans with their cities and villages.
verseByVerse.commentary: In the middle of a chapter about fields stands a man. Balaam was the prophet-for-hire who could not curse Israel, the great comic failure of Numbers. What he did afterwards is not comic: he advised Balak to ruin them from the inside, and it worked at Peor when cursing had not (Num. 31:16). The risen Christ names the problem in a compromising church as the teaching of Balaam, who taught Balak to put a stumbling block before the sons of Israel (Rev. 2:14). Nobody could curse them. They had to be talked into it.

verseByVerse.quote: Moses gave an inheritance also to the tribe of Gad, to the people of Gad, according to their clans. Their territory was Jazer, and all the cities of Gilead, and half the land of the Ammonites, to Aroer, which is east of Rabbah, and from Heshbon to Ramath-mizpeh and Betonim, and from Mahanaim to the territory of Debir, and in the valley Beth-haram, Beth-nimrah, Succoth, and Zaphon, the rest of the kingdom of Sihon king of Heshbon, having the Jordan as a boundary, to the lower end of the Sea of Chinnereth, eastward beyond the Jordan. This is the inheritance of the people of Gad according to their clans, with their cities and villages. And Moses gave an inheritance to the half-tribe of Manasseh. It was allotted to the half-tribe of the people of Manasseh according to their clans. Their region extended from Mahanaim, through all Bashan, the whole kingdom of Og king of Bashan, and all the towns of Jair, which are in Bashan, sixty cities, and half Gilead, and Ashtaroth, and Edrei, the cities of the kingdom of Og in Bashan. These were allotted to the people of Machir the son of Manasseh for the half of the people of Machir according to their clans. These are the inheritances that Moses distributed in the plains of Moab, beyond the Jordan east of Jericho. But to the tribe of Levi Moses gave no inheritance; the LORD God of Israel is their inheritance, just as he said to them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The distribution was made on the plains of Moab, by a man who never crossed the river.

Picture the day. Men hear the names of places they will farm, and each family walks away holding something they can stand on. Levi is handed nothing. That could be read as a consolation prize, and the rest of the Bible will not let it be. Asaph gets to the bottom of it: whom have I in heaven but you? And there is nothing on earth that I desire besides you. My flesh and my heart may fail, but God is the strength of my heart and my portion forever (Ps. 73:25-26).

Everything Reuben was given could be taken away, and eventually was: Assyria carried those eastern tribes off first (1 Chr. 5:26).

14.title: Caleb's Inheritance
14.text: <sup>1</sup>These are the inheritances that the people of Israel received in the land of Canaan, which Eleazar the priest and Joshua the son of Nun and the heads of the fathers' houses of the tribes of the people of Israel gave them to inherit.<sup>2</sup>Their inheritance was by lot, just as the LORD had commanded by the hand of Moses for the nine and one-half tribes.<sup>3</sup>For Moses had given an inheritance to the two and one-half tribes beyond the Jordan, but to the Levites he gave no inheritance among them.<sup>4</sup>For the people of Joseph were two tribes, Manasseh and Ephraim. And no portion was given to the Levites in the land, but only cities to dwell in, with their pasturelands for their livestock and their substance.<sup>5</sup>The people of Israel did as the LORD commanded Moses; they allotted the land.<sup>6</sup>Then the people of Judah came to Joshua at Gilgal. And Caleb the son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite said to him, "You know what the LORD said to Moses the man of God in Kadesh-barnea concerning you and me.<sup>7</sup>I was forty years old when Moses the servant of the LORD sent me from Kadesh-barnea to spy out the land, and I brought him word again as it was in my heart.<sup>8</sup>But my brothers who went up with me made the heart of the people melt; yet I wholly followed the LORD my God.<sup>9</sup>And Moses swore on that day, saying, 'Surely the land on which your foot has trodden shall be an inheritance for you and your children forever, because you have wholly followed the LORD my God.'<sup>10</sup>And now, behold, the LORD has kept me alive, just as he said, these forty-five years since the time that the LORD spoke this word to Moses, while Israel walked in the wilderness. And now, behold, I am this day eighty-five years old.<sup>11</sup>I am still as strong today as I was in the day that Moses sent me; my strength now is as my strength was then, for war and for going and coming.<sup>12</sup>So now give me this hill country of which the LORD spoke on that day, for you heard on that day how the Anakim were there, with great fortified cities. It may be that the LORD will be with me, and I shall drive them out just as the LORD said."<sup>13</sup>Then Joshua blessed him, and he gave Hebron to Caleb the son of Jephunneh for an inheritance.<sup>14</sup>Therefore Hebron became the inheritance of Caleb the son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite to this day, because he wholly followed the LORD, the God of Israel.<sup>15</sup>Now the name of Hebron formerly was Kiriath-arba. (Arba was the greatest man among the Anakim.) And the land had rest from war.
14.overview:
The allotment of the western land begins by lot, a method that removes every human lever, so that no tribe can lobby and no family can be quietly cheated. And then the register stops for one man.

Caleb comes to Joshua at Gilgal, and the two of them are the only ones left of the generation condemned at Kadesh-barnea. He rehearses the day the spies came back, when he alone with Joshua wholly followed the LORD, and what being right cost him.

He is eighty-five, he has counted the years exactly, and his request is not for a quiet valley: give me this hill country, where the giants still live. He gets Hebron, the one place in Canaan already thick with promise.
14.theology:
The lot, and who is really deciding. Land drawn by lot looks like chance and functions as its opposite. Every family that ends up on hard ground knows exactly whose decision it was: the lot is cast into the lap, but its every decision is from the LORD (Prov. 16:33).

Wholly followed. The phrase is repeated three times over one man (vv. 8, 9, 14): he went after the LORD with nothing held back. It is the exact opposite of the verdict the rest of these chapters keep recording about the tribes: they did not drive out, they could not drive out, they left them living in the midst.

Did Caleb earn his hill? No. Hebron was a promise kept, sworn by God at Kadesh, not wages paid. Caleb’s wholehearted following was the shape his faith took, and God himself calls him my servant who had a different spirit (Numbers 14:24). Only one man ever followed the LORD wholly with no lapse at all: Christ, faithful to him who appointed him (Hebrews 3:2) and obedient to the point of death (Philippians 2:8). His people inherit because he followed wholly; then, made new, they begin to follow him with something of Caleb’s undivided heart.

Faithfulness is not exempted from other people's consequences. Caleb was right at forty and it bought him thirty-eight years in a wilderness he had argued against, burying men who had been wrong. God kept him alive through all of it and gave him the ground at eighty-five. Being on the right side of a decision does not remove a believer from the country that made the wrong one.

Asking for the giants. The request in verse 12 is for the hardest terrain on the map, named with its difficulties attached, and it ends it may be that the LORD will be with me: certainty about the promise and humility about himself, in one sentence. This is what faith and patience look like at eighty-five (Heb. 6:12).
14.examples:
Then: An old man walked up to the man dividing the country and asked for the one district everybody else was avoiding, because God had mentioned it to him forty-five years earlier and he had not forgotten the address.

Now: Two questions come out of this chapter, and the second is the harder. What promise are you still counting the years on, and would you recognise it if it arrived? Caleb knew the number of years exactly. And then: what would you ask God for if you were sure he had already granted it? Most requests get smaller with age. Caleb's got steeper, and he still would not say more than it may be that the LORD will be with me. And if your own strength has not lasted like his, the promise never rested on his strength either; it rested on the God who kept him alive.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The western allotment begins, and the writer records who did it: Eleazar the priest, Joshua, and the heads of the tribes (v. 1). The method is stated plainly, their inheritance was by lot (v. 2), and the arithmetic is explained: two and a half tribes are already settled east of the Jordan, Joseph counts as two tribes because of Manasseh and Ephraim, and Levi gets no territory at all, only towns to live in with pasture (vv. 3-4). Verse 5 closes it: they did as the LORD commanded, and allotted the land.
verseByVerse.theology: Drawing lots removes every human lever: no tribe can lobby, no elder can trade a favour, the strongest tribe cannot argue its way to the best ground, and the smallest cannot be quietly cheated.
verseByVerse.examples: Levi is dealt with in half a verse: no portion, only cities to live in and grazing for the animals. The tribe that carried the ark across the Jordan ends the day with somewhere to sleep and nowhere to farm.

verseByVerse.quote: These are the inheritances that the people of Israel received in the land of Canaan, which Eleazar the priest and Joshua the son of Nun and the heads of the fathers' houses of the tribes of the people of Israel gave them to inherit. Their inheritance was by lot, just as the LORD had commanded by the hand of Moses for the nine and one-half tribes. For Moses had given an inheritance to the two and one-half tribes beyond the Jordan, but to the Levites he gave no inheritance among them. For the people of Joseph were two tribes, Manasseh and Ephraim. And no portion was given to the Levites in the land, but only cities to dwell in, with their pasturelands for their livestock and their substance. The people of Israel did as the LORD commanded Moses; they allotted the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The land is divided by lot, and the priest is named before the general. Whatever this is, it is not a military distribution of spoils.

Levi's half verse is the third such note in two chapters, and it will come round again in chapters 18 and 21.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 6–9 — I Wholly Followed the LORD
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Then one man steps out of the crowd. Caleb comes to Joshua at Gilgal and opens with a reminder that they two are the only ones left of the twelve who spied out the land: you know what the LORD said to Moses... concerning you and me (v. 6). He rehearses it: forty years old when he was sent to spy out the land, and he brought back the report as it was in his heart (v. 7); his brothers made the people's heart melt, and he did not (v. 8); and Moses swore that the ground his foot had walked on would be his, because he wholly followed the LORD (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: The phrase runs through the chapter three times and it is Caleb's whole testimony: he wholly followed the LORD, going after God with nothing held back.
verseByVerse.examples: Twice he is called the Kenizzite (vv. 6, 14), and Kenaz is an Edomite clan name (Gen. 36:11, 15). The most single-minded Israelite in the book may not have been born an Israelite at all.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the people of Judah came to Joshua at Gilgal. And Caleb the son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite said to him, "You know what the LORD said to Moses the man of God in Kadesh-barnea concerning you and me. I was forty years old when Moses the servant of the LORD sent me from Kadesh-barnea to spy out the land, and I brought him word again as it was in my heart. But my brothers who went up with me made the heart of the people melt; yet I wholly followed the LORD my God. And Moses swore on that day, saying, 'Surely the land on which your foot has trodden shall be an inheritance for you and your children forever, because you have wholly followed the LORD my God.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
One man steps out of a delegation and opens with the two of them. Concerning you and me, because Joshua and Caleb are the only two left of the men counted and condemned at Kadesh-barnea. Most of those present were children then, or unborn. The rest of that generation is buried in the desert behind them.

His account of the worst day in Israel's history is brief and it does not spare anyone. Ten men came back and made a nation's heart melt, the verb used of Jericho and of the kings of Canaan. What frightened Israel out of the land was not the Anakim. It was a report.

Being right cost him a great deal. Telling the truth did not get Caleb the land at forty; it got him thirty-eight more years in a desert with the people who had been wrong.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–12 — Give Me This Hill Country
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Caleb does the arithmetic out loud. Forty-five years since Moses swore it, most of them spent watching a generation die in a desert, and the LORD has kept him alive through every one (v. 10). He is eighty-five, and claims to be as strong for war and for going and coming as he was at forty (v. 11). And then the request, which is not for a quiet field: give me this hill country, the ground where the Anakim are, with great fortified cities, and a sentence of pure humility at the end of it: it may be that the LORD will be with me (v. 12).
verseByVerse.theology: He asks for the hardest ground on the map. The giants that had frightened ten men into a forty-year detour are still living in those hills, and the eighty-five-year-old who brought back the minority report is asking for that particular address.
verseByVerse.examples: The last clause keeps the whole speech from being bravado. Not "the LORD will be with me", but it may be. Forty-five years of waiting had not made him presumptuous about God; he asks for giants and does not tell God what to do about them.

verseByVerse.quote: And now, behold, the LORD has kept me alive, just as he said, these forty-five years since the time that the LORD spoke this word to Moses, while Israel walked in the wilderness. And now, behold, I am this day eighty-five years old. I am still as strong today as I was in the day that Moses sent me; my strength now is as my strength was then, for war and for going and coming. So now give me this hill country of which the LORD spoke on that day, for you heard on that day how the Anakim were there, with great fortified cities. It may be that the LORD will be with me, and I shall drive them out just as the LORD said."
verseByVerse.commentary:
He has been counting, because a man waiting on a specific promise keeps the date: thirty-eight years watching the men who made the decision die one funeral at a time, then seven years of war. The chapter credits his strength to the LORD who kept me alive. Most men at eighty-five are taking an inventory of what they can no longer do. Caleb is applying for work.

He does not ask for a quiet valley near water, and he says exactly what is up there in the hill country.

Had Joshua not already cut off the Anakim from Hebron (11:21)? He broke their power in the campaign; they held on or came back, and Caleb finished the occupation (15:13–14). Judges 1:10 gives the same victory to Judah, because Caleb fought as a leader of Judah.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Joshua blesses him and gives him Hebron (v. 13), and the writer notes that Hebron belongs to Caleb's family to this day, and gives the reason once more: because he wholly followed the LORD, the God of Israel (v. 14). Verse 15 adds the town's old name, Kiriath-arba, with a note that Arba was the greatest man among the Anakim, and then the sentence that closed the conquest returns: and the land had rest from war.
verseByVerse.theology: Of all the ground in Canaan, Hebron is the one place already thick with promise. Abraham lived there under the oaks, and bought the cave of Machpelah there as the only piece of the land he ever owned: the grave where he, Sarah, Isaac, Rebekah, Jacob and Leah are buried (Gen. 23; 49:31). Caleb asks for the family plot.
verseByVerse.examples: The town's old name honoured a giant, for Arba was the greatest of the Anakim. The name that once frightened the spies became the address of the one man among them who was not afraid.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Joshua blessed him, and he gave Hebron to Caleb the son of Jephunneh for an inheritance. Therefore Hebron became the inheritance of Caleb the son of Jephunneh the Kenizzite to this day, because he wholly followed the LORD, the God of Israel. Now the name of Hebron formerly was Kiriath-arba. (Arba was the greatest man among the Anakim.) And the land had rest from war.
verseByVerse.commentary: Two old men, the last of a generation, settle a promise made in a desert nearly half a century before. Abraham had pitched his tent by the oaks of Mamre here, and Caleb asked for the place where the promise was buried. Hebrews tells sluggish Christians to imitate those who inherit the promises through faith and patience (Heb. 6:12), and it could have named Caleb. He believed God at forty, said so when it was unpopular, paid for it with thirty-eight years he had not earned, and then walked up to the hardest hill in the country at eighty-five and asked for it by name.
verseByVerse.note: “Kiriath-arba” means “the city of Arba”; 15:13 calls Arba the father of Anak.

15.title: The Allotment of Judah
15.text: <sup>1</sup>The allotment for the tribe of the people of Judah according to their clans reached southward to the boundary of Edom, to the wilderness of Zin at the farthest south.<sup>2</sup>And their south boundary ran from the end of the Salt Sea, from the bay that faces southward.<sup>3</sup>It goes out southward of the ascent of Akrabbim, passes along to Zin, and goes up south of Kadesh-barnea, along by Hezron, up to Addar, turns about to Karka,<sup>4</sup>passes along to Azmon, goes out by the Brook of Egypt, and comes to its end at the sea. This shall be your south boundary.<sup>5</sup>And the east boundary is the Salt Sea, to the mouth of the Jordan. And the boundary on the north side runs from the bay of the sea at the mouth of the Jordan.<sup>6</sup>And the boundary goes up to Beth-hoglah and passes along north of Beth-arabah. And the boundary goes up to the stone of Bohan the son of Reuben.<sup>7</sup>And the boundary goes up to Debir from the Valley of Achor, and so northward, turning toward Gilgal, which is opposite the ascent of Adummim, which is on the south side of the valley. And the boundary passes along to the waters of En-shemesh and ends at En-rogel.<sup>8</sup>Then the boundary goes up by the Valley of the Son of Hinnom at the southern shoulder of the Jebusite (that is, Jerusalem). And the boundary goes up to the top of the mountain that lies over against the Valley of Hinnom, on the west, at the northern end of the Valley of Rephaim.<sup>9</sup>Then the boundary extends from the top of the mountain to the spring of the waters of Nephtoah, and from there to the cities of Mount Ephron. Then the boundary bends around to Baalah (that is, Kiriath-jearim).<sup>10</sup>And the boundary circles west of Baalah to Mount Seir, passes along to the northern shoulder of Mount Jearim (that is, Chesalon), and goes down to Beth-shemesh and passes along by Timnah.<sup>11</sup>The boundary goes out to the shoulder of the hill north of Ekron, then the boundary bends around to Shikkeron and passes along to Mount Baalah and goes out to Jabneel. Then the boundary comes to an end at the sea.<sup>12</sup>And the west boundary was the Great Sea with its coastline. This is the boundary around the people of Judah according to their clans.<sup>13</sup>According to the commandment of the LORD to Joshua, he gave to Caleb the son of Jephunneh a portion among the people of Judah, Kiriath-arba, that is, Hebron (Arba was the father of Anak).<sup>14</sup>And Caleb drove out from there the three sons of Anak, Sheshai and Ahiman and Talmai, the descendants of Anak.<sup>15</sup>And he went up from there against the inhabitants of Debir. Now the name of Debir formerly was Kiriath-sepher.<sup>16</sup>And Caleb said, "He who attacks Kiriath-sepher and captures it, I will give him Achsah my daughter as wife."<sup>17</sup>And Othniel the son of Kenaz, the brother of Caleb, captured it. And he gave him Achsah his daughter as wife.<sup>18</sup>When she came to him, she urged him to ask her father for a field.
