Since you have given me the land of the Negeb, give me also springs of water." And he gave her the upper springs and the lower springs.<sup>20</sup>This is the inheritance of the tribe of the people of Judah according to their clans.<sup>21</sup>The cities belonging to the tribe of the people of Judah in the extreme south, toward the boundary of Edom, were Kabzeel, Eder, Jagur,<sup>22</sup>Kinah, Dimonah, Adadah,<sup>23</sup>Kedesh, Hazor, Ithnan,<sup>24</sup>Ziph, Telem, Bealoth,<sup>25</sup>Hazor-hadattah, Kerioth-hezron (that is, Hazor),<sup>26</sup>Amam, Shema, Moladah,<sup>27</sup>Hazar-gaddah, Heshmon, Beth-pelet,<sup>28</sup>Hazar-shual, Beersheba, Biziothiah,<sup>29</sup>Baalah, Iim, Ezem,<sup>30</sup>Eltolad, Chesil, Hormah,<sup>31</sup>Ziklag, Madmannah, Sansannah,<sup>32</sup>Lebaoth, Shilhim, Ain, and Rimmon: in all, twenty-nine cities with their villages.<sup>33</sup>And in the lowland, Eshtaol, Zorah, Ashnah,<sup>34</sup>Zanoah, En-gannim, Tappuah, Enam,<sup>35</sup>Jarmuth, Adullam, Socoh, Azekah,<sup>36</sup>Shaaraim, Adithaim, Gederah, Gederothaim: fourteen cities with their villages.<sup>37</sup>Zenan, Hadashah, Migdal-gad,<sup>38</sup>Dilean, Mizpeh, Joktheel,<sup>39</sup>Lachish, Bozkath, Eglon,<sup>40</sup>Cabbon, Lahmam, Chitlish,<sup>41</sup>Gederoth, Beth-dagon, Naamah, and Makkedah: sixteen cities with their villages.<sup>42</sup>Libnah, Ether, Ashan,<sup>43</sup>Iphtah, Ashnah, Nezib,<sup>44</sup>Keilah, Achzib, and Mareshah: nine cities with their villages.<sup>45</sup>Ekron, with its towns and its villages;<sup>46</sup>from Ekron to the sea, all that were by the side of Ashdod, with their villages.<sup>47</sup>Ashdod, its towns and its villages; Gaza, its towns and its villages; to the Brook of Egypt, and the Great Sea with its coastline.<sup>48</sup>And in the hill country, Shamir, Jattir, Socoh,<sup>49</sup>Dannah, Kiriath-sannah (that is, Debir),<sup>50</sup>Anab, Eshtemoh, Anim,<sup>51</sup>Goshen, Holon, and Giloh: eleven cities with their villages.<sup>52</sup>Arab, Dumah, Eshan,<sup>53</sup>Janim, Beth-tappuah, Aphekah,<sup>54</sup>Humtah, Kiriath-arba (that is, Hebron), and Zior: nine cities with their villages.<sup>55</sup>Maon, Carmel, Ziph, Juttah,<sup>56</sup>Jezreel, Jokdeam, Zanoah,<sup>57</sup>Kain, Gibeah, and Timnah: ten cities with their villages.<sup>58</sup>Halhul, Beth-zur, Gedor,<sup>59</sup>Maarath, Beth-anoth, and Eltekon: six cities with their villages.<sup>60</sup>Kiriath-baal (that is, Kiriath-jearim), and Rabbah: two cities with their villages.<sup>61</sup>In the wilderness, Beth-arabah, Middin, Secacah,<sup>62</sup>Nibshan, the City of Salt, and Engedi: six cities with their villages.<sup>63</sup>But the Jebusites, the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the people of Judah could not drive out, so the Jebusites dwell with the people of Judah at Jerusalem to this day.
15.overview:
Judah is dealt with first and at greatest length: sixty-three verses, a perimeter walked landmark by landmark, and more than a hundred towns counted in batches. It is the longest inventory in the book and it is a deed of property.

Two names on the boundary, Achor and Hinnom, are not neutral (vv. 7-8). In the middle of the register the writer stops for a family: Caleb clears the giants out of Hebron, Othniel takes a town to win a wife, and Achsah asks her father for springs of water. And the last verse is not a total but the one city Judah could not take: Jerusalem.
15.theology:
Promises arrive as addresses. Forty verses of town names are the cashing of a sentence spoken to a childless man who was told to count the stars. God does not fulfil his word in the abstract; he fulfils it in Kabzeel and Jagur and Adadah, until somebody has to count them in batches. Biblical language about inheritance can float free and become a mood, and this chapter nails it to a map.

Two valleys on one boundary. Achor is where Achan of Judah was stoned and buried (7:24-26); Hinnom becomes Gehenna. And Hosea took the first of those names and turned it into a door of hope (Hos. 2:15): God has a habit of reissuing the address of the worst thing that ever happened.

Asking well. Achsah has land and no water, so she gets down off her donkey and says give me a blessing and then names the thing she actually needs (vv. 18-19). Her father, who waited forty-five years for one promise and then asked for a mountain full of giants, gives her both the upper and the lower springs. The man who knew how to ask raised a daughter who knew how to ask, and neither of them was refused. Jesus argues from the same kind of father: if earthly fathers know how to give good gifts, how much more will the heavenly Father give the Holy Spirit to those who ask him (Luke 11:13).

Could not. More than a hundred towns were delivered exactly as promised, and one was not, and the one was the city where the temple would stand and, outside its wall, the hill where the Lion of Judah would be crucified.
15.examples:
Then: Surveyors walked a boundary past a heap of stones over a thief and along a ravine that would one day give hell its name, counted more than a hundred towns into batches, and finished by writing down the name of the one city they could not take.

Now: Take the two verses in the middle. Achsah had been given something real that was useless without one more thing, and she asked for it directly and got more than she named. Most Christians ask God for the field and never mention the springs. And take the last verse as the honest companion to it: a great deal delivered, and one thing standing that will not move yet.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The first and largest allotment is Judah's, and the chapter opens by walking its perimeter. South to the wilderness of Zin on the edge of Edom (v. 1), east along the Salt Sea (v. 5), then the northern line traced landmark by landmark through Beth-hoglah, the stone of Bohan, the Valley of Achor, En-shemesh and En-rogel (vv. 6-7), up the Valley of the Son of Hinnom past the shoulder of the Jebusite, that is, Jerusalem (v. 8), out west past Beth-shemesh and Timnah and Ekron, and ending at the Great Sea (vv. 9-12).
verseByVerse.theology: Two names on this boundary are not neutral. The line runs through the Valley of Achor, where a man of Judah was buried under stones for stealing from God (7:24-26); and it runs along the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, which the New Testament knows as Gehenna. Judah's title deeds are drawn through the valley of its own worst day and past the valley that became a word for hell.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 8 puts Jerusalem on the boundary and calls it the Jebusite. The city that will one day be the centre of everything is at this point a foreign town on the edge of somebody's farmland, and verse 63 says what happened when Judah tried to take it.

verseByVerse.quote: The allotment for the tribe of the people of Judah according to their clans reached southward to the boundary of Edom, to the wilderness of Zin at the farthest south. And their south boundary ran from the end of the Salt Sea, from the bay that faces southward. It goes out southward of the ascent of Akrabbim, passes along to Zin, and goes up south of Kadesh-barnea, along by Hezron, up to Addar, turns about to Karka, passes along to Azmon, goes out by the Brook of Egypt, and comes to its end at the sea. This shall be your south boundary. And the east boundary is the Salt Sea, to the mouth of the Jordan. And the boundary on the north side runs from the bay of the sea at the mouth of the Jordan. And the boundary goes up to Beth-hoglah and passes along north of Beth-arabah. And the boundary goes up to the stone of Bohan the son of Reuben. And the boundary goes up to Debir from the Valley of Achor, and so northward, turning toward Gilgal, which is opposite the ascent of Adummim, which is on the south side of the valley. And the boundary passes along to the waters of En-shemesh and ends at En-rogel. Then the boundary goes up by the Valley of the Son of Hinnom at the southern shoulder of the Jebusite (that is, Jerusalem). And the boundary goes up to the top of the mountain that lies over against the Valley of Hinnom, on the west, at the northern end of the Valley of Rephaim. Then the boundary extends from the top of the mountain to the spring of the waters of Nephtoah, and from there to the cities of Mount Ephron. Then the boundary bends around to Baalah (that is, Kiriath-jearim). And the boundary circles west of Baalah to Mount Seir, passes along to the northern shoulder of Mount Jearim (that is, Chesalon), and goes down to Beth-shemesh and passes along by Timnah. The boundary goes out to the shoulder of the hill north of Ekron, then the boundary bends around to Shikkeron and passes along to Mount Baalah and goes out to Jabneel. Then the boundary comes to an end at the sea. And the west boundary was the Great Sea with its coastline. This is the boundary around the people of Judah according to their clans.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Judah is dealt with first and at greatest length, which is the writer's way of saying what this tribe is going to be. Most names on this circuit meant a great deal to an ancient reader: a spring, a ridge, a stone somebody had set up.

Achan, buried in Achor, was a man of Judah (7:1, 18), and every generation of surveyors after this walked past the stones. Gehenna is the word Jesus uses more than anyone else in the New Testament for final judgment; in Joshua's day it is simply a ravine outside a Canaanite town, later the place where children were burned to Molech.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The register stops for a family. Caleb receives Hebron by the LORD's own command (v. 13) and drives out the three sons of Anak by name (v. 14), then moves on Debir and offers his daughter Achsah to whoever takes it (vv. 15-16). Othniel his kinsman takes it and marries her (v. 17). Then a scene: she urges him to ask her father for a field, gets down off her donkey, and asks Caleb herself: give me a blessing. Since you have given me the land of the Negeb, give me also springs of water — and he gives her the upper springs and the lower springs (vv. 18-19).
verseByVerse.theology: The three giants of verse 14 are named: Sheshai, Ahiman and Talmai. These are the names the spies brought back from Hebron forty-five years earlier, on the journey that ended with Israel feeling like grasshoppers (Num. 13:22, 33). An eighty-five-year-old took their town, and the writer troubles to give their names because they had been a legend and now they are a line in a property record.
verseByVerse.examples: Othniel goes on to become the first of the judges, the man God raises up to deliver Israel when the nation collapses in the next book (Judg. 3:9-11). Israel's first deliverer is introduced here as a young man who captured a town to win a wife.

verseByVerse.quote: According to the commandment of the LORD to Joshua, he gave to Caleb the son of Jephunneh a portion among the people of Judah, Kiriath-arba, that is, Hebron (Arba was the father of Anak). And Caleb drove out from there the three sons of Anak, Sheshai and Ahiman and Talmai, the descendants of Anak. And he went up from there against the inhabitants of Debir. Now the name of Debir formerly was Kiriath-sepher. And Caleb said, "He who attacks Kiriath-sepher and captures it, I will give him Achsah my daughter as wife." And Othniel the son of Kenaz, the brother of Caleb, captured it. And he gave him Achsah his daughter as wife. When she came to him, she urged him to ask her father for a field. And she dismounted from her donkey, and Caleb said to her, "What do you want?" She said to him, "Give me a blessing. Since you have given me the land of the Negeb, give me also springs of water." And he gave her the upper springs and the lower springs.
verseByVerse.commentary:
An old man does what he said he would do. The giants who had been a legend for two generations are cleared out of Hebron in half a verse, and the writer records their names the way an estate agent records a previous owner.

Caleb is still fighting and still recruiting, and his offer is shrewd: he is looking for a son-in-law with nerve, and the test is a walled town.

Othniel takes it, the future first judge of Israel. (The Hebrew can make Othniel Caleb’s younger brother or his nephew, so Achsah married an uncle or a cousin; the marriage laws of Leviticus 18 forbade neither.)

The best scene in the chapter takes two verses. A field in the dry Negeb without water is a technicality, not a farm. So she gets off the donkey and asks her father herself, not for more land but for the one thing that makes the land she has worth having. Caleb does not haggle with his daughter, and gives more than she asked for.

Caleb offers his daughter as a prize: in that world a father arranged marriage, and here the bride-price was courage (cf. 1 Sam 17:25). Scripture records the custom, and then shows that Achsah was no mere prize: she speaks for herself and is heard.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 20–63 — More Than a Hundred Towns, and One That Would Not Fall
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The rest of the chapter is a list, grouped by region and counted as it goes: twenty-nine towns in the far south towards Edom (vv. 21-32), then the lowland in four groups of fourteen, sixteen, nine and the Philistine coast (vv. 33-47), then the hill country in five groups (vv. 48-60), then six more in the wilderness by the Salt Sea (vv. 61-62). And then the last verse, which is not a total: the Jebusites, the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the people of Judah could not drive out, so the Jebusites dwell with the people of Judah at Jerusalem to this day (v. 63).
verseByVerse.theology: The litany repays reading aloud once rather than studying: a deed of property running to more than a hundred addresses, promised to a man who owned nothing in this country but a burial cave.
verseByVerse.examples: The chapter ends on a failure, and the wording has shifted. Earlier the writer said Israel did not drive out Geshur and Maacath (13:13). Here he says Judah could not drive out the Jebusites. Judah will burn it early in Judges, but the Jebusites stay, and Jerusalem is still a Jebusite city generations later, when a shepherd from Bethlehem takes it (Judg. 1:8, 21; 2 Sam. 5:6-9).

verseByVerse.quote: This is the inheritance of the tribe of the people of Judah according to their clans. The cities belonging to the tribe of the people of Judah in the extreme south, toward the boundary of Edom, were Kabzeel, Eder, Jagur, Kinah, Dimonah, Adadah, Kedesh, Hazor, Ithnan, Ziph, Telem, Bealoth, Hazor-hadattah, Kerioth-hezron (that is, Hazor), Amam, Shema, Moladah, Hazar-gaddah, Heshmon, Beth-pelet, Hazar-shual, Beersheba, Biziothiah, Baalah, Iim, Ezem, Eltolad, Chesil, Hormah, Ziklag, Madmannah, Sansannah, Lebaoth, Shilhim, Ain, and Rimmon: in all, twenty-nine cities with their villages. And in the lowland, Eshtaol, Zorah, Ashnah, Zanoah, En-gannim, Tappuah, Enam, Jarmuth, Adullam, Socoh, Azekah, Shaaraim, Adithaim, Gederah, Gederothaim: fourteen cities with their villages. Zenan, Hadashah, Migdal-gad, Dilean, Mizpeh, Joktheel, Lachish, Bozkath, Eglon, Cabbon, Lahmam, Chitlish, Gederoth, Beth-dagon, Naamah, and Makkedah: sixteen cities with their villages. Libnah, Ether, Ashan, Iphtah, Ashnah, Nezib, Keilah, Achzib, and Mareshah: nine cities with their villages. Ekron, with its towns and its villages; from Ekron to the sea, all that were by the side of Ashdod, with their villages. Ashdod, its towns and its villages; Gaza, its towns and its villages; to the Brook of Egypt, and the Great Sea with its coastline.
verseByVerse.commentary: The Philistine coast is listed as Judah's and is not Judah's (13:2-3). Every name here is a real place with real people in it: a well, a threshing floor, a few dozen families, somebody's grandmother. Ziklag is in this list, and David will live there as an outlaw. Beersheba is in it, where Abraham planted a tamarisk tree. Adullam is in it, where David hid in a cave.

verseByVerse.quote: And in the hill country, Shamir, Jattir, Socoh, Dannah, Kiriath-sannah (that is, Debir), Anab, Eshtemoh, Anim, Goshen, Holon, and Giloh: eleven cities with their villages. Arab, Dumah, Eshan, Janim, Beth-tappuah, Aphekah, Humtah, Kiriath-arba (that is, Hebron), and Zior: nine cities with their villages. Maon, Carmel, Ziph, Juttah, Jezreel, Jokdeam, Zanoah, Kain, Gibeah, and Timnah: ten cities with their villages. Halhul, Beth-zur, Gedor, Maarath, Beth-anoth, and Eltekon: six cities with their villages. Kiriath-baal (that is, Kiriath-jearim), and Rabbah: two cities with their villages. In the wilderness, Beth-arabah, Middin, Secacah, Nibshan, the City of Salt, and Engedi: six cities with their villages. But the Jebusites, the inhabitants of Jerusalem, the people of Judah could not drive out, so the Jebusites dwell with the people of Judah at Jerusalem to this day.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The list finishes in the hill country and then out in the wilderness by the Salt Sea, with six towns that are barely towns. The last of them is Engedi, an oasis on a cliff above the Dead Sea where David will one day hide from Saul and cut the corner off his robe rather than kill him.

The counting is meticulous to the end, and then the chapter stops counting. The greatest tribe, with more than a hundred towns, ends unable to take the one city on its boundary that mattered; the Jebusites are still there in the days of the judges (Judg. 19:11-12) and under Saul.

It is the honest shape of this whole section of the book. Judah did not know what was on that ridge. The tribe whose boundary ran through the Valley of Trouble and along the ravine that would give hell its name could not take the city outside whose wall the Lamb of God would be crucified. It was left standing, in foreign hands, on the border of the tribe out of which the Lion of Judah would come.
verseByVerse.note: Achor means “trouble” (cf. 7:26); Engedi (v. 62) is the oasis of 1 Samuel 24.

16.title: The Allotment of Ephraim
16.text: <sup>1</sup>The allotment of the people of Joseph went from the Jordan by Jericho, east of the waters of Jericho, into the wilderness, going up from Jericho into the hill country to Bethel.<sup>2</sup>Then going from Bethel to Luz, it passes along to Ataroth, the territory of the Archites.<sup>3</sup>Then it goes down westward to the territory of the Japhletites, as far as the territory of Lower Beth-horon, then to Gezer, and it ends at the sea.<sup>4</sup>The people of Joseph, Manasseh and Ephraim, received their inheritance.<sup>5</sup>The territory of the people of Ephraim by their clans was as follows: the boundary of their inheritance on the east was Ataroth-addar as far as Upper Beth-horon,<sup>6</sup>and the boundary goes from there to the sea. On the north is Michmethath. Then on the east the boundary turns around toward Taanath-shiloh and passes along beyond it on the east to Janoah,<sup>7</sup>then it goes down from Janoah to Ataroth and to Naarah, and touches Jericho, ending at the Jordan.<sup>8</sup>From Tappuah the boundary goes westward to the brook Kanah and ends at the sea. Such is the inheritance of the tribe of the people of Ephraim by their clans,<sup>9</sup>together with the towns that were set apart for the people of Ephraim within the inheritance of the Manassites, all those towns with their villages.<sup>10</sup>However, they did not drive out the Canaanites who lived in Gezer, so the Canaanites have lived in the midst of Ephraim to this day but have been made to do forced labor.
16.overview:
The house of Joseph receives a broad band across the middle of the country, and there are two tribes here rather than one because of a deathbed in Egypt. Jacob adopted Joseph's two sons as his own (Gen. 48:5), so the brother who was sold to traders ends up with a double share of the land.

Then the chapter ends on a single verse that is the reason it is in the Bible. Ephraim did not lose a battle for Gezer; Ephraim found an arrangement, and the command was quietly replaced by a policy. Israel never took Gezer at all: centuries later a pharaoh did, and gave it away as a wedding present.
16.theology:
Compromise is usually profitable. Ephraim's practical decision paid better than obedience would have. That is what makes verse 10 worth more attention than the nine boundary verses before it: it is the ordinary shape of disobedience among people who would be shocked to be called disobedient.

What is kept because it is useful does not stay in its place. The book of Judges opens by collecting all these verses into one list and then delivering its verdict (Judg. 2:3), and Israel finished up worshipping the gods of the labour force.

Unfinished business gets finished by somebody else. Gezer was never taken by Israel; an Egyptian king settled the matter centuries later (1 Kings 9:16). What God's people leave undone does not quietly disappear; it is settled eventually, by other hands and on other terms.

Was forced labour the sin? Not in the writer’s eyes. God had ordered the Canaanite cults removed from his land (Deuteronomy 7:1-5), and a labour force was a way of keeping the people and their gods within reach. Forced labour was common in that world and Scripture records it without commending it; Israel later felt its weight from its own king (1 Kings 5:13; 9:20-21; 12:4). The fault named here is that a clear command was traded for a profit.

The rejected brother’s portion. The map gives Joseph, the brother who was sold, a double share. Stephen tells Joseph’s story as the first of a pattern in which God’s people reject the deliverer God sends and are then saved by him (Acts 7:9-14, 35, 52). Its last and greatest instance is Christ, handed over by his own brothers and raised to God’s right hand, from where he holds out forgiveness and an inheritance to the very people who rejected him (Acts 2:36-39).
16.examples:
Then: A tribe looked at a fortified town full of people it had been told to remove, weighed the cost, and put them on the payroll instead. It was the sensible decision and it was still there when the book was written.

Now: The test in this chapter is not whether there is open sin in your life. It is whether there is something God told you to end that you have instead made useful: the arrangement that is easier to keep than to break, and that happens to pay. Ephraim's Canaanites were not rebels in the camp. They were staff. The land was a gift before it was a task, and the same is true for the believer: Christ has already won the ground, and his Spirit gives the strength to dismiss what we have kept on the payroll (Gal. 5:16), with mercy for every time we have not (1 John 1:9).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The lot of the house of Joseph runs from the Jordan at Jericho up into the hill country to Bethel (v. 1), on past Ataroth and the territory of the Archites (v. 2), down west through Lower Beth-horon to Gezer, and out to the sea (v. 3). Verse 4 records the two tribes taking it: Manasseh and Ephraim, the sons of Joseph.
verseByVerse.theology: Joseph counts as two tribes because Jacob adopted his two sons as his own on his deathbed, crossing his hands to put the younger in front (Gen. 48:5, 14). The boy who was sold into Egypt gets a double share of the country his brothers sold him out of.

verseByVerse.quote: The allotment of the people of Joseph went from the Jordan by Jericho, east of the waters of Jericho, into the wilderness, going up from Jericho into the hill country to Bethel. Then going from Bethel to Luz, it passes along to Ataroth, the territory of the Archites. Then it goes down westward to the territory of the Japhletites, as far as the territory of Lower Beth-horon, then to Gezer, and it ends at the sea. The people of Joseph, Manasseh and Ephraim, received their inheritance.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The territory runs right across the middle of the country, from the Jordan to the Mediterranean, and it is given to Joseph, who has been dead for a very long time.

Jacob, dying, said Ephraim and Manasseh shall be mine, as Reuben and Simeon are (Gen. 48:5), and would not be corrected about the crossed hands. Nobody in this chapter says what that means for the brother who was thrown into a pit. The map says it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Ephraim's perimeter is traced in the usual way: east at Ataroth-addar as far as Upper Beth-horon (v. 5), north at Michmethath, then round by Taanath-shiloh and Janoah (v. 6), down to Ataroth and Naarah, touching Jericho and ending at the Jordan (v. 7), and west from Tappuah along the brook Kanah to the sea (v. 8). Verse 9 adds the towns set apart for Ephraim inside Manasseh's territory.
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 9 is a small administrative kindness with a long history behind it. Ephraim gets towns inside his brother's allotment, which means the two tribes of Joseph are deliberately kept interleaved rather than cleanly separated.

verseByVerse.quote: The territory of the people of Ephraim by their clans was as follows: the boundary of their inheritance on the east was Ataroth-addar as far as Upper Beth-horon, and the boundary goes from there to the sea. On the north is Michmethath. Then on the east the boundary turns around toward Taanath-shiloh and passes along beyond it on the east to Janoah, then it goes down from Janoah to Ataroth and to Naarah, and touches Jericho, ending at the Jordan. From Tappuah the boundary goes westward to the brook Kanah and ends at the sea. Such is the inheritance of the tribe of the people of Ephraim by their clans, together with the towns that were set apart for the people of Ephraim within the inheritance of the Manassites, all those towns with their villages.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The perimeter walk again: ridges, brooks, towns and a coastline. Ephraim gets the central hill country, which is good ground and defensible, and it will hold the tabernacle at Shiloh for generations, until the days of Eli.

Whatever the practical reason for verse 9, the effect is that the sons of Joseph cannot forget each other. Their fields touch. And the next chapter will show what these two tribes do when they have a grievance, which is come as a pair.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: One verse, and it is the point of the chapter: however, they did not drive out the Canaanites who lived in Gezer, so the Canaanites have lived in the midst of Ephraim to this day but have been made to do forced labor (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: The failure is not that Ephraim lost a battle. It is that they found an arrangement: the command was replaced by a labour policy, and everybody did rather well out of it.
verseByVerse.examples: Gezer never became Israelite by conquest. Centuries later Pharaoh king of Egypt captured it, burned it and killed the Canaanites living in it, and handed it over as a dowry when his daughter married Solomon (1 Kings 9:16). Ephraim's unfinished business was eventually settled by a foreign king, as a wedding present.

verseByVerse.quote: However, they did not drive out the Canaanites who lived in Gezer, so the Canaanites have lived in the midst of Ephraim to this day but have been made to do forced labor.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything before this verse is a boundary description; this is a policy decision. Somebody weighed the cost of removing an entrenched population from a fortified town against the value of a permanent labour supply, and made the sensible decision.

It is the ordinary form spiritual compromise takes. Nobody in Ephraim decided to disobey God; they decided to be practical about something God had told them to end.

What a person keeps because it is useful will not stay in the servants' quarters. Judges, which is the sequel to all these verses, gives the verdict in advance: the peoples left in the land became thorns in your sides, and their gods shall be a snare to you (Judg. 2:3).

17.title: The Allotment of Manasseh and the Complaint of Joseph
17.text: <sup>1</sup>Then allotment was made to the people of Manasseh, for he was the firstborn of Joseph. To Machir the firstborn of Manasseh, the father of Gilead, were allotted Gilead and Bashan, because he was a man of war.<sup>2</sup>And allotments were made to the rest of the people of Manasseh by their clans, Abiezer, Helek, Asriel, Shechem, Hepher, and Shemida. These were the male descendants of Manasseh the son of Joseph, by their clans.<sup>3</sup>Now Zelophehad the son of Hepher, son of Gilead, son of Machir, son of Manasseh, had no sons, but only daughters, and these are the names of his daughters: Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah.<sup>4</sup>They approached Eleazar the priest and Joshua the son of Nun and the leaders and said, "The LORD commanded Moses to give us an inheritance along with our brothers." So according to the mouth of the LORD he gave them an inheritance among the brothers of their father.<sup>5</sup>Thus there fell to Manasseh ten portions, besides the land of Gilead and Bashan, which is on the other side of the Jordan,<sup>6</sup>because the daughters of Manasseh received an inheritance along with his sons. The land of Gilead was allotted to the rest of the people of Manasseh.<sup>7</sup>The territory of Manasseh reached from Asher to Michmethath, which is east of Shechem. Then the boundary goes along southward to the inhabitants of En-tappuah.<sup>8</sup>The land of Tappuah belonged to Manasseh, but the town of Tappuah on the boundary of Manasseh belonged to the people of Ephraim.<sup>9</sup>Then the boundary went down to the brook Kanah. These cities, to the south of the brook, among the cities of Manasseh, belong to Ephraim. Then the boundary of Manasseh goes on the north side of the brook and ends at the sea,<sup>10</sup>the land to the south being Ephraim's and that to the north being Manasseh's, with the sea forming its boundary. On the north Asher is reached, and on the east Issachar.<sup>11</sup>Also in Issachar and in Asher Manasseh had Beth-shean and its villages, and Ibleam and its villages, and the inhabitants of Dor and its villages, and the inhabitants of En-dor and its villages, and the inhabitants of Taanach and its villages, and the inhabitants of Megiddo and its villages; the third is Naphath.<sup>12</sup>Yet the people of Manasseh could not take possession of those cities, but the Canaanites persisted in dwelling in that land.<sup>13</sup>Now when the people of Israel grew strong, they put the Canaanites to forced labor, but did not utterly drive them out.<sup>14</sup>Then the people of Joseph spoke to Joshua, saying, "Why have you given me but one lot and one portion as an inheritance, although I am a numerous people, since all along the LORD has blessed me?"<sup>15</sup>And Joshua said to them, "If you are a numerous people, go up by yourselves to the forest, and there clear ground for yourselves in the land of the Perizzites and the Rephaim, since the hill country of Ephraim is too narrow for you."<sup>16</sup>The people of Joseph said, "The hill country is not enough for us. Yet all the Canaanites who dwell in the plain have chariots of iron, both those in Beth-shean and its villages and those in the Valley of Jezreel."<sup>17</sup>Then Joshua said to the house of Joseph, to Ephraim and Manasseh, "You are a numerous people and have great power. You shall not have one allotment only,<sup>18</sup>but the hill country shall be yours, for though it is a forest, you shall clear it and possess it to its farthest borders. For you shall drive out the Canaanites, though they have chariots of iron, and though they are strong."
17.overview:
Manasseh's register is interrupted almost as soon as it begins. Zelophehad had no sons, and his five daughters hold a new administration to a ruling God had made for them years earlier.

Then two verbs in two verses tell the story of this whole half of the book: Manasseh could not take the best towns in the north, and when it grew strong it still did not (vv. 12-13).

The chapter ends with the house of Joseph asking for more land on the grounds that God has blessed them. Joshua, lobbied by his own tribe, offers them no easier ground, only a forest, an axe, and a promise that the iron chariots will not stop them.
17.theology:
Five women in a land register. The daughters of Zelophehad are named one by one every time Scripture mentions them, and the reason is a case they argued and won. The gospel carries their case to its end: in Christ the Father’s inheritance is no longer held through sons alone, for all who belong to him are Abraham’s offspring and heirs according to promise (Galatians 3:26-29), and husbands are told to honour their wives as heirs with them of the grace of life (1 Peter 3:7).

When the excuse expires. Could not in verse 12 is stated as fact, not blamed. Verse 13 is the sting: once Israel grew strong, the arrangement made in weakness was kept because by then it paid, and that is a different matter from the first failure.

Blessing as a claim. The house of Joseph argues that because God has blessed them they are owed more room (v. 14). Joshua takes the argument seriously and turns it round: if you are numerous, behave like it, and he gives them a forest to clear. Growth is not a title to easier ground.

He refuses his own tribe. Joshua gives his own kinsmen nothing but work and a promise, and he does not pretend the iron chariots are not there: he names them, adds that the enemy is strong, and repeats the instruction anyway. Honest leadership tells people the size of the difficulty and sends them at it.

Was God beaten by iron? A reader meets the iron chariots again in Judges 1:19 and may wonder whether they were too much for God. Chariots were the heavy armour of that world and could not be matched on flat ground. But Joshua’s answer settles the question: you shall drive them out, though they have chariots of iron (v. 18). The limit was never the LORD’s strength; it was Israel’s readiness to trust him on the plain.
17.examples:
Then: Five sisters held a new government to a promise the previous one had made, and got their fields. A tribe that already held a broad band across the middle of the country came to complain that it was not enough, and went away with permission to cut down a forest.

Now: Verse 13 is the searching one. Most people can name something they could not deal with at the time, and the honest question is not whether the excuse was true then, but whether it is still true. Israel grew strong and kept the arrangement. And when the house of Joseph finally said what was really wrong, it was not the size of the land but the iron chariots on the part of it worth having. Joshua's answer named the chariots and did not change the instruction, and it came with a promise: you shall drive out the Canaanites (v. 18). For a Christian that promise is the Spirit's work, God at work in us to will and to do (Phil. 2:13), and the arrangement we kept too long is forgiven when it is confessed.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–6 — Five Women in a Land Register
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Manasseh's allotment begins with Machir, a man of war, who has Gilead and Bashan (v. 1), and the clans of the rest (v. 2). Then the register stops: Zelophehad had no sons, only daughters, and they are named: Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah and Tirzah (v. 3). They come to Eleazar and Joshua and the leaders and say plainly, the LORD commanded Moses to give us an inheritance along with our brothers, and they are given one (v. 4). So Manasseh receives ten portions, because the daughters inherited alongside the sons (vv. 5-6).
verseByVerse.theology: These five had already been to court once, and won (see below). They are now standing in front of a new administration, asking only that the ruling be honoured, and it is.
verseByVerse.examples: Their names are given in full here for the fourth time in Scripture (Num. 26:33; 27:1; 36:11, and this). In a section of the Bible made of place names, five women are named and named again.

verseByVerse.quote: Then allotment was made to the people of Manasseh, for he was the firstborn of Joseph. To Machir the firstborn of Manasseh, the father of Gilead, were allotted Gilead and Bashan, because he was a man of war. And allotments were made to the rest of the people of Manasseh by their clans, Abiezer, Helek, Asriel, Shechem, Hepher, and Shemida. These were the male descendants of Manasseh the son of Joseph, by their clans. Now Zelophehad the son of Hepher, son of Gilead, son of Machir, son of Manasseh, had no sons, but only daughters, and these are the names of his daughters: Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah. They approached Eleazar the priest and Joshua the son of Nun and the leaders and said, "The LORD commanded Moses to give us an inheritance along with our brothers." So according to the mouth of the LORD he gave them an inheritance among the brothers of their father. Thus there fell to Manasseh ten portions, besides the land of Gilead and Bashan, which is on the other side of the Jordan, because the daughters of Manasseh received an inheritance along with his sons. The land of Gilead was allotted to the rest of the people of Manasseh.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The register opens with a firstborn and a soldier, and then stops for five women, in a culture where land ran through sons. Their father had died in the wilderness with no sons, which under the custom of the time meant his name and his portion simply disappeared. The five of them went to Moses and the whole assembly at the tent of meeting and made an argument: why should the name of our father be taken away from his clan because he had no son? Moses did not rule on it. He took the case to God, and God said, the daughters of Zelophehad are right, and made it a statute for Israel (Num. 27:1-11).

Now, with Moses dead, they do not plead or argue their merits. They cite the judgment, and it is granted at once, so Manasseh's allotment is counted in ten portions.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 7–13 — Could Not, and Would Not
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Manasseh's boundary is traced from Asher to Michmethath, down past En-tappuah and the brook Kanah to the sea, with Ephraim to the south (vv. 7-10). Verse 11 lists six good towns Manasseh held inside Issachar and Asher, including Beth-shean, Taanach and Megiddo. And then verses 12-13: they could not take possession of those cities, the Canaanites persisted in living there, and when Israel grew strong they put them to forced labour but did not utterly drive them out.
verseByVerse.theology: The two verbs in two verses are the whole story of this half of the book: first could not, then, once it was possible, did not. The excuse expired and the arrangement stayed.
verseByVerse.examples: The six towns are the best real estate in the north: Beth-shean commanding the Jordan valley road, Megiddo commanding the pass into the plain of Jezreel. Manasseh had the title and never got the keys, and those towns will be trouble to Israel for centuries.

verseByVerse.quote: The territory of Manasseh reached from Asher to Michmethath, which is east of Shechem. Then the boundary goes along southward to the inhabitants of En-tappuah. The land of Tappuah belonged to Manasseh, but the town of Tappuah on the boundary of Manasseh belonged to the people of Ephraim. Then the boundary went down to the brook Kanah. These cities, to the south of the brook, among the cities of Manasseh, belong to Ephraim. Then the boundary of Manasseh goes on the north side of the brook and ends at the sea, the land to the south being Ephraim's and that to the north being Manasseh's, with the sea forming its boundary. On the north Asher is reached, and on the east Issachar. Also in Issachar and in Asher Manasseh had Beth-shean and its villages, and Ibleam and its villages, and the inhabitants of Dor and its villages, and the inhabitants of En-dor and its villages, and the inhabitants of Taanach and its villages, and the inhabitants of Megiddo and its villages; the third is Naphath. Yet the people of Manasseh could not take possession of those cities, but the Canaanites persisted in dwelling in that land. Now when the people of Israel grew strong, they put the Canaanites to forced labor, but did not utterly drive them out.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The boundary walk is standard, and then six towns are listed that Manasseh held on paper. They are the best sites in the north: Beth-shean, sitting where the Jordan valley meets the plain; Taanach and Megiddo, guarding the pass that every army in the ancient world used to get across the country.

The first verb is could not. In the early days Manasseh was not strong enough, and that is stated as a fact rather than a sin. Some things are genuinely beyond a person's strength for a season, and Scripture says so without scolding.

Then the second sentence, and it changes everything: when the people of Israel grew strong. The weakness passed, and at the exact moment the thing became possible, Manasseh did not do it. They put the Canaanites to forced labour instead, which was profitable, and left it there.

The excuse is often true when it is first offered. What matters is whether the arrangement made in weakness is dismantled once the strength arrives, or quietly kept because by then it suits everybody.

Megiddo is on that list of towns Manasseh never took. Solomon will one day fortify it and Josiah will die there (1 Kings 9:15; 2 Kings 23:29), and its name probably lies behind Armageddon (Revelation 16:16).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 14–18 — Ask for More, Get a Forest
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The house of Joseph comes to Joshua with a grievance: why one lot and one portion, when we are a numerous people whom the LORD has blessed all along (v. 14)? Joshua's answer is not more land but an axe: if you are numerous, go up to the forest and clear ground for yourselves (v. 15). They come back with the real objection: the hill country is not enough, and the Canaanites in the plain have chariots of iron (v. 16). And Joshua repeats himself with the promise attached: you are numerous and have great power, the hill country shall be yours, you shall clear it and possess it to its farthest borders, and you shall drive out the Canaanites though they have chariots of iron, and though they are strong (vv. 17-18).
verseByVerse.theology: Joshua is himself an Ephraimite (Num. 13:8, 16). These are his own people asking their own kinsman for a better deal, and he gives them nothing but work and a promise. Nepotism would have been easy and nobody would have objected.
verseByVerse.examples: Their two complaints pull against each other. In verse 14 they are a great people who need more room; in verse 16 they are too weak, they say, to take the ground the chariots hold. A people large enough to need more room is large enough to take it, and Joshua says so in almost those words.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the people of Joseph spoke to Joshua, saying, "Why have you given me but one lot and one portion as an inheritance, although I am a numerous people, since all along the LORD has blessed me?" And Joshua said to them, "If you are a numerous people, go up by yourselves to the forest, and there clear ground for yourselves in the land of the Perizzites and the Rephaim, since the hill country of Ephraim is too narrow for you." The people of Joseph said, "The hill country is not enough for us. Yet all the Canaanites who dwell in the plain have chariots of iron, both those in Beth-shean and its villages and those in the Valley of Jezreel." Then Joshua said to the house of Joseph, to Ephraim and Manasseh, "You are a numerous people and have great power. You shall not have one allotment only, but the hill country shall be yours, for though it is a forest, you shall clear it and possess it to its farthest borders. For you shall drive out the Canaanites, though they have chariots of iron, and though they are strong."
verseByVerse.commentary:
A deputation arrives with a grievance, and the shape of it repays hearing. They have not been treated unjustly; they have a broad band of land across the middle of the country. What they want is more, and the argument they use is that God has blessed them.

God's evident favour becomes the ground of a claim. Joshua gives them an axe and a forest instead: you say you are numerous, so behave like it.

Then the real objection surfaces: the good land has iron chariots on it.

That is the honest sentence in the whole exchange. They did not want more territory in general. They wanted the plain, which is flat, fertile and farmable, and they did not want to fight the people who were sitting on it.

Joshua does not soften and he does not sneer. He gives them back their own words with the promise attached: you are numerous, you have great power, the hill country shall be yours, and you shall drive them out.

He also refuses to pretend: the difficulty is real, he says it twice, and it does not change the instruction. The last word this old general gives his own tribe is not sympathy and not easier land. It is that the ground is theirs and the trees will have to come down.

18.title: Shiloh and the Remaining Allotments
18.text: <sup>1</sup>Then the whole congregation of the people of Israel assembled at Shiloh and set up the tent of meeting there. The land lay subdued before them.<sup>2</sup>There remained among the people of Israel seven tribes whose inheritance had not yet been apportioned.<sup>3</sup>So Joshua said to the people of Israel, "How long will you put off going in to take possession of the land, which the LORD, the God of your fathers, has given you?<sup>4</sup>Provide three men from each tribe, and I will send them out that they may set out and go up and down the land. They shall write a description of it with a view to their inheritances, and then come to me.<sup>5</sup>They shall divide it into seven portions. Judah shall continue in his territory on the south, and the house of Joseph shall continue in their territory on the north.<sup>6</sup>And you shall describe the land in seven divisions and bring the description here to me. And I will cast lots for you here before the LORD our God.<sup>7</sup>The Levites have no portion among you, for the priesthood of the LORD is their heritage. And Gad and Reuben and half the tribe of Manasseh have received their inheritance beyond the Jordan eastward, which Moses the servant of the LORD gave them."<sup>8</sup>So the men arose and went, and Joshua charged those who went to write the description of the land, saying, "Go up and down in the land and write a description and return to me. And I will cast lots for you here before the LORD in Shiloh."<sup>9</sup>So the men went and passed up and down in the land and wrote in a book a description of it by towns in seven divisions. Then they came to Joshua to the camp at Shiloh,<sup>10</sup>and Joshua cast lots for them in Shiloh before the LORD. And there Joshua apportioned the land to the people of Israel, to each his portion.<sup>11</sup>The lot of the tribe of the people of Benjamin according to its clans came up, and the territory allotted to it fell between the people of Judah and the people of Joseph.<sup>12</sup>On the north side their boundary began at the Jordan. Then the boundary goes up to the shoulder north of Jericho, then up through the hill country westward, and it ends at the wilderness of Beth-aven.<sup>13</sup>From there the boundary passes along southward in the direction of Luz, to the shoulder of Luz (that is, Bethel), then the boundary goes down to Ataroth-addar, on the mountain that lies south of Lower Beth-horon.<sup>14</sup>Then the boundary goes in another direction, turning on the western side southward from the mountain that lies to the south, opposite Beth-horon, and it ends at Kiriath-baal (that is, Kiriath-jearim), a city belonging to the people of Judah. This forms the western side.<sup>15</sup>And the southern side begins at the outskirts of Kiriath-jearim. And the boundary goes from there to Ephron, to the spring of the waters of Nephtoah.<sup>16</sup>Then the boundary goes down to the border of the mountain that overlooks the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, which is at the north end of the Valley of Rephaim. And it then goes down the Valley of Hinnom, south of the shoulder of the Jebusites, and downward to En-rogel.<sup>17</sup>Then it bends in a northerly direction going on to En-shemesh, and from there goes to Geliloth, which is opposite the ascent of Adummim. Then it goes down to the stone of Bohan the son of Reuben,<sup>18</sup>and passing on to the north of the shoulder of Beth-arabah it goes down to the Arabah.<sup>19</sup>Then the boundary passes on to the north of the shoulder of Beth-hoglah. And the boundary ends at the northern bay of the Salt Sea, at the south end of the Jordan: this is the southern border.<sup>20</sup>The Jordan forms its boundary on the eastern side. This is the inheritance of the people of Benjamin, according to their clans, boundary by boundary all around.<sup>21</sup>Now the cities of the tribe of the people of Benjamin according to their clans were Jericho, Beth-hoglah, Emek-keziz,<sup>22</sup>Beth-arabah, Zemaraim, Bethel,<sup>23</sup>Avvim, Parah, Ophrah,<sup>24</sup>Chephar-ammoni, Ophni, Geba—twelve cities with their villages:<sup>25</sup>Gibeon, Ramah, Beeroth,<sup>26</sup>Mizpeh, Chephirah, Mozah,<sup>27</sup>Rekem, Irpeel, Taralah,<sup>28</sup>Zela, Haeleph, Jebus (that is, Jerusalem), Gibeah and Kiriath-jearim —fourteen cities with their villages. This is the inheritance of the people of Benjamin according to its clans.
18.overview:
The camp moves out of the Jordan valley and up into the hills, and the first thing built once the land is subdued is not a fort or a capital but the tent of meeting (v. 1).

Then the sharpest sentence in this half of the book: seven tribes are asked how long they will put off taking land the LORD has already given them (v. 3). There is no calf, no Achan, no muttering. These people are perfectly orthodox and completely stationary. What Joshua offers them is a survey team and lots cast before the LORD (vv. 4-10).

Benjamin, the smallest tribe, is drawn first and gets the narrowest strip and some of the most consequential ground in the country: Jericho, Bethel, Gibeon, and Jerusalem in the last verse of the list.
18.theology:
Worship first, and then everything else. The land is subdued and the tent goes up before a single fort or granary. And the tent points beyond itself. The Word became flesh and pitched his tent among us (John 1:14), and the place where God meets his people is now a person: not Shiloh, not even Jerusalem, but the Son, in whom the Father is worshipped in spirit and truth (John 4:21-24). Shiloh could fall. He cannot.

The sin that feels like nothing. Joshua confronts a failure with no dramatic content at all: seven tribes who have not gone in. The clause that makes it a rebuke is which the LORD... has given you. Delay is treated here as something to answer for, and the rebuke is itself a reminder of the gift.

The remedy is the gift already given. Joshua does not wait for a fresh visitation. For the Christian the same Spirit who has given us everything in Christ is the one who moves us to take it up, through his word, prayer and the company of his people. At Shiloh the deadlock broke not because anyone's feelings changed but because there was something specific to do.

Work and lot together. The men measure, describe and write a book; God assigns by lot (vv. 9-10). Every mile was walked by somebody with sore feet, and not one boundary was decided by the men who walked it. It is the same arrangement as the Jordan and Jericho, transacted in an office instead of a battle.
18.examples:
Then: Seven tribes sat comfortably in camp with a country waiting for them, and were asked how long they intended to put it off. The answer they were given was not a sermon but a job: three men each, go and walk it, write it down, bring the book back.

Now: The question in verse 3 is the one to sit with, because it is aimed at people who have done nothing wrong. Name the thing you already have in Christ and have not taken up: the promise not yet rested on, the conversation not had, the discipline not begun. Then notice Joshua's remedy. He did not wait for some new gift. He appointed people, set a task and named the day it was due, and the Spirit who lives in believers is given for exactly that kind of plain obedience (Gal. 5:25).

verseByVerse.ref: v. 1 — The Tent Goes Up at Shiloh
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: One verse, and it changes the centre of the nation. The whole congregation assembles at Shiloh and sets up the tent of meeting there, and the writer adds the reason it was possible: the land lay subdued before them (v. 1).
verseByVerse.theology: The first structure Israel raises once the fighting stops is not a fort, a palace or a granary. It is the tent. Worship is not what the nation does when the practical work is finished; it is the first practical decision made.
verseByVerse.examples: Shiloh holds the tabernacle for generations, and it ends in ruins. Centuries later God tells Jerusalem to go and look at them: go now to my place that was in Shiloh, where I made my name dwell at first, and see what I did to it because of the evil of my people Israel (Jer. 7:12-14).

verseByVerse.quote: Then the whole congregation of the people of Israel assembled at Shiloh and set up the tent of meeting there. The land lay subdued before them.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Until now the camp has been at Gilgal, down in the Jordan valley where the twelve stones stand. Now the whole congregation walks up into the hill country of Ephraim.

Shiloh is where Hannah prayed so desperately that the priest thought she was drunk, and where Samuel first heard his name called in the night. It ends badly: the ark is carried out into a battle and never returns (1 Sam. 4:3-11).

No place is safe because God once lived there, and that was as true on the day the tent went up as on the day it fell.
verseByVerse.note: Shiloh lay north of Bethel, east of the road from Bethel to Shechem (Judg. 21:19).

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 2–7 — How Long Will You Put Off?
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Seven tribes still have no inheritance (v. 2), and Joshua's question to them is the sharpest sentence in this half of the book: how long will you put off going in to take possession of the land, which the LORD, the God of your fathers, has given you? (v. 3). He then gives them a procedure (three men from each tribe, a written survey, seven divisions, and lots cast before the LORD, vv. 4-6) and sets out who is already provided for: Levi, whose heritage is the priesthood, and the two and a half tribes east of the Jordan (v. 7).
verseByVerse.theology: Both halves of the question matter. The land has been given, and they have not gone in. Nobody here is rebelling; they are simply not moving, and Joshua treats that as a thing that needs answering for.
verseByVerse.examples: There is no suggestion that they need more from God. They need to go. The remedy for this kind of delay is never another gift; the gift is the thing lying unclaimed.

verseByVerse.quote: There remained among the people of Israel seven tribes whose inheritance had not yet been apportioned. So Joshua said to the people of Israel, "How long will you put off going in to take possession of the land, which the LORD, the God of your fathers, has given you? Provide three men from each tribe, and I will send them out that they may set out and go up and down the land. They shall write a description of it with a view to their inheritances, and then come to me. They shall divide it into seven portions. Judah shall continue in his territory on the south, and the house of Joseph shall continue in their territory on the north. And you shall describe the land in seven divisions and bring the description here to me. And I will cast lots for you here before the LORD our God. The Levites have no portion among you, for the priesthood of the LORD is their heritage. And Gad and Reuben and half the tribe of Manasseh have received their inheritance beyond the Jordan eastward, which Moses the servant of the LORD gave them."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Seven tribes out of twelve have not taken their land. Not lost it, not been driven out of it: simply not gone.

The sting is in the last clause, has given you, and it is also the comfort: there is no obstacle in heaven and no further permission required. A country sits there with their names on it.

This is the commonest condition in the Christian life. A believer possesses more in Christ than he has ever taken up. The forgiveness is granted and not enjoyed; the prayer is available and not made; the reconciliation is possible and postponed another year. Nothing is being refused. Nothing is being done.

Levi is mentioned for the fourth time in six chapters, in the middle of a rebuke about land. The tribe with nothing to claim is the one tribe that has never held anything up.

Is casting lots a model for guidance today? Here God himself appointed the lot to divide a land he had already promised (Num 26:55; Prov 16:33). The last lot in Scripture came before Pentecost (Acts 1:26); believers now seek God’s will through his word, prayer and wise counsel.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 8–10 — A Survey, a Book, and a Lot
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Joshua does not leave the rebuke to do its own work. The men are sent out with an instruction to walk the country and write it down (v. 8), and they do — up and down the land, and wrote in a book a description of it by towns in seven divisions (v. 9). They bring the book back to Shiloh, and there Joshua casts lots before the LORD and apportions the land (v. 10).
verseByVerse.theology: The cure for passivity here is a task, a team, a method and a deadline: a few men from each tribe walking the hills with a pen.
verseByVerse.examples: The survey is human work done thoroughly, and the allocation is still by lot before the LORD. Israel measures and describes; God assigns. Neither half is decorative, and the book they carried back to Shiloh did not decide a single boundary.

verseByVerse.quote: So the men arose and went, and Joshua charged those who went to write the description of the land, saying, "Go up and down in the land and write a description and return to me. And I will cast lots for you here before the LORD in Shiloh." So the men went and passed up and down in the land and wrote in a book a description of it by towns in seven divisions. Then they came to Joshua to the camp at Shiloh, and Joshua cast lots for them in Shiloh before the LORD. And there Joshua apportioned the land to the people of Israel, to each his portion.
verseByVerse.commentary: The job is specific and not glamorous: a land survey compiled by walking. That is how paralysis is usually broken. Not by a change of feeling but by a task with edges on it: who goes, what they do, what they bring back, and when. Nothing in this passage suggests the seven tribes suddenly became enthusiastic. They were given something concrete to do and a man who expected it done.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Benjamin's lot comes up first, and it falls in the gap between Judah to the south and the house of Joseph to the north (v. 11). The boundary is walked in the usual way (vv. 12-20), and then the towns are listed in two groups — twelve, and then fourteen more, ending with Jebus (that is, Jerusalem), Gibeah and Kiriath-jearim (vv. 21-28).
verseByVerse.theology: Benjamin is the smallest tribe and gets the most consequential few square miles in the country. Jericho is in it. Bethel, where Jacob saw the ladder, is on its border. Gibeon is in it. And Jerusalem is in the list.
verseByVerse.examples: Two men named Saul came out of this tribe. The first was Israel's first king, the people's choice, who ended on Gilboa. The second was a Pharisee from Tarsus who described himself as of the tribe of Benjamin twice in his letters (Rom. 11:1; Phil. 3:5), and who took the gospel to the nations.

verseByVerse.quote: The lot of the tribe of the people of Benjamin according to its clans came up, and the territory allotted to it fell between the people of Judah and the people of Joseph. On the north side their boundary began at the Jordan. Then the boundary goes up to the shoulder north of Jericho, then up through the hill country westward, and it ends at the wilderness of Beth-aven. From there the boundary passes along southward in the direction of Luz, to the shoulder of Luz (that is, Bethel), then the boundary goes down to Ataroth-addar, on the mountain that lies south of Lower Beth-horon. Then the boundary goes in another direction, turning on the western side southward from the mountain that lies to the south, opposite Beth-horon, and it ends at Kiriath-baal (that is, Kiriath-jearim), a city belonging to the people of Judah. This forms the western side. And the southern side begins at the outskirts of Kiriath-jearim. And the boundary goes from there to Ephron, to the spring of the waters of Nephtoah. Then the boundary goes down to the border of the mountain that overlooks the Valley of the Son of Hinnom, which is at the north end of the Valley of Rephaim. And it then goes down the Valley of Hinnom, south of the shoulder of the Jebusites, and downward to En-rogel. Then it bends in a northerly direction going on to En-shemesh, and from there goes to Geliloth, which is opposite the ascent of Adummim. Then it goes down to the stone of Bohan the son of Reuben, and passing on to the north of the shoulder of Beth-arabah it goes down to the Arabah. Then the boundary passes on to the north of the shoulder of Beth-hoglah. And the boundary ends at the northern bay of the Salt Sea, at the south end of the Jordan: this is the southern border. The Jordan forms its boundary on the eastern side. This is the inheritance of the people of Benjamin, according to their clans, boundary by boundary all around. Now the cities of the tribe of the people of Benjamin according to their clans were Jericho, Beth-hoglah, Emek-keziz, Beth-arabah, Zemaraim, Bethel, Avvim, Parah, Ophrah, Chephar-ammoni, Ophni, Geba—twelve cities with their villages: Gibeon, Ramah, Beeroth, Mizpeh, Chephirah, Mozah, Rekem, Irpeel, Taralah, Zela, Haeleph, Jebus (that is, Jerusalem), Gibeah and Kiriath-jearim —fourteen cities with their villages. This is the inheritance of the people of Benjamin according to its clans.
verseByVerse.commentary:
A small tribe is drawn first, and it lands in the narrowest strip on the map, wedged between the two giants, Judah below and the house of Joseph above.

Benjamin was the youngest son, born on the road to Bethlehem while his mother died naming him. His tribe was nearly exterminated in the civil war at the end of the book of Judges, down to six hundred men. It never had the numbers of Judah or Ephraim and never pretended to.

What it has is position.

Jerusalem is on Benjamin's list and it was on Judah's, and neither tribe took it. Judah could not (15:63); Benjamin did not (Judg. 1:21). The city that will hold the temple sits on the boundary between two tribes, and both of them file it under unfinished business.

Gibeah is on the list too, the very next name, and it will be the worst address in Israel: the town whose crime starts the civil war that almost ends this tribe.

The first Saul began by hiding among the baggage and ended by falling on his sword on Gilboa. The second used his tribe once to prove that God had not rejected Israel (Rom. 11:1), and once in the list of what he counted as loss for the sake of Christ (Phil. 3:5).

The smallest tribe, in the narrowest strip of land, produced the king who lost the kingdom and the apostle who carried the gospel out of it to the ends of the earth.

19.title: The Remaining Tribes and Joshua's Own Inheritance
19.text: <sup>1</sup>The second lot came out for Simeon, for the tribe of the people of Simeon, according to their clans, and their inheritance was in the midst of the inheritance of the people of Judah.<sup>2</sup>And they had for their inheritance Beersheba, Sheba, Moladah,<sup>3</sup>Hazar-shual, Balah, Ezem,<sup>4</sup>Eltolad, Bethul, Hormah,<sup>5</sup>Ziklag, Beth-marcaboth, Hazar-susah,<sup>6</sup>Beth-lebaoth, and Sharuhen—thirteen cities with their villages;<sup>7</sup>Ain, Rimmon, Ether, and Ashan—four cities with their villages,<sup>8</sup>together with all the villages around these cities as far as Baalath-beer, Ramah of the Negeb. This was the inheritance of the tribe of the people of Simeon according to their clans.<sup>9</sup>The inheritance of the people of Simeon formed part of the territory of the people of Judah. Because the portion of the people of Judah was too large for them, the people of Simeon obtained an inheritance in the midst of their inheritance.<sup>10</sup>The third lot came up for the people of Zebulun, according to their clans. And the territory of their inheritance reached as far as Sarid.<sup>11</sup>Then their boundary goes up westward and on to Mareal and touches Dabbesheth, then the brook that is east of Jokneam.<sup>12</sup>From Sarid it goes in the other direction eastward toward the sunrise to the boundary of Chisloth-tabor. From there it goes to Daberath, then up to Japhia.<sup>13</sup>From there it passes along on the east toward the sunrise to Gath-hepher, to Eth-kazin, and going on to Rimmon it bends toward Neah,<sup>14</sup>then on the north the boundary turns about to Hannathon, and it ends at the Valley of Iphtahel;<sup>15</sup>and Kattath, Nahalal, Shimron, Idalah, and Bethlehem—twelve cities with their villages.<sup>16</sup>This is the inheritance of the people of Zebulun, according to their clans—these cities with their villages.<sup>17</sup>The fourth lot came out for Issachar, for the people of Issachar, according to their clans.<sup>18</sup>Their territory included Jezreel, Chesulloth, Shunem,<sup>19</sup>Hapharaim, Shion, Anaharath,<sup>20</sup>Rabbith, Kishion, Ebez,<sup>21</sup>Remeth, En-gannim, En-haddah, Beth-pazzez.<sup>22</sup>The boundary also touches Tabor, Shahazumah, and Beth-shemesh, and its boundary ends at the Jordan—sixteen cities with their villages.<sup>23</sup>This is the inheritance of the tribe of the people of Issachar, according to their clans—the cities with their villages.<sup>24</sup>The fifth lot came out for the tribe of the people of Asher according to their clans.<sup>25</sup>Their territory included Helkath, Hali, Beten, Achshaph,<sup>26</sup>Allammelech, Amad, and Mishal. On the west it touches Carmel and Shihor-libnath,<sup>27</sup>then it turns eastward, it goes to Beth-dagon, and touches Zebulun and the Valley of Iphtahel northward to Beth-emek and Neiel. Then it continues in the north to Cabul,<sup>28</sup>Ebron, Rehob, Hammon, Kanah, as far as Sidon the Great.<sup>29</sup>Then the boundary turns to Ramah, reaching to the fortified city of Tyre. Then the boundary turns to Hosah, and it ends at the sea; Mahalab, Achzib,<sup>30</sup>Ummah, Aphek and Rehob—twenty-two cities with their villages.<sup>31</sup>This is the inheritance of the tribe of
