westward to Aznoth-tabor and goes from there to Hukkok, touching Zebulun at the south and Asher on the west and Judah on the east at the Jordan.<sup>35</sup>The fortified cities are Ziddim, Zer, Hammath, Rakkath, Chinnereth,<sup>36</sup>Adamah, Ramah, Hazor,<sup>37</sup>Kedesh, Edrei, En-hazor,<sup>38</sup>Yiron, Migdal-el, Horem, Beth-anath, and Beth-shemesh—nineteen cities with their villages.<sup>39</sup>This is the inheritance of the tribe of the people of Naphtali according to their clans—the cities with their villages.<sup>40</sup>The seventh lot came out for the tribe of the people of Dan, according to their clans.<sup>41</sup>And the territory of its inheritance included Zorah, Eshtaol, Ir-shemesh,<sup>42</sup>Shaalabbin, Aijalon, Ithlah,<sup>43</sup>Elon, Timnah, Ekron,<sup>44</sup>Eltekeh, Gibbethon, Baalath,<sup>45</sup>Jehud, Bene-berak, Gath-rimmon,<sup>46</sup>and Me-jarkon and Rakkon with the territory over against Joppa.<sup>47</sup>When the territory of the people of Dan was lost to them, the people of Dan went up and fought against Leshem, and after capturing it and striking it with the sword they took possession of it and settled in it, calling Leshem, Dan, after the name of Dan their ancestor.<sup>48</sup>This is the inheritance of the tribe of the people of Dan, according to their clans—these cities with their villages.<sup>49</sup>When they had finished distributing the several territories of the land as inheritances, the people of Israel gave an inheritance among them to Joshua the son of Nun.<sup>50</sup>By command of the LORD they gave him the city that he asked, Timnath-serah in the hill country of Ephraim. And he rebuilt the city and settled in it.<sup>51</sup>These are the inheritances that Eleazar the priest and Joshua the son of Nun and the heads of the fathers' houses of the tribes of the people of Israel distributed by lot at Shiloh before the LORD, at the entrance of the tent of meeting. So they finished dividing the land.
19.overview:
The last six lots are drawn, and each carries something more than geography.

Simeon gets no border at all, only towns inside Judah (vv. 1, 9), and within a few generations the tribe has largely dissolved into its neighbour, as Jacob had said on his deathbed (Gen. 49:7).

The four northern tribes follow, and two of their names, Zebulun and Naphtali, will matter far beyond this register.

Dan is given good land against the Philistine border and loses it (v. 47), then marches a hundred miles north to take a quiet town instead, a migration Judges tells in full. And the man who conquered the country is given somewhere to live only after every tribe, and has to rebuild it.
19.theology:
One curse, two histories. Simeon and Levi received the same sentence from their dying father for the same crime, and both were scattered exactly as he said. Levi ended up teaching in forty-eight towns across every tribe; Simeon ended up largely absorbed. The words spoken over them were identical, and God made one of them a vocation.

The map of the Gospels is drawn here. Zebulun and Naphtali are two entries in a property register here and two names in a prophecy about light in Isaiah 9. God was arranging the setting of the incarnation while a clerk at Shiloh was writing down town names.

Leaving the hard place. Dan is the only tribe recorded as losing its inheritance, and its allotment faced the Philistines. They went north and took an easier town, and did not stop being religious when they moved: they set up a stolen idol with a hired priest (Judg. 18:31). A tribe that leaves the ground God assigned does not become irreligious. It builds something else.

Served last. Joshua distributes the entire country for seven chapters and receives his own portion only when the register is closed (v. 49). He asks for one town, and has to rebuild it before he can live in it. The man who bore the name Jesus would bear is served last, and the greater Joshua went further: he came not to be served but to serve and to give his life (Mark 10:45), and had nowhere to lay his head (Matthew 8:20) while he won an inheritance for others.
19.examples:
Then: One tribe got no border and eventually no identity. One lost its land to the Philistines and went north to easier neighbours, taking a stolen idol with it. And the general who had taken the whole country waited until every family was housed, then asked for a town that needed rebuilding.

Now: Dan is the warning and Joshua the model. Dan left the assigned ground because the opposition on it was relentless; Joshua stayed in the assigned order and was served last. Ask which describes the way you have handled the hardest thing God has actually given you. The ground was a gift before it was a battlefield, and the God who gave it gives his Spirit to hold it. Where you have walked away, the greater Joshua stayed at his post to the cross for you, and the way back is open.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The second lot falls to Simeon, whose inheritance lay in the midst of Judah's (v. 1): seventeen towns with their villages (vv. 2-8), because Judah's portion was too large (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: Of the twelve tribes, Simeon is the one that stops being a place on the map.
verseByVerse.examples: The writer gives a practical reason in verse 9, Judah's share was too large; a reader of Genesis hears an older word behind it.

verseByVerse.quote: The second lot came out for Simeon, for the tribe of the people of Simeon, according to their clans, and their inheritance was in the midst of the inheritance of the people of Judah. And they had for their inheritance Beersheba, Sheba, Moladah, Hazar-shual, Balah, Ezem, Eltolad, Bethul, Hormah, Ziklag, Beth-marcaboth, Hazar-susah, Beth-lebaoth, and Sharuhen—thirteen cities with their villages; Ain, Rimmon, Ether, and Ashan—four cities with their villages, together with all the villages around these cities as far as Baalath-beer, Ramah of the Negeb. This was the inheritance of the tribe of the people of Simeon according to their clans. The inheritance of the people of Simeon formed part of the territory of the people of Judah. Because the portion of the people of Judah was too large for them, the people of Simeon obtained an inheritance in the midst of their inheritance.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Simeon does not get a border. He gets towns inside somebody else's country, and the writer explains it as a practical adjustment: Judah's allotment was too big, so Simeon was fitted into it.

The explanation is true and not the whole story. Simeon has no frontier, no coastline, no capital, nothing on the map with his name along the edge of it. Within a few generations he has largely dissolved into Judah, and by the time the tribes are listed in later Scripture he is barely there.

Go back to a deathbed in Egypt. Simeon and Levi had taken swords into Shechem and killed every man in the town, and their father had never forgiven it. His word over them was a curse on their anger: cursed be their anger, for it is fierce, and their wrath, for it is cruel. I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel (Gen. 49:7).

Both were scattered, exactly as he said, and the two outcomes could not be less alike. Levi's scattering became the priesthood, a tribe with no land, deliberately distributed so that every part of Israel had someone to teach it the law. Simeon's scattering was absorption, and it left little behind.

The same curse fell on both, and God did something with one of them. The difference was not in the words spoken at the bedside. Scripture shows where Levi’s story turned: at the golden calf, when Moses cried out for whoever was on the LORD’s side, the sons of Levi came (Exodus 32:26-29). A family under a curse became the tribe that served at God’s altar, which is the gospel in miniature: in Christ, who became a curse for us (Galatians 3:13), the sentence that hung over a life can be turned into a calling.
verseByVerse.note: Several of Simeon’s towns, Beersheba among them, appear in Judah’s list as well (15:26-32).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Four lots follow in order: Zebulun in the north with twelve towns (vv. 10-16), Issachar in the Jezreel valley with sixteen (vv. 17-23), Asher along the coast towards Sidon with twenty-two (vv. 24-31), and Naphtali in the high country with nineteen (vv. 32-39). Each entry follows the same form: the lot came out, the boundary ran, the cities with their villages, the inheritance according to their clans.
verseByVerse.theology: These four tribes get the north, and the north is where the Gospels happen.
verseByVerse.examples: Read quickly, the list is a register of villages. Read with the Gospels open, it is the stage being set: the towns of the ministry of Jesus are entered in this register more than a thousand years early.

verseByVerse.quote: The third lot came up for the people of Zebulun, according to their clans. And the territory of their inheritance reached as far as Sarid. Then their boundary goes up westward and on to Mareal and touches Dabbesheth, then the brook that is east of Jokneam. From Sarid it goes in the other direction eastward toward the sunrise to the boundary of Chisloth-tabor. From there it goes to Daberath, then up to Japhia. From there it passes along on the east toward the sunrise to Gath-hepher, to Eth-kazin, and going on to Rimmon it bends toward Neah, then on the north the boundary turns about to Hannathon, and it ends at the Valley of Iphtahel; and Kattath, Nahalal, Shimron, Idalah, and Bethlehem—twelve cities with their villages. This is the inheritance of the people of Zebulun, according to their clans—these cities with their villages. The fourth lot came out for Issachar, for the people of Issachar, according to their clans. Their territory included Jezreel, Chesulloth, Shunem, Hapharaim, Shion, Anaharath, Rabbith, Kishion, Ebez, Remeth, En-gannim, En-haddah, Beth-pazzez. The boundary also touches Tabor, Shahazumah, and Beth-shemesh, and its boundary ends at the Jordan—sixteen cities with their villages. This is the inheritance of the tribe of the people of Issachar, according to their clans—the cities with their villages. The fifth lot came out for the tribe of the people of Asher according to their clans. Their territory included Helkath, Hali, Beten, Achshaph, Allammelech, Amad, and Mishal. On the west it touches Carmel and Shihor-libnath, then it turns eastward, it goes to Beth-dagon, and touches Zebulun and the Valley of Iphtahel northward to Beth-emek and Neiel. Then it continues in the north to Cabul, Ebron, Rehob, Hammon, Kanah, as far as Sidon the Great. Then the boundary turns to Ramah, reaching to the fortified city of Tyre. Then the boundary turns to Hosah, and it ends at the sea; Mahalab, Achzib, Ummah, Aphek and Rehob—twenty-two cities with their villages. This is the inheritance of the tribe of the people of Asher according to their clans—these cities with their villages. The sixth lot came out for the people of Naphtali, for the people of Naphtali, according to their clans. And their boundary ran from Heleph, from the oak in Zaanannim, and Adami-nekeb, and Jabneel, as far as Lakkum, and it ended at the Jordan. Then the boundary turns westward to Aznoth-tabor and goes from there to Hukkok, touching Zebulun at the south and Asher on the west and Judah on the east at the Jordan. The fortified cities are Ziddim, Zer, Hammath, Rakkath, Chinnereth, Adamah, Ramah, Hazor, Kedesh, Edrei, En-hazor, Yiron, Migdal-el, Horem, Beth-anath, and Beth-shemesh—nineteen cities with their villages. This is the inheritance of the tribe of the people of Naphtali according to their clans—the cities with their villages.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Four tribes in thirty verses, each in the same form: the lot, the boundary, so many cities with their villages. The effect is meant to be cumulative rather than memorable: a country handed over in an orderly way to families who will farm it.

But hold the two names at either end of the list. Centuries later a prophet writing about a northern region wrecked by invasion picks out those two tribes: In the former time he brought into contempt the land of Zebulun and the land of Naphtali... The people who walked in darkness have seen a great light; those who dwelt in a land of deep darkness, on them has light shone (Isa. 9:1-2).

When Jesus left Nazareth for a fishing town on the lake to begin preaching, Matthew stopped the narrative to quote that verse (Matt. 4:13-16). Nazareth is in the hills of Zebulun's allotment; Capernaum is on Naphtali's shore. Neither town is mentioned here (they were nothing then, and one of them probably did not yet exist), but the ground they would stand on is being handed out, by lot, at Shiloh, in a list nobody reads.
verseByVerse.note: Both tribes lay in the region later called Galilee.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 40–48 — The Tribe That Lost Its Land
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The seventh lot goes to Dan, in the fertile lowland near the Philistine border (vv. 40-46). Then a sentence unlike anything else in these chapters: Dan's territory was lost, and they went north and took Leshem (v. 47).
verseByVerse.theology: Dan is the one tribe that could not hold what it was given. The Amorites pressed them back into the hill country (Judg. 1:34), so they left the land God assigned them and took land he had not.
verseByVerse.examples: The book of Judges tells that migration in full (Judg. 18), and it is not a proud story.

verseByVerse.quote: The seventh lot came out for the tribe of the people of Dan, according to their clans. And the territory of its inheritance included Zorah, Eshtaol, Ir-shemesh, Shaalabbin, Aijalon, Ithlah, Elon, Timnah, Ekron, Eltekeh, Gibbethon, Baalath, Jehud, Bene-berak, Gath-rimmon, and Me-jarkon and Rakkon with the territory over against Joppa. When the territory of the people of Dan was lost to them, the people of Dan went up and fought against Leshem, and after capturing it and striking it with the sword they took possession of it and settled in it, calling Leshem, Dan, after the name of Dan their ancestor. This is the inheritance of the tribe of the people of Dan, according to their clans—these cities with their villages.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Dan is given good ground: the fertile lowland west of Benjamin, running down towards the coast. On paper it is one of the better allotments in the country.

It also sits directly against the Philistines, and that turns out to be the whole story. Zorah and Eshtaol, on Dan's list, are where Samson will be born and buried: the strong man who fought that border single-handed and never cleared it.

Other tribes are recorded as failing to take part of what they were given. Dan is the tribe that could not hold what it had. The pressure from the coast was more than they would bear, so they marched about a hundred miles north, attacked a quiet unsuspecting town at the far frontier, and renamed it after themselves.

The details in Judges are worse than this verse lets on. On the way north the Danites steal a household idol and persuade the man's hired Levite to be priest to a whole tribe instead, a better career, they tell him. They set up the stolen idol at Laish, and it stood as long as the house of God was at Shiloh (Judg. 18:30-31). While the tabernacle stood, one of the twelve tribes was running a rival shrine with a stolen god and a bought priest. Centuries later Jeroboam put one of his two golden calves in that same town, because it already had the habit.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 49–51 — The Man Who Was Served Last
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When every tribe has been provided for, Israel gives Joshua an inheritance (v. 49). By command of the LORD they give him the town he asked for, Timnath-serah in the hill country of Ephraim, and he rebuilt the city and settled in it (v. 50). Verse 51 closes the whole distribution: Eleazar, Joshua and the heads of the tribes, by lot at Shiloh, before the LORD, at the entrance of the tent of meeting. So they finished dividing the land.
verseByVerse.theology: The man who conquered the country is given somewhere to live only after every tribe has its portion. He had the authority to take whatever he wanted at any point in seven chapters, and he waited until the register was closed.
verseByVerse.examples: Caleb asked for a mountain full of giants. Joshua asks for one town, and has to rebuild it. The two old men who brought back the minority report at Kadesh take their portions in character.

verseByVerse.quote: When they had finished distributing the several territories of the land as inheritances, the people of Israel gave an inheritance among them to Joshua the son of Nun. By command of the LORD they gave him the city that he asked, Timnath-serah in the hill country of Ephraim. And he rebuilt the city and settled in it. These are the inheritances that Eleazar the priest and Joshua the son of Nun and the heads of the fathers' houses of the tribes of the people of Israel distributed by lot at Shiloh before the LORD, at the entrance of the tent of meeting. So they finished dividing the land.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The first words carry the point: when they had finished distributing.

Every tribe has been provided for. Judah has its hundred-odd towns, Benjamin its twenty-six, Dan has walked north, Levi is about to get its forty-eight, and the register is closed. Only then does anyone give the commander-in-chief anywhere to live.

He has run this distribution for seven chapters. He casts the lots, he has the ear of the priest, the confidence of the nation and the authority of a man God said he would exalt, and at any point he could have taken a valley without anybody objecting. He asks for one town in his own tribal hill country, and by the sound of it not a good one, because he had to rebuild it before he could live there.

The whole distribution is signed off in one verse, and every phrase matters: by lot, at Shiloh, before the LORD, at the entrance of the tent of meeting. Not in a palace, not by negotiation, not according to the size of anyone's army. A nation of former slaves who owned nothing within living memory now hold a country town by town, with the deeds drawn up at the door of a tent, and the man who took it for them lived in a rebuilt house in the hills and was served last.

20.title: The Cities of Refuge
20.text: <sup>1</sup>Then the LORD said to Joshua,<sup>2</sup>"Say to the people of Israel, 'Appoint the cities of refuge, of which I spoke to you through Moses,<sup>3</sup>that the manslayer who strikes any person without intent or unknowingly may flee there. They shall be for you a refuge from the avenger of blood.<sup>4</sup>He shall flee to one of these cities and shall stand at the entrance of the gate of the city and explain his case to the elders of that city. Then they shall take him into the city and give him a place, and he shall remain with them.<sup>5</sup>And if the avenger of blood pursues him, they shall not give up the manslayer into his hand, because he struck his neighbor unknowingly, and did not hate him in the past.<sup>6</sup>And he shall remain in that city until he has stood before the congregation for judgment, until the death of him who is high priest at the time. Then the manslayer may return to his own town and his own home, to the town from which he fled.'"<sup>7</sup>So they set apart Kedesh in Galilee in the hill country of Naphtali, and Shechem in the hill country of Ephraim, and Kiriath-arba (that is, Hebron) in the hill country of Judah.<sup>8</sup>And beyond the Jordan east of Jericho, they appointed Bezer in the wilderness on the tableland, from the tribe of Reuben, and Ramoth in Gilead, from the tribe of Gad, and Golan in Bashan, from the tribe of Manasseh.<sup>9</sup>These were the cities designated for all the people of Israel and for the stranger sojourning among them, that anyone who killed a person without intent could flee there, so that he might not die by the hand of the avenger of blood, till he stood before the congregation.
20.overview:
The land is divided, and God speaks again to ask for something that is not a fort or a shrine: six towns where a man who has killed somebody by accident can go and not be killed. Deuteronomy gives the example: an axe-head flies off the handle and a neighbour is dead (Deut. 19:5). Nobody meant anything, and somebody is dead.

In a world with no police, the dead man's nearest relative, the avenger of blood, comes for the man who did it. God does not abolish him, because the loss is real. He provides a place to run, because a family in the first week of grief is in no state to weigh intent.

Everything about the refuge is public, and its strangest clause is its end: even after a trial clears him, the man stays until the death of him who is high priest at the time (v. 6). His release waits on a funeral he has no part in.

The six are spread three west and three east, so that nobody was much more than a day's run from a gate, and the last verse opens them to the foreigner on exactly the same terms.
20.theology:
Justice and mercy in the same statute. The law does not pretend the killing did not happen and does not treat the avenger as a criminal. It builds a distinction into the legal system, between a murderer and a man who has killed someone, and then builds six towns to make the distinction survivable while it is being established. Israel is given a trial and a place to wait for it.

Freedom by the death of the high priest. Verse 6 is where Christian preachers have long seen Christ. The refugee's exile ends at one moment only: when the high priest dies. A death he had nothing to do with opens the gate and gives him his home back. Hebrews describes Christians in this language, we who have fled for refuge might have strong encouragement to hold fast to the hope set before us (Heb. 6:18), in the letter that spends four chapters on a high priest who died. Hebrews does not cite this law by name, so the link is a pattern rather than a stated type, but it fits the gospel closely.

Refuge that a frightened man can reach. Three cities west and three east, spaced north, middle and south. Mercy in Scripture is characteristically practical: not a principle announced but a road built, near enough to be reached by somebody running.

The stranger, again. A foreigner with no tribe, no land and no clan to protect him gets the same gate on the same terms (v. 9), one more outsider this book quietly brings inside the covenant.
20.examples:
A man whose axe-head killed his neighbour ran for a town he had probably never visited, stood at the gate in front of strangers and told them what he had done, and lived there among people who all knew, waiting, for years perhaps, on the health of an old man in Shiloh he had never met.

For a Christian the picture is close to exact. Everything that fixed that man's position was outside him. He could not buy his way home, earn it or appeal. He was safe and not yet free, and his freedom came through a death that was nothing to do with him. For those who have fled to Christ, that death has already happened.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–3 — A City to Run To
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: God speaks, and what he commands is not a battle but an address: appoint the cities of refuge, of which I spoke to you through Moses (vv. 1-2). Their purpose is stated exactly: so that a man who kills without intent or unknowingly may flee there, and be safe from the avenger of blood (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: The law is drawing a line that every legal system since has had to draw, and drawing it carefully. There is a difference between a murderer and a man who has killed somebody, and a society without that distinction will either execute the innocent or let the guilty walk.
verseByVerse.examples: The avenger was family, not a vigilante, and these cities exist to get between a grieving man and a mistake.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the LORD said to Joshua, "Say to the people of Israel, 'Appoint the cities of refuge, of which I spoke to you through Moses, that the manslayer who strikes any person without intent or unknowingly may flee there. They shall be for you a refuge from the avenger of blood.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Consider the situation this law exists for. A man is chopping wood and the axe-head flies off the handle and kills his neighbour; that is the example Deuteronomy uses (Deut. 19:5). Nobody meant anything, and somebody is dead.

In a world with no police force and no public prosecutor, the dead man's nearest relative comes for the man who did it. The avenger of blood is not a vigilante; he is family, carrying out a duty society expected of him. The word is go'el, used in Leviticus and Ruth of the kinsman who buys back a relative's land or pays his debts, and by Isaiah of God himself as Israel's Redeemer. The nearest relative was responsible for everything a helpless family member could not do for himself, and in a killing that included blood.

So God does two things at once. He does not abolish the avenger, because the loss is real and the demand for justice is not wicked. And he provides a place to run, because grief is in no condition to weigh intent. A society that will not distinguish murder from accident ends by executing the innocent, and one that makes the distinction too easily ends by releasing the guilty. Israel is given six towns and a trial.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 4–6 — Until the Death of the High Priest
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The procedure is set out step by step. The man runs, stands at the entrance of the gate, and states his case to the elders, who take him in and give him a place (v. 4). If the avenger arrives, they are not to hand him over (v. 5). He stays until he has stood trial before the congregation, and then, whatever the verdict clears him of, he stays on until the death of him who is high priest at the time. Then he may go home (v. 6).
verseByVerse.theology: He does not sneak in; he explains himself in the open, and the elders have to keep him against an angry family. Refuge in Israel was a decision made by a whole town.
verseByVerse.examples: Two hearings are in view: the elders at the gate decide whether to take him in, and the congregation later tries the case. Refuge was shelter until a verdict, not an acquittal in advance.

verseByVerse.quote: He shall flee to one of these cities and shall stand at the entrance of the gate of the city and explain his case to the elders of that city. Then they shall take him into the city and give him a place, and he shall remain with them. And if the avenger of blood pursues him, they shall not give up the manslayer into his hand, because he struck his neighbor unknowingly, and did not hate him in the past. And he shall remain in that city until he has stood before the congregation for judgment, until the death of him who is high priest at the time. Then the manslayer may return to his own town and his own home, to the town from which he fled.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The procedure is public from the first minute. He does not slip in at night and hide. He stands at the gate, where the elders sat and business was done, and states his case out loud. They take him in and give him a place: not a cell, but somewhere to sleep and work in a town full of people who now know exactly what he has done.

Then the town has to stand between him and the family. That is not a small thing to ask of strangers: a grieving relative arrives at the gate with a right that everyone recognises, and the elders have to say no and mean it. The reason given is that he did not hate him in the past: motive is weighed by asking what the relationship had been before, as a competent court still does.

Then the strangest and best clause in the chapter. Even after the trial clears him, the man does not go home. His stay has one end date: the death of him who is high priest at the time. His freedom does not depend on compensation, or on the family relenting, or on a term of years, or on anything he can do. He is safe, and he is not home, and only the death of a man he may never have met will end his exile.

When that death comes, the gate opens. No payment is made and no further verdict is delivered. A high priest dies and the man goes back to his own town and his own home.

The letter to the Hebrews reaches for this picture when it describes Christians as people who have fled for refuge… to hold fast to the hope set before us (Heb. 6:18), and it is the same letter that spends four chapters on a high priest who dies.

The picture limps in one place, and the limp is good news. The manslayer was innocent of murder, and the high priest’s death only ended his exile. Those who flee to Christ are not innocent, and their High Priest’s death does more: he put away sin by the sacrifice of himself (Hebrews 9:26), and he lives for ever to intercede for them (Hebrews 7:25). Their refuge is not a town they wait in but the Priest himself.

Israel had a law on its books for centuries in which a man's exile ended, and his old life was handed back to him, by the death of the high priest and by nothing else. Nobody who ran to one of those six gates could have said what it was for. They knew only that the date they were waiting for was somebody else's funeral.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The six are named and placed: Kedesh in Galilee, Shechem in the hill country of Ephraim, and Hebron in Judah on the west side (v. 7); Bezer on the tableland, Ramoth in Gilead and Golan in Bashan on the east (v. 8). Verse 9 states who they were for: all the people of Israel and for the stranger sojourning among them.
verseByVerse.theology: North, middle and south on each side, so that no one was much more than a day's run from a gate. The mercy is within reach of a frightened man on foot.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 9 names the foreigner alongside the Israelite, on exactly the same terms.

verseByVerse.quote: So they set apart Kedesh in Galilee in the hill country of Naphtali, and Shechem in the hill country of Ephraim, and Kiriath-arba (that is, Hebron) in the hill country of Judah. And beyond the Jordan east of Jericho, they appointed Bezer in the wilderness on the tableland, from the tribe of Reuben, and Ramoth in Gilead, from the tribe of Gad, and Golan in Bashan, from the tribe of Manasseh. These were the cities designated for all the people of Israel and for the stranger sojourning among them, that anyone who killed a person without intent could flee there, so that he might not die by the hand of the avenger of blood, till he stood before the congregation.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Three towns on the west of the Jordan, north, middle and south, and three on the east matching them. That spacing is what turns a merciful principle into a merciful provision. A frightened man on foot, with a relative behind him, does not need a doctrine of asylum. He needs to know which way to run and that he can get there before dark.

Two of the names are old friends. Hebron is Caleb's town and holds Abraham's grave. Shechem is where Joseph's bones will be buried (24:32) and where the nation stood between the two mountains to hear the law read. The places thickest with Israel's history are set aside for people running for their lives.

And the last clause does what this book keeps doing: and for the stranger sojourning among them. The foreigner, with no clan to protect him, is named in the statute alongside everybody else. Rahab walked out of Jericho, the Gibeonites carried water to the altar, Caleb the Kenizzite got Hebron, and now the law of refuge is written with the outsider inside it.

21.overview:
Every other tribe is housed, and Levi comes last and has to ask. They ask with a promise rather than a need (v. 2), and the towns are granted at once, out of the other tribes' own inheritance.

Forty-eight cities, in every tribe and every region, complete the sentence Jacob spoke over Simeon and Levi, so that no family in Israel lived far from someone whose calling was to teach the law. Six of them are the cities of refuge from the previous chapter.

Then the summit: not one word of all the good promises that the LORD had made to the house of Israel had failed; all came to pass (v. 45), written by the man who has just spent nine chapters listing what was never taken.
21.theology:
Citing the promise. Three times in these chapters somebody comes to the leadership holding an old word rather than a grievance: Caleb with an oath from Kadesh-barnea, the daughters of Zelophehad with a ruling from Moses, and now the Levites. Every time the answer is immediate. Prayer in Scripture characteristically works this way: not informing God of a need but reminding him of a word.

A curse turned into a calling. Levi and Simeon received the same sentence for the same crime. Simeon largely disappeared into Judah; Levi became the teaching order of Israel. Nothing in the words spoken over them accounts for the difference; God did.

Mercy administered by the landless. The elders who had to stand at the gate and refuse to hand a man over to a grieving family were from the tribe that owned nothing and belonged to no faction. God put the asylum system in the hands of the only people in Israel with nothing to gain by an unjust verdict.

Not one word failed, and Gezer was not taken. Both are true and neither may be softened: God's delivery was complete, and Israel's occupation was not (13:6). And the faithfulness in verse 45 has another edge, which Joshua names two chapters later: the God who kept every good word will keep the other kind by the same reliability (23:15).
21.examples:
The tribe that had carried the ark across the Jordan waited until everybody else was housed, then came and quoted a promise, and the other tribes handed back forty-eight of their own towns.

Verse 45 is the verse to carry home, and the honest way to carry it is where the book puts it, immediately after the list of what was never taken. Nothing God promised you is outstanding. A good deal of ground in your life is still occupied. This chapter refuses to let you use either sentence to excuse the other. The possessing is not done by willpower: the God who gave the land gives his Spirit to those who are his, and where you have left ground untaken, the record that stands for you is Christ's, not yours, and the way back is to come to him and take the next town.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The heads of the Levites come to Eleazar, Joshua and the tribal heads at Shiloh (v. 1) and make their case in one sentence: the LORD commanded through Moses that we be given cities to dwell in, along with their pasturelands for our livestock (v. 2). So by command of the LORD, Israel gives them towns out of its own inheritance (v. 3).
verseByVerse.theology: Levi comes last, after every other tribe is housed, and asks with a promise rather than a need.
verseByVerse.examples: Every Levite house stood on ground some other tribe gave up: Israel paid for its own teachers.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the heads of the fathers' houses of the Levites came to Eleazar the priest and to Joshua the son of Nun and to the heads of the fathers' houses of the tribes of the people of Israel. And they said to them at Shiloh in the land of Canaan, "The LORD commanded through Moses that we be given cities to dwell in, along with their pasturelands for our livestock." So by command of the LORD the people of Israel gave to the Levites the following cities and pasturelands out of their inheritance.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everybody else has been housed, down to Joshua in his rebuilt house in the hills. Levi has been mentioned four times since the register began, always to say it gets nothing, and now the heads of the tribe come and ask.

Look at what they ask with. Not "we have nowhere to live", which was true, and not "we carried the ark across the Jordan", which was also true. They say: the LORD commanded through Moses. Caleb did the same at eighty-five, citing an oath from Kadesh-barnea; the five daughters of Zelophehad did it, citing a ruling Moses had brought back from God. In every case the answer is the same and it is immediate.

Four words carry the cost: out of their inheritance. These towns are not spare land. Every one comes off some other tribe's allotment, already surveyed, drawn by lot and handed over. The men who teach Israel the law are housed at Israel's expense, on ground that families had already been given and had to hand back.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The distribution runs for forty verses. Thirteen towns go to the priests, the sons of Aaron, out of Judah, Simeon and Benjamin (v. 4); ten to the rest of Kohath out of Ephraim, Dan and half-Manasseh (v. 5); thirteen to Gershon in the north (v. 6); twelve to Merari from Reuben, Gad and Zebulun (v. 7). Then each is named, town by town, with its pasturelands, and the total is given: in all forty-eight cities with their pasturelands (vv. 41-42).
verseByVerse.theology: Jacob's curse becomes a commission: the scattering he foretold now puts a teacher of the law within reach of every family in Israel.
verseByVerse.examples: Six of the forty-eight are the cities of refuge of chapter 20.

verseByVerse.quote: The lot came out for the clans of the Kohathites. So those Levites who were descendants of Aaron the priest received by lot from the tribes of Judah, Simeon, and Benjamin, thirteen cities. And the rest of the Kohathites received by lot from the clans of the tribe of Ephraim, from the tribe of Dan and the half-tribe of Manasseh, ten cities. The Gershonites received by lot from the clans of the tribe of Issachar, from the tribe of Asher, from the tribe of Naphtali, and from the half-tribe of Manasseh in Bashan, thirteen cities. The Merarites according to their clans received from the tribe of Reuben, the tribe of Gad, and the tribe of Zebulun, twelve cities. These cities and their pasturelands the people of Israel gave by lot to the Levites, as the LORD had commanded through Moses. Out of the tribe of the people of Judah and the tribe of the people of Simeon they gave the following cities mentioned by name, which went to the descendants of Aaron, one of the clans of the Kohathites who belonged to the people of Levi; since the lot fell to them first. They gave them Kiriath-arba (Arba being the father of Anak), that is Hebron, in the hill country of Judah, along with the pasturelands around it. But the fields of the city and its villages had been given to Caleb the son of Jephunneh as his possession. And to the descendants of Aaron the priest they gave Hebron, the city of refuge for the manslayer, with its pasturelands, Libnah with its pasturelands, Jattir with its pasturelands, Eshtemoa with its pasturelands, Holon with its pasturelands, Debir with its pasturelands, Ain with its pasturelands, Juttah with its pasturelands, Beth-shemesh with its pasturelands—nine cities out of these two tribes; then out of the tribe of Benjamin, Gibeon with its pasturelands, Geba with its pasturelands, Anathoth with its pasturelands, and Almon with its pasturelands—four cities. The cities of the descendants of Aaron, the priests, were in all thirteen cities with their pasturelands. As to the rest of the Kohathites belonging to the Kohathite clans of the Levites, the cities allotted to them were out of the tribe of Ephraim. To them were given Shechem, the city of refuge for the manslayer, with its pasturelands in the hill country of Ephraim, Gezer with its pasturelands, Kibzaim with its pasturelands, Beth-horon with its pasturelands—four cities; and out of the tribe of Dan, Elteke with its pasturelands, Gibbethon with its pasturelands, Aijalon with its pasturelands, Gath-rimmon with its pasturelands—four cities; and out of the half-tribe of Manasseh, Taanach with its pasturelands, and Gath-rimmon with its pasturelands—two cities. The cities of the clans of the rest of the Kohathites were ten in all with their pasturelands. And to the Gershonites, one of the clans of the Levites, were given out of the half-tribe of Manasseh, Golan in Bashan with its pasturelands, the city of refuge for the manslayer, and Beeshterah with its pasturelands—two cities; and out of the tribe of Issachar, Kishion with its pasturelands, Daberath with its pasturelands, Jarmuth with its pasturelands, En-gannim with its pasturelands—four cities; and out of the tribe of Asher, Mishal with its pasturelands, Abdon with its pasturelands, Helkath with its pasturelands, and Rehob with its pasturelands—four cities; and out of the tribe of Naphtali, Kedesh in Galilee with its pasturelands, the city of refuge for the manslayer, Hammoth-dor with its pasturelands, and Kartan with its pasturelands—three cities. The cities of the several clans of the Gershonites were in all thirteen cities with their pasturelands. And to the rest of the Levites, the Merarite clans, were given out of the tribe of Zebulun, Jokneam with its pasturelands, Kartah with its pasturelands, Dimnah with its pasturelands, Nahalal with its pasturelands—four cities; and out of the tribe of Reuben, Bezer with its pasturelands, Jahaz with its pasturelands, Kedemoth with its pasturelands, and Mephaath with its pasturelands—four cities; and out of the tribe of Gad, Ramoth in Gilead with its pasturelands, the city of refuge for the manslayer, Mahanaim with its pasturelands, Heshbon with its pasturelands, Jazer with its pasturelands—four cities in all. As for the cities of the several Merarite clans, that is, the remainder of the clans of the Levites, those allotted to them were in all twelve cities. The cities of the Levites in the midst of the possession of the people of Israel were in all forty-eight cities with their pasturelands. These cities each had its pasturelands around it. So it was with all these cities.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The arithmetic matters. The thirteen priestly towns are drawn from Judah, Simeon and Benjamin, clustered in the south around the place where the temple will eventually stand. The men who will serve the altar are settled within reach of it centuries before there is one. The rest are spread everywhere else, and no tribe is without them.

This is the second half of the sentence Jacob spoke over Simeon and Levi for their swords at Shechem: I will divide them in Jacob and scatter them in Israel (Gen. 49:7). Simeon's scattering was absorption into Judah. Levi's is forty-eight towns in every corner of the country, so that no Israelite family lives far from somebody whose job description Moses had already written: they shall teach Jacob your rules and Israel your law (Deut. 33:10). A tribe sentenced to have no home of its own ended up living in every home in Israel.

Kedesh, Shechem, Hebron, Bezer, Ramoth and Golan are all on this list. The towns that took a frightened man in were held by the tribe with no land, no faction and no stake in anybody's feud: the only people in Israel who had nothing to lose by being fair.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Three verses close the whole allotment and they are the summit of the book. The LORD gave Israel all the land he swore to their fathers, and they took possession and settled there (v. 43). He gave them rest on every side, and not one of their enemies had withstood them (v. 44). And then: not one word of all the good promises that the LORD had made to the house of Israel had failed; all came to pass (v. 45).
verseByVerse.theology: Read against nine chapters of unfinished business, this looks impossible. How can the writer say that not one word failed?
verseByVerse.examples: The answer lies in who had undertaken what: God to give, and Israel to possess. It is Israel's part that is incomplete.

verseByVerse.quote: Thus the LORD gave to Israel all the land that he swore to give to their fathers. And they took possession of it, and they settled there. And the LORD gave them rest on every side just as he had sworn to their fathers. Not one of all their enemies had withstood them, for the LORD had given all their enemies into their hands. Not one word of all the good promises that the LORD had made to the house of Israel had failed; all came to pass.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Everything since chapter 1 is gathered up here: the land sworn to the fathers, given; the possession, taken; the rest, granted on every side. Then the sentence, and it needs facing honestly rather than admiring.

The reader has just come through nine chapters that say the opposite. Judah could not take Jerusalem. Ephraim did not take Gezer. Manasseh left the six best towns in the north in Canaanite hands. Dan lost its whole allotment. The phrase to this day has been used again and again about ground never occupied. How can a writer who recorded all of that say that not one word failed?

Because God had already set out who was doing what: I myself will drive them out from before the people of Israel. Only allot the land to Israel for an inheritance, as I have commanded you (13:6). Every promise on his side was kept, at the Jordan, at Jericho, at Merom, on the day the sun stood still. What is unfinished is not his delivery but Israel's occupation. Verse 45 is a statement about God's record, and read as that, it is exact.

That is the shape of the Christian life too. Nothing promised is outstanding. The blood was shed, the tomb was emptied, the Spirit was given, and the inheritance is deeded. What is patchy is the possessing. This book will not let a reader blame God for Gezer, and it will not let him pretend Gezer was taken.

Not one word had failed. Not one. A nation of slaves who could not have taken a single walled city stood in a country of thirty-one kingdoms, in houses they did not build, eating from vineyards they did not plant, with the tent of meeting at Shiloh and the tribe that had nothing living among them to teach them the law. He said he would, centuries earlier, to a childless man in a foreign country. He did.

And every one of those promises was a down payment on a greater one. All the promises of God find their Yes in Christ (2 Corinthians 1:20). The rest on every side in verse 44 was real, and it was not final: if Joshua had given them rest, God would not have spoken later of another day (Hebrews 4:8). The land was kept by the word of God; the rest that remains is kept by the Son.

Was the promise fully kept? The boundaries promised to Abraham (Genesis 15:18) were reached, for a time, under Solomon (1 Kings 4:21), and Joshua says that God kept every word. Christians differ over whether a land promise to Israel is still to be fulfilled. Dispensational and some other premillennial believers expect one, because the land was sworn to Abraham’s offspring as an everlasting possession (Genesis 17:8). Many Reformed Christians think the New Testament widens the promise rather than repeating it: Abraham is heir of the world (Romans 4:13), and the patriarchs sought a better, heavenly country (Hebrews 11:16). Both sides honour the promise and differ over its final shape, and they should differ as brothers.

22.title: The Eastern Tribes Return and the Altar of Witness
22.text: <sup>1</sup>At that time Joshua summoned the Reubenites and the Gadites and the half-tribe of Manasseh,<sup>2</sup>and said to them, "You have kept all that Moses the servant of the LORD commanded you and have obeyed my voice in all that I have commanded you.<sup>3</sup>You have not forsaken your brothers these many days, down to this day, but have been careful to keep the charge of the LORD your God.<sup>4</sup>And now the LORD your God has given rest to your brothers, as he promised them. Therefore turn and go to your tents in the land where your possession lies, which Moses the servant of the LORD gave you on the other side of the Jordan.<sup>5</sup>Only be very careful to observe the commandment and the law that Moses the servant of the LORD commanded you, to love the LORD your God, and to walk in all his ways and to keep his commandments and to cling to him and to serve him with all your heart and with all your soul."<sup>6</sup>So Joshua blessed them and sent them away, and they went to their tents.<sup>7</sup>Now to the one half of the tribe of Manasseh Moses had given a possession in Bashan, but to the other half Joshua had given a possession beside their brothers in the land west of the Jordan. And when Joshua sent them away to their homes and blessed them,<sup>8</sup>he said to them, "Go back to your tents with much wealth and with very much livestock, with silver, gold, bronze, and iron, and with much clothing. Divide the spoil of your enemies with your brothers."<sup>9</sup>So the people of Reuben and the people of Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh returned home, parting from the people of Israel at Shiloh, which is in the land of Canaan, to go to the land of Gilead, their own land of which they had possessed themselves by command of the LORD through Moses.<sup>10</sup>And when they came to the region of the Jordan that is in the land of Canaan, the people of Reuben and the people of Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh built there an altar by the Jordan, an altar of imposing size.<sup>11</sup>And the people of Israel heard it said, "Behold, the people of Reuben and the people of Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh have built the altar at the frontier of the land of Canaan, in the region about the Jordan, on the side that belongs to the people of Israel."<sup>12</sup>And when the people of Israel heard of it, the whole assembly of the people of Israel gathered at Shiloh to make war against them.<sup>13</sup>Then the people of Israel sent to the people of Reuben and the people of Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh, in the land of Gilead, Phinehas the son of Eleazar the priest,<sup>14</sup>and with him ten chiefs, one from each of the tribal families of Israel, every one of them the head of a family among the clans of Israel.<sup>15</sup>And they came to the people of Reuben, the people of Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh, in the land of Gilead, and they said to them,<sup>16</sup>"Thus says the whole congregation of the LORD, 'What is this breach of faith that you have committed against the God of Israel in turning away this day from following the LORD by building yourselves an altar this day in rebellion against the LORD?<sup>17</sup>Have we not had enough of the sin at Peor from which even yet we have not cleansed ourselves, and for which there came a plague upon the congregation of the LORD,<sup>18</sup>that you too must turn away this day from following the LORD? And if you too rebel against the LORD today then tomorrow he will be angry with the whole congregation of Israel.<sup>19</sup>But now, if the land of your possession is unclean, pass over into the LORD's land where the LORD's tabernacle stands, and take for yourselves a possession among us. Only do not rebel against the LORD or make us as rebels by building for yourselves an altar other than the altar of the LORD our God.<sup>20</sup>Did not Achan the son of Zerah break faith in the matter of the devoted things, and wrath fell upon all the congregation of Israel? And he did not perish alone for his iniquity.'"<sup>21</sup>Then the people of Reuben, the people of Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh said in answer to the heads of the families of Israel,<sup>22</sup>"The Mighty One, God, the LORD! The Mighty One, God, the LORD! He knows; and let Israel itself know! If it was in rebellion or in breach of faith against the LORD, do not spare us today<sup>23</sup>for building an altar to turn away from following the LORD. Or if we did so to offer burnt offerings or grain offerings or peace offerings on it, may the LORD himself take vengeance.<sup>24</sup>No, but we did it from fear that in time to come your children might say to our children, 'What have you to do with the LORD, the God of Israel?<sup>25</sup>For the LORD has made the Jordan a boundary between us and you, you people of Reuben and people of Gad. You have no portion in the LORD.' So your children might make our children cease to worship the LORD.<sup>26</sup>Therefore we said, 'Let us now build an altar, not for burnt offering, nor for sacrifice,<sup>27</sup>but to be a witness between us and you, and between our generations after us, that we do perform the service of the LORD in his presence with our burnt offerings and sacrifices and peace offerings, so your children will not say to our children in time to come, "You have no portion in the LORD."'<sup>28</sup>And we thought, 'If this should be said to us or to our descendants in time to come, we should say, "Behold, the copy of the altar of the LORD, which our fathers made, not for burnt offerings, nor for sacrifice, but to be a witness between us and you."'<sup>29</sup>Far be it from us that we should rebel against the LORD and turn away this day from following the LORD by building an altar for burnt offering, grain offering, or sacrifice, other than the altar of the LORD our God that stands before his tabernacle!"<sup>30</sup>When Phinehas the priest and the chiefs of the congregation, the heads of the families of Israel who were with him, heard the words that the people of Reuben and the people of Gad and the people of Manasseh spoke, it was good in their eyes.<sup>31</sup>And Phinehas the son of Eleazar the priest said to the people of Reuben and the people of Gad and the people of Manasseh, "Today we know that the LORD is in our midst, because you have not committed this breach of faith against the LORD. Now you have delivered the people of Israel from the hand of the LORD."<sup>32</sup>Then Phinehas the son of Eleazar the priest, and the chiefs, returned from the people of Reuben and the people of Gad in the land of Gilead to the land of Canaan, to the people of Israel, and brought back word to them.<sup>33</sup>And the report was good in the eyes of the people of Israel. And the people of Israel blessed God and spoke no more of making war against them to destroy the land where the people of Reuben and the people of Gad were settled.<sup>34</sup>The people of Reuben and the people of Gad called the altar Witness, "For," they said, "it is a witness between us that the LORD is God."
22.overview:
The eastern tribes are discharged with a commendation they have earned over years of war: you have not forsaken your brothers these many days (v. 3). They already had their land when they crossed the river to fight for everyone else's, and now they are sent home rich, with instructions to share the spoil with the families who stayed behind.

Joshua's parting charge is five verbs: love, walk, keep, cling, serve (v. 5). He is warning settled men going home with money, not soldiers facing an enemy.

At the Jordan they build an altar of imposing size, and Israel musters for war in a single verse. The alarm is not stupid, but they concluded before they asked. What saves the day is a delegation sent first, led by Phinehas, the most zealous man in Israel, and he asks a question.

The answer nobody guessed is fear: the eastern tribes were afraid their grandchildren would one day be told you have no portion in the LORD (v. 25). So they built a copy of an altar, never to be lit, and called it Witness.
22.theology:
Inquire before you accuse. Israel gathered for war on an inference about a building nobody had visited. What averted the disaster was a delegation, and its leader was the most zealous man in the nation. Zeal and enquiry are not opposites here. Jesus gives the church the same order of operations: go and tell him his fault, between you and him alone (Matt. 18:15).

The offer inside the accusation. Verse 19 keeps this from being a story about religious hotheads: if your land is unclean, come and take a possession among us. The western tribes offered to cut their own allotments again rather than lose their brothers. That is what zeal for God looks like when it is not merely zeal for being right.

The fear of being written out. The eastern tribes understood that belonging must be visible to survive a generation, and built something that could be pointed at.

One altar, and one sacrifice. The western tribes were right that there could be only one altar, and the gospel shows why the oneness mattered so much. There is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus (1 Timothy 2:5), and one offering, made once for all (Hebrews 10:10-14). Every quarrel in this chapter was about how far a family might live from the one place of sacrifice; in Christ that sacrifice has been made, and those once far off are brought near by his blood (Ephesians 2:13).
22.examples:
A nation that had just finished a war mustered to fight its own brothers over a structure nobody had inspected, and the men on the far bank turned out to be terrified of being told one day that they did not belong.

Two things carry over without adjustment. The first is the procedure: go and ask before drawing a sword, as the man with the strongest convictions in Israel did. The second is the fear. A great deal of what looks like awkwardness or defensiveness in other Christians is the same quiet dread of being told they have no portion in the LORD. Find that out before you decide what you are looking at. Those who have themselves been welcomed in Christ, and given his Spirit of gentleness, can afford to ask first.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–9 — Sent Home with a Blessing
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Joshua calls the eastern tribes and gives them a commendation with no qualification in it: you have kept everything Moses commanded and obeyed my voice, and you have not forsaken your brothers these many days (vv. 2-3). Their brothers now have rest, so they are released to go home (v. 4) with one charge, which packs the whole law into five verbs: love the LORD, walk in his ways, keep his commandments, cling to him, serve him with all your heart and soul (v. 5). He blesses them (v. 6), tells them to take their share of the spoil home and divide it with the brothers who stayed (vv. 7-8), and they part from Israel at Shiloh (v. 9).
verseByVerse.theology: They promised this in chapter 1 and they have just finished paying for it: years of somebody else's war, fought by men who already had their land.
verseByVerse.examples: The fourth verb in verse 5 is cling, the word Genesis uses when a man holds fast to his wife (Gen. 2:24). Joshua's last word to men going home to a comfortable settlement is a word about attachment.

verseByVerse.quote: At that time Joshua summoned the Reubenites and the Gadites and the half-tribe of Manasseh, and said to them, "You have kept all that Moses the servant of the LORD commanded you and have obeyed my voice in all that I have commanded you. You have not forsaken your brothers these many days, down to this day, but have been careful to keep the charge of the LORD your God. And now the LORD your God has given rest to your brothers, as he promised them. Therefore turn and go to your tents in the land where your possession lies, which Moses the servant of the LORD gave you on the other side of the Jordan. Only be very careful to observe the commandment and the law that Moses the servant of the LORD commanded you, to love the LORD your God, and to walk in all his ways and to keep his commandments and to cling to him and to serve him with all your heart and with all your soul." So Joshua blessed them and sent them away, and they went to their tents.
verseByVerse.commentary:
It is a commendation with nothing held back, earned over about seven years. These men already had their land east of the Jordan, their families safe and their cattle grazing, and they were told to leave all of it and fight for other people's inheritance until everybody else was home. They did, with their wives and children on the far side of a river the whole time.

The condition of service was until the LORD gives rest to your brothers as he has to you (1:15). Joshua now certifies that the condition is met. Nobody had to argue about when it was over.

Then the charge, and its order matters. It comes after the LORD your God has given rest (v. 4): the land, the rest and the kept promise are already theirs, and the five verbs describe life with the God who gave them. One sits oddly among the practical ones. Cling is a word about grip and attachment, not about duty, and Joshua puts it between keeping commandments and serving wholeheartedly, as though the outward things will not survive without it.

The audience matters. Not soldiers facing an enemy, but men going home with money in their packs. Joshua knows where the danger is, and it is not on the road. It is in the third year of prosperity, across the river from Shiloh, when nothing whatever is going wrong.

Centuries later a lawyer asked which commandment was the greatest, and the answer he got was this verse's first verb: love the Lord your God with all your heart and with all your soul and with all your mind (Matt. 22:37). Nobody has kept it with all the heart but the one who gave that answer, and he kept it for those who have not. The cleaving the Christian is asked for is the work of his Spirit, who holds us fast to him before we learn to hold fast ourselves.

verseByVerse.quote: Now to the one half of the tribe of Manasseh Moses had given a possession in Bashan, but to the other half Joshua had given a possession beside their brothers in the land west of the Jordan. And when Joshua sent them away to their homes and blessed them, he said to them, "Go back to your tents with much wealth and with very much livestock, with silver, gold, bronze, and iron, and with much clothing. Divide the spoil of your enemies with your brothers." So the people of Reuben and the people of Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh returned home, parting from the people of Israel at Shiloh, which is in the land of Canaan, to go to the land of Gilead, their own land of which they had possessed themselves by command of the LORD through Moses.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They go home rich, and they are told to share it with those who stayed behind: the wives, the older boys, the men too old to march, who ran the farms for seven years and never lifted a sword. Joshua rules that the spoil is theirs too.

It is the principle David will make a statute generations later: as his share is who goes down into the battle, so shall his share be who stays by the baggage. They shall share alike (1 Sam. 30:24).

They part at Shiloh, where the tent of meeting stands. The last thing they see of the rest of Israel is the place where God lives, and then they walk east towards a river they will be on the wrong side of for the rest of their history.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 10–20 — An Altar, and an Army
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: At the Jordan the eastern tribes build an altar of imposing size (v. 10). The news travels, and the reaction is immediate: the whole assembly gathers at Shiloh to make war against them (vv. 11-12). Before marching, they send Phinehas the priest and ten chiefs, one from each tribe (vv. 13-14), and the charge they carry is blunt: what is this breach of faith, this rebellion (v. 16)? They cite two precedents: Peor, whose plague they have not finished paying for (vv. 17-18), and Achan, who did not perish alone for his iniquity (v. 20). And in the middle of the accusation, an offer: if your land is unclean, cross over and take a possession among us (v. 19).
verseByVerse.theology: The alarm is not paranoia. Sacrifice was to be offered at one place only (Deut. 12), and the two examples they cite are both cases where the sin of a few brought wrath on everybody.
verseByVerse.examples: The delegation is ten chiefs, one from each tribe, with a priest at their head: the whole nation comes to ask, not one faction.

verseByVerse.quote: And when they came to the region of the Jordan that is in the land of Canaan, the people of Reuben and the people of Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh built there an altar by the Jordan, an altar of imposing size. And the people of Israel heard it said, "Behold, the people of Reuben and the people of Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh have built the altar at the frontier of the land of Canaan, in the region about the Jordan, on the side that belongs to the people of Israel." And when the people of Israel heard of it, the whole assembly of the people of Israel gathered at Shiloh to make war against them. Then the people of Israel sent to the people of Reuben and the people of Gad and the half-tribe of Manasseh, in the land of Gilead, Phinehas the son of Eleazar the priest, and with him ten chiefs, one from each of the tribal families of Israel, every one of them the head of a family among the clans of Israel.
verseByVerse.commentary:
They stop at the river and build something, and the writer records two facts about it: it is an altar, and it is big. Both facts are about to cause a war. Israel had one altar, at the tent of meeting, and Deuteronomy is emphatic that sacrifice happens at the place God chooses and nowhere else (Deut. 12:13-14). A second altar is not a regional convenience. It is a rival.

The response takes one verse. No debate is recorded, no delay, no committee: the whole assembly gathers, and it gathers to fight. These are men who finished a seven-year war within living memory, now mustering against the brothers they fought it with, over a structure by a river that nobody has been to look at.

Then, before the army moves, somebody has a better idea. They send a delegation, and the choice of leader is deliberate and not obvious. Phinehas is the man who at Peor saw an Israelite bring a Midianite woman into the camp during a plague, took a spear and killed them both, and the plague stopped (Num. 25:7-8). He is the most zealous man in Israel, the last person you would send if you wanted the matter smoothed over. Israel sends its hardest man, with ten tribal chiefs behind him, and what he does when he arrives is ask a question.

verseByVerse.quote: And they came to the people of Reuben, the people of Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh, in the land of Gilead, and they said to them, "Thus says the whole congregation of the LORD, 'What is this breach of faith that you have committed against the God of Israel in turning away this day from following the LORD by building yourselves an altar this day in rebellion against the LORD? Have we not had enough of the sin at Peor from which even yet we have not cleansed ourselves, and for which there came a plague upon the congregation of the LORD, that you too must turn away this day from following the LORD? And if you too rebel against the LORD today then tomorrow he will be angry with the whole congregation of Israel. But now, if the land of your possession is unclean, pass over into the LORD's land where the LORD's tabernacle stands, and take for yourselves a possession among us. Only do not rebel against the LORD or make us as rebels by building for yourselves an altar other than the altar of the LORD our God. Did not Achan the son of Zerah break faith in the matter of the devoted things, and wrath fell upon all the congregation of Israel? And he did not perish alone for his iniquity.'"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The charge is not softened. It is treason against God, put in those words, to men's faces. Whatever else is wrong here, this is not gossip.

Both precedents are on the point. At Peor twenty-four thousand died in the plague, and the man arguing here is the man who stopped it. At Ai one man buried plunder in his tent and thirty-six others were killed for it. He did not perish alone for his iniquity is not superstition; it is the doctrine of chapter 7, learned at funerals. So the alarm is intelligent and the mistake is procedural: they have raised an army on an inference.

Then, in the middle of an accusation of treason, the most unexpected sentence in the chapter. If your side of the river feels far from God, come and live on ours. The western tribes, who have just finished dividing a country into carefully surveyed allotments, offer to cut their own portions again rather than lose their brothers. They arrive armed, they accuse without inquiring, and their opening proposal is to give away their land.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 21–29 — We Were Afraid of Your Children
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The answer begins with an oath so emphatic it is said twice, the Mighty One, God, the LORD! The Mighty One, God, the LORD!, and invites destruction if the charge is true (vv. 22-23). Then the reason, and it is not what anyone expected. They were afraid that in time to come the western children would say to their children, what have you to do with the LORD, the God of Israel? For the LORD has made the Jordan a boundary... You have no portion in the LORD (vv. 24-25). So the altar is a copy, built as a witness and never for sacrifice, so that no descendant of theirs could be told he did not belong (vv. 26-29).
verseByVerse.theology: The answer turns the accusation inside out: the altar at the frontier was built out of loyalty, not rebellion.
verseByVerse.examples: Both sides are frightened of the same thing from opposite ends. The west fears a rival altar splitting the worship of God; the east fears a river splitting the people of God. Nobody in the chapter is indifferent, and that is why it nearly ended in a battle.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the people of Reuben, the people of Gad, and the half-tribe of Manasseh said in answer to the heads of the families of Israel, "The Mighty One, God, the LORD! The Mighty One, God, the LORD! He knows; and let Israel itself know! If it was in rebellion or in breach of faith against the LORD, do not spare us today for building an altar to turn away from following the LORD. Or if we did so to offer burnt offerings or grain offerings or peace offerings on it, may the LORD himself take vengeance. No, but we did it from fear that in time to come your children might say to our children, 'What have you to do with the LORD, the God of Israel? For the LORD has made the Jordan a boundary between us and you, you people of Reuben and people of Gad. You have no portion in the LORD.' So your children might make our children cease to worship the LORD. Therefore we said, 'Let us now build an altar, not for burnt offering, nor for sacrifice, but to be a witness between us and you, and between our generations after us, that we do perform the service of the LORD in his presence with our burnt offerings and sacrifices and peace offerings, so your children will not say to our children in time to come, "You have no portion in the LORD."' And we thought, 'If this should be said to us or to our descendants in time to come, we should say, "Behold, the copy of the altar of the LORD, which our fathers made, not for burnt offerings, nor for sacrifice, but to be a witness between us and you."' Far be it from us that we should rebel against the LORD and turn away this day from following the LORD by building an altar for burnt offering, grain offering, or sacrifice, other than the altar of the LORD our God that stands before his tabernacle!"
verseByVerse.commentary:
The answer begins with three names of God said twice over, El, Elohim, YHWH, about as emphatic as Hebrew gets, and then invites execution if the charge is true. Nobody is offended at being asked. They do not complain about the tone or the assumption; they answer the question under oath.

The reason is nothing anyone had guessed. They were afraid, not of the Canaanites or of Israel's army, but of a sentence not yet spoken, to be said by children not yet born, to children not yet born: you have no portion in the LORD.

Geography produced that fear. The Jordan is a real boundary. They are on the far side of it, out of sight of the tent of meeting, and the ordinary drift of two or three generations would be enough to make their grandchildren strangers. They could see it coming from a hundred miles and forty years away.

So the structure is not an altar for use. It is a copy of one, deliberately shaped like the real thing and deliberately never lit, standing at the river as an exhibit for a conversation that would happen after everyone present was dead.

They understood something easy to miss: belonging has to be visible to survive a generation. Their grandchildren would not have their memories, and children are told who they are by other children. So they put up something that could be pointed at. It is the instinct of the twelve stones out of the Jordan in chapter 4, built for exactly the same reason: when your children ask in time to come.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: When Phinehas and the chiefs hear the explanation, it was good in their eyes (v. 30), and the priest's verdict is generous: today we know the LORD is in our midst, because you have not committed this breach of faith; you have delivered the people of Israel from the hand of the LORD (v. 31). The delegation carries the report home, the assembly blesses God, and the talk of war stops (vv. 32-33). And the eastern tribes name the altar: Witness, for it is a witness between us that the LORD is God (v. 34).
verseByVerse.theology: Nobody in this chapter has to be humiliated for it to end well. The west does not have to admit it was hysterical and the east does not have to apologise for building anything. The delegation asked, the answer was true, and both sides went home believing better of each other than they had that morning.

verseByVerse.quote: When Phinehas the priest and the chiefs of the congregation, the heads of the families of Israel who were with him, heard the words that the people of Reuben and the people of Gad and the people of Manasseh spoke, it was good in their eyes. And Phinehas the son of Eleazar the priest said to the people of Reuben and the people of Gad and the people of Manasseh, "Today we know that the LORD is in our midst, because you have not committed this breach of faith against the LORD. Now you have delivered the people of Israel from the hand of the LORD." Then Phinehas the son of Eleazar the priest, and the chiefs, returned from the people of Reuben and the people of Gad in the land of Gilead to the land of Canaan, to the people of Israel, and brought back word to them. And the report was good in the eyes of the people of Israel. And the people of Israel blessed God and spoke no more of making war against them to destroy the land where the people of Reuben and the people of Gad were settled. The people of Reuben and the people of Gad called the altar Witness, "For," they said, "it is a witness between us that the LORD is God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
There is no grudging here, and no face-saving. The delegation came convinced of treason, heard the explanation, and accepted it completely.

The verdict from the hardest man in Israel is more generous than it needed to be. Today we know that the LORD is in our midst: his brothers' faithfulness is taken as evidence that God is present. And: you have delivered the people of Israel from the hand of the LORD. The accused end the interview as the deliverers. The army that gathered in one verse disperses in one verse, and the last thing it does is worship.

The name is the whole point: Witness. Not "Peace", and not anything about the quarrel. It stands at the river to testify that the men on the far side belong to the LORD. What almost destroyed Israel was not wickedness on either side but two parties jealous for the same God.

The fear underneath it all has been answered since, in terms the eastern tribes could not have known. Nobody in Christ is on the far side of anything. There is one body and one Spirit, one Lord, one faith, one baptism (Eph. 4:4-6), and the people once furthest off, with no portion and no claim, have been brought near by the blood of Christ and are no longer strangers but members of the household of God (Eph. 2:13, 19). No copy of an altar is needed at the frontier. The frontier is gone.

23.title: Joshua's Farewell Charge
23.text: <sup>1</sup>A long time afterward, when the LORD had given rest to Israel from all their surrounding enemies, and Joshua was old and well advanced in years,<sup>2</sup>Joshua summoned all Israel, its elders and heads, its judges and officers, and said to them, "I am now old and well advanced in years.<sup>3</sup>And you have seen all that the LORD your God has done to all these nations for your sake, for it is the LORD your God who has fought for you.<sup>4</sup>Behold, I have allotted to you as an inheritance for your tribes those nations that remain, along with all the nations that I have already cut off, from the Jordan to the Great Sea in the west.<sup>5</sup>The LORD your God will push them back before you and drive them out of your sight. And you shall possess their land, just as the LORD your God promised you.<sup>6</sup>Therefore, be very strong to keep and to do all that is written in the Book of the Law of Moses, turning aside from it neither to the right hand nor to the left,<sup>7</sup>that you may not mix with these nations remaining among you or make mention of the names of their gods or swear by them or serve them or bow down to them,<sup>8</sup>but you shall cling to the LORD your God just as you have done to this day.<sup>9</sup>For the LORD has driven out before you great and strong nations. And as for you, no man has been able to stand before you to this day.<sup>10</sup>One man of you puts to flight a thousand, since it is the LORD your God who fights for you, just as he promised you.<sup>11</sup>Be very careful, therefore, to love the LORD your God.<sup>12</sup>For if you turn back and cling to the remnant of these nations remaining among you and make marriages with them, so that you associate with them and they with you,<sup>13</sup>know for certain that the LORD your God will no longer drive out these nations before you, but they shall be a snare and a trap for you, a whip on your sides and thorns in your eyes, until you perish from off this good ground that the LORD your God has given you.<sup>14</sup>"And now I am about to go the way of all the earth, and you know in your hearts and souls, all of you, that not one word has failed of all the good things that the LORD your God promised concerning you. All have come to pass for you; not one of them has failed.<sup>15</sup>But just as all the good things that the LORD your God promised concerning you have been fulfilled for you, so the LORD will bring upon you all the evil things, until he has destroyed you from off this good land that the LORD your God has given you,<sup>16</sup>if you transgress the covenant of the LORD your God, which he commanded you, and go and serve other gods and bow down to them. Then the anger of the LORD will be kindled against you, and you shall perish quickly from off the good land that he has given to you."
23.overview:
Years have passed, the tribes are settled, and the old man calls the leadership together to say goodbye. He begins with his own age and with what they have seen with their own eyes: it is the LORD your God who has fought for you (v. 3). He is honest that nations still remain, and promises that God will go on driving them out after he himself is gone.

The charge he gives them is the one God gave him on his first day (v. 6; cf. 1:7), with a warning in verse 7 that starts almost at nothing: do not even speak the names of their gods.

The chapter turns on one verb used twice: cling to the LORD (v. 8), or cling to the remnant of the nations (v. 12).

Then Joshua calls them as witnesses that not one good word has failed, and joins to it, with the words just as, the warning that the evil words will come with the same reliability (vv. 14-15).
23.theology:
Cling, with two possible objects.
