The Hebrew dabaq is the verb Genesis uses of a man holding fast to his wife, and Joshua uses it twice here: cling to the LORD (v. 8), or cling to the remnant of these nations (v. 12). The chapter does not present a choice between devotion and indifference. It presents a choice of what the hands are holding, because they will be holding something.

The guard rail is set a long way back. Verse 7 forbids serving and bowing down, which anybody would call idolatry, and before those it forbids mixing, and even to make mention of the names of their gods. Joshua has watched a nation fall away before, and knows the descent begins in vocabulary and social ease, years before anybody kneels.

The same faithfulness, both directions. Not one word has failed of all the good things, and just as those were fulfilled, so the LORD will bring upon you all the evil things. This is one claim about one attribute: God's words happen. The reliability that opened the Jordan is not a warm disposition running in a single direction, and the exile proved it.

Where the two kinds of word met. A believer who trembles at verses 15-16 should follow the story to its end. The evil words did fall, on Israel at the exile, and then once more on the one Israelite who had kept every word: Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us (Galatians 3:13). The God whose warnings are as sure as his promises has made both sure in his Son. For those who are in Christ there is now no condemnation (Romans 8:1), and the faithfulness that makes the warning terrible is the same faithfulness that makes the gospel safe.

The last instruction is the first one. What Joshua tells the nation at the end of his life is what God told him at the beginning of his command. And the summary of the whole charge is not vigilance but affection: Be very careful, therefore, to love the LORD your God (v. 11), an odd thing to be careful about, until you notice that love is precisely what people lose without noticing.
23.examples:
An old man who had watched a river open and a wall fall flat gathered the leaders of a settled, comfortable nation and warned them, not about armies, but about marriages, conversation and the names people use for things.

In everyday life. Verse 7 is the practical one. The question is not whether you are about to bow down to anything, because you are not. It is whether the vocabulary, the assumptions and the friendships of a world that does not know God have begun to be the water you swim in, which is where the descent starts and where it is still easy to stop. And verse 11 is the one to keep: be very careful to love him. Love is not manufactured by trying harder; it is answered love, kindled by the God who fought for you, and kept alive by his Spirit through his word, prayer and his people. Where you find it has cooled, Christ's love for the Father was whole for you, and the way back is open today.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–5 — The LORD Has Fought for You
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: A long time has passed; Israel has rest, and Joshua is old (v. 1). He summons the leadership (v. 2) and puts the whole conquest in one clause: it is the LORD your God who has fought for you (v. 3). The allotment includes nations still standing (v. 4), and God himself will push them back and drive them out (v. 5).
verseByVerse.theology: He argues from their own lifetime, and the verb belongs to God in every sentence. Every command that follows rests on it.
verseByVerse.examples: Nations still remain, and they have been allotted anyway. The promise of verse 5 is future tense, given to men who are about to bury the only leader they have known.

verseByVerse.quote: A long time afterward, when the LORD had given rest to Israel from all their surrounding enemies, and Joshua was old and well advanced in years, Joshua summoned all Israel, its elders and heads, its judges and officers, and said to them, "I am now old and well advanced in years. And you have seen all that the LORD your God has done to all these nations for your sake, for it is the LORD your God who has fought for you. Behold, I have allotted to you as an inheritance for your tribes those nations that remain, along with all the nations that I have already cut off, from the Jordan to the Great Sea in the west. The LORD your God will push them back before you and drive them out of your sight. And you shall possess their land, just as the LORD your God promised you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Years have gone by. The tribes have gone home, the country is quiet, and the old man calls the leadership together to say goodbye. He begins with his own age, without embarrassment. Nothing in this chapter pretends the speaker has time.

Then the whole conquest in one clause, and the subject of every verb in it is God. He argues from sight, not from an appeal or a doctrine: you have seen. They were at the Jordan, at Jericho, on the hillside at Gibeon when the day would not end. Whatever else they do with their lives, they cannot claim they have no evidence.

He is entirely honest about the state of the country. There are nations still standing, allotted anyway, deeds written for ground still occupied, exactly as in chapter 13.

The promise in verse 5 is future tense. He is telling men who are about to bury him that God will go on doing what they watched him do, when the man who led them is not there. The church never has to hear that speech. Its Joshua died once and lives, holds his priesthood permanently because he continues for ever (Hebrews 7:24), and has promised to be with his people always, to the end of the age (Matthew 28:20).

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: The charge is the one God gave Joshua on his first day (v. 6; cf. 1:7). The danger is named precisely: do not mix with the nations that remain, do not so much as speak the names of their gods, do not swear by them or serve them (v. 7). The positive command is one word: cling to the LORD your God (v. 8). Then the evidence: God has driven out great nations, and one man of them puts a thousand to flight (vv. 9-10). And the summary: be very careful to love the LORD your God (v. 11).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 7 is a descent, and it begins with the smallest thing on the list.
verseByVerse.examples: Joshua hands the nation the words once spoken over him (1:7).

verseByVerse.quote: Therefore, be very strong to keep and to do all that is written in the Book of the Law of Moses, turning aside from it neither to the right hand nor to the left, that you may not mix with these nations remaining among you or make mention of the names of their gods or swear by them or serve them or bow down to them, but you shall cling to the LORD your God just as you have done to this day. For the LORD has driven out before you great and strong nations. And as for you, no man has been able to stand before you to this day. One man of you puts to flight a thousand, since it is the LORD your God who fights for you, just as he promised you. Be very careful, therefore, to love the LORD your God.
verseByVerse.commentary:
These are the words God spoke over Joshua just after Moses died: only be strong and very courageous, being careful to do according to all the law... do not turn from it to the right hand or to the left (1:7). Decades later he hands them on without updating them or qualifying them with anything he has learned.

Read verse 7 in order, because it is a descent. The last two items are what anybody would call idolatry; the first two are conversational. Joshua puts the guard rail a long way back from the cliff: nobody arrives at bowing down. They arrive at borrowing the vocabulary, then at finding it convenient, then at using it in an oath because everyone else does, and the knees come last.

Then the positive command, one verb: cling, the word he used to the eastern tribes as they went home (22:5). The arithmetic of verse 10 comes with its explanation attached: not that Israelites are formidable, but that the LORD fights for them, so that nobody takes the statistic home without it. The strength they are told to be strong in is his, given before it is asked for.

And the summary is not vigilance about the Canaanites but care about affection. Be very careful, therefore, to love: the thing people lose without noticing.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 12–16 — The Same Faithfulness, the Other Way
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: If you turn back and cling to the remnant of these nations and intermarry with them (v. 12), God will stop driving them out, and they will become a snare, a trap, a whip on your sides and thorns in your eyes (v. 13). Joshua, about to die, calls them to witness that not one good word has failed (v. 14), and immediately: just as the good things have been fulfilled, so the LORD will bring the evil things if they transgress the covenant (vv. 15-16).
verseByVerse.theology: Verse 12 uses the same verb as verse 8: one word, two possible objects.
verseByVerse.examples: Verses 14 and 15 are joined by just as, and must not be read apart.

verseByVerse.quote: For if you turn back and cling to the remnant of these nations remaining among you and make marriages with them, so that you associate with them and they with you, know for certain that the LORD your God will no longer drive out these nations before you, but they shall be a snare and a trap for you, a whip on your sides and thorns in your eyes, until you perish from off this good ground that the LORD your God has given you. "And now I am about to go the way of all the earth, and you know in your hearts and souls, all of you, that not one word has failed of all the good things that the LORD your God promised concerning you. All have come to pass for you; not one of them has failed. But just as all the good things that the LORD your God promised concerning you have been fulfilled for you, so the LORD will bring upon you all the evil things, until he has destroyed you from off this good land that the LORD your God has given you, if you transgress the covenant of the LORD your God, which he commanded you, and go and serve other gods and bow down to them. Then the anger of the LORD will be kindled against you, and you shall perish quickly from off the good land that he has given to you."
verseByVerse.commentary:
Nobody wakes up and decides to stop holding on to God. What happens is that something else gets hold of the hands. The chapter names the mechanism exactly: association, then marriage, then the slow merging of two peoples, and the gods come with the families.

Four images escalate from inconvenience to blindness. A snare catches a foot. A trap holds. A whip is on the sides, constant and painful. Thorns in the eyes is the worst: the thing you failed to remove ends by taking your sight. These are the nations Israel did not drive out, Gezer, the six towns of Manasseh, the Philistine coast: the people already living down the road.

He is dying, and he calls them as witnesses to God's record. Not one word has failed, the writer's verdict two chapters ago (21:45), now from the man who was there for every one of them. Then the sentence most readers would rather he had not said: faithfulness means a God whose words happen. All of them.

Every syllable of this came true. Centuries later Jerusalem burned and the survivors walked to Babylon, and the prophets who watched it said precisely what Joshua said here: that God had kept his word. Even then the same prophets promised a new covenant, written on the heart (Jer. 31:33), so that judgment was never God's last word to his people.

The old man's final argument is not that God is dangerous. It is that God is consistent, and that everything good they possess, the fields, the towns, the rest, came from a character they are now being asked to trust in the dark, without him, after he is buried.

Was the ban on intermarriage racial? No: Rahab and Ruth joined Israel by faith. The danger was idolatry (Deut 7:3–4). The principle carries over: a Christian should marry only in the Lord (1 Cor 7:39).

24.title: The Covenant at Shechem
24.text: <sup>1</sup>Joshua gathered all the tribes of Israel to Shechem and summoned the elders, the heads, the judges, and the officers of Israel. And they presented themselves before God.<sup>2</sup>And Joshua said to all the people, "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, 'Long ago, your fathers lived beyond the Euphrates, Terah, the father of Abraham and of Nahor; and they served other gods.<sup>3</sup>Then I took your father Abraham from beyond the River and led him through all the land of Canaan, and made his offspring many. I gave him Isaac.<sup>4</sup>And to Isaac I gave Jacob and Esau. And I gave Esau the hill country of Seir to possess, but Jacob and his children went down to Egypt.<sup>5</sup>And I sent Moses and Aaron, and I plagued Egypt with what I did in the midst of it, and afterward I brought you out.<sup>6</sup>"'Then I brought your fathers out of Egypt, and you came to the sea. And the Egyptians pursued your fathers with chariots and horsemen to the Red Sea.<sup>7</sup>And when they cried to the LORD, he put darkness between you and the Egyptians and made the sea come upon them and cover them; and your eyes saw what I did in Egypt. And you lived in the wilderness a long time.<sup>8</sup>Then I brought you to the land of the Amorites, who lived on the other side of the Jordan. They fought with you, and I gave them into your hand, and you took possession of their land, and I destroyed them before you.<sup>9</sup>Then Balak the son of Zippor, king of Moab, arose and fought against Israel. And he sent and invited Balaam the son of Beor to curse you,<sup>10</sup>but I would not listen to Balaam. Indeed, he blessed you. So I delivered you out of his hand.<sup>11</sup>And you went over the Jordan and came to Jericho, and the leaders of Jericho fought against you, and also the Amorites, the Perizzites, the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Girgashites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites. And I gave them into your hand.<sup>12</sup>And I sent the hornet before you, which drove them out before you, the two kings of the Amorites; it was not by your sword or by your bow.<sup>13</sup>I gave you a land on which you had not labored and cities that you had not built, and you dwell in them. You eat the fruit of vineyards and olive orchards that you did not plant.'<sup>14</sup>"Now therefore fear the LORD and serve him in sincerity and in faithfulness. Put away the gods that your fathers served beyond the River and in Egypt, and serve the LORD.<sup>15</sup>And if it is evil in your eyes to serve the LORD, choose this day whom you will serve, whether the gods your fathers served in the region beyond the River, or the gods of the Amorites in whose land you dwell. But as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD."<sup>16</sup>Then the people answered, "Far be it from us that we should forsake the LORD to serve other gods,<sup>17</sup>for it is the LORD our God who brought us and our fathers up from the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery, and who did those great signs in our sight and preserved us in all the way that we went, and among all the peoples through whom we passed.<sup>18</sup>And the LORD drove out before us all the peoples, the Amorites who lived in the land. Therefore we also will serve the LORD, for he is our God."<sup>19</sup>But Joshua said to the people, "You are not able to serve the LORD, for he is a holy God. He is a jealous God; he will not forgive your transgressions or your sins.<sup>20</sup>If you forsake the LORD and serve foreign gods, then he will turn and do you harm and consume you, after having done you good."<sup>21</sup>And the people said to Joshua, "No, but we will serve the LORD."<sup>22</sup>Then Joshua said to the people, "You are witnesses against yourselves that you have chosen the LORD, to serve him." And they said, "We are witnesses."<sup>23</sup>He said, "Then put away the foreign gods that are among you, and incline your heart to the LORD, the God of Israel."<sup>24</sup>And the people said to Joshua, "The LORD our God we will serve, and his voice we will obey."<sup>25</sup>So Joshua made a covenant with the people that day, and put in place statutes and rules for them at Shechem.<sup>26</sup>And Joshua wrote these words in the Book of the Law of God. And he took a large stone and set it up there under the terebinth that was by the sanctuary of the LORD.<sup>27</sup>And Joshua said to all the people, "Behold, this stone shall be a witness against us, for it has heard all the words of the LORD that he spoke to us. Therefore it shall be a witness against you, lest you deal falsely with your God."<sup>28</sup>So Joshua sent the people away, every man to his inheritance.<sup>29</sup>After these things Joshua the son of Nun, the servant of the LORD, died, being 110 years old.<sup>30</sup>And they buried him in his own inheritance at Timnath-serah, which is in the hill country of Ephraim, north of the mountain of Gaash.<sup>31</sup>Israel served the LORD all the days of Joshua, and all the days of the elders who outlived Joshua and had known all the work that the LORD did for Israel.<sup>32</sup>As for the bones of Joseph, which the people of Israel brought up from Egypt, they buried them at Shechem, in the piece of land that Jacob bought from the sons of Hamor the father of Shechem for a hundred pieces of money. It became an inheritance of the descendants of Joseph.<sup>33</sup>And Eleazar the son of Aaron died, and they buried him at Gibeah, the town of Phinehas his son, which had been given him in the hill country of Ephraim.
24.overview:
Joshua does not gather them at Shiloh, where the tent of meeting stands. He takes them to Shechem, where the promise of the land was first spoken to Abram (Gen. 12:6-7), to ask whether they will keep it.

God's speech runs twelve verses in the first person. It opens with an embarrassment (v. 2), and then the verbs are all his: I took, I led, I gave, I sent, I brought out.

Then the demand, which reveals that they still have the old gods (v. 14), and the famous choice, which is not between belief and unbelief but between gods (v. 15).

The people answer well, and Joshua refuses their answer (v. 19) and makes them say it again until it costs something. Then a covenant, a stone that has heard, and three graves: Joshua, given the title servant of the LORD in his own obituary; Joseph's bones, waiting four hundred years for burial; and Eleazar. The book ends with a burial and no successor.
24.theology:
Grace before demand. Twelve verses of history precede a single word of requirement, and the history is told entirely with God as subject, beginning with a family of idolaters (v. 2). Everything Israel has is on the list of things done to them, ending with a land they had not worked for and vineyards they had not planted (v. 13).

The choice is never between God and nothing. Joshua names the two alternatives and both are gods: the old family religion from beyond the Euphrates, or the local Amorite gods, ancestral or fashionable (v. 15). Everyone at Shechem was going to serve something. The famous verse is a demand to say which god, out loud, today.

A refused profession. The people give a confession that is accurate, evidently sincere and immediate, and Joshua answers you are not able (v. 19). He had heard this nation promise everything at Sinai and break the promise before Moses came down the mountain. It is the method of the Lord who told an eager crowd to sit down and count the cost first (Luke 14:28-30). And you are not able is not the last word on it. The answer Scripture gives is not a stronger promise from the people but a better covenant, in which God writes his law on the heart (Jeremiah 31:33), enacted through a better mediator (Hebrews 8:6-10): the greater Joshua, who came to do God’s will (Hebrews 10:7) and did for his people what they could not do for themselves.

One generation. Israel served the LORD all the days of Joshua and of the elders who had known all the work that the LORD did for Israel (v. 31). Judges finishes the sentence: and there arose another generation after them who did not know the LORD or the work that he had done (Judg. 2:10). Everything in this book about stones and questions and children was aimed at that gap, and the gap opened anyway. Which is why the rest for the people of God is still spoken of as future, and why there had to be another Joshua (Heb. 4:8-9).
24.examples:
Then: A nation stood where the promise had started, heard its history with God as the subject of every sentence, and was asked which god it would serve. It answered well and was told it could not do it. It insisted, and was sent home to throw out the idols it had been carrying since Mesopotamia.

Now: Verse 14 is the searching one, not verse 15. The famous verse gets hung in kitchens; the verse before it says the people making that fine confession still had the old gods in their houses. It is entirely possible to have seen God work, to be genuinely grateful, to be at the meeting and mean every word, and to have kept something on a shelf at home. Joshua would not let them leave with the decision in the air; he attached it to an object. The order is the same for us: first what God has done, then the putting away, and the strength to do it is the Spirit who inclines the heart. And when the shelf is found full again, the covenant does not rest on our record but on the one who kept it for us.

verseByVerse.ref: vv. 1–13 — Everything God Did, in the First Person
verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Joshua gathers all the tribes to Shechem, and they present themselves before God (v. 1). What follows is God speaking, a history told entirely in the first person. Your fathers lived beyond the Euphrates and served other gods; I took your father Abraham (vv. 2-3). I gave Isaac, Jacob and Esau, I sent Moses and Aaron, I plagued Egypt, I brought you out (vv. 3-6). I put darkness between you and the Egyptians, I gave the Amorites into your hand (vv. 7-8). I would not listen to Balaam (vv. 9-10). I gave Jericho and seven nations into your hand and sent the hornet, not by your sword or by your bow (vv. 11-12). And I gave you a land you did not work for, cities you did not build, vineyards you did not plant (v. 13).
verseByVerse.theology: Count the verbs. Almost every sentence has God as its subject and Israel as its object, and the two things Israel is credited with are crying out at the sea and going over the Jordan.
verseByVerse.examples: Before the nation promises anything, it is reminded that its ancestry gives it no standing at all.

verseByVerse.quote: Joshua gathered all the tribes of Israel to Shechem and summoned the elders, the heads, the judges, and the officers of Israel. And they presented themselves before God. And Joshua said to all the people, "Thus says the LORD, the God of Israel, 'Long ago, your fathers lived beyond the Euphrates, Terah, the father of Abraham and of Nahor; and they served other gods. Then I took your father Abraham from beyond the River and led him through all the land of Canaan, and made his offspring many. I gave him Isaac. And to Isaac I gave Jacob and Esau. And I gave Esau the hill country of Seir to possess, but Jacob and his children went down to Egypt.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Shechem is not casual. It is the first place Abram stopped when he walked in from Mesopotamia, and where God first said the sentence everything since has depended on: to your offspring I will give this land (Gen. 12:6-7). It is where Jacob made his household hand over their foreign gods and hid them under the terebinth (Gen. 35:4). It lies between Ebal and Gerizim, where the nation heard the law read (8:33), and Joseph's bones will be buried there before the chapter ends.

God's speech begins not with a promise but an embarrassment. Abraham's father Terah is named, and the family religion is stated flatly in the opening line of a covenant renewal.

Then the verbs start, and they do not stop for eleven verses. I took. I led. I made. I gave. Nothing is a response to anything Abraham did. He is taken out of a family of idol-worshippers by a God he was not looking for. The whole history of Israel begins with a man being collected.
verseByVerse.note: “The River” is the Euphrates (ESV note).

verseByVerse.quote: And I sent Moses and Aaron, and I plagued Egypt with what I did in the midst of it, and afterward I brought you out. "'Then I brought your fathers out of Egypt, and you came to the sea. And the Egyptians pursued your fathers with chariots and horsemen to the Red Sea. And when they cried to the LORD, he put darkness between you and the Egyptians and made the sea come upon them and cover them; and your eyes saw what I did in Egypt. And you lived in the wilderness a long time. Then I brought you to the land of the Amorites, who lived on the other side of the Jordan. They fought with you, and I gave them into your hand, and you took possession of their land, and I destroyed them before you.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The exodus in three sentences, and the subject is the same every time. Follow the pronouns. The speech began with your fathers, at a distance of centuries. By verse 6 it is I brought your fathers out... and you came to the sea. Most of the men at Shechem were children at the Red Sea or not yet born, and God speaks to them as though they had been there. That is how Israel was taught to remember, and how the church learns to: nobody reading this was at Golgotha either, and the New Testament speaks to Christians as people who were crucified with him.

One clause is given to Israel's own contribution: they cried to the LORD. Then a detail from Exodus easy to lose: he put darkness between you and the Egyptians. The pillar moved round behind them and stood in the gap all night, darkness on one side and light on the other (Ex. 14:19-20). God did not only open a road; he stood in the doorway while they used it.

Forty years in nine words. God's own summary of the wilderness is brief, and the brevity is a mercy; the details are in Numbers and they are not flattering.

verseByVerse.quote: Then Balak the son of Zippor, king of Moab, arose and fought against Israel. And he sent and invited Balaam the son of Beor to curse you, but I would not listen to Balaam. Indeed, he blessed you. So I delivered you out of his hand. And you went over the Jordan and came to Jericho, and the leaders of Jericho fought against you, and also the Amorites, the Perizzites, the Canaanites, the Hittites, the Girgashites, the Hivites, and the Jebusites. And I gave them into your hand. And I sent the hornet before you, which drove them out before you, the two kings of the Amorites; it was not by your sword or by your bow. I gave you a land on which you had not labored and cities that you had not built, and you dwell in them. You eat the fruit of vineyards and olive orchards that you did not plant.'
verseByVerse.commentary:
Israel very likely knew nothing about Balaam at the time: a king hiring a prophet to curse them while they sat in their tents in the valley below. God's account is one clause: I would not listen to Balaam. The threat was real, the fee offered, the prophet willing, and nothing happened because God declined to hear him. Everyone has a stretch of life like that, danger arranged by people they never met, which came to nothing for reasons they are only told afterwards.

Israel had swords and used them, at Jericho and Ai and Merom. God says the country was not taken by them. The hornet is most likely the terror God sent ahead of Israel (Exod 23:27–28); some take it literally. The point is plain: it was not by your sword or by your bow.

The speech ends with an inventory of unearned things: the land, the cities, the vineyards, the olive trees. Every man listening stood on ground he had not cleared, in a house he had not built. Moses had warned them what that does to a heart: then take care lest you forget the LORD (Deut. 6:10-12). It is the last thing God says before asking for their allegiance: not a threat, and not an argument, but a list of what they have been given.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Now the demand: fear the LORD, serve him in sincerity and faithfulness, and put away the gods that your fathers served beyond the River and in Egypt (v. 14). Then the famous sentence, framed as a dare: if serving the LORD is evil in your eyes, choose today which gods you will have instead, the old ones from beyond the river or the local ones of the Amorites; but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD (v. 15). The people answer at once and confidently: far be it from us to forsake the LORD, he brought us out of slavery, he did the signs, he kept us on every road, he drove out the nations; we will serve him, for he is our God (vv. 16-18).
verseByVerse.theology: Joshua declares for his own house before he has heard what anyone else will choose.
verseByVerse.examples: Verse 14 asks for sincerity and faithfulness before it mentions idols: the inward and the outward together.

verseByVerse.quote: "Now therefore fear the LORD and serve him in sincerity and in faithfulness. Put away the gods that your fathers served beyond the River and in Egypt, and serve the LORD. And if it is evil in your eyes to serve the LORD, choose this day whom you will serve, whether the gods your fathers served in the region beyond the River, or the gods of the Amorites in whose land you dwell. But as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The second half of the demand should stop a reader. They still have the old gods. After the Jordan opened, after Jericho fell, after the sun stood still and the tent of meeting was pitched at Shiloh, there are household idols in the camp, some from the old family religion beyond the River and some picked up in Egypt. They had been carried across the desert and into the promised land, and were presumably sitting in Israelite houses that afternoon. It is the ordinary condition of religious people.

The most quoted sentence in the book is usually quoted with the frame taken off. Both alternatives Joshua names are gods, and his contempt for both is audible in the way he lists them.

Then the last clause: but as for me and my house, we will serve the LORD. He includes his household: a man declaring publicly what will be served under his roof, and taking responsibility for it.

Does “choose” teach free will? The command is a real summons, and each must answer it. But Joshua at once warns, You are not able to serve the LORD (v. 19): the people cannot keep covenant in their own strength. The call to choose and the need for God to change the heart belong together (Deut 30:6). And “as for me and my house” is a father’s resolve to lead his household in serving God, not a promise that every child will believe; it commits him to lead, teach and pray.

verseByVerse.quote: Then the people answered, "Far be it from us that we should forsake the LORD to serve other gods, for it is the LORD our God who brought us and our fathers up from the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery, and who did those great signs in our sight and preserved us in all the way that we went, and among all the peoples through whom we passed. And the LORD drove out before us all the peoples, the Amorites who lived in the land. Therefore we also will serve the LORD, for he is our God."
verseByVerse.commentary:
The answer comes back immediately and it is a good one. It is not vague enthusiasm; they give reasons, and the reasons are the right ones.

They rehearse God's own speech back to him. He brought us out of slavery. He did the signs where we could see them. He kept us on every road we travelled and among every people we passed through. He drove out the nations. Every clause is accurate, and it is offered as the ground of their commitment.

By any ordinary standard this is exactly the response the ceremony was designed to produce. The history has been recited, the demand has been made, and the nation has answered with a confession that is theologically sound and evidently sincere.

Joshua does not accept it.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Joshua refuses their profession (vv. 19-20). The people insist (v. 21), and he makes them witnesses against themselves (v. 22) and tells them again to put away the foreign gods (v. 23). The covenant is made and written in the Book of the Law, and a large stone is set up under the terebinth as a witness, for it has heard all the words of the LORD (vv. 24-27). Then he sends everybody home (v. 28).
verseByVerse.theology: Joshua is not being difficult; he is refusing a cheap yes. A commitment that has not been told what it will cost is not worth witnessing.
verseByVerse.examples: The stone is a witness because there is nobody else left to be one. Moses is dead, Joshua is going, and the generation that saw the Jordan will soon be buried. So a rock is stood up under a tree at Shechem, and told what it has heard.

verseByVerse.quote: But Joshua said to the people, "You are not able to serve the LORD, for he is a holy God. He is a jealous God; he will not forgive your transgressions or your sins. If you forsake the LORD and serve foreign gods, then he will turn and do you harm and consume you, after having done you good." And the people said to Joshua, "No, but we will serve the LORD." Then Joshua said to the people, "You are witnesses against yourselves that you have chosen the LORD, to serve him." And they said, "We are witnesses."
verseByVerse.commentary:
This is the most startling thing anybody says in the book, said by a preacher to a congregation that has just made a good confession. He tells them, to their faces, that they cannot do what they have just promised.

He is not being cynical. He is doing what an honest man does when a promise is made too quickly by people who have not counted the cost. This nation said at Sinai all that the LORD has spoken we will do, and had a golden calf in the camp before Moses got down the mountain. Joshua was on the mountain path when they heard the noise.

The two words he uses about God are the reason. Holy: wholly other and not to be handled casually. Jealous: the word for a husband's response to a rival, not for petty envy.

The hardest clause is the last: he will not forgive your transgressions or your sins. Read alongside the rest of Scripture, and alongside the God who has just described centuries of carrying this people, it is plainly not a denial that God forgives. It is a statement about covenant treachery: he will not simply overlook a people who take his covenant and then keep idols in the house.

They push back, and they are right to. This is what Joshua was after: not a smaller commitment but a considered one. So he makes them say it again as a legal act. Witnesses against yourselves: their words are entered as evidence, and everyone knows which way it will point if the promise fails.

Joshua's method is to make it harder before he lets anybody agree, to tell them what God is like before they say yes. Jesus does the same with a crowd of eager followers: sit down first and count the cost, like a man building a tower (Luke 14:28-30).

verseByVerse.quote: He said, "Then put away the foreign gods that are among you, and incline your heart to the LORD, the God of Israel." And the people said to Joshua, "The LORD our God we will serve, and his voice we will obey." So Joshua made a covenant with the people that day, and put in place statutes and rules for them at Shechem.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Having accepted their word, he makes it concrete, and it is the same instruction as verse 14 because nothing has actually happened yet. The idols are still in the tents. Joshua will not leave a decision in the air where it can be admired. Go home and get rid of the things.

The second half is the inward half: incline your heart to the LORD. Neither substitutes for the other. A man can throw out an idol and keep his heart where it was, or feel deeply about God and still have the thing on a shelf. The inclining they are commanded is what God himself promised to do: I will give you a new heart, and put my Spirit within you, and cause you to walk in my statutes (Ezek. 36:26-27).

Only now is the covenant made. The whole ceremony has been an exercise in slowing a willing people down.

verseByVerse.quote: And Joshua wrote these words in the Book of the Law of God. And he took a large stone and set it up there under the terebinth that was by the sanctuary of the LORD. And Joshua said to all the people, "Behold, this stone shall be a witness against us, for it has heard all the words of the LORD that he spoke to us. Therefore it shall be a witness against you, lest you deal falsely with your God." So Joshua sent the people away, every man to his inheritance.
verseByVerse.commentary:
Two things are done to make the day survive the people who were in it: it is written down, and a rock is stood up.

The stone has heard. It is a striking thing to say and Joshua says it deliberately. A covenant needed witnesses, and he does not have any.

Moses is dead. Eleazar is old and about to die. Joshua is near the end and knows it, and every man who saw the Jordan open will be buried within a generation. There is nobody left who can stand up in twenty years and say what was promised at Shechem.

So he uses a stone, because stone outlives men. This is the last in a line of stone markers in the book: the twelve at Gilgal, the twelve in the riverbed, the stones over Achan, the heap at Ai's gate, the law written on stones at Ebal, the stones over the cave at Makkedah, and now this. Israel's history is being marked in rock by people who knew exactly how short memory is.

That is the last thing he does. He sends them home, each man to the land that was drawn for him by lot, in a country that had been a promise to a childless idolater's son centuries earlier.

The “sanctuary of the LORD” at Shechem was the sacred place where Abraham and Jacob had built altars (Gen 12:6–7; 33:20), not a rival to the tabernacle at Shiloh.

verseByVerse.sectionOverview: Joshua dies at a hundred and ten and is buried in the town he asked for (vv. 29-30). Verse 31 gives the verdict on his generation, with a time limit built in: Israel served the LORD all the days of Joshua and of the elders who outlived him and had known all the work the LORD did. Then Joseph's bones, carried out of Egypt and through forty years of wilderness, are buried at Shechem in the field Jacob bought (v. 32). And Eleazar the priest dies and is buried in the hill country of Ephraim (v. 33).
verseByVerse.theology: The book ends with three funerals and no successor. There is no Joshua to follow Joshua, and the next book will open on a nation with no leader, going down the list of what each tribe failed to take.
verseByVerse.examples: Joshua dies at a hundred and ten, the age at which Joseph died (Gen. 50:26), whose bones are buried in the same passage.

verseByVerse.quote: After these things Joshua the son of Nun, the servant of the LORD, died, being 110 years old. And they buried him in his own inheritance at Timnath-serah, which is in the hill country of Ephraim, north of the mountain of Gaash. Israel served the LORD all the days of Joshua, and all the days of the elders who outlived Joshua and had known all the work that the LORD did for Israel. As for the bones of Joseph, which the people of Israel brought up from Egypt, they buried them at Shechem, in the piece of land that Jacob bought from the sons of Hamor the father of Shechem for a hundred pieces of money. It became an inheritance of the descendants of Joseph. And Eleazar the son of Aaron died, and they buried him at Gibeah, the town of Phinehas his son, which had been given him in the hill country of Ephraim.
verseByVerse.commentary:
The title in that sentence has been withheld for twenty-four chapters. From chapter 1, one man has been called the servant of the LORD, and it is Moses, long after his death. Joshua enters as the man who waited on him, and is given the title in his obituary: not when the Jordan opened or the sun stood still, but when he is dead, in the town he asked for and had to rebuild.

Servant is the highest title this book knows, and the New Testament names one higher. Moses was faithful in all God’s house as a servant, but Christ is faithful over God’s house as a son (Hebrews 3:5-6). Joshua earned the servant’s name by a lifetime and could not hold his people beyond his own generation; the Son keeps every one the Father gives him (John 6:37-39).

The verdict on the generation has a time bomb in it. The nation held while there were men alive who had personally seen the river open, and Judges finishes the sentence (Judg. 2:10). One generation is the whole distance between Shechem and the collapse.

The second grave is four hundred years in the making. Joseph, dying in Egypt as second man in the kingdom, made his brothers swear: God will surely visit you, and you shall carry up my bones from here (Gen. 50:25). Moses took the coffin out on the night of the exodus (Ex. 13:19), and for forty years, through the sea and the wilderness and every camp, somebody carried the bones of a man who had died before any of them were born. They bury him in the field his father bought, in the country God had promised, where the nation has just renewed its covenant. An old man's confidence in a promise, expressed as an instruction about a coffin, is honoured four centuries later by people he never met.

The third grave is the priest who stood beside Joshua at every distribution. No new Joshua is named, no charge given, nobody stands up to say be strong and courageous. The next book opens with a nation asking who will go up first.

Yet what has been buried here, and where, is full of hope. Joseph's bones lie in Canaan because a dying man believed God would keep a promise. And a stone stands at Shechem, where Abram was first told to your offspring I will give this land, and the offspring are in it.

Not one word had failed. The LORD had fought for Israel, and the man who bore the name Jesus would later bear had brought them in and could not keep them there, and the book knows it. There would have to be another day, and another rest, and another Joshua (Heb. 4:8-9).

Stephen says Abraham bought the tomb at Shechem (Acts 7:16). He is compressing two purchases, Abraham’s cave at Hebron and Jacob’s field here, into one sentence.
verseByVerse.note: Jacob had bought the field on his return to Canaan and set up an altar there (Gen. 33:19-20).
